“Because you’re colder.”

She didn’t say anything for a while. Then she let her head rest against his arm as she walked, and he slowed down a little to match her, and didn’t tell her to walk straight.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old wall ran along the back road for a quarter of a mile, between the street and the water. It was stone, old, darker than the night, and somebody long ago had put iron lamps along the top of it, and the light came down from them in round gold pools on the pavement, one after another, all the way along.

She slowed down.

“It’s pretty.”

“Yes.”

“Did you bring me here on purpose?”

“The road happens to go this way.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

He looked down at her. “Would you like it to be?”

“Yes.”

He stopped under one of the lamps. She turned to face him.

She was in his jacket with his pen in the pocket and his slippers on her feet and her shoes in her hand, and the light was coming down on both of them, and the city was a long way off.

“I hated tonight,” she said.

“I know.”

“She talked about my future as if I weren’t standing there. Nine men. And then July.” She looked down at the rabbits on her feet. “I wish I could tell her. All of it. About you.”

“One day, perhaps.”

“But tonight I just want to be your girlfriend. Nothing else. Just that.”

His face changed. He put his hand up and moved the loose strand of hair off her cheek and tucked it behind her ear.

“Just that,” he said.

He kissed her.

He’d meant to be gentle. The first one was, a slow press, asking. She answered by dropping the silver sandals onto the pavement and putting both hands flat on his chest, and going up on her toes in her rabbit slippers, and opening her mouth under his. He made a sound low in his throat. His hand went into her hair and the last of the careful afternoon’s pins came out and went somewhere, and the whole smooth arrangement came down at last over his wrist, and he kissed her harder, his other arm round her inside the jacket, so she was pressed against him through his thin cold shirt from her chest to her knees. She could feel his heart going.

When he lifted his head she was smiling against his mouth.

“What?” he said.

“I like you.”

“I like you too.”

“Only like?”

He looked at her, under the lamp. Something went across his face, and she watched him almost say it, and not.

“Very much,” he said.

“Better,” said Yu Jie, and kissed him again, because he’d looked so stricken.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped at the corner one block before her building.

“This is it?”

“Almost.”

“I live there.” She pointed down the street, at the tall pale block with a lit glass lobby and a doorman behind a desk.

“I know. And the man on that desk will tell your mother’s driver who walked you home, and your mother’s driver will tell your mother.” He took his hand off her arm. “This is far enough.”

She looked at him. She understood. She hated it, and she understood.

“You’re still being careful.”

“Yes.”

He handed her the sandals. She took them.

“Goodnight, Dr. Wei.”

“Goodnight, Miss Shen.”

“Very formal.”

“Very late.”

She laughed and turned away.

She’d taken two steps when she felt a tug on her sleeve. She looked round. He’d caught the cuff of his own jacket between his fingers, the one hanging over her hand, and he pulled. Not hard. Just enough.

She came back.

“One more minute,” he said.

“Only one?”

“Perhaps two.”

“You’re negotiating.”

“I’m trying to be reasonable.”

“You’re failing,” said Yu Jie, and he pulled her the rest of the way into his arms.

She put her cheek against his chest. His shirt was cold right through and his heart under it was loud. He bent his head and kissed her hair, and kept his mouth there.

“Text me when you’re inside,” he said into it.

“I will.”

“And when you’re changed.”

“All right.”

“And when you’re in bed.”

“Are you going to supervise my whole night?”

“Only the rest of it.”

She touched his face. “You’re freezing. Go home.”

“In a minute.”

She kissed him once, and then again, because of how he looked after the first one. Then she stepped back, and he let go of her sleeve.

At the end of the block she turned round. He was still on the corner, in his white shirt, under the street light. She lifted her hand. He lifted his.

He waited until the glass doors had closed behind her. Then he turned and walked home, and he took the long way back too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Not Stuck: Inside.

Not Stuck: Changed.

Not Stuck: In bed.

Not Stuck: I miss you.

He was standing under a lamp by the old wall when the last one came. He looked at it for a while.

Miles: I miss you too.

Not Stuck: I’ve stolen your jacket.

Miles: I noticed.

Not Stuck: And there was something else in the pocket.

A photograph came through. Two White Rabbits in the palm of her hand, on his black sleeve.

He’d forgotten. He’d put them in at six o’clock in case she was hungry and couldn’t say.

Not Stuck: You brought me sweets to a gala.

Miles: I thought you might want them.

Not Stuck: You thought right.

Miles: Eat them tomorrow. It’s late.

Not Stuck: You’re not my professor right now. You can say goodnight without an instruction.

Miles: Goodnight, sweetheart.

Not Stuck: …

Not Stuck: You can’t just SAY that.

Miles: Why not?

Not Stuck: Because now I’m never going to sleep.

He put the phone in his pocket, and laughed out loud, by himself, on the harbour road at half past one in the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the flat, in the dark, Yu Jie lay under her duvet in an old T-shirt with his jacket on over it. The sleeves came down past her fingers. The collar touched her cheek every time she turned her head.

On the bedside table the silver sandals lay on their sides next to the pink slippers with the rabbits on, and the purple pen was beside her phone.

She unwrapped one White Rabbit and put it in her mouth, and held the other one in her hand, and turned her face into the collar of his jacket.

She fell asleep like that, with the sweet still in her fist.

chapters.title: The Thesis Draft Covered in Red Pen
chapters.desc: He’s not her supervisor. He reads it anyway, all night, and finds the flaw that would have sunk her in May.
chapters.epigraph: “Your gap doesn’t close.”
chapters.content:
The department had been back from the holidays for three days when the email came from Professor Ruan, on the Thursday evening, with a file attached.

She asked me to send you this. She wants an opinion from someone who understands the theory and isn’t responsible for marking it. I told her you’d refuse. She said you’d read it anyway. — L.R.

The file was a hundred and eighteen pages long.

He told himself he’d read the introduction and send her a few questions. He wasn’t her supervisor. He wasn’t going to rewrite her thesis for her.

At a quarter to nine he was on page twenty-three. At half past twelve he reached her numerical results, which were beautiful, and sat back and looked at her figures with something warm and painful in his chest.

At a quarter past one he reached page sixty-seven, and stopped.

He read the paragraph again, and the equation under it. He opened the paper she’d cited and checked it against hers. He checked it a second time, and a third.

Her code was fine. Her numbers did exactly what she’d told them to. The trouble came earlier, before she’d calculated anything at all. She’d treated the false magnetic field that came from stretching the sheet as if it were even, the same strength everywhere across the patch of graphene she was studying. In the middle of the patch that was reasonable. Near the corners it wasn’t, not without proof. And the heart of her thesis was a claim about the corners.

It ran through the next two chapters like a crack through a plate. If she went into her examination in May with it, any competent examiner would find it in ten minutes.

He opened a blank document.

He knew how to fix it. He could have written his method out on a single page and sent it to her by two o’clock, and the thesis would have been finished.

And the answer would have been his. It was her thesis.

He closed the blank document. He opened the comments.

p. 67. What justifies treating the field as uniform here? Does that hold at the corners?

p. 68. Which boundary condition is this? Please separate the bulk approximation from the finite edge.

p. 69. Can you show that the localisation length is still comparable when the field varies?

He didn’t tell her the answer. He asked her where she’d stopped asking.

By half past three the document was a map of questions. Some were small. Some were large. And some were only him.

This paragraph is doing three jobs. It shouldn’t be allowed to get away with it.

You introduce a variable here and then abandon it. Is it lost, or am I?

This is good. Give it room.

At four he reached the end. There was a good thesis in there, a really good one, with one mistake in it that could have swallowed all of it.

He’d written two hundred and twelve comments. Under the last one, at the very end, he typed a single line and left it there.

Your gap doesn’t close.

Then he saved the file.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him in his office at a quarter past eight on Friday morning, in yesterday’s turtleneck, with a full cup of coffee gone cold by his keyboard.

“Miles?”

“Good morning.”

She came round the desk and saw her own thesis open on his screen, and the little number beside the comments.

“Two hundred and twelve?”

“Yes.”

“You read all of it?”

“Yes.”

“Last night?”

He took his glasses off. “Mostly.”

She put both hands on his shoulders. “You haven’t slept at all, have you,” said Yu Jie, and bent and kissed his forehead, and he shut his eyes. “Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me yet.” He turned the screen towards her. “Page sixty-seven.”

She read it. He watched her face, and he knew the exact second she understood: her eyes went from his question to her equation and back to the paragraph before, and then she went still, and then she reached past him and opened her own files on his laptop without asking, and for five minutes there was no sound in the office but the keys.

“Oh,” she said.

He waited.

“Oh no. I’ve treated it as uniform. All the way out.”

“In a region where it isn’t.”

“In the middle it’s fine.”

“In the middle it’s fine.”

“Not at the corners.”

“Not without showing that the error’s under control.”

She sat down on the edge of his desk.

“That would have been the viva,” she said. “That would have been it. In front of everyone.”

She turned and looked at him. “Why didn’t you just tell me how to fix it?”

“Because I don’t want to give you a solution you haven’t worked through yourself.”

“You could have.”

“I could have. It would have been mine, then. Not yours.” He reached for the cold coffee.

She took it out of his hand. “No. You’re going home to sleep.”

“I’ve got a lecture at ten.”

“Then you’ve got an hour and a half. Go.” She was already printing the comments. At the door, as he put his coat on, she said, without turning round, “Miles. Thank you.”

This time he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t ask him for the answer. Not once.

She took the comments home and stuck the rude ones on the fridge, where Tao Tao read them over her cereal and laughed until milk came out of her nose. She spent a week on the strain profile and the comparison. She went to Professor Ruan with a new set of assumptions and explained why the old one wasn’t good enough, and Professor Ruan listened with her glasses pushed up into her hair and then told her to defend the new one, and Yu Jie did, and they disagreed about one boundary condition for an entire afternoon.

Yu Jie went back to the lab and tested it. She came back the next day with a new figure.

“Better,” said Professor Ruan.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t look so pleased. Your discussion’s too long. Your conclusion’s more confident than your data.”

“I know.”

“Good. That’s progress.”

When she admitted in the corridor that lunch had been a biscuit, there’d be a box of dumplings in the department fridge the next morning with her name on it in his small upright hand.

He never asked how it was going. She never told him. They were careful, and they waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Wednesday, nineteen days after that grey morning, it snowed.

Not much. Enough to lie in a thin white line along the window ledges and blur the edges of the courtyard and make the whole fourth floor go quiet. Miles was at his board when she came in without knocking and put a fat new stack of paper down on his desk.

He looked at it. A hundred and twenty-six pages. There was a purple tab on the side, marking the corners.

He sat down and read it. She stood on the other side of the desk with her hands behind her back and tried not to look as if she were going to be sick.

She hadn’t used his method. She’d kept the framework she’d built and split the sheet into two regimes, the middle and the edge, and tested the change from one to the other instead of forcing a single answer across the lot. There was a figure he’d have liked to frame.

“You changed the method,” he said.

“Yes.”

“It isn’t how I’d have done it.”

Her face fell. “Oh.”

“It’s better.”

She stared at him.

“It’s cleaner than mine. It’ll stand up in May.” He closed the folder. “It’s yours.”

“I was so frightened I’d ruined it.”

“You found a problem before somebody else found it for you.”

“You found it.”

“I asked a question.”

“Two hundred and twelve. Some of them were rude. I made a list.”

He laughed. She’d been trying to make him do that all morning, she realised, and there it was.

Then she put her other hand in her pocket and took something out and put it on his desk.

It was a pen. A purple pen, with a cat on the end. Not hers. This cat’s face had come out of the mould slightly crooked, so that one ear was noticeably bigger than the other and it looked permanently surprised.

“You had mine long enough,” she said. “This one’s yours. It keeps asking questions.”

He picked it up. He turned it over. He didn’t say anything, and when he did his voice wasn’t quite right.

“Thank you.”

“Do you like it?”

“Very much.”

She looked past him, at the board, and he saw her eyes change. There was a proof on it from yesterday, his own, half done.

“There’s something wrong with that,” she said.

“There isn’t.”

“Line four.”

She took the chalk out of his hand and started writing, fast, explaining.

“You’re assuming...”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m not, look...” She turned round with chalk on her fingers and her face alight and stopped. “Why are you smiling?”

“Because you’re arguing with me.”

“I’m correcting you.”

She turned back to the board. And he looked at her: her thesis on his desk, the snow on the sill, the crooked purple cat in his hand, and her at his board in her white shirt with chalk on her cheek, arguing about line four with exactly the face she’d had in September, pretending to be stuck.

He put the pen down. He came up behind her and put his hands on her waist and lifted her.

“Miles!”

He set her back against the board, right on top of her own handwriting, so her feet left the floor and her shoulders pressed into line four and her hands came down on his shoulders to hold on.

“What are you doing?”

“Interrupting.”

“You can’t just...”

He kissed her. She made a sound into his mouth and then wound her arms round his neck and her legs round his waist, and he held her up against the board with his whole body and kissed her until neither of them could breathe, until the chalk on her fingers was all through his hair.

When he finally lifted his head there was a perfect smudged print of her proof across the back of her white shirt.

“You’ve interrupted my proof,” she said, breathless.

“I know.”

“That’s academically irresponsible.”

“Probably.”

“You look very pleased with yourself.”

“I am,” said Miles, and she pulled his head back down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed the afternoon. At five he made tea and sat beside her on his little sofa.

“Can I ask you something?” she said.

“Of course.”

“Have you been with anyone? Before me?”

He didn’t answer straight away. It wasn’t that he minded. He wanted to get it right.

“Once,” he said.

She waited.

“A long time ago. A conference, when I was twenty-five. I thought I was supposed to have done it by then. I didn’t know how to tell her I wasn’t interested in her, not really, so I didn’t, and it happened, and in the morning we were both very polite.” He looked down into his tea. “She didn’t matter. Not because she wasn’t a person. Because there wasn’t anything between us that either of us wanted to keep. I didn’t see her again.”

She was quiet for a while. “Are you nervous?” she said. “About us?”

He knew exactly what she meant. He took her hand.

“Yes.”

“Me too.”

“I know. You’re holding my hand very hard.”

She looked down and loosened her fingers, and he laughed, and she leaned on his shoulder.

At seven the snow got heavier.

Tao Tao: are you coming home? it’s a blizzard. I’m making noodles

She looked at the message. Then at him.

“Can I stay?” she said. “With you. Tonight.”

He understood the question under it. He’d have understood it in any language.

“Because of the snow?”

“No. Not because of the snow.”

He came across the room and touched her face.

“Be sure,” he said.

“I’m sure.”

“If you change your mind, at any point...”

“I’ll tell you. And you’ll stop. I know.” She put her hand flat on his chest. “Miles. I want to be with you. Not because I owe you, or because we’ve waited, or because I’m frightened you’ll change your mind. Just because I want you.”

Yu Jie: I’m staying out. Don’t wait up.

Tao Tao: !!!!!!!!!

✦ ✦ ✦

His staff flat was small, with a window over the courtyard, which was white now from wall to wall. The fridge, she noticed, had real food in it.

They made soup and ate it at the little table by the window with the snow coming down outside, and when the last bowl was in the cupboard she stood in the middle of his kitchen and looked at him and the whole flat went quiet.

He crossed the kitchen and kissed her, slowly, as if there were all the time in the world, and then he asked, “Are you comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Still sure?”

“Yes.” She touched his mouth. “Stop asking.”

“That seems unlikely,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the bedroom he didn’t turn on the big light. The snow did it for him, coming grey-white through the thin curtains, so she could see him and not much else.

He asked first. He asked every time. Could he undo this button. And this one. He did them one at a time, the way he’d done up her cardigan in November, from the bottom, slowly, with his knuckles brushing her skin now instead of cloth, and when the white shirt with her chalk proof printed on its back finally slid off her shoulders he stood looking at her for so long that she began to laugh.

“What?”

“I’m taking notes.”

“Miles.”

“You’ve got a freckle here.” He touched it, low on her collarbone, with one finger. “I didn’t know that. And here.” Her ribs. “And you’ve gone pink. All the way down. Did you know that happens?”

“Stop narrating.”

“I can’t. It’s my training.”

She pulled his turtleneck over his head to shut him up, and his glasses came off with it and went somewhere on the floor, and he stood there blinking at her, half-blind and rumpled, with his hair on end.

“Can you see me?”

“You’re within my focal range,” he said, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on to him, and then she stopped laughing, because he’d put his mouth to the side of her neck where he’d kissed her in November, and this time he didn’t stop.

It was slow. He was careful with her, so careful, a hand on her face, a question in her ear before everything, and his voice when he asked got lower and rougher each time, and she started to answer before he’d finished. She was careful with him too. She could feel how unsure he was underneath all that patience, how badly he wanted to get it right. When he hesitated she pulled him closer. When she went quiet he stopped and asked what she needed, and she told him, and watched his face change.

Somewhere along the way it stopped being funny. She didn’t notice when. One moment she was laughing into his shoulder at something he’d said about her knees, and the next he was over her in the grey light with his hands framing her face and his eyes dark without his glasses, saying her name as if it were the only word he still knew, and there was nothing funny left in the world at all. She took the lead then. She rolled him onto his back on his narrow bed with the snow light on his skin and showed him exactly what she wanted, and he let her, and looked up at her as if he’d never seen anything like her, as if he were seventeen and nothing had ever gone wrong.

When she finally took him inside her they both stopped breathing, and then she moved, and he gripped her hips, and it wasn’t careful at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, much later, she woke in the dark.

The snow had stopped. He was asleep with one arm over her waist and his face pressed into her hair. Without his glasses, without the furrow between his eyebrows, he looked younger than she’d ever seen him, and his mouth had gone soft.

She touched his cheek. His eyes opened at once.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.” She smiled into the dark. “Your comments were very helpful.”

He made a sound that was half a laugh. “You’re thinking about that now?”

“The last one. Your gap doesn’t close.” She put her hand on his chest. “I thought it was a warning. When I first read it. I cried.”

“It wasn’t a warning.”

“I know. It took me about a week.” She was quiet for a moment. “It means there’s always somewhere left to go. Doesn’t it.”

He pulled her in closer under the covers and kissed the top of her head and didn’t answer, because she was right, and because he wasn’t sure he could say anything just then that wouldn’t be too much.

“Thank you for reading it,” she said.

“Thank you for writing it,” said Miles.

Across the campus, in the dark, in office 412, a hundred and twenty-six pages lay on his desk beside a crooked purple cat with one surprised ear, and the snow lay white along the window ledge, and the date in the corner of the board said 20 JUNE — 16:00 under a long smudge where somebody had been kissed against it.

chapters.title: Rumours in the Department Kitchen
chapters.desc: A photograph on the student forum. A man’s tuxedo jacket at half past one in the morning. Then Miles hears what the postdocs are saying, and finds out he has a temper after all.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not responsible for my anger.”
chapters.content:
The photograph went up on the student forum at seventeen minutes past nine on the last Saturday of January.

It wasn’t a good photograph. It had been taken from above, through a window, at night, with a phone, and the flash had caught a drainpipe and turned it white. Half of it was the corner of a building. Nobody ever found out whose phone it had been on for six weeks, or why it came out when it did.

But the girl in it was clear enough.

She was standing in a narrow street behind a hotel, barefoot, with a pair of silver sandals hanging from two fingers. She was laughing. And she was wearing a man’s dinner jacket, dark charcoal, far too big for her, with the sleeves down over her hands.

Who does this jacket belong to?? Shen Foundation gala, 1:30 a.m. Interesting way to end an evening.

Three minutes later, someone answered.

isn’t that the girl from physics?

Shen Yu Jie. the foundation heiress. her family owns the library

wait

WAIT. isn’t that Dr. Wei’s jacket? he was there. my cousin waitered it. he was the only man there who looked like he wanted to die

By half past nine there were forty comments. By a quarter to ten, Tao Tao had found it. At ten to ten, Yu Jie was sitting across from her in the café by the south gate, holding her phone in both hands and wishing she’d never learned to read.

It was much worse on a bigger screen. The jacket was unmistakable. She remembered putting the purple pen into its pocket. She remembered the warmth of it, and the service corridor, and the cold hitting her like water, and laughing in the street because she’d got out. She’d never once looked up.

“Why would anybody care?”

“Because you’re in a man’s jacket at half past one in the morning,” said Tao Tao, “after a party where your mother walked you past nine eligible men.” She scrolled. Her face changed. “There’s another one.”

“Show me.”

“Maybe don’t.”

“Tao Tao. Show me.”

The second post was newer. It had no picture. Just a paragraph.

Since everyone’s asking about Shen Yu Jie, maybe someone could explain why she’s always in office 412. Some of us have been working for years to get where we are. Funny how certain people get certain kinds of attention.

Under it:

her family funds half the university, what did you expect

wouldn’t be surprised if the degree was arranged in first year

maybe that’s why she doesn’t need to worry about her thesis

Yu Jie read the last one twice. Her fingers went still round the paper cup.

Tao Tao took the phone out of her hand. “That’s enough.”

“They don’t know anything.”

“No. They don’t know about the corners, or the nineteen days, or the two hundred and twelve rude questions on our fridge.” Tao Tao put the phone face down. Then she picked her own phone up and started tapping, with her jaw set.

“What are you doing?”

“Closing something.”

“What?”

Tao Tao sighed. “Don’t be angry. There’s a sort of. Pool. In the second-year group chat. Since about November. On whether you and Dr. Wei were...” She stopped. “It was a joke.”

“How many people?”

“Not many.”

“How many, Tao Tao.”

“Enough.” She hit something hard with her thumb. “I’ve reported it. And I’ve told Ah Dong to tell everyone that the next person who puts money on your life gets their cell cultures contaminated.”

For once Tao Tao didn’t try to make her laugh. She reached across the table and took Yu Jie’s cold hand.

“Listen to me. You earned your place. You wrote every word of that thesis. You don’t owe any of them a thing.”

Yu Jie nodded. Her hand stayed cold.

“Does Miles know?”

“No.”

“Are you going to tell him?”

She locked the phone.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because he’ll want to know who posted it. He’ll go to Professor Cen. He’ll make it into something enormous, and it’ll be about him, and then it’ll be true.” She looked out of the window. “I don’t want him to worry. He’s only just started laughing.”

Tao Tao looked at her.

“You’re both impossible,” she said.

“Thank you.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles found out on Tuesday. Not from her. Not from Ling Hao. He found out because he went into the department kitchen at eleven to make tea and heard somebody laughing.

There were three postdocs and a visiting student round the kettle. The talk didn’t stop when he came in. He took his mug down from the cupboard.

“Well,” said Zeng Bo, “if I had her family, I suppose I’d find a degree a lot easier too.”

Somebody laughed.

Miles stopped with his hand on the cupboard door.

“Office 412’s very popular these days,” said Zeng Bo. He was thirty-four, a postdoc in the optics group, on his third contract in five years, with a good haircut and a habit of talking loudly enough for the next room. “Maybe we should all try the expensive jewellery and the right surname.”

Miles put his mug down on the counter. He didn’t do it loudly. It was enough. The laughing went thin.

Zeng Bo looked round. “Dr. Wei.”

“Would you say that again?”

“Nothing important.”

“I thought I heard you talking about Shen Yu Jie.”

“Just the forum.” Zeng Bo leaned back against the counter. “You know how it is. People notice things.”

“People notice a photograph of a student in a jacket.”

“And people notice when a student gets a great deal of attention from certain members of staff.”

The kitchen went quiet.

“Are you suggesting something?” said Miles.

Zeng Bo shrugged. “I’m saying people are talking. Her family funds the place. Everybody knows.”

“And you believe that makes her degree unearned?”

“I’m saying it’s hard to know how much of it’s hers.”

Miles looked at him.

“Have you read her thesis?” he said, very quietly.

Zeng Bo blinked. “What?”

“Have you read it?”

“No.”

“Have you looked at how she derives the pseudomagnetic field? Or how she handles it at the corners, where it stops being uniform?”

“I don’t work in that area.”

“Then what is your opinion based on?”

Zeng Bo’s smile had gone. “I was making a general observation.”

“No. You were making a specific accusation about a student whose work you haven’t read.” Miles picked up his mug, and then put it down again. His hand was steady. His voice hadn’t risen at all. But something in it had gone very cold, and the visiting student by the window had stopped breathing. “She found a serious flaw in her own work. She rebuilt the analysis herself, in under three weeks, and the result is better than what most people in this building could have produced. She did it on her own.”

“And how would you know that?”

Miles was quiet for a second. He had to be careful. He knew exactly how much of it he’d read. He knew exactly how many questions he’d written. And none of that was his to tell a kitchen.

“Her work is available through the proper channels,” he said. “You’re welcome to read it before you form a view.”

Zeng Bo gave a small, ugly smile. “Well. I suppose you would know.”

“Yes,” said Miles.

The smile went.

“And I would also know,” said Miles, “that making insinuations about a student’s academic integrity, particularly in connection with her family, in front of witnesses, is harassment under the university’s code. Section four. I’d be very happy to show you.”

Zeng Bo straightened up off the counter. “Are you threatening me?”

“I’m informing you.”

“That’s absurd.”

“Then you’ll have no trouble explaining your comments if a report is made.”

“You’re taking this awfully seriously,” said Zeng Bo.

“I am,” said Miles.

He picked up his mug, without any tea in it, and walked out. He didn’t slam the door. The kitchen stayed silent after.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao found him twenty minutes later at the window of 412, looking down at the courtyard, with the empty mug still in his hand.

“I heard,” said Ling Hao, and shut the door. “From three people. Did you actually threaten Zeng Bo with a harassment report?”

“I told him what his remarks could be.”

Ling Hao looked at his back for a while. “You’re angry.”

“Yes.”

Ling Hao sat down. “Have you talked to her?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because she hasn’t told me.” Miles put the mug down at last. “It’s been on the forum since Saturday. Tao Tao will have shown her by ten o’clock that morning. And she came in here on Monday and asked me about a citation and smiled at me and said nothing at all.”

“Maybe she doesn’t want you to know.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of.”

Ling Hao was quiet. Then he said, more gently than usual, “You’re not angry with her.”

“No.”

“You’re angry that she thinks she has to protect you from something that’s happening to her.”

Miles looked at his hands.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three, Professor Cen took his coffee in the department kitchen, standing beside Zeng Bo, and said a few quiet sentences to him about evidence and proper processes that nobody else heard and that made Zeng Bo stare at the kettle for some time after he’d gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Cen came to 412 at half past three and shut the door behind him.

“Have you got a minute, Miles?”

“Of course.”

He sat down in Yu Jie’s chair, which was too small for him. “I’ve heard about Zeng Bo.”

Miles’s face didn’t move. “I see.”

“You should have come to me before you went at him.”

“Perhaps.”

“Perhaps.” Professor Cen looked at him over his reading glasses. “You’re not usually quick to anger.”

Miles didn’t answer.

“Well.” Professor Cen put a thin folder on the desk. “There’s something else you need to know. It’s about the examination panels.”

“Mine?”

“Hers.” He opened it. “Shen Yu Jie’s thesis examination. The provisional roster. We drew it up last September, before term started, from whoever’s research was nearest each topic.”

Miles looked down.

His name was there. Under Professor Ruan’s. Above the two external examiners.

He read the line twice.

“Since September,” he said.

“Since the first week of September. It’s provisional. The formal assignments go to the faculty in February. You’d have had the letter next week.” Professor Cen took his glasses off. “I expected you to say something.”

“Take me off.”

“I expected you to say that.”

“Professor Ruan’s her supervisor. I’ve read parts of her draft. I’ve never assessed any of her work.”

“That distinction matters.”

“It isn’t enough.”

“No,” said Professor Cen. “It isn’t.”

“I can’t examine her.”

“Then you’ll be recused.”

“Today.”

“Today.” He closed the folder. “I’ll have the roster changed. We’ll find someone else.”

There was a long pause.

“You understand why this matters,” said Professor Cen. “Not just because of whatever there is between you two. Because of how it looks. And because of the forum. People are already hunting for a reason to say her work isn’t hers. We can’t hand them a real procedural irregularity to point at.”

“I understand.”

“Does she know you were on it?”

“No.”

“Then tell her.” Professor Cen stood up and went to the door, and stopped with his hand on it. “And, Miles. Don’t let caring about her turn into a public fight that makes her life harder. She’s a fine student. Let the work speak.”

The door closed.

Miles sat looking at the folder for a long time.

Since September. Since before the first Wednesday, before the harmonic oscillator and the purple pen and the second mug. Before the graph, and the back stairs, and October. His name had been sitting on a list under hers the whole time, and he’d stood at his board in October and promised her nobody would ever be able to say her degree came from him.

He closed the folder and sat still.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t come to the fourth floor that afternoon.

He noticed at four. He noticed again at five, and at six. He didn’t message her. He knew she had chapters to finish and that she’d been working hard, since October, to keep her work and him on opposite sides of a wall.

At eighteen minutes past seven he opened their conversation.

The last message was from that morning.

Not Stuck: Don’t forget to eat lunch.

Miles: I won’t.

He’d forgotten.

He started typing.

I heard what they’re saying.

He deleted it.

You don’t have to keep things from me.

He read it back. It sounded like a reprimand. He deleted that too.

I’m sorry.

He didn’t know what he was apologising for.

He deleted it.

Then his thumbs moved before he could think.

I love you.

He looked at the three words on the screen.

He’d said them in his head more times than he could count. He’d said them to the back of her neck while she slept, in January, in the snow light, without a sound. He’d as good as said them to Aurelia, holding a plate. He’d never said them to her.

He imagined her reading them tonight, of all nights, and wondering whether he only meant sorry.

His thumb stayed over the arrow.

Then he deleted it, and put the phone face down on the desk.

A minute later it buzzed.

Not Stuck: Are you still at work?

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: Have you eaten?

He looked at the empty mug.

Miles: Not yet.

Not Stuck: That’s unacceptable. I’m bringing you something.

Miles: You don’t have to.

Not Stuck: I know.

Not Stuck: I want to.

He looked at the empty box where the three words had been. He could still send them. He could tell her now.

He wanted to see her face when he did. So he put the phone down and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came twenty minutes later in a thick grey cardigan, with her hair tied up anyhow and a paper bag in one hand and a small frown that said she’d already decided he was going to be difficult.

“Dinner,” she said. Two vegetable buns from the place by the gate, a tub of soup, a little box of cut fruit. “Why do you look like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’ve been thinking too hard.”

He shut the door behind her. There wasn’t any point pretending.

“Zeng Bo said some things in the kitchen this morning.”

She went still.

“About the forum,” said Miles.

She put the bag down on his desk carefully. “You saw it.”

“I heard about it. In a kitchen. From a man who said your family bought your degree.”

Her face tightened.

“I was going to tell you,” she said.

“All right.”

“I didn’t want you to be angry.”

“I was angry.” He came a step closer and didn’t touch her. “I should have asked you what you wanted before I did anything. I didn’t. I told him to read your thesis before he opened his mouth again, and that the code has a section on harassment.”

“Of course you did,” she said, and her voice wobbled.

“Yu Jie. Don’t protect me from things that are happening to you.”

“I wasn’t...”

“You were. You came in yesterday and asked me about a citation and smiled.”

She looked away. “I didn’t want you to be angry because of me.”

“You’re not responsible for my anger,” said Miles. “And you’re not responsible for making me comfortable while people are cruel to you.”

Her eyes filled. She turned her face away fast.

“I hate that they think I didn’t earn it,” she said. “I worked so hard. I spent nineteen days on those corners. I thought I’d have to start the whole thing again. And now they’re saying my family bought it.”

“Your work is yours.”

He held out his hand. She took it.

“Professor Cen told me something today,” he said. “When the department drew up the examination panels last September, before term started, they put me on yours. Provisionally.”

Her hand went still in his. “What?”

“Since the first week of September. Before the harmonic oscillator. I didn’t know. Nobody tells you until February.” He kept hold of her. “I’ve asked to be taken off. He’s agreed. Someone else will do it.”

“Does Professor Ruan know?”

“She will.”

“Does it mean...”

“No. It doesn’t change your thesis, or your supervisor, or a single line you’ve written. We’ll make sure the procedure’s right. That’s what matters now.”

She looked at him. Then she put her forehead against his chest, and he put his arms round her, and he didn’t tell her it would be fine and he didn’t tell her to ignore them. He just held her until her breathing went slow.

“Did you really threaten Zeng Bo with a harassment report?” she said, into his jumper.

“I told him what the code says.”

She pulled back and looked at him. “You’re not usually like that.”

“No.”

“You’re angry.”

“Yes.”

“I’ve never seen you angry.”

“Neither had I,” said Miles. “Apparently.”

She laughed, a little, wetly. Then she went up on her toes and kissed him, not a short kiss, with both hands holding his face, as if she were the one who had something to say and couldn’t find the words either.

When she drew back she said, “Don’t fight everybody for me.”

“I’ll try to choose.”

“Good.” She glanced at the bag on the desk. “Now eat.”

“You’re very authoritative.”

“Somebody has to be,” said Yu Jie, and this time he didn’t argue.

chapters.title: Miles Recuses Himself
chapters.desc: One page, written at his one table between midnight and four. The most honest document in the history of the department. Then the Wednesday rules change, and Ling Hao brings croissants.
chapters.epigraph: “Physics only was this afternoon.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past midnight, Miles sat at the one table in his staff flat with a sheet of blank paper in front of him.

The table was barely big enough for the paper and his laptop, and one leg had a square of cardboard under it. There was a form on the university website, a single page with boxes. He could have filled it in, in five minutes, and let the department do the rest.

But the form didn’t ask the questions that mattered. It didn’t ask whether he’d read her draft. It didn’t ask whether he had any reason to favour her, or whether what he felt for her could ever bend his judgement. It didn’t ask whether he loved her.

He picked up his pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

To: Professor Cen, Head of Department

Re: Formal declaration of a personal relationship, and request for recusal

I am writing to declare a personal relationship with Shen Yu Jie, a final-year undergraduate in this department.

The relationship began in October. I understand that it creates both an actual and a perceived conflict of interest in any academic, supervisory, examining or administrative decision that concerns her.

I was listed on the provisional examining panel for her thesis from September. I did not know this until yesterday. I ask to be removed from that panel immediately and completely, and from any other process that may affect her academic progress.

I have also read a full draft of her thesis, at her request, passed to me by her supervisor. I wrote comments in the form of questions. I did not provide a method, a derivation or a solution, and I have not supervised, assessed or marked any of her work. I recognise, nevertheless, that my involvement could raise questions about the independence of her assessment. I ask the department to keep a record of this declaration, to review my comments, and to make sure that her work is examined by people who have no connection to her.

I want to be plain that my feelings for Shen Yu Jie are not casual. I love her.

That is exactly why I must not be placed anywhere my judgement, however carefully I use it, could be questioned and turned against her. I do not want her achievement diminished by my position in this department. I do not want her ever to have to defend the legitimacy of her own work because of something I failed to do.

I ask that this declaration be kept confidential as far as university policy allows. I will provide anything else that is needed.

Miles Wei

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it once. Then again.

He thought about changing the sentence in the middle. I love her. It looked almost embarrassingly bare, sitting there among all the procedure, like a man who’d turned up to a committee meeting without a jacket.

He left it.

At one he printed it, signed it, scanned it, and attached it to an email to Professor Cen. Then he didn’t send it.

There’s a particular fear in making something private official. Once it was sent, it couldn’t be unsent.

He thought of her face the night before when she’d said now they’re saying my family bought it. He thought of his own name, typed on a list under hers in September, and how easily a careless decision could become a permanent question mark beside someone.

At fourteen minutes to four, he sent it.

Then he closed the laptop and went to bed, and didn’t sleep much.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Cen read it at twenty past eight, twice.

The second time he read it as a man who’d known Miles Wei since he was a doctoral student taking notes in pencil at the back of every seminar. Then he rang Professor Ruan, and she was in his office in twelve minutes, still in her coat, smelling of cigarettes. She read it standing up, and looked up.

“He could simply have filled in the form,” said Professor Cen.

“Yes. Instead he’s written you a confession.”

“A formal declaration.”

“Cen. I know what a formal declaration looks like.” She put the paper down on the desk. “He’s named every possible source of conflict. He’s told you about the draft, which nobody would ever have known. He’s asked you to investigate him. This is a man making very sure that he’s the only one in the room anybody can blame.”

Professor Cen didn’t answer.

She looked at the sentence in the middle. Then she let out a breath.

“Well,” said Professor Ruan. “At least we know why he went for Zeng Bo in the kitchen.”

“Good,” said Professor Cen. “Somebody should have shut that man up in October.”

Professor Ruan laughed, short and surprised.

“What will you do?”

“Take him off the panel today. Put Ling Hao on. He’s never met the girl except across a corridor.” Professor Cen tapped the letter. “And I’ll ask the research committee to look at Miles’s comments on her draft, so there’s a record that he never supervised or marked her. That should protect her.”

“Will you tell her?”

“That’s his to do.”

“He’s very good at writing difficult things to committees,” said Professor Ruan, picking up her bag. “And very bad at saying them. I’ll tell her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to eleven the department office sent him an email.

Following your declaration of a personal conflict of interest, you have been removed from the provisional examining panel for Shen Yu Jie. Dr. Ling Hao has been appointed in your place, subject to the usual approval.

He read it. He closed it.

He felt relief, and then the small cold finality of seeing someone else’s name where his had been.

Ling Hao was in the doorway ten minutes later with a paper bag.

“Congratulations. You’re unemployed as an examiner.”

“That’s not a position.”

“It was a very prestigious one.” He put the bag down. Croissants, still warm. “I’ve been appointed in your place. I expect a generous handover.”

“There’s nothing to hand over.”

“I’ll read what she submits, cold,” said Ling Hao, sitting down. “And I won’t discuss it with you. Not one word.”

“Good.”

“You’re taking it well.”

Miles looked at the email still open on his screen. “I’m relieved.”

“You’re also disappointed.”

Miles didn’t answer.

“That’s allowed,” said Ling Hao, and pushed the bag across the desk. “Eat. Coffee isn’t breakfast.”

The next email came before lunch.

To maintain clear professional boundaries, consultations between students and any member of staff with a declared conflict of interest will now take place in the glass consultation rooms on the second floor, and must be booked through the department system.

Nobody had forbidden him to talk to her. They’d only made sure nobody could mistake what the talking was.

“Your new office is a fish tank,” said Ling Hao, from the doorway again, an hour later. “Shall I bring you a little plastic castle?”

Miles gave him a look. Ling Hao grinned.

“Croissants next Wednesday, then,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Ruan found Yu Jie that afternoon in the administrative corridor, collecting a form for her thesis submission.

“Shen Yu Jie. A minute.”

She took her into the empty meeting room at the end and shut the door.

“Dr. Wei sent a formal declaration to the head of department last night,” she said. “About your relationship.”

Yu Jie went completely still.

“He’s asked to be taken off your examining panel and out of anything that could touch your assessment. He’s been taken off. Dr. Ling will examine you instead.”

“Good,” said Yu Jie, slowly.

“There’s more.” Professor Ruan looked at her over her half-moon glasses. “It was a letter. One page. Written between midnight and four in the morning.”

Yu Jie looked down. “Of course it was.”

“He told the department that he’d read your draft. He explained exactly what his comments were and weren’t. He asked to have his own conduct investigated, so that nobody could ever say your work wasn’t independent.” She paused. “And he wrote one more thing.”

“What?”

“He wrote that he loves you.”

The room went quiet.

“He hasn’t said it to me,” she whispered. “He’s never said it.”

“No,” said Professor Ruan. “He wouldn’t have, would he. He’s very good at declaring things to committees.”

Yu Jie laughed, and it came out wrong, and her eyes filled.

“I’m telling you,” said Professor Ruan, more gently, “because I don’t think you should have to hear it from a rumour in a kitchen.” She stood up. “Your Wednesdays have moved to the glass room on the second floor, by the way. The department wants everything visible.”

“That’s fair.”

“It is.” At the door Professor Ruan stopped. “He’s trying very hard to do the right thing, Yu Jie.”

“I know.”

When she’d gone Yu Jie sat alone in the meeting room for a long time. She thought of him at that little table in his flat, the one with the cardboard under its leg. Writing it a sentence at a time. Stopping at three words. Deciding to leave them in.

She took out her phone.

I heard about your letter.

She deleted it. She wanted to say it to his face.

✦ ✦ ✦

The glass room was on the second floor, at the end of the corridor by the stairs. It had a narrow table, two chairs, a whiteboard, and walls made entirely of glass, so that everybody walking past could see in from every side.

At two o’clock she came in with her laptop and a folder of graphs. He was already there, standing at the whiteboard with a marker, his sleeves pushed up. The room was bright.

“Hello,” he said.

“Hello.”

She sat down. He sat down opposite her. For a moment they just looked at each other across the narrow table, in full view of the second floor.

Then she opened her notebook.

“I’ve been thinking about the corners.”

“All right.”

“I don’t think the thesis should be the last thing I write about them. The way the field changes near the boundary, I don’t think the localisation length’s the only thing it affects. I think the shape of the corner matters. The angle.” She turned the laptop round. “I think there might be a second paper.”

He studied her graph. “Perhaps.”

“That’s not very enthusiastic.”

“It’s a preliminary result. Call it a question.”

She wrote across the top of a clean page: Second question: corner geometry and edge localisation.

“What’s your central hypothesis?” he said.

For nearly an hour they worked, in a glass box, with the whole department going past. A second-year stopped outside to look at the whiteboard. Miles looked up. The boy waved, awkwardly. Miles nodded to him. Yu Jie hid her face behind her laptop.

At eight minutes past three she closed her notebook and put a small cardboard box on the table.

It was a box of white chalk. Ordinary classroom chalk. When he opened it, the sticks were wrapped in a twist of tissue paper.

“For your pocket,” she said. “You leave it everywhere. There’s chalk in my coat.”

He took a stick out. It left a white smudge on his fingertip.

“Thank you,” he said, and put the box in the inside pocket of his jacket.

Their eyes met. A student went past the glass.

“Next Wednesday?” he said.

“Next Wednesday.”

They left separately. It was the right thing to do. It was also hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to six she knocked once on the door of 412.

He opened it. She came in. He shut the door.

She looked at him for a moment. Then she took two handfuls of his jumper and pushed him back against the inside of his own door and kissed him so hard his head hit the wood.

She was angry, and it was in her mouth and her hands, and he caught her waist and let her.

When she let go she was breathing fast.

“You wrote it down,” she said.

He went still.

“That you love me. To Professor Cen. On university paper. At four in the morning.”

“Professor Ruan told you.”

“Yes.”

“I was going to tell you.”

“When? At the next committee meeting?”

The corner of his mouth moved. “Possibly.”

She glared at him. He laughed, quietly, against the door. Then her face changed.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I wanted to say it properly.”

“Writing it to the head of department was properly?”

“It was necessary.”

“You can write it to a committee but you can’t say it to me?”

The teasing went out of his face.

“I can,” he said. “I don’t want to say it because I’m afraid of what’s going to happen to you. Or because the department’s watching. Or because I think you need comforting.” His thumb moved along her cheek. “I want to say it because it’s true.”

“Then say it.”

He put his forehead against hers. “Not like this.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’re angry.”

“I’m not angry.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“I’m a bit angry,” said Yu Jie.

“I know.”

“Then when?”

“When I can say it without it sounding like an apology.”

She looked at him. Then something in her face gave.

“All right,” she said. “But you don’t get another nineteen days.”

He laughed out loud. “I won’t.”

She kissed him again, slowly this time. Then she put her hand on the little box of chalk in his jacket.

“Come home with me,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left separately. The snow from last week had melted and the pavements were dark and wet, and she was waiting for him by the old wall under the first lamp. When she saw him she smiled, and he walked up to her and took her hand, and they went the rest of the way together, and nobody stopped them.

Tao Tao was at the lab until midnight. The flat was warm and untidy, a book face down on the sofa, socks abandoned by the rug, and he stood looking at it all and smiling.

She made tea. They drank it on the sofa with her leaning against his shoulder. Then she put her cup down.

“Are you sure you want me to stay?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Yu Jie...”

“Physics only was this afternoon,” said Yu Jie.

He stared at her for a second. Then he laughed, properly, helplessly, with his head back against the sofa, and she watched him do it with her whole face.

She took his hand and led him to her bedroom, and at the doorway he stopped.

“Are you sure?”

“Miles.”

“I’m only asking.”

“I know,” she said, and pulled him in, and shut the door.

There was no whiteboard in there, no roster, no department notice, nobody asking either of them to explain anything. There was her lamp with a scarf over it turning everything gold, and her unmade bed, and the two of them.

He asked, the way he always asked. She answered by pushing his jacket off his shoulders and letting it drop, chalk box and all, onto her floor. He laughed at that. Then she took his glasses off and put them on her bedside table, carefully, folded, the way she’d watched him do it a hundred times, and he stopped laughing.

She took the lead. She’d been angry all afternoon and she was still a little angry, and he let her be, let her push him down onto her bed and hold his wrists and kiss him as if she were making a point. When he hesitated, out of habit, out of all those years of being careful, she smiled against his mouth and told him he was allowed to want this too. That he was allowed to want her. Out loud.

So he told her. Not the three words. Everything else. He told her in a low wrecked voice exactly what he wanted, a step at a time, the way he’d explain a derivation, and she did every one of them, unbuttoning him and then herself while he watched, and laughed, and then she didn’t. When she sank down onto him he said her name like a proof he’d finally finished, and she rode him slowly with the gold light on his face until neither of them said anything that made any sense.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest. His fingers moved slowly through her hair.

“You’re thinking,” he said.

“I’m always thinking.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She lifted her head. “Do you regret it? The letter.”

“No.”

“Even the part where you made yourself the only person anybody could blame?”

He was quiet. “I didn’t want anyone to question your work because of me.”

“I don’t want you carrying everything on your own.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He looked up at her. “I’m learning.”

She put her head back down. After a while he brushed her hair away from her face.

“There’s something I haven’t told you.”

“What?”

“I didn’t write that sentence because I thought it would help the department understand the conflict.” His hand stopped in her hair. “I wrote it because it’s true.”

She lifted her head again and looked at him.

“I love you,” said Miles.

There was no letter. No committee. Nobody else in the room. Just him, without his glasses, looking straight at her, in her lamp light, letting her see every bit of his face.

She smiled, small, and it shook.

“I love you too.”

He shut his eyes. She kissed him. And when she settled down against him again, he held her a little tighter than before, and didn’t let go.

Across the campus the glass room stood empty. And on her bedroom floor, in the inside pocket of a dark jacket, a small box of chalk waited for next Wednesday.

chapters.title: She Cries in a Stairwell
chapters.desc: New Year’s Eve dinner at the museum, with the Yans at the table and the forum on her mother’s phone. Not because of him. Because of her mother.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re Yu Jie, and you get to decide what that means.”
chapters.content:
The museum had been shut to the public since four.

By seven its great hall had become a dining room. Long tables ran beneath the glass roof in ivory linen and white orchids, and the old galleries round the edge glowed gold, and outside the tall windows the city was getting ready for the new year: red lanterns strung across the streets, families hurrying home with bags of food, and somewhere over the harbour a firework going off far too early.

The Shen Foundation’s New Year’s Eve dinner wasn’t, strictly speaking, a family occasion. It was only the evening on which everyone in the Shens’ orbit was expected to appear.

Yu Jie sat beside her mother. Across the table sat the Yans.

Yan Zhiyuan was in a dark suit and a plain silver watch, as polished as always, talking easily to everyone. His father was discussing a reception at the ministry with Shen Ruolan. His mother was admiring the new exhibition. Yu Jie smiled when she was supposed to, and answered when she was spoken to, and once she even laughed, when Mrs. Yan said how hard it was these days to find young people who could get through a dinner without looking at their phones.

It was a good performance. Her mother seemed satisfied.

“Zhiyuan says you’ve been working hard on your thesis,” said Mrs. Yan.

“Yes. It’s nearly finished.”

“How wonderful. Your mother says you’ve done well.”

Yu Jie glanced at her mother. “Professor Ruan has been generous with her time.”

“And after June you’ll have so much more time for yourself.”

“I hope so.”

“She will,” said Shen Ruolan. “We’ve already talked about her plans for the summer.”

Yu Jie looked at her mother. They hadn’t. Her mother had talked about them, and Yu Jie had been in the room. It wasn’t the same thing.

Across the table, Yan Zhiyuan saw her face. He didn’t interrupt. He turned instead to her father and asked about the museum’s new collection of trade porcelain, and the conversation slid neatly away down a different road, and she could have kissed him for it, in a purely diplomatic sense.

Her phone buzzed under the table.

Yan Zhiyuan: You look as though you’ve been sentenced to a long committee.

Yu Jie: I have.

Yan Zhiyuan: Survive till pudding. The chocolate is worth it.

She looked up. He was listening to his father with perfect attention and didn’t look at her at all.

Yan Zhiyuan: For what it’s worth, you’re doing it beautifully.

She put the phone away. She liked him. Not the way her mother wanted. But he knew the difference between being polite and being comfortable, and he had never once asked her to be someone else.

Her mother had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble came after dinner.

Yu Jie had slipped away to the east gallery, where the family had lent the museum an exhibition of old photographs for the new year. It was quieter there. She stood in front of a portrait of her grandmother as a young woman, in pearls, looking straight into the camera with a calm that had always slightly frightened her.

“You’ve got her face.”

Her mother was behind her.

“Ma.”

“Your grandmother was beautiful.”

“She was.”

“She understood what it meant to represent a family.”

Yu Jie looked at the photograph. “She was also a chemist.”

Her mother’s expression barely moved. “Before she married your grandfather.”

Then she took her phone out of her evening bag.

“Do you know what people are saying about you?”

Something tightened under Yu Jie’s ribs. “Who?”

“People.”

Her mother held the phone out. On the screen was the forum. The photograph. Yu Jie in a narrow street behind the Harbour Hotel, barefoot, laughing, holding her silver sandals, in a man’s charcoal dinner jacket with the sleeves down over her hands.

Her mother swiped. The comments.

isn’t that the Shen heiress?

that’s Dr. Wei’s jacket isn’t it

office 412 again

I suppose being a Shen makes everything easier

Another swipe. The second post, the one about her degree.

“Do you understand how this looks?” said Shen Ruolan.

“It looks like somebody took a picture of me after the gala.”

“It looks like a girl from this family wearing a lecturer’s jacket in the middle of the night.”

“He lent it to me because I was cold.”

“And why were you with him?”

Yu Jie said nothing.

Her mother’s voice dropped. “Don’t insult me by pretending I can’t see what’s going on.”

Yu Jie looked at the screen again. She’d read all of it before, at the café table with Tao Tao, and tried not to think about it since. In her mother’s hand it looked different. It looked less like gossip and more like evidence.

“Is that why you put the Yans at our table tonight?”

“Don’t make this about them.”

“Then what’s it about?”

“You.”

Yu Jie laughed once, without anything in it. “That’s what everybody keeps telling me.”

“You’ve been careless.”

“I haven’t done anything wrong.”

“That isn’t the same as being careful.”

“Have you read my thesis, Ma?”

Her mother stopped. “What?”

“Have you read one chapter? Do you know what I changed in January? Do you know what was wrong with the corners and how I fixed it?”

“I’m not discussing your coursework.”

“Why not?”

“Because it isn’t the problem.”

Yu Jie stared at her. She couldn’t find a single word.

Her mother put the phone away. “This family cannot afford another scandal.”

“Another?”

Something moved across Shen Ruolan’s face and was gone. “Don’t twist my words.”

“I didn’t.”

“Your grandfather spent his whole life building this family. Your father has spent his protecting it. You have been given every chance there is.”

“And I’m grateful.”

“Then behave like it.”

Yu Jie pressed her hands together, hard. “I’m not a pearl you can put back in a box every time someone looks at me.”

Her mother went still.

“Don’t speak to me like that.”

“Then don’t talk about me as if I need polishing.”

Shen Ruolan took a breath, and when she spoke again her voice was perfectly controlled.

“The engagement will be in late June. After your graduation. The Yans and I have agreed the timing.”

“No. You agreed it.”

“Zhiyuan is an excellent match. His family understands ours. He has a career, and he’ll be posted overseas in the autumn, to the mission. The foundation’s been talking about an international partnership. You’ll go with him once the wedding’s arranged, and learn how to manage the family’s interests abroad.”

The floor seemed to tilt.

From the hall came the sound of the dinner going on without them: glasses, a laugh, somebody tapping a microphone to announce the next part of the evening.

“You’ve decided everything.”

“I’m giving you a future.”

“You’re giving me an itinerary.”

“Yu Jie.”

“I haven’t even graduated.”

“Which is why it will be after you graduate.”

“Late June.”

“Yes.”

“Eight days after.”

“It’s a suitable date.”

Yu Jie thought of the twentieth of June. Sixteen hundred hours. Two hundred and fifty-five atoms on her wall, most of them still uncoloured. She thought of a man in a glass room saying call it a question. And here was her mother telling her what the answer would be.

“You can’t arrange my marriage like a foundation lunch.”

“I can arrange an introduction. I can make plans. I can offer you a life where you never have to struggle.”

“I don’t want that life.”

“You don’t know what you want.”

“I do.”

Her mother studied her. Then, lower: “Is it him?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer.

“Dr. Wei.”

“Don’t.”

“Is that why you’re so determined to stay in that department? Is he why you’ve become so difficult?”

“He isn’t the reason.”

“Then what is?”

The answer was so obvious she almost laughed.

“Me,” said Yu Jie.

For the first time all evening, Shen Ruolan looked genuinely displeased. “You’re making a mistake.”

“Maybe.”

“Do you think he can give you what the Yans can?”

Yu Jie opened her mouth, and nothing came out of it. Because how could she explain? That he had never promised her an easy life. That he had never once asked her to be less clever or less loud or less herself. That he’d read a hundred and eighteen pages of her thesis in one night not to own it but to understand it. That he’d written a letter at four in the morning to take himself out of her way, because he loved her, and said so, to the head of department, in writing.

You couldn’t explain something to someone who had already decided it was worth nothing.

So she said nothing at all.

Her mother turned the pearl bracelet on her wrist. “Come back to the dining room.”

“I need a minute.”

Her mother went.

Yu Jie stood in front of her grandmother, who wore her pearls in the photograph with the face of a woman nobody had ever asked whether she wanted them.

She didn’t go back to the dining room.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got as far as the back staircase before the first tear came.

It was an old service stair behind the galleries, stone, smelling of floor cleaner, with one narrow window looking out over a dark courtyard. She sat down on the landing and tried to breathe.

She told herself she wasn’t going to cry. She was twenty-two. She’d nearly finished a thesis. She’d survived a forum, a department kitchen, a conflict-of-interest review and nineteen days of corners. She could survive one conversation with her mother.

Then she thought of the mission. Late June. A wedding. A whole life already written out for her in somebody else’s handwriting.

And she cried properly. Not the small, pretty crying she’d learned to do at family dinners. Her shoulders shook. She put her hand over her mouth. She cried until her eyes hurt and then she went on.

Her phone buzzed.

White Rabbit: Are you still at the museum?

She’d told him that morning where she’d be, and that she’d rather be anywhere else.

Yu Jie: Yes.

White Rabbit: Where?

Yu Jie: Somewhere quiet.

The answer came at once.

White Rabbit: Stay there. I’m coming.

He found her eleven minutes later.

He was in his dark coat, with his hair on end from the wind and from his hands, and he stopped at the top of the stairs.

“Yu Jie.”

She looked up. His face changed. He came down the stairs two at a time and didn’t ask a single thing. He sat on the step beside her and opened his arms, and she went into them, and the moment her face touched his coat she started crying all over again.

He held her. One hand flat between her shoulder blades. The other cupped round the back of her head. He didn’t tell her to calm down. He didn’t tell her it would be all right. He just stayed.

After a while he said, very low, “Breathe with me.”

She tried. He breathed slowly and she followed him, in and out, again, and again, until the shaking started to ease.

“She knows,” she said into his coat.

“About us?”

“About the forum. The photograph. Your jacket. She had screenshots.”

“All right.”

“She says people are talking.”

“I know.”

She pulled back to look at him. “You know?”

“I’ve seen them. Since the kitchen.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t think repeating them to you would help.”

She looked down. “She says I’ve embarrassed the family. She says the engagement’s in late June. To Yan Zhiyuan. And then he’s posted overseas, and I go with him.”

His jaw went tight. That was all. He didn’t move.

“Did you agree?” he said.

“No.”

“Then it isn’t decided.”

“She thinks it is.”

“That doesn’t make it so.”

“She thinks I’ve got everything,” said Yu Jie, and her voice broke again. “She thinks I could have a good life if I’d just stop being difficult. She thinks I’m ungrateful.” She pressed her face back into his shoulder. “What if she’s right? What if I’m being selfish? What if I’m throwing away something good because I want something else?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He rested his cheek against her hair.

“My parents are teachers,” he said.

She lifted her head. He almost never talked about them.

“At a secondary school, out in the suburbs. My father teaches mathematics. My mother teaches literature. Ordinary people, very good at what they do. They think education’s meant to make you more able to choose your own life.” He looked at the narrow window. “My father always said a student who’s memorised every answer and never learned to ask a question hasn’t learned anything.”

A small wet smile came onto her face. “That sounds like you.”

“He said it first.” His thumb moved under her eye. “My mother’s less patient. She once told a parent she couldn’t teach his son to think if he insisted on doing the thinking for him.”

“Did he complain?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“She made him tea. So he’d have to sit down while she explained why he was wrong.”

Yu Jie laughed, a very small one. It was there, though.

“I grew up in a house where they thought you should be allowed to become what you were able to become,” said Miles. “Not what somebody else had already imagined for you. They got plenty wrong. They’re not perfect. But they never once made me feel that being their son meant I owed them a particular life.”

“I don’t think my mother knows how to love me without planning me.”

“Perhaps she doesn’t know how to love you without trying to protect you.”

“That doesn’t make it hurt less.”

“No,” he said. He didn’t excuse her mother. He didn’t tell her to forgive anybody. “You’re allowed to be hurt by someone who loves you. And you’re allowed to disagree with them.”

She leaned back against him. “She calls me her jewel. She says I have to understand what I represent.”

He was quiet.

“You’re not a jewel,” said Miles. “You’re a physicist.”

She looked up.

“You’re the physicist who spent nineteen days finding a better way through a problem I thought I understood. You’re the one who saw a boundary condition in somebody else’s seminar while the rest of the room was admiring the slides. You stood up in front of a hundred and forty second-years and asked me if zero-point energy applied to people.” He brushed a tear off her cheek. “You’re not an ornament. You’re not a family symbol. You’re not something to be polished and put somewhere safe. You’re Yu Jie, and you get to decide what that means.”

She couldn’t speak at all.

Then she took two fistfuls of his coat and kissed him.

It wasn’t careful. It had everything in it she hadn’t been able to say in the gallery, the anger and the fear and the exhaustion and the no. She kissed him hard enough to push him back against the stair rail, and his arm came round her waist and held her there, and he kissed her back the same way, as if he’d been as frightened as she had, on the walk over, and had only just been allowed to stop.

When she drew back she put her forehead against his.

“I’m not going overseas.”

“All right.”

“I’m not getting engaged to him.”

“All right.”

“I’m graduating on the twentieth of June. At four.”

“I remember.”

“And I’m going to finish my thesis, and submit it, and stand in that room in May and answer every question they ask. And then I’m going to decide what happens next.”

“That’s yours to decide.”

“I don’t know how to tell her.”

“You don’t have to work that out tonight.”

“But I will.”

“I know.”

She kissed him again, slowly this time.

“You’re not going to tell me to be patient?”

“No.”

“Or to think about the consequences?”

“I expect you’ve thought about them.”

“I have.”

“Then I won’t repeat what you already know.”

“You’re very annoying,” she said, and he said he’d been told, by her, frequently, and she laughed into his collar.

They sat on the cold stone landing together until the noise of the dinner had faded away to nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Monday morning, the first thing she did was look at the calendar on her wall.

She hadn’t touched it since New Year’s Eve. Most of the atoms were still empty. The last square, the twentieth of June, had a star in it in purple pen, and after it the paper simply stopped.

She picked up her pen and drew another square after the star. Then another. Then a row of them, running on past graduation into the days her mother had already claimed. She didn’t put atoms in them. She left them empty, and at the bottom of the new row she wrote, in capitals:

NOT A PEARL.

Then, underneath:

A PHYSICIST.

Her phone buzzed.

White Rabbit: Good morning.

Yu Jie: Good morning, White Rabbit.

White Rabbit: Have you eaten?

Yu Jie: Not yet.

White Rabbit: Please eat before you start work.

Yu Jie: You’re not my supervisor.

White Rabbit: I’m aware.

Yu Jie: You’re not my mother either.

White Rabbit: I’m relieved.

She laughed, and took a photograph of the wall, and sent it.

There was a pause.

White Rabbit: You’ve made it longer.

Yu Jie: I’ve got more squares to fill.

A longer pause.

White Rabbit: I like that.

She looked at the empty squares running off the edge of her plans. For the first time since the museum, the future didn’t look like a room somebody else had furnished for her. It looked like a blank page, and she had a pen.

chapters.title: The Grant Nobody Applied For
chapters.desc: Five years of funding, a laboratory with a four-metre tank that can make a horizon, and a donor who wants no name. Miles is overjoyed for exactly two days.
chapters.epigraph: “Try being happy before you design the entire building.”
chapters.content:
Professor Cen sent for him at a quarter past nine on the second of March, a Monday, which was never a good sign.

Miles went down with a notebook and a coffee and the revised lecture schedule, in case that was what it was about. It wasn’t. Cen pointed at the chair across the desk, waited until he’d sat in it, and opened a green folder with the care of a man laying out cards he already knew would win.

“A charitable trust has approved a research award,” he said. “Four million, over five years. For a programme in experimental analogue gravity. Your programme.”

Miles put the coffee down.

“Mine.”

“Your own laboratory. The trust read your publications and the proposal you sent round two years ago, the one the faculty told you was a lovely idea for some other decade. They’ve funded all of it. Set-up, equipment, a technician, two doctoral places, five years of running costs.” Cen turned the folder round so it faced him. “They’d like the old optics basement under the east wing, if you’ll have it.”

Miles read the first page. Then the second. Then the first again.

“You’re welcome to read it a third time,” said Cen. “It won’t change.”

He didn’t answer. He’d reached the equipment schedule, and on the equipment schedule there was a tank.

It was described in the dry language of procurement. A circular acrylic tank, four metres across, with a drain at its centre and pumps round the rim, so that the water could be made to circle inwards and down like a bath emptying. A wave-maker. A high-speed camera array above, and lasers to read the surface to a fraction of a millimetre. He had drawn this tank in the margin of a notebook when he was twenty-six. He’d never shown anybody the drawing. He didn’t show people his notebooks.

The idea was older than him and not his own. Water flowing inwards gets faster as it nears the drain. Somewhere there is a circle where the water runs inward faster than a ripple can travel out against it, and any small wave that strays inside that circle is carried down whatever it does. It isn’t a black hole. Nothing is being crushed. But for the waves on the surface the geometry is the same, a horizon they can’t climb back over, and the mathematics that describes it is the mathematics of curved spacetime. Groups abroad had built tanks like it. One of them, a few years ago, had sent waves past a spinning vortex and watched them come back out larger than they went in, carrying away a little of the spin, exactly as a rotating black hole was supposed to allow. He’d read that paper on a train and missed his stop.

“An effective horizon,” he said.

“I’m told that’s the point.”

“I’ll need to see the pump specifications before anything’s ordered. And the floor loading. Four metres of water is—“

“Facilities will assess it.”

“The drainage in that basement is forty years old.”

“Miles.”

He looked up.

“You’ve had the money for about four minutes,” said Cen. “Try being happy before you design the entire building.”

Miles looked at the folder. And then something happened to his face that Cen, who had known him nine years, had seen perhaps twice: he smiled with the whole of it, open and disbelieving, like a boy who’d been told the holidays were starting early.

“All right,” he said.

“Good. Who’s the trust?” said Cen, before Miles could ask it, and answered himself. “Anonymous. They’ve asked for no name on the door, no plaque, no announcement and no meeting. No say in the science. Standard reporting, independent review, the work stays yours and the university’s.” He shut the folder and kept his hand on it. “Which brings me to the other thing, and I’d rather you heard it from me.”

He took a single sheet out of his drawer.

It was a copy of a letter to the Vice-Chancellor, on stationery with a little embossed tree at the top, and it was signed Shen Ruolan. It was courteous. It expressed concern. It mentioned the student forum and the photograph after the winter gala and the department’s recent conflict-of-interest arrangements, and wondered, with regret, whether those arrangements had been sufficiently independent of the department itself. It noted that Dr. Wei was due before the appointments council in April. It asked whether the university might think it wiser to pause his review until the matter had been fully examined.

It didn’t accuse him of anything. It was cleverer than that.

Miles read it twice and put it down square on the desk.

“She knows I’m off the panel.”

“She knows.”

“She knows Ling Hao replaced me. That Yu Jie’s supervisor and examiners are all independent.”

“She isn’t saying the procedures don’t exist. She’s asking whether they’re enough. That’s a question nobody can ever finish answering, which is why people ask it.” Cen watched him. “The council will read your declaration and the recusal record. I’ll see to it. Does Yu Jie know?”

“Not yet. Please let me tell her.”

“That’s yours to decide.” Cen pushed the coffee back across the desk to him. “And Miles. Don’t make the mistake of thinking every move that woman makes is a bill you have to pay personally. The review is yours. The laboratory is yours. Don’t let them get mixed up.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The basement smelt of dust and old rubber.

Its last occupants had moved to a newer building three years ago and left behind empty benches, dead equipment and a row of labels for instruments that no longer existed. The ceiling was high. There was a drainage channel along the floor, a water main in the corner, and a line of narrow windows near the top of the far wall where the March light came in grey and thin.

Miles stood in the middle of it on Tuesday morning with his hands in his coat pockets and saw the tank as clearly as if it had been there. The camera gantry above it. A darkened bay for the lasers. A desk by the door for whoever sat up at three in the morning watching the data, which would be him.

He wrote 4 m in his notebook and drew a circle and rubbed it out and drew it again, a little further from the wall.

He hadn’t told her yet. He’d meant to ring her the minute he left Cen’s office, and then he’d stood in the corridor with the letter folded in his pocket and found he couldn’t tell her the first thing without the second, and he didn’t want to put the second in her hands by phone.

So he’d sent her a message instead.

Miles: Can I see you tonight? I’ve got news. Most of it good.

Not Stuck: Most of it?

Miles: Tonight.

Not Stuck: Second lamp. Seven. Bring the good part first.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were two lamps on the old path between the physics building and the gardens, iron ones, set far enough apart that a person walking from one to the other seemed for a few steps to belong to neither. Yu Jie had told him once it made people look as if they were walking between two worlds. He’d pointed out that it was just the inverse square law. She’d told him he was hopeless.
