She was under the second lamp when he got there, in a cream coat with her hair down, and the moment she saw his face she said, “Oh. It’s good, isn’t it.”

He told her the good part first.

He meant to be brief. He wasn’t. He told her about the tank and the vortex and the horizon, about waves going in and coming out stronger, about the two doctoral places and who he might ask, about the first experiment and the second, and he found halfway through that he’d taken his hands out of his pockets to draw the flow in the air between them, and he didn’t put them back. She didn’t interrupt once. She stood with her chin tucked into her collar and watched him, and her eyes went bright, and at one point she pressed her lips together hard as if she were trying not to say something.

“Your kingdom,” she said when he finally stopped.

“It’s a basement.”

“Your Majesty’s basement. With a moat.”

He laughed out loud, there on the path, and she looked at him as though he’d handed her something.

Then she put both hands flat on his chest and stood on her toes and kissed him.

It was a long one. Her fingers curled into his coat. He put his hand at the small of her back, under her hair, and felt her smile against his mouth and then stop smiling and kiss him harder, the way she did when she’d decided something. When she drew back her cheeks were pink in the lamplight.

“Tell me Wednesday,” she said.

“Tell you what?”

“Wednesdays. In the glass room. Every week, tell me all of it. What went wrong with the pumps. Which students you like. What the water did.” She tucked her hair behind her ear. “Even if it takes the whole hour.”

“It will take the whole hour.”

“Especially then.”

He should have told her the second thing then. He had it ready. But she had her forehead against his collar and she was laughing at something about moats, and he thought: tomorrow. In the glass room. Properly, sitting down, with tea. One more evening of this.

He’d think about that choice a great deal over the next fortnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve been smiling at your monitor for eleven minutes,” said Ling Hao from the doorway of 412 on Wednesday morning.

“I’m reading pump specifications.”

“You’re smiling at a pump.”

“It has a variable flow rate.”

“I’m going to tell my wife you’ve left me for a pump.” Ling Hao came in and took a biscuit out of the tin without asking, as he had for nine years. He looked at the green folder by Miles’s elbow. “Anonymous, still?”

“Still.”

“Four million’s a lot of anonymity.”

“The university did its due diligence. I’m not going to go poking at a gift.”

Ling Hao ate the biscuit, looking out of the window at the library wing across the square, where the Shen Foundation’s little tree was carved over the door.

“Her grandmother was a chemist,” he said. “Did you know that? Shen Lihua. The library wing was her. There’s a separate trust in her name for science and education, outside the main family foundation. Zeng Bo applied to it for a fellowship once. It funds lab work and nothing else.” He finished the biscuit. “And in January you showed Yu Jie your old proposal, the one with the tank in the margin, and told her it would never happen. You told me so yourself the next morning. You were very pleased she’d asked.”

Miles had stopped smiling.

“That doesn’t prove anything.”

“No. I’m not saying it does.” Ling Hao brushed the crumbs off his jumper. “I’m saying you’ve already thought it. You thought it on Monday and put it in a drawer. Don’t take it out and decide what it means on your own. Ask her.” He went to the door and stopped. “Ask her, Miles. That’s all. Don’t do the other thing you do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to the glass room at half past five with his jasmine tea in a paper cup and a coffee for herself.

The second floor was empty by then. The consultation room had glass on three sides, so that anyone walking down the corridor could see in, which was why they’d chosen it in February, and nobody was walking down the corridor. She put the tea in front of him and sat down and pulled her chair in.

“Right,” she said. “Tell me about the pumps.”

He didn’t drink the tea. She saw that.

“Do you know anything about the trust that funded the laboratory?”

There was a pause. It lasted perhaps half a second. A year ago he wouldn’t have seen it. He’d spent six months learning her face.

“Ling Hao thinks it’s my grandmother’s,” she said.

“Is it?”

She put the coffee down. “Yes.”

The glass room went quiet. Down in the square somebody was chaining up a bicycle.

“It’s not the family foundation,” she said, fast and low. “It’s not my mother’s. My grandmother left part of it for me to direct when I turned twenty-one. It’s for exactly this. Laboratories. Equipment. People who need years to ask a question properly. I told the trustees about us, all of it, before they voted. I didn’t vote. They’re independent, they read your papers, they read the proposal, they said yes on their own.”

“When?”

“January.” She looked at him. “After you showed me the drawing.”

He got up. He went to the glass wall and stood with his back to her, looking at the dark corridor and his own reflection in it.

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I knew you’d refuse.”

“Yes. I would have.”

“That’s why.”

He turned round. “Your mother wrote to the Vice-Chancellor last week. She’s asked them to pause my review in April.”

The colour went out of her face. “What?”

“Cen showed me on Monday.”

“You’ve known since Monday?”

“I meant to tell you last night. I wanted—“ He stopped. He’d wanted one more evening. It sounded worse aloud than it had under the lamp. “It doesn’t matter. Do you understand what this looks like now? A student from a donor family funds the private laboratory of the man she’s involved with, anonymously, a month after the forum, a month before his review. The trustees will be asked whether they were independent. The council will be asked whether I knew. Your mother won’t even have to say anything. She’ll just have to forward the deed.”

“It isn’t like that.”

“It doesn’t matter what it’s like. It matters what it looks like.”

“That’s my mother’s sentence,” said Yu Jie. “Word for word.”

He heard it. He should have stopped there. He was tired, and frightened in a way he hadn’t let himself feel since Monday, and for two whole days he’d been happier than he could remember being, and every bit of that happiness had turned out to be something she’d arranged.

“So you bought me,” he said.

She went white.

He looked away, at the corridor, and said the rest of it to the glass. “I didn’t think you were like them.”

He knew as he said it. He would have given a great deal, then and afterwards, to put those words back.

Yu Jie stood up.

“Like who?” Her voice was quite steady. “Like my mother? Like the people who think money decides what somebody should become?”

“Yu Jie—“

“I didn’t buy you. I didn’t buy your work. You did the work. You did it years ago, you drew it in a notebook and put it away because nobody would pay for it, and I watched you look at it in January like a man looking at a photograph of somebody who’d died.” She had her hands in fists at her sides. “You wrote a letter at four in the morning and took yourself off my panel. You didn’t ask me first. You decided what was right for me and you did it and you took the consequences. I did exactly the same thing.”

“It isn’t the same.”

“Why not?”

“Because I was giving up power over you. You’ve just given yourself some over me.”

That landed. He saw it land. She stood still in the middle of the glass room.

“Is that what you think?”

“I think you wanted to give me something so badly that you decided I didn’t need to know.”

She opened her mouth and shut it again. He watched her recognise it. It was what she’d said to him in February, in this room, about the letter.

“I wanted you to be happy,” she said. “I wanted to see you in that basement. I wanted you to have five years to build something nobody could take off you. I did it because I love you.” Her voice cracked on it, finally. “I thought that was allowed.”

He took a step towards her.

“Don’t,” she said.

He stopped.

She picked up her bag. She was not crying. She’d gone past it into something quieter and much worse.

“I’ll tell the trustees and the university everything they want,” she said. “I know the process matters. I know you’re right that I should have told you. But don’t you ever tell me again that I’m like them. You don’t know what it’s like when somebody decides what your whole life should be and calls it love. I do.”

She went to the glass door and opened it.

He let her. Not because he wanted her to go. Because if he stood in front of that door now, he’d be making one more decision for her, and he’d just been told, rightly, that he had no business making those.

“I hope you get your laboratory,” she said from the corridor. “I hope you build every single thing you wanted.”

Then she was gone, and the lights in the corridor clicked off one by one behind her on their timers.

There were two cups on the table. His jasmine tea, which she’d queued for at the café by the east gate because the machine upstairs did it wrong. Her coffee, barely touched. Between them lay the floor plan of the basement, and in the middle of the floor plan a circle four metres across, drawn in blue, with nothing in it.

chapters.title: He Finds the Name
chapters.desc: A purpose clause in a trust deed, initialled S.Y.J. Then a diplomat in a perfect suit comes to Thursday office hours with no physics question at all.
chapters.epigraph: “Start by listening. You’re quite good at it when you remember.”
chapters.content:
At twenty-six minutes past one on Thursday morning, Miles gave up on sleep.

He’d turned the lamp off twice and on twice. He’d turned the pillow over. He’d put his phone face down on the floor and then picked it up again because he’d thought of something to look up, and then he hadn’t been able to remember what it was. In the end he got up and went through to the kitchen and sat at the table with the folded cardboard under one leg and a cup of tea he didn’t drink.

He took a sheet of graph paper out of the drawer and wrote on it, in capitals:

I AM AN IDIOT.

He looked at it. Then he drew two axes under it out of pure habit, and labelled one time and the other judgement, and stared at them, and crossed both labels out. It wasn’t that kind of problem. He knew exactly what he’d done. He’d been handed the one thing he’d wanted for ten years and been so frightened of how it looked that he’d turned round and put the fear into the hands of the person who’d given it to him. He hadn’t asked how the trust worked. He hadn’t asked what her grandmother had meant it for. He had looked at the money and seen her mother’s face.

Underneath, he wrote:

AND I HURT HER.

Their messages were still open on his phone. The last thing she’d sent, on Tuesday night, before the lamp, was a photograph of a half-eaten bowl of noodles and one word.

Not Stuck: Evidence.

He’d laughed at it. He typed I’m sorry and looked at it for a minute and deleted it. An apology at half past one in the morning from a man who didn’t yet understand what he was apologising for was just another way of asking her to make him feel better.

At three he was still awake. At four the birds started.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Ruan was already in Cen’s office when he got there at twenty to nine, standing by the window with a fat folder under her arm and the smell of her first cigarette still in her cardigan.

“Sit down,” said Cen. “There’s something you should read.”

“The university completed its due diligence before it accepted the award,” said Ruan, and put the folder on the desk open at a page she’d marked with a bus ticket. “Source of funds, governance, approval process. It’s in order. All of it. The trustees minuted her declaration of interest in January and she left the room for the vote.” She tapped the page. “That’s not what I want you to see. Read the purpose clause.”

It was a trust deed, some years old, drawn up for a woman called Shen Lihua, for the support of education and science. The opening clauses were the usual dense legal stuff. Then there was a paragraph that wasn’t.

The trust shall support scientific inquiry that approaches difficult questions through observation, experiment and the patient construction of knowledge. It shall give researchers room to ask questions without any obligation to produce convenient answers for any donor, family, institution or private interest. No donor, beneficiary or member of the founder’s family may direct the conclusions, recruitment, publication or ownership of any work it funds.

In the margin, beside the amendment that had added it, were three initials in purple ink.

S.Y.J.

“She wrote that last spring,” said Ruan. “A year before your laboratory was anybody’s idea. The trustees adopted it in May. She didn’t write a rule to get you funded, Miles. She wrote a rule so that her own family could never buy anybody with that money. And then she put you forward under it.”

Miles read the clause again. Room to ask questions. He’d sat in the glass room and heard every fact she’d given him and understood none of it.

“I knew Lihua,” said Ruan.

He looked up.

“Not well. When I was a young lecturer she sat on the faculty’s science board for a few years, the only donor on it who’d actually read the papers. She was her husband’s wife at every dinner and a chemist the rest of the time. One spring she asked me up the hill road to see the old glasshouse at the back of the house. She’d made it into a laboratory. A proper bench, a balance in a glass case, a fume cupboard her husband had paid somebody a ridiculous sum to put in.” Ruan took off her half-moon glasses and let them hang on their chain. “Years later she took me out to see it again. There was a child’s chemistry set on the bench. Six bottles and a spirit lamp. It was for Yu Jie. She was five. Lihua let her grow copper sulphate crystals on a string, blue as anything, and Yu Jie sat and watched one for a whole afternoon because she couldn’t believe something you couldn’t see was building itself in front of her.”

Miles didn’t say anything.

“She took a kitchen timer apart once, to find out why it ticked. Couldn’t put it back together. Ruolan was furious. Lihua gave her a screwdriver and told her to try again.” Ruan put her glasses back on. “The thing she used to say to that child was that science isn’t having the answer ready. It’s being honest enough to find out you were wrong.”

The words went into him like a splinter.

“She wanted the girl to have one thing that was hers,” said Ruan. “Not the name. Not the company. Something she could use to choose. And Yu Jie used it on you.” She looked straight at him. “And you were cruel to her.”

“I know.”

“No, I don’t think you do yet.” Her voice didn’t go up. That was worse. “You’ve spent your whole working life insisting that an idea should be judged on its own merits and not on whose it is. You’ve been right about that. You’ve been tiresome about it. And the first time that girl did something you didn’t understand, you decided what it meant before you’d asked her a single question. You looked at her and saw exactly what her mother sees. A surname and a bank account.”

Miles sat with his hands on the folder and let it land.

“The award stands,” said Cen, after a moment. “The council will have the trustees’ minutes. Your review goes ahead on the ninth of April in the ordinary way. Shen Ruolan’s letter will be answered separately, by people above my head.” He folded his hands. “What you do about Yu Jie isn’t an administrative matter.”

“No.”

“So don’t try to fix it with another declaration.”

Ruan picked up her folder. At the door she said, without turning round, “Start by listening. You’re quite good at it when you remember.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday office hours were still in 412, at two, with the door wedged open on its rubber stop. Nobody had come to one for weeks. At four minutes past two, somebody did.

Miles saw the suit before he saw the man. Navy, beautifully cut, a white shirt and a tie with a pattern so discreet you had to be standing quite close to be sure it was there. Yan Zhiyuan stood in the doorway as if he’d been sent round by a tailor to show what could be done.

“Dr. Wei. May I?”

“Are you taking physics, Mr. Yan?”

“I’m not.”

“Then your question’s probably outside the syllabus.”

“Almost certainly.” Yan came in and sat down and laid a slim grey folder on the desk between them. “It’s about her mother. I don’t think she’s going to stop at a letter.”

He opened the folder. Copies, all of it: the letter to the Vice-Chancellor, and another, to a member of the university council Miles had met once at a dinner, and a page of handwritten notes in a hand Miles didn’t know.

“My mother’s,” said Yan. “From a lunch on Sunday with Mrs. Shen. My mother writes everything down. It’s how my father has survived thirty years in government.” He turned the page round. “Mrs. Shen’s view is that if the forum and the funding can be made to look bad enough before April, the council will find it simpler not to make you permanent, and you’ll go somewhere else. And Yu Jie, without you in the building, will come to her senses by June.”

Miles read it twice. It was set out calmly, in somebody else’s mother’s handwriting. His job. His laboratory. Her.

“Why are you showing me this?”

“Because I don’t agree with it.” Yan sat back. “And because I was supposed to be the senses she came to.”

Miles looked at him.

“At the gala,” said Yan, “I asked her to pretend we were courting. Slowly, very properly. A few dinners, a photograph or two, and in the spring we’d decide we didn’t suit. It would have kept her mother busy and kept mine from asking questions.” He saw Miles’s face and stopped. “She hasn’t told you.”

“No.”

“She will have meant to.” Yan said it gently, and it still went in. “She made conditions. No engagement. No promises. Nothing that hurt anybody who didn’t deserve it. We had two dinners, in January, and talked about you for most of the second one. But her mother’s stopped hearing the word pretend. She’s started talking to mine about silk.”

There was a long silence in 412. Somewhere down the corridor a printer started up and stopped.

Miles had sat on a stone staircase three weeks ago and held her while she cried about an engagement in June, and had never once asked her whether there was any more to it. And she’d kept this back, too, for two months, because she’d decided it would only worry him. It was the same mistake from the other side. He could see that now, which was a strange kind of comfort, like finding out that the hole in the boat was on both ends.

“You’re not going to marry her,” he said.

“No.” Yan looked at his hands. “I told her there was somebody I couldn’t be seen with. I said she. It was easier, at a gala, with my father two tables away.” He lifted his head. “His name is Remy. He’s an interpreter. We met at a conference three years ago, when he corrected my pronunciation in front of forty delegates and a minister.”

“Were you wrong?”

“Appallingly.” Something moved across Yan’s face that had nothing diplomatic in it at all. “He still does it. He’ll be explaining a clause to me and I’ll realise I’ve stopped listening and I’m watching his hands. My family know there’s a colleague I see a great deal of. They don’t know what he is to me. I’ve been trying for a year to find a way to tell them that doesn’t end with my father walking out of a restaurant.”

“Is there one?”

“I doubt it.” Yan smiled slightly. “But I’m not going to marry somebody else to save myself the walk.”

Miles thought about a letter he’d written at four in the morning, and about the moment you stopped arranging your life around what other people would call it.

“She didn’t buy you,” said Yan. “If that’s what you said to her. And from her face on Wednesday night, I think it was.”

“You saw her?”

“She rang me from the bus. She wanted to know whether the trust’s terms would protect you if the council looked at them. That was her whole conversation. Not how she felt. Whether you’d be all right.” He gathered the copies into the grey folder. “She gave you a guarantee, Dr. Wei. That the work would have somewhere to happen, whatever her mother did, whatever happened in April. Five years in which nobody could take the basement off you. You can decide whether to accept it. But don’t confuse it with a price.”

He stood up and straightened a cuff that didn’t need it.

“I’ll leave these with you. Please don’t make her regret trying to be generous. She’s had a great deal of practice at regret already, for twenty-two.”

He went out. The rubber stop held the door exactly where it had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past four Ling Hao came in for a biscuit and found the bin full of small yellow squares.

He looked at the bin. Then at Miles, who was writing on another one.

“How many?”

“I don’t know.”

Ling Hao fished them out and laid them on the desk in a row, like a man doing patience. I’m sorry. I was wrong. I was wrong to assume. I should have trusted. I should have asked before I. Yu Jie, I. Yu Jie. A tidy little diagram of a vortex, for some reason, crossed out. There were eleven.

“You’re trying to write a paper,” said Ling Hao.

“I’m trying not to make it about me.”

“Then stop trying to make it perfect.” He pushed the scraps into a heap. “Don’t explain why you did it. Don’t tell her what you’ve learnt from the trust deed, she wrote the trust deed. Don’t list your intentions. You hurt her. Tell her you know how. And then let her talk.”

“She deserves better than a sticky note.”

“Probably. But she’s spent four months writing you terrible jokes on pink paper. That’s how you two talk. Don’t use it instead of a conversation. Use it to ask for one.”

Miles took one more square off the pad.

I called your gift a price. I decided what it meant before I asked you, and that was cruel, and I’m sorry. I’d like to listen, if you’ll let me.

He read it. Then he looked at Ling Hao.

“No,” said Ling Hao, before he could ask. “No note’s enough. You’ll have to say it to her face. But it’ll get you as far as the door.”

Miles folded it once and put it in his breast pocket, where the purple pen had ridden all night at the gala. He picked up his coat.

“Shall I throw these away?” said Ling Hao, looking at the heap.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Evidence,” said Miles, “that I can be an idiot eleven different ways,” and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wasn’t in the library. She wasn’t in the glass room, or the café by the east gate, or the reading room on the third floor where she sometimes hid when Tao Tao had friends over. Outside Professor Ruan’s office a first-year he half recognised told him she’d gone about twenty minutes ago, with her bag, towards the bus.

He took out his phone.

Miles: Are you still on campus?

He waited. Nothing came. He typed I need to talk to you, and looked at the word need and deleted the whole thing. He wasn’t going to turn this into one more thing she had to manage for him.

The sky over the sports hall had gone the colour of wet slate. A wind had come up off the harbour, and the first drops were hitting the windows of the stairwell sideways.

He thought of her on the museum stairs three weeks ago, with her face pressed into his coat, while he told her she was a physicist and not a jewel. And then he thought of himself in the glass room, saying you bought me, as if her one free choice in twenty-two years had come with a receipt.

He knew where she lived. He’d stopped a block short of her door for five months so that nobody would see him walk her home.

He went down the back stairs and out into the rain, and he didn’t stop a block early.

chapters.title: Their First Real Fight
chapters.desc: An intercom by a blue door, in the rain. “You bought me a lab.” “I bought you time.” Both of them are right. That’s the problem.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t buy you a lab. I bought you time.”
chapters.content:
By seven the rain had turned into the kind that makes a city look unfinished. The streetlamps ran. Cars went past with their headlights smeared across the road, and the plane trees along the pavement bent and dripped and bent again.

Miles had walked the whole way. He’d watched the rain gather on his office window for an hour that afternoon, and he’d known perfectly well what it was doing, and he hadn’t thought about an umbrella once. He stood now in front of the tall pale building where she lived, under its little steel awning, in front of a pair of blue glass doors with a doorman’s desk lit up behind them, and the water ran off his hair and down inside his collar.

He’d rehearsed it all the way over the hill and thrown every version away, because every version started with because.

The doorman, a small man in a brown cardigan, came to the glass and opened it a hand’s width. Miles took the folded yellow square out of his breast pocket and asked whether he’d be kind enough to take it up to Miss Shen on nine. The man looked at the note, and at him, and went to the lift without a word. He came back four minutes later with empty hands and a nod.

Miles pressed the button beside her flat number.

The intercom crackled.

“Yes?”

“It’s me.”

There was a pause.

“I know,” said Yu Jie. “Old Huang rang up. He says you look like a drowned heron.”

Behind the blue glass Old Huang gave him a look of mild professional sympathy and went back to his newspaper.

“Will you come down?”

“No.”

She didn’t say it angrily. That was what made it go through him.

“All right,” he said.

He put his forehead against the cold wall beside the panel, then took it away again, because she might have a camera up there and he wasn’t going to make her watch that.

“Why are you here, Miles?”

“Because I owe you an apology.”

“I’ve got it in my hand. Ling Hao rang Tao Tao to say there were eleven before it.”

“Ling Hao is a traitor.”

“He’s on my side.” A breath. “So you’ve apologised.”

“No. I’ve written that I’m sorry. I haven’t listened to you yet.” He kept his voice level. “Please let me say this much. Then I’ll do whatever you want.”

The rain drummed on the awning over his head. He imagined her standing at the little table by her front door with her hand on the receiver, in the big grey cardigan she wore for working, perhaps, with her hair tied up in a pencil. He didn’t know. He’d lost the right to assume things about her for a while. That was what he’d come to say.

“Go on,” she said.

“I was wrong. I saw the grant and then I saw your name behind it, and I thought about the council and your mother’s letter and what people would say, and I decided what you’d meant before I knew what you’d done. I made it smaller than it was. I called it a purchase because I was frightened of what it would mean to take something from you.” His voice had gone rough. He let it. “And I told you you were like them. After everything you’ve told me about that house. You’ve spent your whole life trying to make one thing that was yours and not your name’s, and when you did, I looked at it and saw a cheque.”

The intercom said nothing.

“I’m sorry, Yu Jie.”

There was a small sound through the speaker. Not quite a breath.

“You think I bought you a lab,” she said.

“I did think that.”

“I didn’t buy you a lab. I bought you time.” He heard her move, closer to the receiver. “Five years, Miles. Five years in which you don’t have to write an application every other month and sit in front of a committee being polite to people who think the tank’s a toy. Five years when nobody can ring you in October and say they’re terribly sorry but the pumps have to go. Do you know how many napkins you’ve drawn that tank on? I’ve got three in my bag. You draw it when you’re thinking and don’t notice.”

“I know you listen.”

“No. You know I listen when it suits you.” It came out hard and then softened at the edge, as if she’d heard herself. “I listened when you told me what you wanted and I listened when you told me what you were scared of. And I thought, for once in my life, I’ve got something that can actually help. Not a dinner. Not a name. Help.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you make me ashamed of it?”

He could have said a dozen true things. Every one of them would have been an excuse. So he told her the one underneath them.

“Because I was ashamed.”

The rain seemed to get louder.

“I’ve spent my whole life making sure I never owed anybody anything I couldn’t pay back,” he said. “I know how to make do. I know how to refuse things before they turn into favours. My parents are proud of that, and so am I, mostly. I didn’t know how to take something that size from you and still be sure where I stopped and where your kindness started.”

“Those aren’t the same thing.”

“I know that now.”

“Do you?” she said. “Because you keep treating my kindness as if it’s a threat.”

He opened his mouth to tell her it wasn’t her kindness he was afraid of, it was how much he wanted it. He shut it again. That was just his fear, wrapped up nicely so she’d have to hold it.

“You’re right,” he said.

There was a long silence.

“Are you going to give it back?” she said.

“I don’t think I can keep it.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“The university’s process has to be—“

“Don’t,” said Yu Jie, sharp and sudden through the crackle, and he stopped. “Don’t hide behind the university. This isn’t about the university. The trustees approved it. The research is independent, it’s in the deed, I wrote it into the deed, Ruan’s read it, Cen’s read it. You don’t get to decide the money’s wrong because taking it makes you uncomfortable.”

“I can’t keep your money, Yu Jie.”

“And I can’t make you take it.” Her voice was shaking now, though not with crying. “But it isn’t yours to decide what happens to it. Do you understand? That isn’t your choice. I made it. I went to the trustees and I left the room and I made sure nobody in my family could ever tell you what to find. I thought about all of it for two months. I’m not a child who’s bought her teacher an apple.”

He pressed his hand flat against the wet wall.

“I know you’re not.”

“Then please stop making me sorry I did it.”

She said that last part so low he nearly lost it in the rain.

“I don’t want you to regret anything.”

“I do, though,” she said. “I regret every minute I spent imagining you walking into that basement. I thought you’d be so happy. I was so stupid.”

“I was happy. I’ve never been happier than I was on Monday.”

“And then you found out it was me.”

He had nothing to say to that, because it was true, and it was the worst thing he’d ever done.

“Do you know what the worst part is?” she said. “I didn’t need you to thank me. I didn’t need you to say I was generous or wonderful or that I’d saved your career. I just wanted you to know why.”

“I know why now.”

“Now,” she said, and let the word sit there.

He could have asked her again to come down. He could have told her he loved her, which she knew, and which would only have been one more thing she had to answer. He looked at his ruined shoes and asked the only thing he hadn’t asked on Wednesday.

“What do you need from me?”

The question seemed to throw her. For a while there was only the rain and the hiss of the line.

“I need you not to come on Wednesdays,” she said. “For a while. I don’t want you waiting in the glass room with my tea. I don’t want to sit across from you and pretend we’re fine because it’s Wednesday and that’s what we do on Wednesdays.”

He made himself breathe.

“All right.”

“And don’t ask Ruan to check on me. Don’t ask Tao Tao how I am. Don’t walk past the café by the east gate four times a day pretending you need a sandwich.”

The corner of his mouth tried to move, and didn’t manage it.

“I won’t.”

“I mean it, Miles.”

“I know you do.”

He heard her let out a long breath.

“I don’t want to stop loving you,” she said. “I’m not going to. But I can’t keep being the one who makes everything easy for you while you make everything hard for me. Not this time.”

“I understand.”

“Good.”

The line clicked and went dead.

He stood under the awning for a minute longer. I’d like to listen, if you’ll let me, he’d written. She had let him speak. She hadn’t let him in. For tonight, that was the answer, and he’d asked for it.

A window opened somewhere above him.

“Dr. Wei!” Tao Tao was leaning out of the ninth floor with her hair in a towel. “Are you planning to drown? That’s not a rhetorical question, you look terrible.”

“I’m fine.”

“Of course you are. Men who stand outside in the rain in March are always fine.” She vanished.

A few minutes later the blue doors opened and Old Huang came out with a yellow umbrella with a cartoon duck printed on it. He held it out, and when Miles didn’t take it straight away he simply put it in his hand.

“Miss Tao brought it down,” he said. “She says don’t bring it back wet.”

“Thank you.”

“And this.” Old Huang took a square of yellow paper out of his cardigan pocket. “Miss Tao brought this as well. It’s from Miss Shen.” He looked at the umbrella, and the coat, and Miles’s face, and decided not to say whatever he’d been going to. “Go home before you catch something, sir.”

He went back inside.

It was his note. On the back, in purple, she’d written three words.

I heard you.

It wasn’t forgiveness. It wasn’t an invitation up. It wasn’t nothing.

He put it in the inside pocket of his coat, where it would stay dry, and opened the duck umbrella, and walked home under it in the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Yu Jie stood by the little table in the hall with her hand still on the receiver.

She’d stood there all the time he was talking, with his yellow note in her other hand. Halfway through she’d turned it over and written on the back of it against the wall, so hard the pen nearly went through. When the line went dead she’d held it out without a word, and Tao Tao, hovering in the doorway in her towel, had taken it and the duck umbrella and gone down in the lift.

She knew he was soaked. She knew he’d walked over the hill without an umbrella, and would deny being cold to anyone who asked. She also knew that if she’d gone down to him she’d have forgiven him in about four seconds, on the wet step, before she’d finished being hurt. Not because what he’d said was small. Because she loved him, and loving him made it terribly easy to reach for him and stop thinking.

Her phone buzzed.

Tao Tao: Did he get the umbrella

Yu Jie: Yes.

Tao Tao: Good. It’s my favourite.

Yu Jie: You have six umbrellas.

Tao Tao: I HAVE FIVE NOW

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh. Then another message came, from the other room, where Tao Tao was clearly lying on her bed with her face in a pillow.

Tao Tao: are you ok

She typed yes. Deleted it. Typed not really. Deleted that.

Yu Jie: I don’t know yet.

Tao Tao sent back a single heart, and nothing else, which was why she’d been her best friend since they were twelve.

The trust papers were on the dining table where she’d left them that afternoon, in a neat stack with her grandmother’s seal at the top. She sat down in front of them, took a clean sheet of paper and uncapped her pen.

Things to do, she wrote at the top.

It looked like a shopping list. It was far too small for what she was feeling. She crossed it out and wrote underneath:

Things I am going to decide for myself.

That was better.

1. The money. Find out exactly how it can be returned to the trust, and do it myself, in person, if anybody does it. Not him. Not Ma. Me.

2. Tell them no.

Her pen stopped there. Two letters. She could already hear her mother’s voice: the reasonable disappointment, the reminders about the family, the suggestion that she was overtired and emotional and would feel differently after a good night’s sleep. She pressed harder.

No to the Yans. No to going abroad. No to having my life planned for me in somebody else’s handwriting.

3. The thesis. Finish the revisions. No favours. Let Ruan and the panel do their jobs.

4. Decide what the trust is for, now that it’s mine to decide.

She looked at the seal at the top of the stack, the little tree. She thought of the glasshouse at the back of the house on the hill, long before it had been pulled down. A bench, a spirit lamp, six bottles. Her grandmother’s thin hand on her shoulder, and a drop of something clear going violet in a dish. Her grandmother hadn’t told her what was going to happen. She’d asked her what she saw.

Look first, she’d said. Don’t decide what happened before you’ve looked.

Yu Jie had looked. She’d made her decision. She wasn’t going to apologise for it. But she could decide what came next.

Her phone lit up again, and for one foolish second her heart leapt.

Ma: We need to discuss the engagement arrangements this weekend. The Yans are waiting for an answer.

She read it twice. Then she turned the phone face down on the table and added one more line to the list.

5. Stop letting people mistake my silence for yes.

She put down the pen. The rain went on against the window.

Somewhere on the other side of the hill, Miles was walking home under a duck. He’d be going over every sentence, trying to find the exact place where he should have said something different, as if there were one right answer and he’d only got the algebra wrong. She knew him. But this wasn’t a problem with one answer. She didn’t need him to understand the grant. He understood the grant better than anybody alive. She needed him to understand her, and she wasn’t ready to explain it again.

She took her phone back and opened his name.

White Rabbit.

She wanted to tell him to dry his hair. She wanted to ask whether he’d eaten. She wanted to tell him that the box of chalk he’d given her in the glass room in February was in her coat pocket right now, and had been every day since, and that she’d held it all the way through the intercom.

She locked the phone and put it down.

For once, she’d let the silence be hers.

chapters.title: Two Weeks of Not Speaking
chapters.desc: Wednesdays are empty. He keeps the door open anyway. Ling Hao eats for two. Somewhere in the basement, a water tank is waiting.
chapters.epigraph: “I trust it more than mine.”
chapters.content:
At eighteen minutes to nine on Wednesday the eleventh of March, Miles put two cups of jasmine tea on the table in the glass room.

He didn’t mean to. His hands did it, the way they found the light switch in the dark. Two scoops from the tin, the water just off the boil, the white mug for him and the blue one with the chip for her, set down across from each other so the handles pointed the same way. He’d done it every Wednesday since February. It was only when he sat down and looked at the empty chair that he remembered.

He moved her cup away from the edge of the table, where it would cool too fast, and opened his laptop.

The corridor was busy. Second-years went past with folders and looked in through the glass, and two of them came in with questions, and he answered both properly. He’d always been better at other people’s questions than his own.

At a quarter past ten Ling Hao came to the door and looked at the two cups.

“You’re still doing that?”

“There’s no rule against making two cups.”

“There’s no rule against eating two lunches either.” Ling Hao came in, picked up the blue cup and drank from it. He made a face. “That’s stewed.”

“She likes it strong.”

“She isn’t here, Wei.”

He put the cup down and sat on the edge of the table and asked about the laboratory, and Miles told him the tank was coming tomorrow, four metres, acrylic, a steel ring for the base, and the supplier had confirmed the dimensions twice. He said it all in the voice of a man reading out a train timetable.

“You’re allowed to be happy about it,” said Ling Hao.

“I am happy about it.”

“Your face is making a convincing case for the defence.” Ling Hao got up. “Eat something today. Food. Not coffee.”

“I know what food is.”

“Your history suggests otherwise.”

At eleven Miles poured the blue cup down the sink in the kitchen at the end of the corridor and rinsed it and put it back on the shelf. He didn’t make another.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night he tried to write her a letter.

He did it on paper because he couldn’t bear another blank document blinking at him. Yu Jie, he wrote, and stopped. He’d already apologised. He’d stood in the rain and said it through a speaker grille. Anything he wrote now would just be another way of asking her to answer him.

I’ve been thinking about what you said. That sounded like the opening of a referee’s report. He crossed it out.

I miss you. That was true, and it was the worst thing he could send, because it asked her to feel sorry for him when she’d asked for room. He crossed it out harder.

Then he wrote, smaller:

I always thought being independent meant refusing anything I couldn’t pay back. I don’t think that was ever quite right. I think I just got comfortable having very little to lose. You gave me something I’d wanted for ten years, and I behaved as if taking it would make me less myself. It didn’t occur to me until the rain that refusing it was also a way of telling you I didn’t trust your judgement. I do. I trust it more than mine.

He read it. Then he folded it once and put it, without an envelope, in the bottom drawer of his desk, under her pink notes, the cat in glasses and you’re my favourite boundary condition and all the rest.

He wasn’t going to send it. But the next time he opened the drawer, it would be there, and that would have to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tank came on Thursday morning at six minutes past nine, twenty minutes late, on a lorry that reversed down the service ramp behind the east wing three times. It came in eight curved panels of clear acrylic, each one taller than a man, and a ring of steel, and a driver who apologised three times and then explained at length that it was heavier than it looked.

Miles didn’t mind. He stood at the bottom of the ramp with Ling Hao, Cen and two technicians and watched the first panel come off on its straps, and the grey March light went through it and came out the other side bent.

It took all day. By four o’clock the ring was bolted down and the panels stood in a circle on it, clamped and sealed, and the thing was what it was meant to be: a great clear drum, four metres across and chest high, with a drain the size of a dinner plate at the bottom of it and nothing at all inside. The basement lights caught in its walls and broke up into pieces, the ceiling, the pipes, the technicians, his own face standing at the edge, all of it curved and stretched out of true.

At half past two Miles had crouched by the western side with the floor plan and said, “Three centimetres.”

The senior technician had looked at him. “Sorry?”

“The clearance on this side. It needs three more. Your measurement yesterday included the packing frame.”

The man had checked. There’d been a pause. “You’re right,” he’d said, and Ling Hao, leaning on a pillar, had told him not to bother arguing, Dr. Wei had been waiting for this tank since he was twenty-six.

Now Miles walked once round it, slowly, the whole way. He could see the water going round in it. The first wave coming in from the rim. The first run that didn’t work, and the second, and the night some student would stand where he was standing and say, That’s not what the model says, and be right. It was everything he’d drawn on napkins for ten years.

And the person who’d put it here wasn’t in the room.

“She’s going to want to see it,” said Ling Hao, beside him.

“Yes.”

“Don’t send her a photograph.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“And don’t ask me to send her one, either. I’m not a carrier pigeon.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday evening Professor Ruan came down the basement stairs with a lit cigarette, saw the fire notice on the door, swore, and put it out on the sole of her shoe.

“So this is the famous drum.”

“This is it.”

She walked halfway round it with her hands in her cardigan pockets. “Big.”

“That’s the idea.”

“You look terrible, Miles.”

“Thank you.”

“Are you sleeping?”

“Yes.”

She looked at him over her half-moon glasses until he said, “Some.”

“Good. Now you’ve stopped lying, I’ll tell you something. She asked you not to ask me about her, I expect. You haven’t. So this doesn’t count.” Ruan sat on an upturned crate, which no one else in the department would have dared. “She’s working fourteen-hour days. She’s in my outer office before eight. I came back for my reading glasses last night at a quarter past nine and she was still there. She’s sleeping on my sofa.”

He’d been holding a pump manual. He put it down.

“She’s what?”

“Three nights this week. She keeps her coat folded at one end and a cushion behind my filing cabinet that she thinks I haven’t seen. She goes home to change and shower and comes straight back.” Ruan pulled a thread off her cuff. “She’s got a thesis to finish in eight weeks, a family arranging her wedding over her head, a trust that’s suddenly hers to run, and a mother who treats every word she says as an opening offer. And she’s trying very hard not to come and find you. That takes a lot of hours. You fill them up with work, or you go and knock on someone’s door.”

“She shouldn’t be doing it alone.”

“Then don’t make it about you,” said Ruan sharply. “There’s something else. Yesterday I heard her on the telephone in the corridor, booking a meeting with her father. At his office. Friday next, at four. Without her mother. She was very clear about that.”

Miles looked at the tank.

In five months of stories Yu Jie had told him very little about her father. A tall man, always on the phone to other time zones. A man who didn’t contradict his wife at dinner.

“About the engagement?”

“She didn’t say. I didn’t ask. She’s not meeting him because you two had a fight. She’s meeting him because she’s got something to say to her family, and she’s going to say it. Let her.” Ruan got up and dusted off the back of her skirt. “Do you have a blanket?”

“What?”

“At the staff flats. A proper one. My sofa’s horsehair and older than you are, and my heating’s been broken since Tuesday.”

He understood. “Yes.”

“Bring it tomorrow. Evening. I’ll be in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the only proper blanket he owned, thick and grey, which Wei Lan had bought him two winters ago after she’d come round and found him sleeping under a thin duvet and his own overcoat. She’d told him he lived like a student who’d been fined. He carried it across the campus on Sunday at twenty past seven, folded over his arm like a waiter’s cloth.

Ruan opened the door before he knocked.

The sofa was in the little inner room, under the window: brown, narrow, its cushions humped. There was a pile of journals at one end, a paper cup on the floor, and over the arm a cream cardigan with a small cat embroidered at the cuff. He knew that cardigan. He’d buttoned it up for her in November.

Ruan took the blanket and shook it out and spread it over the cushions and tucked the end in, briskly, like a nurse.

“She’ll ask where it came from.”

“Tell her it’s yours.”

“It isn’t mine.”

“It’s on your sofa.”

Ruan looked at him. “No note?”

“No.”

“Good.” She held the door. As he went past her she said, “Miles. She isn’t the only one who’s allowed to be tired. Go home. Eat something that didn’t come out of the machine on the second floor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie found it at twenty-two minutes to eight on Monday morning.

She’d come in with two folders and a coffee she hadn’t drunk, in her coat, because the heating still wasn’t working and she’d spent all of Sunday at the outer desk with her sleeves pulled down over her hands. She went into the little room to drop her bag on the sofa, and stopped.

It was grey and thick and soft. There was a loose thread on one corner. She knew that thread. She’d pulled at it once, sitting on his floor in January with a hundred and twenty-six pages of thesis spread round her like a fort, and he’d taken her hand away and said it was Wei Lan’s, so she’d better not unravel it.

“Professor Ruan?”

Ruan came to the door with a file. “Morning.”

“Where did this come from?”

“It’s a blanket.”

“I can see it’s a blanket.”

“Then we’re making progress.” Ruan opened her file. “Somebody left it.”

“Who?”

“Somebody who owns a blanket.” Ruan didn’t look up. “Use it. That sofa’s uncomfortable enough without you getting pneumonia on it. I can’t examine you if you’re in hospital.”

“You’re not examining me.”

“I’m supervising you, which is worse.” She went back to her desk.

Yu Jie stood looking at the grey wool. Then she sat down on the sofa and put her face in it, just for a second, because nobody could see. It smelt of the soap he used and the cold air of his flat and, very faintly, of chalk.

She folded it carefully over the back of the sofa, so that it would be there that night. She didn’t ask again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday, Ling Hao made Miles walk to Bell Street for breakfast.

“Something with nutritional value,” he said. “Not a pastry you can eat with one hand while answering email. Go to the bakery. Tell my wife I sent you. She’ll make you sit down.”

Shu Mei made him sit down. She brought him two steamed buns and a glass of hot milk, as though he were nine, and stood over him until he’d eaten the first. She was a small square woman with flour to the elbows and a pencil behind her ear, and she had known him as long as she’d known Ling Hao, and she had never once in nine years told him anything she didn’t mean.

When he got up to pay she put a paper bag on the counter.

“That one’s yours.”

It said Dr. Wei on the side in purple ink, in capitals.

“Who left it?”

“A young woman. Half past seven, before we’d got the trays out. She stood outside till I opened, in the cold, like a fool.” Shu Mei wiped her hands on her apron. “She said to tell you to eat them before they go brown. She also said not to tell you anything else. So I haven’t.”

He opened the bag.

Inside was a small plastic box, and inside the box were three oranges, peeled and pulled apart into segments, with every scrap of white pith taken off, lined up like soldiers, the way she’d left them in his fridge in November when he’d had the flu and couldn’t keep anything else down. One segment had been split in half, because it was too big to sit flat with the others.

He knew the hands that had done it. He could see her doing it, at the dining table in the tall pale building, at midnight, with the skins piling up by her elbow and her face set like stone.

“Which way did she go?”

Shu Mei pointed up the hill, towards the university. Then she looked at him with her arms folded and said, “And you’re not going after her. I can see it on you. Sit down and finish your milk.”

He didn’t go after her. He didn’t ring. He took the box to the basement and put it beside his laptop on the bench next to the empty tank and ate the segments one by one over the course of the morning, slowly, as if they were medicine.

There were three oranges. He ate every piece.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday he made one cup of tea.

His hand went to the blue mug on the shelf, and he took it back, and made his own, and carried it to the glass room and sat down. Students came at seventeen minutes past nine and at twenty to ten. At half past ten Ling Hao put a sandwich in front of him and stood there till he’d eaten half of it.

The whiteboard was clean. There was a faint grey ghost on it where somebody’s old equation had been wiped off, and nothing else.

“You going to leave it blank all day?” said Ling Hao.

“I’ve nothing to put on it.”

“That’s never once been true.” Ling Hao held out a marker. Miles didn’t take it. Ling Hao put it down on the ledge and went away.

At sixteen minutes past twelve Miles got up and took the cap off the marker.

He thought about writing something useful. An equation, a diagram, something that belonged in a consultation room. Instead he wrote two words, in plain capitals, and stood back.

STILL HERE.

It wasn’t an apology. It didn’t ask her to come back. It didn’t ask her anything. It was only true.

He wiped it off with the side of his hand. He looked at the clean board. Then he wrote it again, and left it, and went down to the basement for the rest of the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody rubbed it out. The cleaners didn’t, and the students who used the room on Wednesday afternoon didn’t, and on Thursday morning at five past eight, when Yu Jie came along the second-floor corridor carrying a signed form for the faculty office, it was still there.

She hadn’t meant to come that way. It was only the shortest route.

The glass room was empty. A table, two chairs, a white mug on the windowsill. And on the board, in his narrow, careful capitals, pressed so hard into the marker that the strokes were almost black:

STILL HERE.

She stopped. She didn’t go in. She didn’t rub it out. She didn’t take out her phone. She held her folder against her chest and stood there until her eyes stung, and then she went to the faculty office and handed in her form.

That night she sat on Ruan’s sofa with the grey blanket over her knees and her laptop open on a pile of journals. The radiator, which a man had kicked at four o’clock, was finally ticking. She’d been reading the same paragraph about corner states for twelve minutes.

She shut the laptop and opened her messages. There was nothing new from him. There hadn’t been for two weeks. She scrolled up past the noodles to the long bright run of January.

I saw the board, she typed. She looked at it and deleted it.

Were the oranges all right? Deleted.

She put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa and pulled the blanket up to her chin. Tomorrow at four she was going to the fortieth floor to see her father, on her own, with a folder, and she wasn’t going to tell anybody until it was done.

Downstairs, in the dark basement, the tank stood empty, waiting for its water. On the second floor, behind the glass, two words waited on the board.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Gives the Money Back
chapters.desc: The fortieth floor of the Shen Building, alone, with four pens in her hair. Her father has never once asked her about an equation. Today, he asks.
chapters.epigraph: “Still angry. Still peeling oranges.”
chapters.content:
The fortieth floor of the Shen Building had a different kind of silence from a library’s. In a library, silence meant people were thinking. Up here it meant people were waiting. The carpet ate footsteps. The glass kept the city at a polite distance, the harbour flat and silver far below, the cranes on the container docks moving like slow insects. Even the receptionists spoke as if each sentence had been costed.

Yu Jie came out of the lift at four minutes to four on Friday the twentieth of March in a cream blouse and dark trousers and the small gold earrings her grandmother had given her at eighteen. She’d put her hair up that morning while she read, without thinking, and it was held there now by four pens. A black fountain pen, two blue biros, and her purple cat with its little gold crown, the one that had spent a whole autumn in a drawer in office 412 and come back to her on the night of the gala.

The receptionist looked at the pens. Yu Jie smiled at her the way she’d smiled at nine men in a row in December.

“I’ve an appointment with my father. Four o’clock.”

“Of course, Miss Shen. He’s expecting you.”

His office was at the end of the corridor behind two sets of glass doors. He was standing at the window with his hands behind his back when she went in, tall and silver-haired, in a grey suit that had cost as much as a car, with his phone face down on the desk, which she’d never seen before in her life.

He turned round and looked at her hair.

“Four pens?”

“Three that work.”

“Which one doesn’t?”

“The black one.”

“Then why is it there?”

“It looks important.”

He considered that seriously, as he considered everything. “Your grandmother used to do that. Pencils behind her ears. A thermometer, once, at dinner. Your grandfather pretended not to see.” He gestured at the chair across the desk. “Sit down. Have you eaten?”

“Toast. And an egg.”

He nodded as though that were an acceptable report and poured her a glass of water from the sideboard and put it in front of her and sat. On the desk between them lay a thin folder and a single sheet of letter paper with the little tree at the top.

“I’ve known about the trust since January,” he said.

She’d been reaching for the water. She stopped.

“The trustees came to see me after the vote. As a courtesy, they said. They wanted the family to understand it had no say.” He folded his hands on the blotter. “I knew about your amendment last spring. I knew you’d put Dr. Wei’s work forward and stepped out of the room. I didn’t tell your mother.”

“Why not?”

“Because she would have tried to stop you.” He looked at the window. “And because I wanted to see if you’d do it yourself. Without either of us telling you what to do.”

“That was a test.”

“Yes. I suppose it was.”

“That isn’t fair.”

“No,” said her father. “It wasn’t.”

She had not, in twenty-two years, heard him say that anything he’d done wasn’t fair. She sat back in the chair and found she didn’t know what to do with her hands.

“Ma’s written to the university,” she said. “Twice. She’s trying to stop his review.”

“I know.”

“She’s using the forum and the grant to make him look bought.”

“I know that too.”

“Does she know you know?”

“Not yet.”

Yu Jie laughed, once, without any amusement in it. “Everybody in this family knows everything except the people who’re meant to be talking to each other.”

He didn’t argue. He opened the thin folder and took out a sheet of handwriting, old, in faded blue ink, and turned it round so that she could see it. It was her grandmother’s hand. She’d have known it anywhere.

“She wrote me this the winter before she died. I’ve had it in my desk ten years.” He didn’t read it out. He put two fingers on one line. “She says you’ll grow up wanting to take apart whatever we give you. Even if it works perfectly well. Because you’ll want to know how it works. She says we’re not to mistake that for disobedience.” His fingers moved down. “And she says that if you ever choose a life we don’t understand, we’re to try to understand it before we try to stop it.”

Yu Jie looked at the faded ink until it went blurry.

“Did you?”

He was quiet for a while.

“Not enough,” he said.

Out of the window a helicopter crossed the harbour, tiny, and went behind a tower.

“When I was nineteen,” said her father, “I wanted to build bridges.”

She stared at him.

“Not buildings. Not companies. Bridges. I did two years of civil engineering before your grandfather needed me. I liked load calculations. I liked the idea that you could work out the weight, and the wind, and what steel does when it’s cold, and build something that would carry people over water long after you’d gone home.” He looked down at the blotter. “I came into the company. I was good at it. I became extremely good at it. I always thought there’d be time to go back.”

“And there wasn’t.”

“There never is. That’s the thing nobody tells you at nineteen.” He looked up at her, and she saw something in his face she’d never once seen there. Regret, and all of it for himself. “I don’t want you to make my mistake. So. Tell me what you came to say.”

She took a breath. She’d written it out on a sheet of paper in Ruan’s office at two in the morning, and she didn’t need the paper.

“I want to close the foundation’s university fund,” she said. “The donor fund. The one that paid for the library wing and the gala and the plaque on the physics building. It’s the part Ma uses. She writes to the Vice-Chancellor on that paper, she sits on the committees, she promises things and takes them away, and everybody up there is a little bit afraid of her because of it. I don’t want our name to be something you can lean on people with. I want it closed, and everything left in it moved into Nai Nai’s trust, under her deed, where nobody in this family can ever tell a scientist what to find.”

He didn’t move.

“That’s a very large decision.”

“I know.”

“Your mother will be beside herself.”

“That’s the one I know best of all.”

“And the award to Dr. Wei? That’s already in the trust.”

“I’m giving it back to the trustees.” She’d decided that one at four in the morning, with the grey blanket round her shoulders. “I’ve written to ask them to hold it. Not cancel it. Hold it, until the council has decided about his post in April without it on the table. So nobody can ever say the money bought him his job. Then they can look at his proposal again from the beginning, on their own, without me, and decide whatever they decide.” She swallowed. “I’m not going to make another decision for him. I’ve just made one for me.”

Her father looked at her across the desk for a long moment. Then he pushed the folder towards her.

“Those are the papers to close the fund. I had them drawn up in February. The trustees have seen them. They need my signature and yours, as the family’s seat on the board.”

She stared at him. “In February?”

“I said I wanted to see if you’d do it.” He uncapped his own pen. “I didn’t say I wasn’t ready if you did.”

She read every page. He let her. It was legal language and transfer schedules and three clauses she had to read twice, and the sun moved down the glass while she did it. When she reached the signature page she pulled the black fountain pen out of her hair, and it was dry, of course, so she put it back and took out the purple cat instead.

Her father watched the little crown come out of her hair.

“That one works?”

“Always.”

She signed. Shen Yu Jie. Then the next page, and the next. By the end her wrist ached.

He gathered them up and squared them and put them in an envelope. Then he picked up the single sheet with the tree at the top and handed it to her. It was already signed.

It was a letter to the Vice-Chancellor, four short paragraphs. It said that Shen Ruolan had written to the university without his knowledge or authority. That the family’s past gifts gave it no right whatever to comment on any academic appointment, review or award. That he withdrew both letters in full, and apologised to the university, and to Dr. Wei, for the trouble they had caused.

She read it twice.

“You’re sending this?”

“It went by hand at three. That’s a copy.” He put his pen away. “I should have had this argument with your mother a long time ago. I’ll have it tonight.”

Something in her chest moved, like a door that had been stuck for years shifting a quarter of an inch in its frame.

“Is he the reason you’re doing this?” said her father. “Dr. Wei?”

“No,” she said at once. Then, more carefully: “He’s part of my life. A big part, if he’ll—“ She stopped. “But this is mine. I’d want Nai Nai’s money kept clean if I’d never met him.”

“Good,” said her father. “She’d have liked that answer.” He leaned back. “Yan Zhiyuan came to see me last Thursday.”

Her head came up.

“He was extremely polite. He sat where you’re sitting and told me he wouldn’t be marrying you, that he’d never meant to, and that your mother had mistaken his attending dinners for an agreement. He said there was somebody else. He didn’t say who.” Her father’s mouth moved slightly. “I gather you know.”

She did know, now. He’d told her two days after the rain, in the back of a teahouse near the ministry, in a low voice, with his tea going cold in both hands, and she’d cried, and he’d laughed at her for crying.

“I know,” she said. “It isn’t mine to tell.”

“No. I told him he should have said so sooner. He said he’d been trying to help you. A pretend courtship, I’m told.”

“It was meant to buy me time.”

Her father rubbed his forehead. “Your mother would have been delighted.”

“She was.”

He laughed. It was a short, low sound, and it surprised them both. She couldn’t remember the last time she’d heard it.

She stood up and picked up her bag. She’d got as far as the first set of glass doors when he said her name.

“Yu Jie.”

She turned round.

“Tell me about your equation.”

She stood there with her hand on the door.

“Your thesis,” he said. “You said something about stretched graphene at dinner once. I didn’t understand a word.”

He had never asked. Not when she’d chosen physics at seventeen. Not when she’d changed her topic in second year. Not on any of the nights she’d come home lit up with a result, or come home and gone straight to her room because a derivation had beaten her. He’d asked about her grades. Her timetable. Her responsibilities. Never the equation.

“Do you actually want to know?”

“Yes.”

She came back and sat down. For twenty-three minutes she told him about electrons in a sheet one atom thick, and what happens when you stretch the sheet, and how the strain makes the electrons behave as though there were a magnetic field where there isn’t one, and why the edges of the sheet matter, and the corners most of all. She drew him a hexagon on the back of a board agenda, and a triangle of hexagons, and a little spike of states at each corner like a lamp left on.

He asked what happened at the corners. She told him. He asked whether you could measure it. She told him about simulations, and a second paper, and Dr. Mao’s group in the north who had the right microscope.

He didn’t understand all of it. He didn’t pretend to. He asked questions, real ones, and a bad one, and laughed at himself for the bad one.

When she went down in the lift at a quarter to five, she had the hexagons folded small in her pocket, because he’d given them back to her and said she might need them, and for the first time in her life she hadn’t had to make her life sound simple before somebody would listen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to four that afternoon, while she was still on the bus, Professor Cen had come down the basement stairs and found Miles at a laptop on the bench beside the tank.

The pumps were in. A temporary control desk ran along the east wall, a nest of cables taped to the floor. The tank stood in the middle of it all, dry, catching the lights.

“Have you eaten?” said Cen.

“Ling Hao brought noodles.”

“Did you eat them?”

“Most of them.”

Cen nodded and held out a small envelope.

Miles knew the writing before he’d taken it. It was folded once inside. Five words, in purple.

Still angry. Still peeling oranges.

He didn’t smile straight away. Something round his eyes let go first. He held the paper by its edges, as if it might come apart.

“She left it in my pigeonhole first thing,” said Cen. “With instructions that it was to be delivered by hand and not before this afternoon. I’ve no idea why the afternoon.”

Miles thought he knew. She’d wanted him to have it while she was in a room on the fortieth floor. So that he’d know where she was without being told.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t make any decisions because of a note,” said Cen.

“I won’t.”

“And don’t make any because you’re afraid of what she’ll think of you.”

“I won’t do that either.”

“Good.” Cen looked at the dry tank for a while with his hands in the pockets of his camel coat. “Her father’s written to the Vice-Chancellor. A copy came down to me an hour ago. He’s withdrawn both of his wife’s letters. Entirely.” He turned to go. “And she’s asked her trustees to put your award on hold until after the council. She wrote to me as well. I think you should know that she did it for your sake and that she’d be furious if you thought she’d done it for her own.”

He went up the stairs.

Miles stood alone with the tank.

He read the note again. He could hear her in it: the small defiance, and the affection she hadn’t quite managed to put away, and her absolute refusal to let him off.

Then he opened the grant file and read the conditions again, all of them. The purpose clause. The independent trustees. The prohibition on any donor directing the work. He’d read them before and understood them. This time he read them without looking for a reason to say no, and found there wasn’t one. There never had been. The thing had been given freely and properly. His only objection to it had been himself.

And now it was on hold, because of him, and she’d done that too.

He closed the file and opened a new document, and typed a title at the top: Laboratory plan, years one to five, without the award.

He sat there till half past eight. What the department’s equipment budget could cover. What could be bought second-hand from the group that had moved out of the basement. Which cameras could wait. Which of the pumps could be hired by the month. The two doctoral places, which would have to become one, and then perhaps none. He wrote three funding applications in outline, and he hated every word, and he went on.

Ling Hao came down at seven and read the title over his shoulder.

“You’re going to pay for it yourself.”

“Some of it. The department will help. I’ll phase the rest. It’ll take longer.”

“You hate writing applications.”

“Yes.”

“Is this to prove something to her?”

“No.” Miles looked at the dry tank. “It’s because I want to keep it. Whatever the trustees decide. Whatever she decides. I want to keep it.”

Ling Hao looked at him. Then he pulled up a stool.

“Show me,” he said, “and if you put me down as a cost I’ll put you down as a fire hazard.”

At nine o’clock Yu Jie let herself into Ruan’s outer office, and Ruan, who was still there with a red pen and somebody else’s thesis, looked at her over her glasses and said, “Well?”

“He asked about my equation.”

Ruan put the pen down.

“Did he understand it?”

“No. He asked about the corners.”

“Then he understood more than most of my committee.” Ruan went back to her red pen. After a minute, without looking up, she said, “Miles brought the blanket. Sunday. Himself. I said it was mine.”

Yu Jie sat down on the sofa and pulled the grey wool over her knees.

“I know,” she said. “It’s got his thread on it.”

chapters.title: The Perfect Jewel Says No
chapters.desc: Sunday dinner at the museum, with the Yans, a seating plan for two hundred, and a sample of engagement silk. She puts down her chopsticks. Then the diplomat puts down his.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m a physicist. You can’t wear me.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past two on Sunday morning, Yu Jie gave up on sleep.

She’d been lying on her back for an hour looking at the ceiling. Her phone was face down on the bedside table. She’d turned it over twice in twenty minutes and found the same screen both times, because she’d asked him not to write, and he was the kind of man who did what you asked. That was the trouble with asking somebody who loved you for space. If they gave it to you, you missed them. If they didn’t, you had every right to be furious.

Eighteen days. She’d told herself she wouldn’t count, and she’d counted anyway, the way you count stairs in the dark.

She missed him in ridiculous ways. The way he read a whole problem before he answered, his eyes going down the page and one finger tapping once on the table. The way he said her name when she was about to do something stupid, as though he’d already worked out the consequences and was waiting politely for her to catch up. The white mug. The terrible jokes. Especially the jokes, which was deeply inconvenient, because she couldn’t think of a single one now without wanting to tell him she’d thought of it.

She turned the phone over and scrolled back through January. An argument about whether a cat could be treated as a classical system. A reminder to take an umbrella. A photograph of a lopsided oscillator on a whiteboard, captioned This is what happens when you let Ling Hao near a marker.

She smiled. Then she stopped.

I miss you, she typed. It would take less than a second.

She locked the phone. She wasn’t ready to talk to him. She was only tired of pretending that being angry meant she’d stopped loving him, and those weren’t the same thing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The private dining hall at the museum had been laid for two hundred.

She found that out at five past six, when she came in from the rain and saw the seating plan on an easel by the door: twenty-five round tables, a centrepiece of white orchids, and under the little tree crest, in a gilt frame, a mounted sample of ivory silk.

It was an invitation. Gold thread round the border. The two families’ names embroidered side by side, Shen and Yan, and a date in late June. Eight days after her graduation.

“You’ve seen it, then.”

Her mother was at her shoulder in deep blue and a rope of pearls, with her hair up so perfectly that it looked carved.

“It’s hand-stitched,” said Shen Ruolan. “The silk’s from the old mill in the hills. We need to confirm the design by Tuesday.”

“Then confirm it without me.”

Her mother’s smile didn’t move. “Don’t be difficult. Not tonight.”

“Is Ba coming?”

The smallest pause. “Your father has been called away.”

He hadn’t. Yu Jie knew where he’d been on Friday night, and what he’d said, because she’d heard the end of it on the phone from Yu Ming at midnight. Her mother had lost the university fund in an afternoon. Tonight was what she did with the loss: two hundred people and a square of silk, so that the next thing would be too public to undo.

The Yans came in. Zhiyuan was in a dark suit with his hair just so, and his face was pleasant and closed, and he looked at the easel and then at her, and his eyes said ah.

He came over and stood beside her in front of the silk.

“You look tired.”

“I haven’t slept.”

“Neither have I.” He studied the gold thread. “I haven’t agreed to any of this, in case you wondered.”

“Neither have I.”

“Then that’s something.”

Her mother came to take them to the top table. Zhiyuan offered her his arm. She looked at it, and at him, and he gave her the smallest nod, and she took it. Not because she was going to marry him. Because tonight, at least, they were going to walk in on the same side.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were speeches. The museum’s director. Her mother, thanking the Yans for a long and valued friendship. Mr. Yan, on the importance of families who understood each other. The silk sat on its little stand in the middle of the room, and every few minutes somebody looked from it to the top table and smiled at her as if she were part of the collection.

She ate almost nothing.

“You’re holding your chopsticks like a weapon,” said Zhiyuan, very low, without moving his lips.

She loosened her fingers. “Are you always this calm?”

“No. Only in public. In private I’m a wreck.”

Across the table her mother was explaining the arrangements to Mrs. Yan. The east gallery for the reception. The guest list closed by the end of the month. The silk only a sample, of course, but she thought the gold was right, didn’t Mrs. Yan think so?

Then she turned to Yu Jie. “Don’t you think so, darling?”

“No,” said Yu Jie.

The table went quiet.

“You’re overtired. We’ll talk about the design later.”

“I don’t mean the design.”

She put her chopsticks down. They made a small sound on the porcelain rest, louder than they should have.

“I’m not going to marry Zhiyuan.”

It was the startled quiet of people who’d been waiting for a different answer and had already started clapping in their heads.

“Not here,” said her mother, through her smile.

“Where, then? In front of the embroiderer?”

Beside her, Zhiyuan looked down at his plate. She thought he might be trying not to laugh.

“This has been agreed between two families.”

“Then somebody should have asked one of the two people in it.”

“Your father and I have spent your whole life protecting your future.”

“From what, Ma?”

“From mistakes you’re too young to see.”

“Physics?”

“Don’t be childish.”

She’d spent years at tables like this learning to make herself smaller. She knew how to smile at people she disliked and how to take compliments she hadn’t earned and how to answer every question about her future without giving anybody a reason to be offended. She’d been polished till there wasn’t a rough edge left on her. That was what a jewel was. A thing you could hold up to the light and admire and hand down and put wherever you liked.

She looked at the silk. Then at her mother.

“I’m a physicist,” she said. “You can’t wear me.”

Her mother’s face did nothing at all, which was worse than anything it could have done.

“I spend my days with things that don’t behave the way they’re supposed to,” said Yu Jie. “I ask questions. I test what everybody assumes. I change my mind when the evidence changes. The evidence hasn’t changed. I don’t want to marry him, and he doesn’t want to marry me.”

She turned. Zhiyuan was looking at her. Then he laid his own chopsticks down across the rest, very precisely, the way he’d sign a treaty.

“No,” he said. “I don’t.”

“Zhiyuan,” said his father.

“She’s right. I should have said so in October.” He looked across the table at his parents. “I went to the dinners because you asked me to. I was polite because I respect Mrs. Shen. Neither of those was a promise to marry anyone.”

“You told me you were willing to consider it,” said her mother, and her voice had gone very quiet.

“I was willing to meet her. And I’m glad I did.” He looked at his father. “There’s another reason. You’ve asked me for a year why I never bring anybody home.”

Yu Jie saw his hands. They lay flat on the tablecloth, perfectly still, except that his right thumb was pressing into the edge of his napkin so hard the nail had gone white. She’d never seen him frightened before.

“I love someone,” he said. “His name is Remy. He’s an interpreter, the best I’ve ever worked with, and he thinks I’m an idiot, and he’s right about that more often than I like.” He breathed in. “I’m not going to marry Yu Jie. I’m not going to marry anybody. I’m going to go on loving him, and I’d rather you knew.”

Nobody at the top table moved. At the next table somebody put a glass down very carefully.

Mr. Yan pushed his chair back. “Enough.”

“Ba—“

“You will not do this here.”

“You asked me to come here,” said Zhiyuan. “You asked me to sit beside a square of wedding silk I’d never seen and smile. I didn’t make this a spectacle. The easel did.”

His father stood. The chair legs scraped on the stone. He walked out between the round tables without looking back, and two hundred people looked carefully at their soup.

Zhiyuan didn’t follow him.

His mother hadn’t moved. She was looking at her son as if she were trying to find the boy she knew inside the man. Then she reached across the tablecloth and took his hand. Her fingers were shaking.

“Is he kind to you?” she said.

Zhiyuan stared at her.

“This Remy. Is he kind?”

“Yes,” he said. “Ma, he is.”

“Does he make you happy?”

He nodded. He couldn’t say it.

“Then I hope he knows how lucky he is.” She held on. “I don’t know how to explain this to your father yet. But I’m not going to pretend I didn’t hear it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother stood up.

“Yu Jie. Come with me.”

“No.”

“Now.”

“No, Ma.”

Shen Ruolan leaned down, one hand on the back of her chair, and spoke so low that only Yu Jie and Zhiyuan could hear it.

“Do you understand what you’ve done? You’ve humiliated two families in front of everyone who matters. You think you can walk out of this? The name, the protection, everything you’ve been given?” Her pearls swung forward and touched Yu Jie’s shoulder. “Then you’ll walk out with nothing. No allowance. No flat. No card. No more playing at being an ordinary student while this family pays for it.”

The old instinct rose up in Yu Jie, the one she’d had since she was six: lower your voice, say sorry, say you didn’t mean it, make it all right. She let it go past her like a car in the rain.

“All right,” she said.

Her mother stared at her. “You don’t know what that means.”

“I know what it means to make my own choices.”

“Your little laboratory. Your professor—“

“Don’t.” It was quiet, and it stopped her mother dead. “Don’t use him to frighten me.”
