“Do you think he’ll stay? A man like that? With all of this round his neck? Then ask yourself why he isn’t here.”

It went somewhere tender. She missed him so much that sometimes even hearing his name hurt. She could have told her mother everything, the rain, the intercom, the oranges, the eighteen days. That he wasn’t here because she’d asked him not to be. That he’d done exactly what she asked, every single day, which was more than anyone at this table had ever done.

“You don’t know anything about him,” she said, and stood, and picked up her bag.

Zhiyuan stood too. His mother let go of his hand, and nodded once, and said, “Ring me tomorrow.” He bent and kissed her cheek.

They walked out of the hall together through two hundred people pretending not to watch.

In the corridor by the cloakroom, under a portrait of somebody’s admiral, her father was standing in his overcoat with rain on his shoulders. He’d come in by the side door. She didn’t know how long he’d been there.

“Ba.”

He looked at her. Then at Zhiyuan, whom he thanked with a small bow, as if he’d just been handed a document that was in order.

“Your grandmother would have been very proud,” he said to her.

He said it simply, without ceremony, as though it were a fact about the weather. Her eyes stung.

“I was so scared.”

“Of course you were. It doesn’t make you wrong.” He put his hand on her shoulder, briefly, heavily, the way he’d done once when she was small and had fallen off a wall. “Go on. I’ll see to your mother.”

He went past her into the hall.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the museum gates the rain had stopped. The cars waited in a line along the kerb with their lights on, and the gold from the museum’s windows lay across the wet steps.

Zhiyuan stopped by the gate. So did she.

“Well,” she said.

“Well.”

“That was terrible.”

“It was the worst dinner of my life, and I’ve been to state banquets.” He let out a breath that shook. “My father will ring me tomorrow and tell me I’ve destroyed the family.”

“Mine might send me a spreadsheet.”

He laughed, helplessly, and put his hand over his eyes.

“Are you frightened?” she said.

“Yes.”

“So am I. Are you free?”

He thought about it, honestly, the way he did everything.

“Not entirely. But I’m not pretending any more.”

She stepped forward and put her arms round him. He went rigid for half a second, and then he held on. Nothing like the way Miles held her: two people who’d just walked out of a room where everybody else had decided what their lives would be.

“You’re going to be all right,” she said into his lapel.

“I hope so.”

“Remy loves you. Your mother loves you.”

His arms tightened. “And you?”

She thought about her mother’s pearls on her shoulder. About her father in the corridor with rain on his coat. About the grant on hold and the tank in the basement and a man she hadn’t spoken to for eighteen days.

“I think so,” she said.

A car slid up to the gate and washed them both in its headlights.

“Ring him,” she said. “Now. Don’t wait till you get home.”

“I will.” He opened the door and stopped. “Yu Jie. Don’t ever let her tell you being loved means doing as you’re told.”

The car pulled away. She watched the tail-lights until they turned the corner, and only then noticed that her hands were shaking. She put them in her coat pockets, and her fingers found the box of chalk.

Frightened and free. She’d never felt the two at once before. It was strange. It was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past eleven she sat on the edge of her bed in the flat that wouldn’t be hers much longer, with her shoes still on, and opened his name.

She still didn’t know what she wanted to say about the grant, or about how it had felt to have to defend what she’d done before he’d trust it. She was still angry. But she’d done something tonight, and she hadn’t done it for him, or because Zhiyuan had helped, or because her father had come in out of the rain. She’d done it because she didn’t want that life.

She typed and deleted and typed.

Yu Jie: I said no tonight.

She sent it before she could stop herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the east-wing basement Miles was still at the bench beside the dry tank, with the plan for five years without the award open on his laptop, staged and costed now down to the cable ties. His phone buzzed against the bench.

Not Stuck: I said no tonight.

He didn’t move for several seconds. Then he picked it up.

He didn’t ask what she meant. He could think of three things she might have said no to, and he’d learnt, the hard way, not to assume he knew all of them.

Miles: I’m glad you said what you wanted.

Miles: I hope you weren’t on your own.

The dots came. Went. Came.

Not Stuck: I wasn’t.

He wanted to ask who’d been with her. Whether she was safe. Whether she’d eaten. Whether her mother had been cruel, whether she was crying, whether she was cold. He wanted to tell her that he missed her so much his hand still went to her blue mug every Wednesday before he could stop it.

Miles: Good.

A minute went by.

Not Stuck: I miss the jasmine tea.

He looked at the white mug beside his laptop. It was empty. He touched the handle.

Miles: I’ll make it whenever you want.

Nothing came. He waited.

Not Stuck: Not yet.

He read the two words. His chest went tight, but he didn’t mistake them for a no. Yet was a word that pointed somewhere.

Miles: All right.

He put the phone down beside the mug. The silence between them hadn’t gone. But for the first time in eighteen days, it had a door in it.

chapters.title: Cut Off
chapters.desc: The bank card fails at the canteen. A letter from the family office. Seven days to leave. She packs one suitcase, and finds out what she owns.
chapters.epigraph: “May I hold you?”
chapters.content:
The first thing Yu Jie lost was lunch.

It went at seventeen minutes to one on Monday the twenty-third of March, at the noodle counter in the main canteen, between a bowl of beef noodles and a bottle of water. The woman behind the counter tapped her card on the reader and the reader gave a short, rude little beep.

“Sorry, love. Try again?”

She tried again. The same beep. She tried the other card, the one she never used, and that beeped too.

“Shall I cancel it?”

“Yes. Sorry. I’m so sorry.” She stepped out of the queue with her face burning and opened her bank’s app, which told her, politely, that access to her account had been restricted by its administrator. She’d never known it had one.

Then her phone buzzed.

Ma: I have instructed the family office to suspend your allowance and all associated accounts with immediate effect. You have chosen to reject the arrangements made for you. You must now take responsibility for the consequences of that choice.

She read it once and locked the phone. She found she wasn’t hungry any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past three, a letter came to the flat by courier, in an envelope with the family office’s seal on the back.

She opened it standing in the hall with her university card still on its lanyard round her neck. It was short and correct. The apartment she occupied was the property of the family and was being withdrawn from her use. She was to vacate it within seven calendar days, return all keys and access cards, and remove her personal belongings. The last paragraph explained, courteously, what would happen if she didn’t.

Seven days.

She looked round the flat. The sitting room was far too big. Her mother had chosen the sofa and the curtains, and a decorator had chosen the dining table, a woman who’d called her a delightful young lady and asked whether she preferred champagne or ivory. Even the floor lamp had turned up one day without anybody asking her. She’d lived here three years, and the place had never once felt like hers.

And it wasn’t only hers. Tao Tao had the other bedroom, and paid her share every month into an account Yu Jie had just discovered she didn’t control.

She took a photograph of the letter and sent it.

Tao Tao: WHAT

Tao Tao: Im coming home. Don’t touch anything. Don’t cry till I get there

She went into the kitchen and opened the fridge and looked into it. Milk, half a bag of greens, two eggs, a tub of congee. A little plastic box of orange segments with the pith off, which she’d done for herself at midnight out of pure habit because her hands had needed something to do.

She sat down at the decorator’s table and began to laugh.

It wasn’t a happy sound. She laughed because it was absurd. Because she’d said no to a wedding and been evicted for it, like something out of a very old novel. Because she’d spent twenty-two years being told she was the family’s jewel and had just found out that a jewel could be repossessed along with the cabinet.

Then she stopped laughing and put her forehead down on the cool champagne-or-ivory wood until she heard Tao Tao’s key in the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday morning Tao Tao came back from the supermarket with two bags of food, bought on her own card, and a new notebook.

“Right,” she said. “We’re making a list.”

“Of what?”

“Everything you own.”

Yu Jie looked round the flat. “That’ll take all day.”

“No. Everything you own. Not the sofa. Not the lamp. Nothing your mother bought, nothing she can say belongs to the family. Yours.” She put the notebook down on the table and held out a pen. “Go on.”

For the first few minutes Yu Jie didn’t write anything. Then she began.

1. My purple cat pen.

2. My laptop. (Bought with my research bursary.)

3. My physics books.

4. My thesis notebooks, all nine.

5. The clothes I bought myself. (About a third.)

6. Nai Nai’s gold earrings.

7. Nai Nai’s chemistry set. Six bottles and a spirit lamp.

8. The little screwdriver with the yellow handle.

9. My old problem sheets.

10. The shoebox of photographs.

11. A box of chalk.

12. A paper bag of White Rabbit sweets.

She stopped.

Tao Tao read it upside down. “That’s it?”

“That’s what’s mine.”

“What’s the screwdriver?”

“Nai Nai gave it to me when I was five. I took a kitchen timer apart with it.”

“Did you put it back together?”

“No.”

“Good,” said Tao Tao. “We don’t keep evidence.” She tapped number eleven. “Chalk?”

Yu Jie didn’t answer that. Tao Tao looked at her face and didn’t ask again. She tapped number twelve instead, and Yu Jie said, “Last September. He’d bought two bags, because he didn’t know which kind I liked, and they’re both the same kind,” and her voice did something on same, and Tao Tao reached over and took the pen out of her hand.

At the bottom of the page she wrote:

13. Yu Jie.

“You’d left yourself off,” she said.

They sat at the table without saying anything for a while. Then Tao Tao squeezed her hand.

“I’ll go to my aunt’s across the harbour,” she said. “She’s got one sofa and four cousins and a parrot, or I’d take you, I swear I would. But we’ll find you somewhere.” She blew her nose. “And if she thinks she can throw you out like an old sofa I’m going to send her an invoice for emotional damages.”

“You’re not a lawyer.”

“I’ll become one. Out of spite.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles had decided about the tea on Sunday night, after Not yet, sitting by the dry tank. If yet was a word that pointed somewhere, then there ought to be tea at the end of it. Not on the off chance. Every week. So that whenever yet arrived, it would already be poured.

So on Wednesday the twenty-fifth he made two cups, on purpose this time. His in the white mug and hers in the blue one with the chip by the handle, strong, the way she liked it, and he set hers across the table and sat down with his work.

At five past ten Miles had to go to the east wing to see a man about a pump. He shut his laptop and left. The blue mug stayed where it was.

At seventeen minutes past ten Yu Jie came down the second-floor corridor with her laptop under one arm and the purple cat holding up her hair, looking for Ruan, and she wasn’t going to look into the glass room. Then she did.

It was empty. Two chairs. The white board, with a faint grey ghost of two words on it, rubbed out and written so many times that the ghost had become permanent. And on the table, on her side, the blue mug.

She stopped.

She didn’t go in. She stood outside the glass and looked at it the way you look at a lit window from the street. The tea had gone cold. She could tell from the colour.

She wanted to go in and put her hands round it and tell him her mother had cut her off at a noodle counter. She wanted him to look at her over the table and say right, let’s work it out, and then work it out.

She wanted him there. And because she wanted it so badly, she made herself walk on.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Thursday she’d packed the chemistry set and the notebooks and the shoebox and the screwdriver into two cardboard boxes, and her clothes lay across the bedroom floor in two piles: the third she’d bought and the two-thirds she hadn’t. She’d thought leaving would feel like losing something. It felt like finding out she’d never been allowed to own very much in the first place.

On the shelf above her desk, behind the textbooks, she found the White Rabbits.

It was the second of the two bags, soft at the corners now. There were two sweets left in it, still in their wrappers. She sat down on the floor with it in both hands and stayed there, in the empty room, for longer than she’d meant to.

Then she put it in the box with the notebooks, on top, where it wouldn’t get squashed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The suitcase belonged to Tao Tao’s cousin. It was navy blue and very old, and its handle only came up if you pressed a little metal button at exactly the right angle while thinking kind thoughts about it. By Friday night everything that was hers had gone into it, and into two boxes and a canvas bag. Tao Tao’s went into her cousin’s car in four trips and a laundry basket.

Yu Jie stood at the sitting-room window looking down over the harbour. She’d once thought this view meant she was lucky. She’d never chosen it. She’d never chosen anything in it, not the street or the walls or the colour of the cushions. She’d just been put inside it, like a ring in a box.

“Anything else?” said Tao Tao from the doorway.

“No,” she said. “I think that’s all of me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-eight minutes past eleven on Monday the thirtieth of March, Yu Jie handed over her keys.

The man from the family office walked round the flat with a clipboard and asked her to sign at the bottom of each page. One apartment key. One building card. He called her Miss Shen and held the door. It shut behind her with a soft expensive click.

Tao Tao had already gone with the second box in her cousin’s car, to drop it at the department before her lab shift. Old Huang carried the first one down for her and shook his head and said nothing.

The suitcase wheel broke at the corner.

It happened just past the entrance, where the pavement dipped towards a storm drain. She was dragging the case with one hand and carrying the box against her hip with the other and the canvas bag was sliding off her shoulder, and the front wheel went into the grating and there was a sharp crack and the whole thing lurched sideways.

She stopped. She pulled. The wheel came off in her hand.

It was a little black plastic wheel. She was too tired even to be angry with it. She’d slept badly for a week. She’d spent the morning signing for her own life in triplicate. She hadn’t really spoken to Miles in twenty-six days.

She put the box down and crouched and tried to push the wheel back on. It wouldn’t go. She tried again, and her fingers were shaking, and it slipped out of them and bounced once on the kerb and went through the grating into the drain with a small, final splash.

Yu Jie looked at the space where it had been.

Then she sat down on the pavement beside her broken suitcase and cried.

Not prettily. She put both hands over her face and sobbed like a child, on the corner, in the middle of the morning, with people walking round her. She cried because she was tired and because she was frightened. Because she’d spent her whole life being told she was precious and had never once learned how to ask for help without feeling ashamed of it. Because she wanted her grandmother. Because she wanted her mother to love her without needing to own her.

And because she wanted Miles. She wanted him so much it was like a stitch in her side. She wanted to ring him and say I’ve got nowhere to put my books and have him say of course, in that voice, as if the answer were obvious. But she’d asked him for space. And he’d given it to her, every single day.

A car slowed. Somebody asked if she was all right. She couldn’t answer.

Her phone buzzed in the canvas bag. She ignored it. It buzzed again. She dug it out with wet fingers.

Tao Tao: where are you. Old Huang rang me. are you on the corner

She sent a pin. It was all she could manage.

Tao Tao: Stay there. I’m in the lab and I can’t get out. I’ve sent someone

She didn’t know how long it was. Ten minutes. Less. She heard a bicycle bell, and the tick of a freewheel, and somebody’s feet hitting the pavement hard as they got off.

“Yu Jie.”

She looked up.

Miles was standing over her in his dark coat with a grey scarf round his neck and his hair blown on end, holding a bicycle by its handlebars. He looked at the suitcase. At the box. At her face.

He leaned the bicycle on the railings and crouched in front of her, far enough away that she didn’t feel crowded.

“Are you hurt?”

She shook her head.

“Did you fall?”

“The suitcase.” Her voice broke completely on it.

He looked at the suitcase. “I see.”

“May I move these?”

She nodded. He picked up the box first and then the bag and put them against the wall, out of the way of feet. When he turned round she was still sitting on the kerb with her face wet and her hair coming down round the purple pen.

He unwound the scarf from his neck. He held it out to her across the space between them.

“Would you like this?”

She looked at it. Then at him. She nodded.

He waited until she reached for it before he let go. It was warm from him. She put it round her neck and it smelt of his soap and the cold air and his flat, and her face crumpled all over again.

He didn’t reach for her. He didn’t tell her not to cry. He didn’t tell her that everything was going to be all right. He stayed where he was, crouched on the pavement in his good coat, and waited.

Then he said, very low, “May I hold you?”

It was the question that undid her. Nobody had asked her anything all week. They’d told her.

“Yes,” she said.

He moved in and gathered her up, and she went into his arms so fast that he had to put a hand down on the pavement to keep his balance. Then that hand was between her shoulder blades and the other was round the back of her head, careful of the pen, and she had her face in his coat and both fists in its lapels, and she cried as she hadn’t cried since the museum stairs, and he held her through all of it and didn’t say a word.

When it eased, she said into his coat, “I’m sorry.”

His hand stopped moving. “For what?”

“Not the crying.”

He understood. He held her a little tighter.

“You don’t have to be sorry for asking me for room,” he said. “I needed to be asked.”

“I missed you,” she said.

He breathed in. For twenty-six days he’d tried very hard not to turn that sentence into something she owed him. Now she’d said it, he didn’t want to answer too fast.

“I missed you too,” he said.

“I’m still angry.”

“I know.”

“I’m still angry now.”

“I know you are.”

She pulled back far enough to look at him. “You’re not supposed to just agree with everything.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I’m trying not to start an argument on a pavement.”

She laughed, a wet, broken, astonished sound, and it was the first time he’d heard her laugh in nearly a month.

The purple pen had slid sideways in her hair. He lifted his hand towards it and stopped.

“May I?”

She nodded. He straightened it, carefully, and pushed a strand of hair back behind her ear with one finger.

“Tao Tao sent you,” she said.

“She rang me in a meeting with the faculty board and told me you were sitting on the corner with a broken suitcase and that if I didn’t get here in ten minutes she’d come out of a sterile hood and kill me.” He looked at the case. “It’s a very poor suitcase.”

“Are you defending it?”

“No. I’m criticising its construction.”

She laughed again, and then her face went, and he put his hand on her cheek and wiped the wet off it with his thumb.

“Where are you going tonight?” he said.

“Tao Tao’s aunt’s. On the sofa. With the parrot.”

“And your books?”

“In the physics building. Under Ruan’s desk.”

He was quiet. He didn’t say come home with me. She watched him not say it. He didn’t assume she’d want to, and he didn’t turn the worst morning of her life into an invitation.

“There’s somewhere else,” he said instead. “If you want it. It isn’t mine. It’s a room. You can see it and say no.”

She looked at him.

“You’ve found me a room?”

“I’ve found a room,” he said. “Whether it’s yours is up to you.”

She wiped her face with the end of his scarf. Then she held out her hand, and he took it and stood and pulled her up, and she didn’t let go.

They stood together on the corner beside a broken suitcase and two cardboard boxes and a bicycle against the railings, while the city went past them both. She was frightened. She was still angry. She owned twelve things and a thirteenth. But she wasn’t sitting on the pavement on her own any more, and when he looked down at her, she held on.

chapters.title: Miles Finds Her a Room
chapters.desc: Not his. A slanted attic above a bakery on Bell Street, a landlady who once threw a rolling pin at a health inspector, and bread at four in the morning. He carries the suitcase, and doesn’t go in.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I chose to stay.”
chapters.content:
A bicycle isn’t built to carry a suitcase. Miles found that out about four minutes after they left the corner.

He’d lashed the case across the saddle with two elastic cords and walked the contraption along with one hand on the handlebars and the other flat on top of the case, while its one remaining wheel bumped the crossbar like a small animal objecting to its circumstances. Yu Jie walked on the other side with the box against her chest and his scarf round her neck.

Halfway down the hill she stopped, unwound the scarf and held it out to him, because his throat above his collar had gone pink with cold.

“You’re cold,” he said.

“So are you, and you’re the one pushing.” She waited. “That isn’t how scarves work, Miles.”

He took it back.

Bell Street was an old lane on the east side of the university, narrow pavements and brick shopfronts and a tailor who’d been there longer than the street lamps. On the corner, the windows of Ling’s bakery were fogged from the heat inside, and a handwritten card in the glass said Bread from 4 a.m. Beside the shop door a second, narrower door led to a steep staircase.

Yu Jie looked at the bakery, and at him. It was where she’d left his oranges.

The narrow door opened before he’d knocked twice. Shu Mei stood there with her sleeves rolled to the elbow, a wooden spoon in one hand and flour in her eyebrows. She looked at Miles, at Yu Jie, and at the suitcase lashed to the bicycle, and said, “You’re late.”

“We’re three minutes early,” said Miles.

“I expected you four minutes ago.” She turned to Yu Jie and her face changed. “The orange girl. I knew it would be you. Come up. Don’t block the door, the dough’s proving and it hates a draught.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The attic was up two flights so steep they were nearly a ladder. Its ceiling sloped so sharply that you could stand up straight in only half the room. A small window was set into the slope of the roof. There was a narrow bed under it, a wooden desk, a wardrobe, a shelf, and a kitchenette with two rings and a kettle. The boards were old and scrubbed pale. A yellow rug lay beside the bed. The whole room smelt faintly of bread.

On the desk there was a lamp, brass, with a green shade. On the shelf there was a plain white mug, a little bigger than it needed to be.

Yu Jie stopped in the doorway.

“Furnished,” said Shu Mei. “The stove works if you shout at it. Don’t hang anything off that beam. The last tenant put a hammock on it.”

“What happened?”

“The hammock came down. And so did he, and so did some of my ceiling.”

She told Yu Jie the rent. It was a good deal less than Yu Jie had braced herself for. “One month’s deposit. No family guarantee, no nonsense. Can you count? Good. I need someone on the till. Four mornings a week, six till ten, paid weekly. I’ll teach you the bread. If you break something we’ll talk about it. If you see the health inspector coming, you shout before he’s through the door.”

“Why?” said Miles, from the landing.

“Because he once told me I couldn’t keep the flour sacks by the back door, and I threw a rolling pin at him.”

Yu Jie stared. “You threw a rolling pin at a health inspector?”

“I missed.”

“That’s not the important part.”

“It was to him.” Shu Mei went down for the forms.

Yu Jie stood in the half of the room where she could stand up straight. Not an allowance. A job, at a till, before dawn, for a wage she’d earn herself.

“I’ll take it,” she said. “Both.”

Miles brought the suitcase up, checked the window latch, and stepped back out onto the landing.

“Is it all right?”

“Yes.” She looked at him. “How did you find it so fast?”

“Tao Tao asked around,” he said, and went down to bring up the box.

✦ ✦ ✦

Shu Mei told her at four o’clock, coming up with a pile of towels.

“Your friend found you a good room.”

Yu Jie was shelving books, first by subject and then by height. “Tao Tao?”

Shu Mei gave her a peculiar look. “No. The tall one. He came round on Thursday night, the day of the rain, dripping on my floor, and asked if the attic was free. Asked whether the window got enough light for somebody who studied. Measured the desk three times with a tape measure. I told him I was born in this building and didn’t need a physicist measuring my furniture.” She put the towels on the bed. “He bought the mattress and the lamp, and that mug, because he said you liked white ones. He tried to pay part of your rent and I wouldn’t let him, and he said good, it ought to be a room you could afford by yourself.” She straightened a towel. “And he asked me not to tell you. So I haven’t.”

Yu Jie sat down on the bed with a book in her hands.

The night of the rain. He’d walked here under a duck umbrella from her door, after she’d told him to stay away, because he’d read Yan’s folder that afternoon and known what her mother did to people who said no. Before the bank card. Before she’d known herself that she’d need anywhere at all.

“He also asked if the ovens would be too loud in the mornings,” said Shu Mei. “I told him bread doesn’t make a noise. People do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The calendar went up first.

She took it out of the back of her thesis notebook and opened it on the desk. Two hundred and fifty-five atoms, most of them coloured in now, and the star on the twentieth of June, and after it the row of empty squares she’d drawn the morning after the museum stairs. NOT A PEARL. A PHYSICIST. She found the roll of tape and stood on the chair to reach the bit of wall above the desk where the slope began.

She heard him on the stairs before she saw him. He’d fetched the second box from under Ruan’s desk, and he set it down on the landing and didn’t come in. He stood just outside the open door with his hands at his sides and watched her tape the corners.

“That’s crooked,” he said.

“It’s not.”

“Left side. Two millimetres.”

She climbed down. She looked at him, standing out there on the bare boards with his scarf still round his neck and his hair on end from the bicycle, keeping exactly one step of landing between himself and her room. As if her door were a line on a chart that he’d sworn not to cross.

“Shu Mei told me,” she said.

He didn’t pretend not to know what.

“You found this room on the night I told you to stay away. You measured my desk. You bought a mattress. You stood in my attic with a tape measure before I knew I’d have to leave the flat.” Her voice was going. She let it. “Do you know how angry I want to be with you?”

“I can imagine.”

“You keep doing this. You make tea I won’t drink. You find a room I don’t know I need. You buy a lamp. And then you stand outside the door as if I’ll break if you come any closer.”

“I didn’t want to decide for you.”

“I know. But sometimes I want you to decide you love me enough to just come in.”

His face changed, very slightly. She saw it.

“I do,” he said.

“Don’t say it like that. Like you’re answering a question in a seminar.”

“I’m trying to be accurate.”

“You’re impossible.”

She took hold of the front of his coat in both fists and pulled him over the threshold.

He stumbled half a step and said her name, and she kissed him.

It wasn’t gentle. It had everything in it: twenty-six days of silence, the noodle counter, the clipboard, the pavement, the drain, a blue mug going cold on the wrong side of a glass wall. For a heartbeat he stood still with surprise. Then his hands came to her waist and closed there, and he kissed her back so hard she went up on her toes, and the door swung shut behind him on its own.

When she pulled back, they were both out of breath. She put her forehead against his.

“I missed you.”

“I know.”

“I’m still angry.”

“I know.”

“Stop knowing things.”

His thumb moved on her waist. “All right.”

She laughed, helplessly, against his mouth, and kissed him again, slowly this time, and he cupped her face in both hands and let her.

Then he looked past her at the calendar over the desk, two millimetres out.

“Does it feel like yours?”

“Yes,” she said. “Because I chose to stay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The bakery woke up before the university did.

At seven minutes past four on Friday the third of April, the ovens were already hot. By nineteen minutes past, Yu Jie had dropped a tray, and Shu Mei had told her that if she was going to drop things she could at least do it quietly. At a quarter past five she served a customer without a single mistake, and Shu Mei, kneading, nodded once without looking up.

At ten o’clock Shu Mei counted notes into an envelope and handed it over.

“Four mornings, less the apron.”

It wasn’t much. Yu Jie held it in both hands like a certificate.

“Don’t thank me,” said Shu Mei. “You worked.”

She smiled at every single customer for the rest of the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday night, Miles filled the tank alone.

The technicians had gone. He opened the valve at nine and sat on a crate and watched the water climb the clear walls, the whole great drum of it filling like a held breath, until it reached the first line on the acrylic.

Then he switched off the basement lights and picked up a torch from the bench.

He shone it down through the surface at a slant. The beam went in and bent, the way any beam bends going from air into water, and on the floor of the tank it made a lozenge of light. He put his hand into the water at the rim and moved it, once, and a ripple went out across the surface, and the lozenge broke into bright shaking lines that ran over the bottom of the tank like a net being shaken out. The surface had become a lens with a thousand bad corners, and the light went wherever the water told it.

It wasn’t the experiment. That would take waves and a vortex and months of failure. But he stood there in the dark with his sleeve wet to the elbow and watched the light bend because the water moved, and he found he was smiling at nobody.

He sent her a photograph.

Miles: First light.

Not Stuck: It’s beautiful.

Miles: It’s only refraction. The measurement’s months off.

Not Stuck: I said the light was beautiful, Dr. Wei.

Not Stuck: Have you eaten

He looked at the empty paper cup on the bench.

Miles: I’m about to.

Not Stuck: That’s not convincing. Go and eat. Goodnight, White Rabbit.

A minute later she sent him a photograph of her wall. In the first of the new squares after the star she’d drawn, very small, a loaf of bread. Underneath it she’d written: First wage. First room. First light.

He saved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The council sat on Thursday the ninth of April at nine o’clock, at a long table under portraits of former Vice-Chancellors, twenty people with folders. Miles sat at the far end with his hands flat on his own.

They asked about his papers and his teaching. They asked about the award on hold, and he showed them his plan for five years without it, and two of them read it twice. One woman asked him straight out about Yu Jie. He told her: disclosed in writing, removed from the panel before it was formal, never her supervisor, never her assessor. Cen confirmed the record. Ruan, speaking for the department, said that the trust had been written to stop exactly the family interference this council was being asked to worry about, and that if they turned down good science because they disliked whose grandmother had paid for it, they’d be doing the interfering themselves.

Then Shen Guoqiang, who had asked to be heard and been allowed ten minutes, stood up at the other end of the table.

“My wife wrote to this university without my authority,” he said. “I’ve withdrawn her letters. My daughter has made several decisions this year I didn’t understand at first. I’m still learning to. But it isn’t for this council to decide whether she’s allowed to make them.” He looked down the table at Miles for the first time. “If Dr. Wei’s work is good enough, keep him on its merits. If it isn’t, let him go on its merits. Don’t use my family as an excuse to avoid doing either.”

He sat down. He didn’t look at Miles again.

At sixteen minutes to twelve they voted. Nineteen to one. Permanent.

Ling Hao, outside the door, grabbed him by both shoulders and shook him and said, “Congratulations, you miserable man.”

In the corridor, Shen Guoqiang held out his hand, and Miles shook it.

“She rang me on Sunday,” said Yu Jie’s father. “She says the ceiling slopes and she’s been paid. She sounded prouder of the wage than of the Faculty Medal shortlist.” He let go. “I’m told she chose the room herself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday the fourteenth of April, at twenty-six minutes past eight, his phone lit up.

Not Stuck: Are you free tonight?

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: Come over.

He was on Bell Street by ten to nine. The stairwell smelt of bread. Before he could knock at the top she’d opened the door, in a soft blue jumper and bare feet, with her hair up round the purple cat.

“Come in,” she said, and this time he didn’t stop at the line.

The room had changed in a fortnight. A small plant leaned towards the window. On the wall by the mug she’d taped a photograph of a woman in a lab coat with a pencil behind each ear, laughing at whoever held the camera.

“Nai Nai,” said Yu Jie. She shut the door and came up behind him and put her arms round his waist, and laid her cheek between his shoulder blades. “I didn’t ask you over to carry anything.”

“I noticed there was nothing to carry.”

“I asked you because I wanted you here.” Her arms tightened. “Stay tonight.”

He turned round inside her arms.

“Are you sure?”

“Miles.” She took his face in her hands. “I’ve been sure since the threshold.”

He kissed her. It began quietly, like coming home after a long time away, and it didn’t stay quiet for long. She pulled his jumper over his head and he hit his skull on the beam and swore, and she laughed so much she had to hold onto him, and he kissed her through it until she stopped. He undid the little buttons at the back of her collar one by one and asked about each of them, as he always did, and she answered each one with her mouth on his throat.

The bed was very narrow. They didn’t need it to be wider. She pulled him down under the slope of the ceiling and he went, carefully, mindful of the beam, and then not carefully at all, because she’d hooked her leg round his and wasn’t letting him be careful. When he pushed into her she arched off the narrow mattress and pulled him deeper. After four weeks of keeping apart they were greedy with each other, and clumsy, and tender in the middle of it in a way that made her eyes sting. She said his name into his shoulder like an answer to something. He said hers against her ear, again and again, as if he’d been saving it.

It was a long time before either of them was still, and she came first, biting his shoulder.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest and the lamp off and a strip of streetlight under the curtain. His hand moved slowly up and down her back.

“Do you remember the bent oscillator?” she said. “September. Six o’clock. When you said you’re right.”

“I remember the chalk handprint you left on my board. I didn’t wash it off for a week.”

“You didn’t.”

“Eight days. Ling Hao asked if it was evidence.”

She laughed into his skin. “I thought I’d live in that big flat forever. I thought having everything meant being safe.”

“And now?”

“Now I’ve got a till and a plant and a ceiling that’s trying to kill you.”

“It nearly succeeded.”

“If you die in here I’ll have to explain to Shu Mei that my boyfriend was defeated by an attic.”

He laughed, low and real, the whole of his chest moving under her cheek. She went still, listening.

“That sound,” she said. “I missed that one most.”

He held her closer. Down below on Bell Street a lorry went by, and the first light came on in the bakery kitchen, and the smell of tomorrow’s bread began to rise up through the floor. She fell asleep in the first room she’d ever chosen for herself, with him beside her, and the beam above them both.

chapters.title: The Thesis Defence
chapters.desc: Nearly three hours in room 301, with an external examiner from the capital who has a score to settle. Miles waits in the corridor and doesn’t sit down.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t try to be perfect. Try to be precise.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past seven on Friday the fifteenth of May, Yu Jie found out her defence suit had a secret.

It was hanging in the attic wardrobe in a garment bag Tao Tao had brought round the night before. Charcoal grey, cut close at the waist, with a jacket that made her shoulders look braver than she felt. Under it, a cream silk blouse. On the shelf, a small box with two pearl studs in it.

She turned round. Tao Tao, on the bed with a slice of toast, swallowed and said, “Fine. Aurelia Chen. She rang me last week. Don’t ask how she got my number, I think she just has everybody’s number. She said she’d heard about your mother and the bank card from four different women at a charity lunch, and that nobody was going to stand up in front of a committee in a borrowed jacket while she had a tailor.” Tao Tao took another bite. “If you try to pay her back she’ll be offended for a year.”

There was a card in the inside pocket, on thick cream paper, in a big looping hand.

For the young woman who knows exactly what she’s defending. Wear it like armour. — A.

Yu Jie read it twice and laughed out loud, and then had to sit down on the bed beside Tao Tao because her eyes had filled.

Over the desk the calendar had thirty-six squares left. In today’s she’d drawn a tiny blackboard, and under it, in purple: Today I defend my work.

At twenty-six minutes past eight Professor Ruan rang.

“Have you eaten? Good. Take water. Not too much coffee. You’re not there to show them how fast you can answer. Take your time. You know that thesis better than anyone who’ll be in the room, and that includes me.” A pause, and the click of a lighter on the fifth-floor balcony. “Don’t try to be perfect. Try to be precise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The panel had been fixed in April. Ruan in the chair, as the department’s rules required. Ling Hao as internal examiner, in Miles’s old place. Professor Dai from the university in the south, who was seventy and kind and had written the textbook half of them had learned from. And, because he had asked for it in writing after reading her final draft, Dr. Mao.

Dr. Mao of slide nineteen. Dr. Mao, who had stood at the front of a seminar in December and listened to an undergraduate ask, in two sentences, why his derivation used one edge and his figure another, while Miles Wei laughed out loud in the front row. His paper had been sent back by the referees in March. The department had found no formal reason to refuse him.

“He may be difficult,” Ruan had told her.

“Then he can ask me about slide nineteen,” Yu Jie had said, and Ruan had looked at her for a long moment and then smiled her rare, crooked smile.

Room 301 was at the end of the third-floor corridor. Professor Cen was going in as she arrived, in his camel coat, with a folder; the head of department could sit in on any defence and ask what he liked, and he’d told her in March he intended to. Ling Hao put his head out with a coffee, looked her up and down, and said, “Don’t mind Mao. I’ll mind him for you. Go on, physicist.”

Miles was at the window opposite.

He’d been there forty minutes. He had a notebook he wasn’t reading and a coffee he hadn’t touched, and he was standing, because of course he was. When she came round the corner his eyes found her at once and stayed.

She saw him see the suit, and the pearls, and the purple cat holding up her hair. She saw him think something and not say it, not here, not with her about to walk into that room.

She lifted one hand, palm out, fingers spread, across the width of the corridor.

He looked at it. Then he lifted his own, the same way. For a second their two hands stood in the air facing each other with four metres of corridor carpet between them, not touching, which was the point.

“Don’t stand there the whole time,” she said.

“I’ll try.”

They both knew he was lying. She went in, and the door shut, and Miles looked at his watch. Two minutes past nine.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hour went well.

Ruan began with why strained graphene, and Yu Jie told them: that stretching a sheet one atom thick makes its electrons move as if a magnetic field were threaded through it, though there’s no magnet anywhere; that if the stretch isn’t even, the false field isn’t either; and that she’d been wrong, in her first draft, to treat it as if it were. Ling Hao asked about the numerical method. She answered without looking at her notes.

Then Dr. Mao opened his copy of the thesis at page sixty-seven.

She knew the page. Everybody in the room except Dr. Dai knew the page.

“Your first derivation assumed the field was uniform,” said Dr. Mao.

“Yes.”

“And your conclusion rested on it.”

“Yes.”

“Then your first conclusion was wrong.”

She folded her hands on the table. “In the form I first wrote it, yes.”

“So why should we believe the second?”

She didn’t answer straight away. Then she stood up and went to the board and picked up a piece of chalk.

“Because the second doesn’t rest on that assumption at all.”

She drew him a triangle of hexagons and split it into regions. In the middle of the sheet, where the strain was gentle, the simple picture held, and she said exactly how far it held and where it began to fail. Near the corners she’d thrown the simple picture away and used the real, uneven field, point by point. And the boundary between the two regions wasn’t a line she’d drawn for convenience. She’d tested it, and shown where the approximation broke and by how much.

“And the localisation length?” said Dr. Mao.

“It changes.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” she agreed. “It isn’t. The answer is that it depends on where you are, and on the shape of the corner, and the old result was only ever true in the middle.” She drew three more lines. “This is where it stops being true.”

He asked about stability near the corner, and the shape of the edge, and whether the effect was really the strain field or only the geometry, and she told him that was the right question and she’d only half answered it, and wrote the half she hadn’t on the board.

Dr. Mao stopped interrupting. He began writing things down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past ten Miles was still standing.

He’d looked at his watch seventeen times. He’d read one page of his notebook so often he could have recited it backwards.

The door of 301 opened and Ling Hao came out for a document he’d left in his pigeonhole, and stopped.

“Sit down. You’re not a lamp post, Wei.” Ling Hao looked at him. “She’s doing well.”

“Define well.”

“I’m not allowed to grade her in the corridor.” He softened. “She’s defending her own work. That’s all she needs. Let her.”

He went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-two minutes to twelve, Professor Cen, who hadn’t said a word all morning, cleared his throat.

“Miss Shen. How do your boundary conditions change the spectrum of edge states, and how sure are you that the localisation survives across all the geometries you looked at?”

Yu Jie looked at the board. Then she smiled.

It was the smile she got when somebody finally asked the question she’d been hoping for all along.

“That’s the part I like best,” she said, and picked up the chalk.

She talked for eleven minutes. About how a corner isn’t just two edges meeting but something with its own rules. About how easy it would be to see an effect of shape and call it an effect of the field, and how she’d tried to tell the two apart, and where she’d succeeded and where she hadn’t yet. She didn’t claim more than she’d shown. She didn’t hide what she hadn’t. When Cen asked what she was least sure of, she wrote it up in a box.

Then she stepped back and put the chalk down, with white all over her fingers.

“Thank you, Yu Jie,” said Ruan. “Sit down.”

The questions got harder after that. She didn’t feel she was defending herself any more. She was defending the work. She knew the difference now.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four minutes to twelve they sent her out.

Miles was exactly where she’d left him. He didn’t ask how it had gone. He lifted his hand, palm out, and she lifted hers, and they stood like that across the corridor.

“I think it went well,” she whispered.

“I thought it would.”

“How long have you been standing?”

He looked at his watch. “Two hours and fifty-four minutes.”

She laughed, a little wildly. “Was it horrible?”

“Yes,” he said. “It was the worst three hours of my life, and I’ve had flu.”

She went and stood at the window for the twelve minutes it took them, and didn’t try to guess.

Then Ruan opened the door and called her in, and said, “Congratulations, Yu Jie. Distinction, subject to the usual corrections,” and the word went past her once without landing and came round again and did.

Dr. Mao closed his copy of the thesis.

“I have one more question,” he said. “Have you thought about a doctorate? I’d like to talk to you about one. In my group, in the capital. Your corners. Extended to the whole family of strained lattices.” He looked at her over the table without any expression at all. “You were right about my boundary conditions. It cost me a paper. I’d rather have you working on my side of the board than against it.”

Ruan made a small noise that might have been a laugh.

“I’d like to hear more,” said Yu Jie, carefully.

When she came out the second time she was smiling so widely that Miles knew before she said a word. She crossed the corridor this time. She stood in front of him with chalk on her hands.

“Distinction.”

“I heard.”

“I got a distinction.”

“I know.”

“Say something, then.”

“I’m so proud of you,” he said, “that I can’t think of a single equation.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The celebration began with terrible coffee.

Yan Zhiyuan came across the square at one o’clock in a pale grey suit, and beside him walked a man Yu Jie had never seen but knew at once: tall, untidy dark hair, a soft jacket with the elbows gone shiny, and the wary look of somebody who’d been told a university celebration would be fun and didn’t believe it. He was carrying a cardboard tray of four paper cups and a white box.

“Remy,” said Zhiyuan, and the way he said it was the whole story.

“Congratulations.” Remy handed her a cup.

She drank. Then she stopped. Her face did something it hadn’t done once in room 301.

“Is it bad?” said Tao Tao, in her lab coat.

“It’s very,” said Yu Jie, “strong.”

“I told him not to buy it from the van,” said Zhiyuan.

“You said to buy coffee,” said Remy. “You didn’t specify good coffee.”

“I didn’t think I had to specify.”

“With me you always have to specify.” Remy opened the white box. Inside was a small cake, leaning to one side, with uneven white icing and, in wobbling blue capitals, CONGRATULATIONS, PHYSICIST. “I made it. He said it would be more personal. It isn’t straight.”

“It’s perfect,” said Yu Jie, and meant it.

For the next half hour she was surrounded. Tao Tao hugged her twice and cried once. Ruan shook her hand very hard and told her to get her corrections in by the first of June. Remy asked whether she’d eaten anything but toast, and when she admitted she hadn’t he looked at her with quiet, total disapproval, like an aunt.

And through all of it Miles stood near enough to be one of them and far enough not to be the middle of it. He watched her laugh. He watched her hold the lopsided cake as if it were made of glass. Once she turned and found his eyes on her, and smiled, and he smiled back, and that was all. He wanted to give her the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave her the night instead.

At twenty to ten she stood beside him on the third-floor landing of the staff flats, out of the suit now and into a soft jumper, with the jacket over her arm and the cake box under the other. He unlocked the door and stood back for her. She went in, and turned round, and he was still standing there with the keys in his hand.

She’d smiled all day until her face ached. Now, in the dark little hall that smelt of his books, she wanted him.

She put the cake down on the shoe rack and took hold of his coat. He said her name, half a laugh, and she went up on her toes and kissed him, and he put the keys down on the table without looking and his hands came to her waist.

“I got a distinction,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.”

“You stood in a corridor for three hours.”

“Yes.”

“Haven’t you got anything to say?”

He looked at her. Then he bent, put one arm behind her knees and the other behind her back, and lifted her clean off the floor.

She shrieked. “Miles!”

“Yes?”

“You can’t just pick me up!”

“I appear to have.” He held her easily, close against his chest. “Shall I put you down?”

She looked at him. Then she wound both arms round his neck.

“Don’t you dare.”

He kissed her in the doorway, holding her, until she forgot what she’d been going to say, and then he carried her the rest of the way.

It was slow, at first, because he wanted it slow, because he’d been waiting since two minutes past nine. He laid her down and knelt over her and kissed the chalk dust still in the creases of her knuckles, one hand and then the other. She pulled him down by his shirt and told him she didn’t want slow, and he said she’d waited three hours for her examiners and she could wait a little for him, and she laughed and bit his lip and he stopped being patient altogether. He got her dress off and she got his shirt off and he came into her still half-dressed, his trousers round his knees, both of them laughing and then gasping. She held onto his shoulders. He said her name like something he’d been carrying in his pocket all day. The small room got warm, and then warmer, and the lamp stayed on, because neither of them could be bothered to reach it.

At half past eleven they decided they needed cake.

The box wouldn’t fit in his fridge, so the only sensible thing was to eat it. It was a little dry and the icing was too sweet. She ate it sitting on his kitchen counter in his shirt and declared it excellent. He said it was edible. She said that was worse.

At one o’clock she put a dab of icing on his nose. He looked at her with enormous dignity. Then he put a dab on her cheek. She gasped, and went for his hand, and he stepped back round the table, and she went round after him, and somewhere in the chase the box slid off the counter and landed upside down on the floor.

They both stopped.

There was icing on his sock.

Yu Jie laughed so hard she had to sit down on the kitchen floor. He crouched beside her, and tried to look stern, and couldn’t, and laughed too, with his head down against her shoulder, the real laugh, the whole of him shaking with it. At two in the morning they were still sitting on his kitchen floor amid the wreckage of CONGRATULATIONS, PHYSICIST, and when she reached for a piece from the unspoilt side he caught her wrist and said a floor wasn’t a plate, so she kissed him instead. He tasted of icing.

Later, on his sofa, with tea, she said, “I don’t know what to do about Mao.”

“That’s all right.”

“The capital’s a long way.”

“Yes.”

“You’re not going to tell me what to do.”

“No. You can ask me what I think.”

She thought about it. “What do you think?”

“I think you should take it seriously. Find out if it’s the work you want to spend four years on.” He turned his cup round in his hands. “Then decide if you want the life that comes with it.”

“Would you want me to stay?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“I would like you to stay,” he said. “Very much. But I won’t have you stay because I asked. I want you to choose the work you want. Not the work that keeps you near me.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder.

“You’re very inconvenient,” she said. “I wanted you to tell me to stay.”

“I know.”

“And you won’t.”

“I won’t.”

She sighed, enormously, and kissed his jaw. The last thing she thought before she slept wasn’t the doctorate, or the board, or Dr. Mao’s face over page sixty-seven. It was him laughing on the kitchen floor with icing on his sock. She wanted to remember it. So she did.

chapters.title: Graduation Day, 4:01 P.M.
chapters.desc: The ceremony ends at four. Eighty-seven steps from the Great Hall to the fourth floor. The first minute she stops being a student in his department.
chapters.epigraph: “Now there’s nothing between us that needs a line.”
chapters.content:
At seven minutes past four on the morning of her graduation, Yu Jie was peeling oranges behind the counter of Ling’s bakery.

The ovens had been going for an hour. The first trays of milk buns were out, and the shop was full of the warm, sweet, faintly scorched smell that had got into her hair and her clothes and her dreams over the past two months. Shu Mei stood at the long table with a pencil behind her ear, slapping dough.

“Not so thick.”

“I’m taking the skin off.”

“You’re taking half the fruit off. You’re taking its future.”

Yu Jie laughed and started another. She’d learned that Shu Mei had a firm opinion about everything. Bread was sliced at one angle and no other. Flour was not kept by the back door, whatever anybody from the council said. Customers who asked whether yesterday’s bread was fresh were told that yesterday’s bread was, by definition, yesterday’s. And oranges were peeled properly or not at all.

“These are for your Dr. Wei,” said Shu Mei.

“He forgets to eat.”

“Men who forget to eat are trouble.”

“He isn’t trouble.”

“All men are trouble. Some are just better dressed.” Shu Mei looked at the clock. “Go upstairs at seven. You’ve got hair to do and a face to put on. You’re getting a medal, not delivering bread.”

She’d been doing it most mornings since April, between customers: three oranges, every scrap of pith off, segments in a plastic box, the box in the fridge behind the counter. Sometimes he ate them at his desk by nine. Sometimes the box sat by his elbow in the basement till three. Once he’d sent her a photograph of it, empty.

White Rabbit: Evidence of compliance.

Yu Jie: I’m very proud of you.

White Rabbit: I know.

Today she put the box in her bag before she went upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tao Tao came at twenty to nine, with a bunch of yellow roses and her hair still wet, and stopped in the attic doorway.

Yu Jie was at the mirror on the back of the wardrobe door, fastening Aurelia’s pearls. The dress was ivory, plain, with a fitted waist and a skirt that fell just past her knees; she’d bought it herself, with six weeks of wages, from a shop on Bell Street run by a woman who’d dressed brides for forty years and had given her a discount on condition that she came back and showed her the medal. There was no purple pen in her hair today. A small pearl clip held it instead.

“You’re really graduating,” said Tao Tao.

“Apparently.”

“First Class. With Distinction. And the medal.”

“That’s what the letter says.”

Tao Tao looked at her up and down and didn’t say anything. Then she looked at the photograph by the lamp, Nai Nai in her lab coat with a pencil behind each ear.

“She’d have tried to scratch the medal with a screwdriver. To see if it was real gold.”

“She’d have succeeded,” said Yu Jie, and they both laughed, and then they both had to fix their eyes.

The calendar over the desk was full. Two hundred and fifty-five atoms, all coloured in now, every one of them, in purple and blue and once, on a very bad day in March, in black. The last square had the star in it, and 20 JUNE — 16:00, and underneath, this morning, she’d drawn a small door.

“Ready?” said Tao Tao.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie. Then: “No.”

“Good. That’s the correct answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Great Hall was full to the back.

Families filled the aisles and the galleries. Photographers crouched at the ends of rows. Somebody’s grandmother had brought a folding stool and was refusing, magnificently, to move it. Yu Jie sat with the physics graduates in the fourth row, in her gown, with her hands folded on her programme and her heart going like a bird’s.

There were speeches about the future of inquiry. There was a choir. There was the long, slow river of names.

She knew who was where. Tao Tao, six rows back, holding her phone up at an angle that meant she’d photograph every second of it. Ruan and Cen in the front row of the faculty seats, Ruan in a gown that didn’t fit and a hat she’d clearly been made to wear against her will. Ling Hao near the end of the same row, waving, which you weren’t supposed to do.

Miles wasn’t there. He’d told her on Wednesday that he’d decided not to walk in the procession, that he’d had nothing to do with this year’s examinations and there was no role for him on the stage. She’d known the real reason. He didn’t want her graduation to have him in it anywhere. He wanted it to be entirely hers.

She’d let him. She knew where he’d be.

“Shen Yu Jie.”

She stood up and walked across the stage. The Vice-Chancellor shook her hand and gave her the certificate. First Class, with Distinction. Then the dean stepped forward with a small velvet box, and read out the Faculty Medal, and the applause went up through the hall like weather.

She held it in both hands. The metal was cool and heavier than she’d expected.

She thought of a pen rolling under a chair in September. Of a flat line on a blackboard. Of two hundred and twelve comments in red. A triangle of hexagons in room 301, and a man standing outside it for three hours because he couldn’t make himself sit down.

She didn’t look for her mother. Her mother wasn’t there. There’d been no message that morning, no flowers, no note from the family office, and she’d stopped expecting her mother to arrive at the moments when she most wanted to be seen.

But at the very back of the hall, by the great doors, a tall silver-haired man in a dark suit had stood up.

He was clapping. Not loudly. Not to be noticed. Steadily, by himself, as people around him sat back down, as though he’d decided he would go on until he was sure she’d seen.

She saw. Across the whole length of the hall, their eyes met. Her father smiled.

By the time the ceremony ended his seat was empty. He’d slipped out by the side door before the lights came up, the way he did everything that mattered to him.

“He came,” said Tao Tao, finding her in the crush with an arm round her shoulders.

“He came,” said Yu Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

The photographs took longer than anybody had planned. Yu Jie with her year. Yu Jie with Ruan, who held her by both shoulders and told her she’d earned every square inch of the day and then took her hat off with enormous relief. Yu Jie with Cen, who said the department would miss somebody who asked difficult questions and hoped she’d still come to the seminars.

“Especially yours,” she told Ling Hao, who appeared at her elbow.

“This is why I didn’t want her to graduate,” Ling Hao told Cen. He looked at his watch. Then at her. “It’s twenty to.”

She was already moving.

“Don’t run in those shoes!”

“Too late!”

It was eighty-seven steps from the side door of the Great Hall to the fourth-floor landing of the physics building. She knew because she’d counted them in October, the day she’d drawn her first atom, walking slowly so that it would take longer. She knew the turn on the second flight and the window that stuck in wet weather and the noise the fire door made on the fourth floor when it swung shut behind you.

Today she took them two at a time. The medal thumped against her chest. Her gown flew out behind her.

She came through the fire door breathless with her hair coming down, and stopped.

The door of 412 was shut. She looked at her watch. Two minutes to four.

She’d imagined this a hundred times. Him opening the door before she’d knocked. Him waiting behind it, already smiling. Herself saying something devastatingly clever. Now she was here she couldn’t think of a single word.

She looked at the brass number. She lifted her hand. Then she put it down again.

Three fifty-nine.

From the stairwell she could hear voices, far away, coming up. Somebody laughing. A door below. She stood in the corridor in her gown with her heart in her throat and watched the last minute go round.

Four o’clock.

She smiled at the door. She didn’t knock. For one more minute she wanted to be exactly what she’d been since September: the girl in the corridor with a question she already knew the answer to. One minute at the very end of the interval. One minute to be sure.

At one minute past four, she knocked.

He opened the door.

He was in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, and his round glasses, and there was a line of chalk on one cuff. He looked at her for a long moment without saying anything. At the gown, and the medal, and her flushed face, and her hair coming loose round the pearl clip.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“It’s one minute past four.”

“I know.”

“May I come in?”

He stood back, and she went in, and he didn’t close the door.

The office was what it had always been. The bookshelves. The small sofa. The kettle and the jasmine tin. The white mug, and beside it a blue one with a chip by the handle. And the board.

He’d drawn the graph again.

He must have done it that morning, with the metre rule, exactly as it had been on the eighth of October, from memory. The two axes, perfectly straight. TIME along the bottom. PERSONAL INVOLVEMENT up the side. The single flat line lying along the time axis, with its small neat arrow and the words PROFESSIONAL DISTANCE. And at the far end, in the bottom corner, where it had stayed all year through every lecture and every seminar and every cleaner’s damp cloth, her own slanting chalk.

20 JUNE — 16:00.

She stared at it. Then at him.

“You never rubbed my date off.”

“No.”

“Not once. All year.”

“Ling Hao offered to. Several times. I told him it was load-bearing.”

She went to the board. She traced the air under the long flat line with one finger, all the way to her date.

“Is it over?” she said.

He came and stood beside her. He picked up a piece of chalk.

“That was the condition.”

He put the chalk to the board at the end of the flat line, exactly where it met her date. And he drew it on. A little way flat at first. Then it lifted. Slowly, then not slowly, up and away from the axis in a long clean curve that ran right off the top corner of the board.

Under it, he wrote two words.

NOT CONSTANT.

She looked at it until it blurred.

“What’s the function?” she said, and her voice wasn’t steady.

“Undetermined.”

“That isn’t a function.”

“It is until we’ve got more data.”

She laughed. It came out wet.

“The old line was a boundary,” he said. “It had to be there. It kept your work yours. It kept your degree beyond any question. I’m not sorry I drew it.” He put the chalk down on the ledge. “But it was only ever meant to run to your date. You put the end on it. I just kept it till we got here.”

“And now?”

“Now there’s nothing between us that needs a line.” He looked at her. “Except whatever we decide to draw.”

She stepped close. He didn’t move.

“May I kiss you?” he said.

She’d waited two hundred and fifty-five days for him to ask her in this room with that door open. She found she couldn’t speak. She nodded.

He glanced at the doorway. The corridor was bright and empty. Somewhere down it a student went past with a bundle of gowns.

“Shall I shut it?”

“No,” she said. “I don’t want to hide from the door any more.”

He looked at her for one more moment. Then he bent his head and kissed her.

It began very gently, with a question still in it, and somewhere in the middle it turned into a smile against her mouth. She held the front of his shirt in both hands. He put one hand at her waist and the other along her cheek, his thumb under her ear, and kissed her as if they had all the time in the world, which, for the first time, they did. It was less dramatic than she’d imagined, and better. It was ordinary. Nobody counting minutes. Nobody watching the door. Just the two of them in his office, with the door wide open and the whole department free to walk past.

When they drew apart she put her forehead against his.

“Hello, Miles.”

“Hello, Yu Jie.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were found about forty seconds later.

The voices from the stairwell came through the fire door all at once: Tao Tao, and Ling Hao, and behind them Ruan and Cen and two of Yu Jie’s year and somebody’s little brother who’d simply followed the crowd. Ling Hao saw the open door first. He stopped. He looked at Miles, and at Yu Jie, and at the board, and he closed his eyes and said to the ceiling, “Finally.”

Tao Tao made a noise like a kettle.

Yu Jie stepped back, scarlet. “Hello.”

“Don’t you hello us,” said Tao Tao, pointing.

Cen came to the doorway and looked past them at the board, at the old straight line and the new curve rising out of the end of it, and something in his long face went soft. Ruan came and stood beside him with her hat in her hand. She read NOT CONSTANT, and then she looked at Yu Jie, and gave her one small, satisfied nod, as though a calculation had come out the way she’d always known it would.

“Congratulations, Yu Jie,” said Ruan. “On the degree. Naturally.”

“Naturally,” said Yu Jie.

“That’s an optimistic gradient,” said Ling Hao.

“Do you have a concern?” said Miles.

“Several.”

“Keep them to yourself.”

Tao Tao had both arms round Yu Jie and was saying you’re done, you’re actually done into her hair. And Miles, standing by his own board with half the fourth floor crowded into his doorway, could have made a dry remark and stepped away. He could have waited till they’d gone.

He took her hand instead. He turned her round, gently, out of Tao Tao’s arms. And in front of all of them, with the door open, he kissed her again.

Tao Tao shrieked. Ling Hao groaned and put his face in his hands. Cen laughed out loud, a deep surprised sound none of them had heard from him before. Ruan looked at the ceiling and said, quite distinctly, “About time.”

When Miles let her go, Yu Jie was laughing so hard she couldn’t stand up straight. She kept hold of his hand. For once, he didn’t look towards the corridor.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went in the end, all of them, in twos and threes, Tao Tao last, walking backwards with her phone up. Ling Hao stopped in the doorway long enough to say that he’d had money on the kiss at four and also on the graph, and that the graph was the one he’d really wanted to win, and that he was going to buy Shu Mei a new oven with it.

Then it was quiet. The late sun came across the floor. Yu Jie sat on the edge of his desk in her gown and took the plastic box out of her bag.

“Oranges,” she said. “I peeled them this morning between the buns.”

He opened it and took a segment and ate it, and looked at her as if she’d handed him the medal.

“You’re keeping the graph?” she said.

“For a while. It isn’t finished.”

“How do you mean to finish it?”

He wiped his fingers on his handkerchief. Then he did a thing she’d never seen him do: he looked shy.

“I’d like to ask you out,” he said. “Properly. Tomorrow. Not office hours, not a consultation. Out.” He glanced at the board. “I’ve been working on how to ask since October.”

“Since October?”

“I had a great deal of time and nothing I was allowed to do with it.”

She looked at him. She looked at the board. NOT CONSTANT.

“Miles Wei,” she said slowly. “What have you done?”

“Nothing yet.” The corner of his mouth went up. “It’s a proof.”

“A proof of what?”

“Come tomorrow and find out.”

She stared at him. Then she started to laugh, helplessly, holding onto the edge of his desk.

“You’re going to ask me out with a proof by induction.”

He didn’t deny it. He took another segment of orange out of the box, and he looked at her, and his whole face was smiling.

chapters.title: A Proof by Induction
chapters.desc: Sunday, a closed building, a key. Miles asks her out the only way he knows how: on a chalkboard, with a base case, an inductive step, and a very small mistake he made on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “You haven’t proved your inductive step.”
chapters.content:
The university was shut on Sundays. This, Miles had told her over the phone on Saturday night, was not an important obstacle.

“It’s a closed building,” Yu Jie said at half past eleven on Sunday the twenty-first of June, opening the attic door to find him on the landing with a paper bag from Shu Mei’s counter in one hand and a ring of keys in the other.

“Yes.”

“With the doors locked.”

“Yes.”

“And you’ve got keys.”

“I do.”

She narrowed her eyes at him. She was in a pale blue cotton dress, barefoot, with her hair down because she’d been told to expect something and had decided to look as if she hadn’t been. “Dr. Wei. Are you planning a crime?”

“I’m planning lunch.”

“That’s what a criminal would say.”

He held out his free hand. She looked at it, the way she’d looked at it at the bottom of the hill road in December, and took it.

They walked up through the Sunday streets, hand in hand, with nobody about. Bell Street was still asleep. The light lay in long warm stripes across the pavement. She told him about Shu Mei’s new sourdough, which had a name and a temper, and about Tao Tao, who had sent her seventeen photographs from graduation, eleven of them of Ling Hao in the background of other people’s pictures. He listened, and asked questions, and seemed content to let her fill the quiet.

At the university gates she stopped and looked at their joined hands.

“Yesterday I walked out of here with a degree,” she said. “Today you’re walking me back in.”

“I thought you’d like to see it without having to defend anything.”

She looked up at him, and her face went soft. “That’s actually quite romantic.”

“I’ll try not to let it happen again.”

“Too late.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The physics building, which the university insisted on calling the Hall of Science in its brochures and nobody else ever did, smelt of old wood and floor polish and the particular clean emptiness of a place with no people in it. Their footsteps went ahead of them up the stairs. He unlocked the side door, and the fire door on the fourth floor, and 412.

She stopped on the threshold. The graph was still on the board, the old flat line and the new curve climbing off the top corner, NOT CONSTANT. The other half of the board was clean.

He shut the door. The latch clicked, and before the sound had finished he’d crossed the room and taken her face in both hands and kissed her.

There was nothing careful in it. No ear on the corridor. No space left for anybody’s sake. His fingers went into her hair at the back of her head and she caught the front of his shirt and went up on her toes, and she smiled against his mouth when he pulled her closer, and then stopped smiling, because he’d been waiting since four o’clock yesterday to do that properly and it showed.

When he let her go, her nose was still against his.

“You could have done that on the stairs.”

“I wanted to shut the door first.”

“You really have changed. You used to leave the room if a second-year saw you holding my tea.”

“That was a very observant second-year.”

She kissed him again, quickly, and stepped back, and saw the box of chalk on his desk. It was the twin of the box she carried in her coat pocket.

He picked it up and turned it over once in his hand.

“Would you like to see something?”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably not.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

He went to the clean half of the board. He stood there a moment with a stick of chalk between his fingers, looking at the empty slate the way he looked at it before a lecture. Then he began to write, in capitals, in his small straight hand.

A PROOF BY INDUCTION

She leaned on the edge of his desk. “Ambitious title.”

“I’ve been working on it.”

“Since when?”

“October.”

“That’s a long time for one proof.”

“It’s a long proof,” he said, and went on.

PROPOSITION. For every n ≥ 0: I want to see you on day n.

She pressed her lips together hard.

BASE CASE. n = 0. Today. True.

“Is there a problem?” he said, without turning round.

“Not yet.”

INDUCTIVE HYPOTHESIS. Suppose that, for some k, I want to see you on day k.

INDUCTIVE STEP. Then I want to see you on day k + 1.

He drew a line underneath, and wrote the thing every first-year learns to write at the bottom of one of these, as if it were a law of nature:

P(0) and P(k) ⇒ P(k+1), therefore P(n) for every n ≥ 0

Then, beneath it, smaller:

COROLLARY. Will you have dinner with me tonight? And tomorrow?

He put the chalk down on the ledge and stood back and folded his arms.

She looked at the board for a long time. Then she looked at him.

“That’s it?”

“That’s the proof.”

“It’s not finished.”

“Isn’t it?”

“You haven’t proved your inductive step.” She came off the desk and stood beside him and ran one finger down under his lines without touching the slate. “Your base case, fine. You want to see me today. I accept that. But all your hypothesis tells me is that you want to see me on day k. It doesn’t tell me a single thing about day k plus one. You’ve just said it does.”

“Perhaps I was being optimistic.”

“Perhaps you were being lazy.”

“I’ll accept that criticism.”

She looked at the board again. Then she stopped, and looked harder, and turned slowly to look at his face, which was perfectly composed except for the very corner of his mouth.

“You did it on purpose.”

He said nothing.

“You left the hole on purpose. You wrote a proof with a gap in it so that I’d have to—“ She took the chalk out of his hand. “You absolute fraud.”

“I prefer teacher.”

She turned her back on him and wrote, underneath his step, in her slanting hand, slightly smaller than his because she was trying very hard not to let her handwriting know he was watching her:

CORRECTION. The proposition is one-sided. It proves that he wants to see her. It says nothing at all about her.

REVISED HYPOTHESIS. On day k, both of them choose to see each other.

REVISED STEP. On day k + 1, both of them are free to choose it again.

She stopped. Then she wrote one more line underneath, and underlined it.

The choice must be made freely at every step.

He read it. He didn’t say anything for a while.

“What?” she said, turning round with the chalk still in her fingers.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a very unconvincing face for nothing.”

“I like your correction.”

“Of course you do. It’s mathematically superior.”

“It is.”

“And ethically superior.”

“That too.”

“And much more romantic.”

“I’m not sure that’s a mathematical category.”

“It is now.” She tapped the chalk on her lip, frowning at his proposition. “Your domain’s a problem as well. Every n. You’re claiming it for every day from now on.”

“Yes.”

“That’s a large commitment for a first date.”

“I hoped you wouldn’t object.”

“I’m considering it.”

He waited. He didn’t hurry her. He never did, when the answer mattered.

Then she turned back to the board, crossed out the question mark after tomorrow, and wrote underneath his corollary:

ANSWER. Yes.

And then, after a moment, in brackets, so small he had to lean in:

(For all n.)

He read it twice.

“Are you sure?” he said.

“I’m not promising to like every restaurant.”

“I wouldn’t expect you to.”

“Or every film. And I reserve the right to change my mind. And if you ever write me another one-sided proof I’ll mark it in red.”

“That’s fair.”

“But yes.”

Something went across his face. He’d never been a man who wore what he felt carelessly. But his eyes changed, and the smile that came was the one she’d learned to think of, privately and possessively, as hers.

“Yes?”

“Yes, Miles.”

He took her hand. Then, so suddenly that she shrieked, he caught her round the waist and lifted her off her feet and spun her right round in the middle of his office. The chalk flew out of her fingers. Her bare heel caught a stack of second-year scripts and sent them sliding off the desk in a fan. A pen rolled off the edge and under the sofa.

“Miles!”

“You said yes.”

“I know what I wrote!”

He put her down with her back against the board and kissed her before she could say anything else. The slate was cool through her dress. Somewhere under her shoulder blade she felt INDUCTIVE STEP smudge into her cotton. She laughed into his mouth, and put one hand round the back of his neck, and he kissed her until she’d stopped laughing and started something else, and the scripts lay where they’d fallen.

When he drew back at last, she was breathless and he was flushed to the ears.

“You’ve got chalk on my dress,” she said.

He looked down at her shoulder. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be.” She brushed a little dust off his shirt, and then, deliberately, pressed her chalky thumb to his collar and left a white print there. “Now we’re even.”

“Is that a correction?”

“To your appearance. You were looking far too respectable.”

He laughed. Not the short surprised breath she’d spent the autumn coaxing out of him. A whole laugh, warm and careless, filling the quiet room.

She rose up and kissed the corner of his mouth. “I like that one.”

“You’ll hear it again.”

“Is that a promise?”

“It’s a proposition.”

“Then I’ll want a proof.”

“I’ll work on one,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were on their knees picking up the scattered scripts when somebody knocked. Three sharp raps.

Yu Jie froze with a handful of second-year wave functions. “Are we in trouble?”

“No.”

“That’s what people say right before they’re in trouble.”

He went and opened the door.

Zeng Bo stood in the corridor with a folder under one arm and a takeaway coffee in the other hand, in a T-shirt that said I’M ONLY HERE FOR THE LASER, with the expensive haircut and the expression of a postdoc on his third contract who had come in on a Sunday to finish a fellowship application and had heard a woman shriek through a fire door.

He looked at Miles. At the chalk on Miles’s collar. At the room, the scripts, the woman on the floor in a blue dress with chalk on her shoulder, smiling. At the board.

His eyes went slowly down it. The title. The proposition. The base case. The hole. The correction in a different hand. The corollary. The answer.

He read the line in brackets twice.

“Dr. Wei,” he said.

“Zeng Bo.”

“It’s Sunday.”

“Yes.”

“The building’s locked.”

“You appear to have a key too.”

Zeng Bo took a sip of his coffee. His mouth had begun to do something he was trying hard to stop.
