“Is that a proof by induction?”

“An attempt.”

“An attempt,” Zeng Bo repeated. He came two steps into the room and stood in front of the board like a man at an exhibition. “Your base case is trivial.”

“Thank you.”

“Your inductive step’s a disgrace.”

“It’s been pointed out.”

“Good. Somebody here’s doing real mathematics.” He nodded at Yu Jie’s correction. “That’s much better. The original was unilateral.”

“Exactly,” said Yu Jie, from the floor.

“And the corollary?”

“Accepted.”

Zeng Bo looked at Miles. “By both parties?”

Miles looked at Yu Jie. She smiled at him.

“Yes,” he said.

Zeng Bo looked between them for a moment longer. Then he said, very quietly and with enormous feeling, “Oh, Dr. Wei,” and picked his coffee up, and turned for the door.

“Zeng Bo.”

“I think the floor should know.”

“No.”

“It’s a major result.”

“Zeng Bo.”

He stopped in the doorway and looked back at the board, and when he spoke again his voice had changed. “Congratulations,” he said. “Both of you. Really.”

Then he was gone, and for perhaps twelve seconds the corridor was silent.

Miles closed his eyes. “He’s going to tell everyone.”

“Probably.”

“He’ll make it sound worse than it is.”

“It sounds quite good to me.”

From down the corridor, Zeng Bo’s voice rang off the walls. “LING HAO! Are you in? Come and look at this!”

A door opened somewhere. Ling Hao’s voice, muffled, from 413, where he’d evidently been marking on a Sunday too: “What?”

“WEI’S IN LOVE!”

There was a pause. Then Ling Hao, with the boundless satisfaction of a man whose every prediction had finally come true, bellowed back: “I KNOW!”

Yu Jie sat down on the floor among the scripts and laughed until she had to put her hand over her mouth. Miles looked at the ceiling.

“I should have locked the door,” he said.

“You did.”

“I should have locked the building.”

“You did that too.”

“Then I underestimated the staff.”

She looked up at him from the floor, bright-eyed, with chalk on her cheek. He crouched in front of her and wiped it off with his thumb.

“Your proof’s been published,” she said.

“Without peer review.”

“Ling Hao will review it.”

“He’ll reject it on principle.”

“Then we’ll resubmit.”

She took out her phone and held it up before he could object.

“What are you doing?”

“Evidence,” she said. “Of the day Dr. Wei wrote a proof he couldn’t finish without me.”

“That isn’t what happened.”

“It’s exactly what happened.”

In the photograph he was standing by the board with chalk on his collar and his hand held out to pull her up, and his face was helpless, and behind him, in his straight capitals and her slanting script, was a proof neither of them had written alone.

She saved it. She took his hand and let him pull her up, and took the keys out of his other hand, and towed him to the door.

“Lunch,” she said. “Then dinner, because it’s in the corollary.”

“And after that?”

She looked back once at the board.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

He locked 412 behind them. And for the first time since a pen had rolled under his chair, he didn’t have to work out how long it would be before he saw her again.

chapters.title: The First Date Has a Lesson Plan
chapters.desc: Four pages, timed to the minute, with learning objectives. She reads it, folds it into a paper plane, and takes him to the night market instead.
chapters.epigraph: “You forgot to ask me what I wanted to do.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter past six that evening Miles climbed the two steep flights above Ling’s bakery carrying a folder.

Yu Jie opened the attic door, looked at the folder, and said, “No.”

“You haven’t seen inside it.”

“I know you.”

“That’s a strong basis for an objection.”

“It’s a folder, Miles. On our first date.”

“Technically it’s a document.”

She leaned on the door frame in a yellow sundress she’d bought that afternoon with two mornings’ wages, and held out her hand for it with the expression of someone accepting a sample of unknown origin. It was dark blue. On the front, in his small straight capitals, it said FIRST DATE: SHEN YU JIE AND MILES WEI.

There were four pages.

Page one had a title, the date, and a short paragraph on the purpose of the evening. Page two was a timetable. 18:30–18:45 Arrival and refreshments. 18:45–19:30 Dinner. 19:30–20:00 Walk by the harbour (allow extra time if conversation ongoing). Page three was a list of possible activities with estimated durations and a contingency for rain. And page four was headed Learning objectives.

She read it aloud, slowly, so that he’d have to hear it.

“By the end of the evening, both participants should: one, have spent time together off campus. Two, have identified at least one shared interest that isn’t physics. Three, have eaten a meal without discussing work for forty minutes or more. Four, wish to arrange a second date.”

She lowered the pages.

“You’ve written a lesson plan.”

“A date plan.”

“With learning objectives.”

“I thought it would help to be clear about what we hoped to get out of it.”

“Is there an assessment?”

He hesitated. It was a very small hesitation. She saw it.

“Miles. Is there an assessment?”

“Not formally. I’d thought of a short discussion at the end.”

She made a small strangled noise and turned away and put her face in the doorframe for a moment. When she turned back she’d got hold of herself, mostly. She went to her desk, squared the four pages against each other, and began to fold them.

“What are you doing?”

“Improving it.”

She folded them in half lengthways, and then the corners down, and then the edges back, with the brisk confidence of a girl who’d spent most of her childhood in rooms full of adults who wouldn’t notice what she did with the menu. When she’d finished it was a very respectable paper plane.

“I spent some time on that,” he said.

“I can tell. The structure’s good. The timing’s ambitious. The objectives are far too prescriptive and the contingencies are excessive.” She held the plane up and sighted along it at him. “And you’ve made one fundamental mistake.”

“Which is?”

“You forgot to ask me what I wanted to do.”

He was quiet for a second. Then he nodded slowly.

“That’s fair.”

“Thank you.” She opened the window over the street. “Schedule withdrawn?”

“Schedule withdrawn.”

“You’re learning.”

She threw it.

It sailed out over Bell Street on the evening air, beautifully, in a long flat glide, past the tailor’s sign and the streetlamp and down, and in through the open window of the number eleven tram as it went rattling past the corner. Somebody inside gave a shout. A man by the window held up four sheets of folded paper and turned them round and read the front, and his face did something astonishing, and the tram took him away round the bend.

Yu Jie put both hands over her mouth.

Miles stood at her shoulder and watched his evening leave without him.

“It’s going somewhere,” she said, through her fingers.

“Without us.”

“Perhaps it’s got a better offer.”

There was a pause. Then he laughed out loud, at the window, at the empty street, and she turned round and looked at him laughing with such delight that he stopped and kissed her instead, quickly, in the window, where anybody on Bell Street could have seen.

“Come on,” she said, taking his hand. “Before it gets to the next stop and finds someone else to date.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The night market behind the station wasn’t on any of his four pages.

You couldn’t see it from the main road. She led him down a passage between a shuttered pharmacy and a shop that sold phone cases, and then the passage opened out, all at once, into a long crowded lane strung with bare bulbs and lanterns, stall after stall of it, steam going up into the lights. The air was thick with garlic and sesame and frying dough and charcoal smoke. A man was calling out the price of roasted chestnuts. Somebody’s radio was playing a love song older than either of them. Two small boys pushed past with paper cups of cut fruit held up like trophies.

Miles stopped dead.

“Is this the night market?”

“The real one. The one on the main road’s for tourists.”

“And this?”

“This is for people who want to eat.” She towed him into the crowd.

He went without a word of complaint. At the first stall she bought skewers of grilled mushrooms and fed him one. At the second she made him taste a bowl of broth before he was allowed to put anything in it, and stood watching him with her arms folded until he said it was good, and then very good, and then that it was the best thing he’d eaten all year, which she accepted. They shared fried tofu out of a paper boat and a cup of hot sweet soy milk, and something wrapped in a lotus leaf that she refused to name until he’d bitten it.

“What is it?”

“Food.”

“I’d gathered.”

He bought her a paper bag of candied hawthorn, red and glassy on their sticks, and she held the bag out to him.

“You don’t like sweet things.”

“I’ve never said that.”

“You pretend you don’t.”

“I prefer less sweet things.”

“That’s because you haven’t tried enough of them.” She watched him eat one. “Well?”

“Acceptable.”

“Try enthusiastic.”

He ate a second one, with great enthusiasm, looking at her the whole time, and she laughed so much she had to hold onto a lamp post.

Halfway down the lane she saw the dumpling stall and stopped.

It was tiny. A low counter, a stool, and on the stool an old woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and two big enamel bowls in front of her, one of chopped chives and egg and one of minced prawn, a stack of round white wrappers, and a bamboo tray already lined with dumplings so neat they looked machine-made.

“I want to make them,” said Yu Jie.

The old woman looked up at her. “You?” She looked at Miles. “And him?”

“Especially him,” said Yu Jie. “I’ve never seen him do anything with his hands that didn’t involve chalk.”

“I can cook,” said Miles.

“You can heat soup.”

“I’ve made dumplings.”

“How many?”

He considered. “Several.”

“He’s lying,” Yu Jie told the old woman, who laughed out loud and cleared a space on the counter and put two stools in front of it.

“Come on, then. Both of you. Not too much filling. Too much and it bursts in the pot.”

Miles took his coat off and folded it over the stool and listened to her instructions with the face he wore for safety briefings. She put a spoonful of prawn on a wrapper for him and showed him how to fold it. He brought the edges together, pinched, and produced something that looked like a dumpling that had been in a serious accident.

The old woman leaned over to look at it, and laughed till she wheezed.

“That’s one.”

“It’s sealed,” said Miles.

“It’s ugly,” said Yu Jie.

“It’s functional.”

“Not everything functional is beautiful.”

He gave her a look. She gave him a beautiful one back.

The second was better. The third was worse. By the fifth he’d understood the principle and his pleats still ran off in different directions like frightened sheep. By the seventh Yu Jie was laughing so much she had to put both hands flat on the counter.

“Stop laughing.”

“I can’t.”

“It’s distracting.”

“I’m so sorry.”

“You aren’t.”

“No.”

“Your husband’s very serious,” the old woman said to her.

Yu Jie nearly dropped her wrapper. “He’s not my—“

“Not yet,” said Miles, without looking up from dumpling eight.

The stall went quiet around her. Even the steam seemed to stop for a moment. The old woman glanced at him, and smiled to herself, and went back to her own folding as if she hadn’t heard a thing.

“Not yet?” Yu Jie whispered.

He did look up then. “Would you rather I’d said no?”

She looked down at her hands very fast.

“No.”

“Then it seemed the more accurate answer.”

Her face was burning. Dumpling nine tore. Ten was nearly respectable. Eleven had too much filling and split down one side the moment he pinched it, and he looked at it with such open disappointment that she leaned over.

“Give it here.”

“I can do it.”

“I know you can.”

She took a fresh wrapper and a little water from the bowl and put the filling in, and then she put his hands round hers. His fingers were warm and much bigger than hers. She laid her thumbs over his, on the dough.

“Not so hard. You’re pressing too much.”

“I’m trying to make it secure.”

“You’re trying to make it survive an earthquake.” She moved his thumb. “There. Hold. Turn it a little. Now pinch.”

The dough folded under their four hands and held.

They both looked down at it. It wasn’t perfect. It was, unmistakably, a dumpling.

“Twelve,” she said.

He looked at it. Then at her. He was smiling in a way she’d seen once before, by a dark tank, in a photograph he’d sent her at midnight.

“It’s acceptable,” he said.

“It’s lovely.”

“It’s uneven.”

“It’s handmade, Dr. Wei. You’re allowed to be proud of one dumpling.”

“I am,” he said, and the old woman took it from them and laid it on the tray with her own, among all the perfect ones, as if it belonged.

She dropped the whole tray into the boiling pot. They stood and waited by the counter with the steam on their faces. Yu Jie leaned against his shoulder, and he put his hand at the small of her back, and his thumb moved once against the cotton.

“You keep her,” the old woman said to him.

She said it the way she might have told him to mind the steam. Yu Jie felt him go still. She looked up at him and didn’t tease, for once. She just waited to see what he’d do with it.

He didn’t look away from her.

“I’m going to,” he said.

The old woman nodded, once, satisfied, and fished the dumplings out.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate them at a folding table beside the stall with black vinegar and a dish of chilli oil. She put a great deal of chilli on hers. He put on a little. She reached over and put a great deal more on his.

“Is this an experiment?”

“Yes.”

“What are we measuring?”

“How much you trust me.”

“That’s a dangerous method.”

“Only if you don’t.”

He ate it. He chewed. He swallowed. Then he reached for his water and drank all of it, and she laughed until there were tears on her face.

“You’re meant to build up a tolerance.”

“That isn’t how capsaicin works.”

When they got up, the old woman waved away the money Yu Jie tried to give her for the lesson.

“Come again,” she said. Then, to Miles: “Practise. And next time bring her.”

“I mean to,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The market thinned out behind them as they walked back towards the station. The shops on the side streets had their shutters down. They turned into a narrow lane lit by one yellow lamp over a doorway, beside a tailor’s with a deep green shutter and a faded sign, and he was listening to her tell him about a woman at the bakery that morning who’d ordered six loaves and then sworn she’d only asked for three, when she stopped talking.

“What?” he said.

“I was thinking that this is our first date.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t bring a lesson plan.”

“I did. It’s on the number eleven.”

“It’s probably met someone by now.”

“I hope they’ll be very happy.” He lifted their joined hands and put his mouth to her knuckles. “Did you enjoy it?”

She looked at him in the lamplight. There was nothing left of the man with the folder. Just Miles, in a quiet street, holding her hand, waiting for an answer as if it mattered more than anything he’d been asked in a seminar.

“Yes,” she said. “Did you?”

“Yes.”

“Even though the schedule was abandoned?”

“Because of it.” He tucked a strand of hair behind her ear. “I liked seeing you somewhere you weren’t waiting for anything. Not office hours. Not a defence. Not a date in a corner of my board.”

“I liked seeing you be bad at something.”

“I’m not usually bad at things.”

“I know. That’s why it was so interesting.” She touched his cuff, where there was still, somehow, a little chalk from that morning. “You looked so serious. You were trying to make the perfect dumpling.”

“There’s nothing wrong with wanting to do a thing properly.”

“No. But sometimes you can just make something with somebody.”

His face changed. He put his hand on her cheek.

Then he kissed her, there in the lane, and the green shutter was cool and ridged behind her back. Far off she could hear the last of the market packing up, plates being stacked, someone calling a price for whatever was left. He kissed her slowly, with one hand on her face and the other spread at her waist, as if the night were a long one and he meant to use all of it. When he drew back she went after him a little way, not willing to let it end.

“Still enjoying the date?” he said against her forehead.

“I’m considering it. There’s room for improvement.”

“I’ll take it under advisement.”

She caught the front of his coat and kissed him again, harder, and this time he laughed into her mouth.

They stayed until the lamp over the doorway flickered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bakery was dark when they got to Bell Street. Shu Mei had left the shop light on and a note taped inside the glass in black marker: Y.J. Lock the BACK door. And stop giving the good pastries away.

“I don’t give the good pastries away,” said Yu Jie.

“You gave me one yesterday.”

“You’re not away.”

She let herself in and put the chestnuts he’d bought her on the counter and came back out, and he was waiting on the step, under her lit window.

“Well,” she said.

“Well.”

“Thank you for dinner. And the dumplings.”

“You made most of them.”

“You made twelve.”

“Eleven and a half. One was structurally compromised.” He hesitated. “I’ll prepare a revised plan for next time.”

“Don’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because I want to see what you come up with when you haven’t prepared anything.”

“That’s much harder.”

“I know.” She stepped down onto the step below his so that their faces were level. “Goodnight, Miles.”

He seemed to expect her to go in. She took hold of his lapels instead and kissed him.

It wasn’t hurried, and it wasn’t one of her teasing ones, meant to make his ears go red. She kissed him the way you sign something you mean. When she let go, his hand was still at her waist.

“Was that part of the assessment?” he said.

“No.”

“Then what was it?”

“My answer.”

He understood. She watched it reach his eyes and stay there.

“Then I think the date went well,” he said.

She kissed him once more, quickly, and went in, and he stood on the step until he heard the attic door shut two floors up. Then he turned for home. His phone buzzed before he’d reached the corner.

Ling Hao: Zeng Bo says you took her on a date

Miles: Yes.

Ling Hao: Did you make a schedule

He stopped under the streetlamp and looked back up at her window.

Miles: Four pages.

Ling Hao: I KNEW IT

Ling Hao: did she reject it

Miles: She folded it into a plane and it got on a tram.

Ling Hao: HAHAHAHAHAHA. Shu Mei’s crying

He thought of the old woman’s stall, and Yu Jie’s thumbs on his over dumpling twelve, and you keep her.

Miles: I think I’ll let her plan the next one.

Ling Hao: smartest thing you’ve done all year

He put his phone away and walked home in the warm dark, smiling at nobody, like a fool.

chapters.title: Holding Hands in Public
chapters.desc: Across the campus in July, past the canteen, the library café and the department kitchen. He keeps checking whether anyone is looking. Everyone is. Then a society photographer gets the picture the forum never did.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you don’t have to protect me from people looking at us.”
chapters.content:
The first time Miles let go of her hand, they were passing the canteen.

It was the first Monday in July, and the campus had gone into its summer rhythm: summer-school students, doctoral students crossing between laboratories with coffee, staff with folders, a few undergraduates who hadn’t noticed the term was over. Yu Jie was telling him about her argument with Shu Mei over the shop window.

“She says the custard buns go at the front because they sell best. I say the sesame rolls, because they’re prettier.”

“Which sells more?”

“Custard buns.”

“Then Shu Mei’s right.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I’m on the side of the sales data.”

“I’m going out with the wrong man.”

Their fingers were laced together. Two second-years came out of the canteen doors as they went by, and one of them looked at Miles, and then at their hands, and then at Miles again, with his eyebrows climbing, and Yu Jie felt Miles’s fingers loosen.

She tightened hers before he could take his hand away.

“Don’t,” she said, looking straight ahead.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“You were going to.”

The students went past. He was quiet for a few steps.

“I’m sorry.”

“For what?”

“I don’t know.” He looked down at her. “Habit.”

She stopped walking, and lifted their joined hands a little between them like evidence.

“Miles. I’ve graduated. I was a graduate yesterday. I’ll be a graduate tomorrow. It’s not going to wear off.”

“I understand the distinction.”

“Then you don’t have to protect me from people looking at us.”

His thumb moved over her knuckles.

The second time was outside the library café. The third was by the department kitchen, when he saw Zeng Bo through the glass and her hand slipped out of his as if it had been greased.

She stopped. He turned round.

“Again?”

“Zeng Bo.”

“Zeng Bo is holding a sandwich. Was he going to attack us with it?”

She held her hand out. He looked at it. The corridor was bright and full: somebody pinning a poster to the board, somebody shouting at the printer, a lecturer going past under a stack of scripts. Miles took her hand, and this time he kept it, and they walked on down the corridor and straight into Mr. Pei.

Mr. Pei ran the department office. He had run it for twenty-three years, through four heads of department and a flood, and he knew where every form and every body was buried. He stopped dead with a folder in his arms and looked at their hands, and a slow, enormous smile spread over his face.

“Well,” he said. “At last.”

“Good morning, Mr. Pei,” said Miles warily.

“I did wonder how long it would take you.” Mr. Pei shifted his folder. “You know there were seven pools.”

Miles went very still. “Seven what?”

“Betting pools, Dr. Wei. On the pair of you.” Mr. Pei counted them off on the corner of his folder with evident pleasure. “Whether you were. When you’d admit it. Whether Miss Shen would ever stop bringing you problems she’d already solved. The Wednesday office hours, separately. The gala, separately. Whether you’d ever be seen holding her hand in this building. And whether you’d ever smile on the fourth floor without looking as if you’d just found a sign error in somebody’s thesis.”

Yu Jie had both hands over her face.

“Who organised these?” said Miles.

“I’m an administrator, Dr. Wei. I don’t involve myself in that sort of thing.” Mr. Pei tucked the folder under his arm. “I merely know where the forms are. Congratulations. It’s very nice to see you both.”

He went off down the corridor humming.

“Seven,” said Miles.

“I think we should be proud. We’ve been a reliable source of entertainment for a whole year.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

She lifted his hand and kissed his knuckles. He looked at her. And then, there in the corridor, he turned her hand over and kissed the middle of her palm, and folded her fingers closed over the place, and walked on holding it.

She went pink to her collarbones and didn’t say a word all the way to the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday afternoon she kissed him in the lift.

She’d come up with two paper cups of jasmine tea and found him coming out of a meeting with Cen, and they got into the lift on the fourth floor together, and nobody else did. She pressed the button for the ground floor. The doors shut. She looked at the little numbers going down above the door.

“Do you know what I’ve just realised? This is the first time I’ve ever stood in a lift with you without listening for someone getting in.”

“That’s true.”

“It’s rather nice.”

She put the cups down on the floor, went up on her toes and kissed him.

His hand came to her waist. The lift went past three, and past two. When she drew back she looked up at the numbers.

“We’ve missed the third floor.”

“We’re going down.”

“I know,” she said, and kissed him again, and when the doors opened on the ground floor she was still kissing him, with one hand flat on his chest and his hand spread across her back, and a boy with a bicycle helmet under his arm was standing outside staring at them both.

“Sorry,” said the boy.

Miles reached past her, quite calmly, and held the doors. “Go ahead.”

The boy got in and stood very close to the wall and looked at the ceiling. When he got out on the first floor he turned round and said, with tremendous courage, “Congratulations, Dr. Wei.”

“On what?” said Miles.

The boy panicked. “The... graduation?”

“Thank you,” said Miles, and the doors closed on Yu Jie laughing against the lift wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday they lay on the lawn behind the library.

It was hot and bright, with a breeze moving the plane trees. Students lay scattered across the grass reading, or talking, or asleep with their bags under their heads. Yu Jie lay on her back with her head in his lap. He’d brought a book. He hadn’t turned a page in twenty minutes.

“You’re watching me,” she said, without opening her eyes.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re there.”

“That’s not a very sophisticated explanation.”

“It’s accurate.” He closed the book and put it down on the grass.

“What are you doing?”

“Taking a break from pretending to read.”

He bent over her. He brushed a strand of hair off her forehead with one finger and traced the line of her temple and her cheek, slowly, the way he’d follow a curve on a page. Then he kissed her mouth, barely, the lightest touch. Then her cheek. Her jaw. Then the place just under her ear.

She went perfectly still.

He stopped. “All right?”

She nodded. He did it again. Her fingers closed in his shirt.

“That’s unfair,” she whispered.

“What is?”

“You’ve found something.”

“What have I found?”

She turned her face away into his leg, smiling, scarlet. He kissed the same place again, very slowly, and she made a small sound she’d never made in public in her life and put both hands over her face.

“Too much?”

“No.” She looked at him between her fingers. “You look so serious doing it.”

“Would you like me to look less serious?”

“I’d like you to stop looking at me.”

“That’s difficult. You’re right here.”

She took his hand from her cheek and kissed his fingertips, one by one, and then held it against her mouth.

“Do it again,” she said. “Not here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat, that evening, was warm and smelt of the oranges in the bowl on the table, which seemed to refill themselves however many she ate. He made tea. She didn’t drink it. She sat on his sofa with her legs under her and watched him across the room until he asked what she was doing.

“Observing.”

“What’s the difference between that and staring?”

“Observing’s scientific. Staring’s romantic.” She held out her arms. “Come here.”

He came. She pulled him down beside her and then didn’t let him stay beside her. She climbed into his lap with her knees either side of him and took his glasses off and put them on the arm of the sofa, and he looked up at her with his naked, short-sighted eyes and said her name like a question.

“You found something on the lawn,” she said. “Find it again.”

He found it. He took his time. He kissed her throat and under her ear and the hollow of her collarbone, with his hands spread on her back under her shirt, until she was holding onto his shoulders and couldn’t keep still. Every time he asked, she said yes. Every time she said yes he went slower, out of pure wickedness, until she pulled his head up by his hair and kissed him so hard the sofa creaked.

They never made it to the bedroom. The sofa was too short and the cushions went onto the floor and so, after a while, did they, laughing, tangled up in his shirt, and then not laughing at all, her skirt pushed up and his trousers kicked off, and when he moved inside her on the rug she hooked her ankles behind his back and held him there. The window was open. The evening came in warm over the sill with the sound of somebody’s radio in the next block, and the light went orange and then blue, and neither of them noticed it go. When it was over she lay on his chest on the rug with the cushions round them like a collapsed fort, and he traced the place under her ear with one finger, very lightly, and she shivered all over and told him he was never to tell anybody about it.

“Who would I tell?”

“Ling Hao. Zeng Bo. Mr. Pei. He’d open a pool.”

He laughed, and she lay listening to it in his chest. “I used to count Wednesdays,” she said. “I thought when the date came, everything would be easy.”

“And is it?”

“Not everything. This is.”

He kissed the top of her head.

“Do you still worry? When people see us?”

“Sometimes. Habit.”

“Then we’ll have to practise.”

“Practise what?”

“Being seen,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday morning Professor Cen found Miles in front of the noticeboard, reading the summer-school timetable for the third time without taking any of it in.

“Getting used to being a public man?”

Miles looked at him. “I’m not sure what you mean.”

“Mr. Pei has told me about the seven betting pools,” said Cen. “And that you kissed Miss Shen’s hand outside the canteen. And that a first-year in the lift congratulated you on graduating.”

“Is there some reason the whole department is discussing my hands?”

“Because for a year you behaved as if holding hers would bring down the building.” Cen looked at the noticeboard with him. “You were right to be careful, Miles. You were right to write that letter, and to make sure every part of her degree was beyond question. But she’s graduated. You’re not responsible for her future in this department, because she hasn’t got one in it. You can stop treating every corridor as if it’s a disciplinary hearing.” He turned to go. “You’re allowed.”

“Allowed what?”

“Go and kiss your girlfriend, Dr. Wei,” said Cen over his shoulder, and walked off down the corridor in his camel coat with the air of a man who had settled something.

Miles found her on the lawn under the big plane tree, flat on her back with a book over her face against the sun.

“Hello,” she said, from under the book.

“Hello.”

“What happened? You look strange.”

“Cen told me something.”

She sat up. “What?”

He held out his hand and pulled her to her feet, and before she could ask again he bent and put one arm behind her knees and the other behind her back and swung her up off the grass. She shrieked. He turned her, carefully, so that for a moment her head was lower than his and her hair fell down towards the lawn and her upside-down face was right in front of his, and he kissed her like that, in the middle of the grass, in full view of the library windows.

When he set her right way up she was laughing so much she had to hold onto him.

“What was that?”

“My answer to Cen.”

Three students had stopped reading. One of them was openly applauding.

She straightened his collar for him. “You’re improving.”

“Am I?”

“Very fast,” she said, and he took her hand and walked her back to the building without once looking round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the university’s research office gave a reception at the Harbour Hotel, and Miles was asked to say five minutes about the new laboratory. Yu Jie went as his guest, in cream, with her grandmother’s earrings.

Half the room were trustees and donors. A good many were people she knew from her mother’s dinners. One of them was Mr. Huo, who had been the third man in her mother’s line at the gala and the first, years ago, when she was nineteen. He found her by the windows while Miles was surrounded.

“Shen Yu Jie. You’ve grown up.” He smiled. “I hear you’ve been spending time with Dr. Wei.”

“Yes.”

“An interesting choice. Your mother must be terribly disappointed.”

“My mother and I disagree about my life.”

“Families often do. But they generally know best.” He laughed indulgently. “You’re young. You may feel differently in a few years.”

Miles was beside her before she’d answered. He didn’t hurry. He simply arrived, close enough that his shoulder touched hers, and put his hand flat at the small of her back.

“Good evening.”

“Dr. Wei. I was congratulating Miss Shen. I do hope you understand the complications of this arrangement.”

“I’m not sure which arrangement you mean.” Miles’s voice didn’t change at all. “Whatever complications there are, I expect Yu Jie will deal with them as she sees fit. She doesn’t need anyone to speak for her. Least of all me.”

It was very quiet and very polite, and it changed the air between the three of them completely. Mr. Huo excused himself.

“You didn’t need rescuing,” Miles said when he’d gone.

“I know.”

“I only wanted you to know I was there.”

“I did know.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it, in the middle of the trustees, and didn’t look to see who’d noticed.

At nine they came out onto the wide pale steps above the harbour, and she stopped halfway down.

“I used to be so careful how I looked beside anyone,” she said. “In case it upset her. In case people talked. In case I made trouble for somebody.” She looked up at him. “I’m tired of letting other people decide what my life looks like. Also, you’re very handsome.”

“That was an unexpected conclusion.”

“It’s an important one.”

She kissed him. It was meant to be a small kiss. It wasn’t, once his hand came up along her jaw. Neither of them heard the shutter on the other side of the road until it clicked a second time.

A young man with a camera lowered it. “Sorry! Harbour Daily. We’re covering the reception.” He recognised her. “Miss Shen. I can delete it if you’d like.”

Miles looked at her and didn’t answer for her.

“Keep it,” said Yu Jie.

It ran on page six on Monday, under a piece about summer research. PHYSICIST AND GRADUATE AT THE HARBOUR HOTEL. His hand along her jaw, her fingers in the front of his jacket, the water a blur of lights behind them. It was a very good photograph.

Tao Tao: GOOD MORNING CELEBRITY

Tao Tao: PAGE SIX

Tao Tao: HE LOOKS LIKE HE’S FORGOTTEN HIS OWN NAME

By ten, Ling Hao had printed it and stuck it to the door of 412. Miles took it down. Ling Hao put it back.

Miles bought two copies. He kept one in his desk drawer, with her notes. The other he posted to his parents, with a card that said only I thought you’d like to see this.

His mother rang on Wednesday while he was in the basement, adjusting a pump.

“Miles,” she said, and her voice wasn’t steady.

“Ma? What’s wrong?”

“Nothing’s wrong.” She made a small sound. “Your father’s read it four times. He says it’s a very well-composed photograph.” Another sound. “You look happy, son.”

He put his hand on the edge of the bench.

“I am.”

His mother began to cry. Quietly, not unhappily, as though she’d been holding something for a very long time and had finally been allowed to put it down.

“I haven’t seen you look like that in a picture since you were sixteen,” she said. “When can we meet her?”

“Soon.”

“Don’t make her wait. And you’d better know your sister’s already rung. She’s having her for dinner in August. She says she has questions.”

“I’m sure she does.”

“Are you happy, Miles?” said his mother again, as if she needed to hear it twice.

He looked at the photograph of the photograph on his phone. Yu Jie smiling against his mouth, one hand in his lapel.

“Yes, Ma,” he said. “I’m happy.”

chapters.title: Yu Jie Gets a Job
chapters.desc: A research assistant post in the capital, five hours north. He asks her what she wants, and makes himself listen to the answer. Then the last night of August, the door of the staff flat, and a question he asks at every step.
chapters.epigraph: “Then it’ll be hard.”
chapters.content:
The offer came on the last Thursday of July, in the middle of the morning rush.

Yu Jie felt her phone go under the till and ignored it. A man wanted two sesame rolls and a custard bun. A woman wanted to know whether the sourdough was today’s. From the kitchen Shu Mei was announcing that whoever had moved her good knife was going to be sorry they’d ever been born. By the time the queue had gone, Yu Jie had forgotten the phone altogether. It was nearly eleven when she looked.

It was from Dr. Mao.

She read it once, and then again, and then sat down on the little stool behind the counter.

A research post in his group in the capital, for one year, from September, with the chance of more. Paid, properly. Her own corners, extended to whole families of stretched lattices, on a real computer cluster, with her name on the paper that came out of it. At the end he’d written: At your defence you showed me that you know not only how to get a result but when to distrust the assumptions that gave it to you. I’d be glad to have you.

She read that sentence several times.

She should have been excited. She was excited. Underneath it was something else she didn’t want to look at.

The capital was five hours north by train. Five hours from Bell Street. From the till, and the attic with the beam, and Tao Tao, and the fourth floor. From him.

She locked the phone and put it in her apron pocket and went back to the counter.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell him that evening. Or on Friday, or Saturday. She told herself she needed to think first. On Sunday she decided she’d tell him after dinner. On Monday she decided she’d better speak to Dr. Mao again first.

On Tuesday Shu Mei found her staring at a tray of bread that was already arranged.

“What’s the matter with you?”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve put the custard buns in with the sesame rolls. That’s how I know.” Shu Mei wiped her hands on her apron. “Is it the boy?”

“No.”

“Money?”

“No.”

“Work, then.” Shu Mei folded her arms. “Ah.”

So Yu Jie told her, all of it, to the cloth she was using on a counter that was already clean.

“And you’re looking at that cloth as if it insulted your mother,” said Shu Mei. “What does he say?”

Yu Jie stopped wiping.

“I haven’t told him.”

Shu Mei stared at her.

“I don’t know what I want yet. I don’t want him to think I’m asking him to decide.”

“Then don’t ask him to decide. Tell him.” Shu Mei took the cloth out of her hand. “Listen to me. You’ve had people tell you what to do your whole life, and now you’d rather drive yourself off a cliff than let anybody near the wheel. I understand. But letting a man sit beside you in the car isn’t the same as giving him the keys.” She threw the cloth into the sink. “Go and tell him. Now. I’ll do the till.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The basement was half dark. The tank was half full, and a technician was on his knees at the far side with a torch in his mouth, doing something to a pump. The work lamps put thin, shaking lines of light across the water and up the clear walls, and Miles was at the control desk reading numbers off a screen.

He looked up when he heard her on the stairs, and saw her face, and put the tablet down.

“What’s happened?”

“Why does something have to have happened?”

“Because you’ve been standing on the bottom step for thirty seconds without saying anything.”

“Perhaps I like looking at you.”

“I’d be delighted if that were the reason.”

She laughed, not very well, and came down the last step and stood in front of him.

“Dr. Mao’s offered me a job. A research post in his group. A year, from September.” She swallowed. “It’s in the capital.”

His face changed, a little. Only a little.

“When did he offer it?”

“Thursday.”

She saw him take in the five days and not say anything about them.

“That’s excellent,” he said. “His group’s very strong, and it’s your own work. Did he send the details?”

“It’s five hours away, Miles.”

“Yes.”

The pump at the far side came on with a low hum. A small wave went out across the tank and slapped softly against the wall.

He didn’t ask whether she’d take it. He didn’t tell her to stay. He didn’t tell her five hours was too far, or not far at all.

“What do you think?” he said.

“I don’t know.”

“Do you want it?”

“I think so.”

“Tell me why.”

“Because the work’s interesting. Because I want to know if the corners can turn into something bigger than a thesis. Because I want to learn to do research properly, not because somebody’s given me a deadline.” She looked at the water. “And because I think I’d be good at it.”

“I think you would be very good at it,” he said, without a moment’s pause. “You’re patient with numerical work. You know the minute an approximation stops being useful. You don’t mind being wrong if it gets you nearer the answer. That’s most of what research is.”

“I’d miss you.”

He took her hand.

“I’d miss you too. But I don’t want you to turn down something you want because you’re frightened of what the distance might do to us.”

“I didn’t come down here to make you tell me to go.”

“I know.”

“Or to stay.”

“I know. You came to tell me.” He lifted her hand and kissed her fingers. “Thank you for telling me.”

She looked at him, and her eyes had gone bright. “That’s all?”

“Would you like more?”

“Yes.”

“I’m proud of you,” he said. “I’m glad somebody with a microscope has seen what you can do.” He held her hand against his chest. “And I would like you to stay here. I like you being near. I like the bakery and the evenings and the mornings you come down those stairs with two cups and tell me I’ve forgotten to eat. I like knowing I might see you on the way to work. But I’m not going to let liking it turn into an instruction.”

“And if I go?”

“Then we’ll work out how to see each other.”

“And if it’s hard?”

“Then it’ll be hard.”

“And if you get tired of trains?”

“I’ll tell you.”

“And if I get lonely—“

“Yu Jie.” He brought her hand up to his mouth. “We don’t have to solve every possible problem before you decide.”

“You always want to solve everything.”

“It’s a professional weakness.”

“It’s a personal one.”

She laughed, with her eyes still wet, and then she put her face into his chest. He wrapped both arms round her and held her there by the half-full tank while the pump hummed.

“I thought you’d be upset,” she said into his shirt.

“I am.”

She pulled back to look at him.

“I’m upset that five hours is going to feel like a very long way,” he said. “I’m not upset with you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They settled it in small pieces over the next fortnight, the way you put up a shelf. The post began on the second of September. The institute had a graduate residence with a room she could have until Christmas while she found her feet. Tao Tao sent forty-one photographs of rooms in the capital, all of them unsuitable. Shu Mei said the till would be there whenever she came home. Wei Lan, at the dinner she’d been threatening since July, fed Yu Jie four courses in a small hot flat full of children’s drawings and asked her thirty-one questions, and at the end of the evening took her into the kitchen and said, very low, “He sent us that photograph in a card with one line on it. He hasn’t sent us anything in a card since he was sixteen,” and hugged her so hard her ribs creaked.

And Miles made a list.

It started on a sheet of graph paper beside his computer: Trains. Departure times, both ways. Return times. Every weekend between September and Christmas. Then he checked the timetable again.

On the second Friday of August a photograph came through on her phone.

White Rabbit: 4 September. 18:20. Here to there.

Yu Jie: What’s this?

White Rabbit: A train ticket.

Yu Jie: I can see it’s a train ticket.

White Rabbit: Then we’re making progress.

White Rabbit: And 11 September, the other way, so you can come home.

She rang him. He answered on the first ring.

“How many have you booked?”

“Until Christmas.”

There was a silence.

“All of them?”

“All the ones that exist. Every other weekend one way, the others the other way. They can be changed if your work needs it. I’ve put them in a timetable.” He paused. “Would you like to see the timetable?”

She sat down on the edge of the attic bed with the phone against her ear, laughing, with a catch in it.

“You don’t have to do this. It’s expensive.”

“I budgeted.”

“Since when?”

“Since the basement.” His voice was quite calm. “I don’t know how often we’ll manage once you start. I thought it would be easier to secure the weekends first and change them afterwards than to try to find them later.”

“You made a timetable for missing me.”

“I did.”

“Of course you did,” she said, and then couldn’t say anything else.

“Yu Jie?”

“Send me the timetable,” she said. “I want to put it on my wall.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The last night of August came in with rain.

She’d spent the day five hours north, carrying boxes into a narrow bright room in the institute residence with a desk under the window and a row of trees outside. On the desk she put two photographs: herself and Tao Tao at graduation, and page six of the Harbour Daily, which she’d printed herself on the bakery’s printer.

Then she got the seven o’clock train back south, because her first day wasn’t until Wednesday and she wasn’t going to spend her last night anywhere but one place.

Yu Jie: On the train. Coming to yours.

White Rabbit: I’ll leave the light on.

Yu Jie: I’ve got a key.

White Rabbit: I know.

Yu Jie: So why leave the light on?

White Rabbit: So you’ll know I’m waiting.

It was after midnight when she let herself in. The lamp was on by the sofa. There was food on the kitchen counter under a plate, and a jam jar of yellow chrysanthemums on the table, which was so unlike him that she stood in the doorway and looked at them.

He came out of the bedroom in a soft grey T-shirt, barefoot, and they looked at each other across the room.

She put her bag down. He crossed the room and took her in his arms. He kissed her hair, and then her forehead, and then her mouth, and then he just held her, with his face in her neck.

“Long day?”

“Very.”

“Have you eaten?”

“On the train. It was awful.”

“I made something. It’s less awful.” He drew back and looked at her. “Are you staying?”

“The whole night,” she said. “I’m not going anywhere till the morning train. I want to wake up here.”

They ate late, at his little table with the cardboard under the leg: noodles, greens, braised tofu he’d learned from Shu Mei, which was better than anything he’d made before and which she told him so about three times. She told him about the residence, and the woman next door who’d already asked her to join a running club.

“What if I’m not good enough?” she said, putting her chopsticks down.

“Then you’ll learn.”

“What if I make mistakes?”

“You will.”

“Miles.”

“Everybody does. You’ll find them, and fix them, and understand why they happened. That’s the job.” He reached across and took her hand. “And you won’t have to do any of it on your own. Even from five hours away.”

She held on.

“Can we not talk about tomorrow for a while?” she said. “Can we just be here?”

“Yes.”

He took her to bed. There was no hurry in it. He asked before everything, and she answered before he’d finished. He undressed her slowly in the lamplight, and kissed the place under her ear until she pulled his shirt off over his head and tangled her fingers in his hair. He kissed his way down her body and stayed between her thighs until she was gripping the sheet, and when he came up over her and into her the rain came down hard on the window and then softer. She held his face in both hands at one point and looked at him, just looked, for so long that he asked what she was doing, and she said she was memorising, and he said she’d see him on Friday, and she said she knew and was memorising anyway. Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest, and his heart under her ear went slowly back to normal, and his hand moved up and down her spine.

“Are you awake?”

“Yes.”

“Of course you are.”

“Would you like me to pretend?”

“No. I like knowing you’re awake.”

For the first time since Dr. Mao’s email, she let herself think about the morning without trying to make it less frightening. She’d wake up here. They’d have breakfast. She’d go. And he’d still be here when she came back. It wasn’t the same as staying. It was something.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, he tried to make her eggs.

He’d left the pan to answer the technician about a pump, and by the time she came into the kitchen in his shirt the bottom had welded itself to the metal.

She stopped in the doorway. “Did the eggs have a thermal event?”

“Possibly.”

“They’re very dark.”

“I’d noticed.”

“I’ll make another lot.”

“No. I want those.” She took a fork and cut a corner and ate it, and her face did several things in a row. “Interesting.”

“That’s not encouraging.”

“They’ve got character.”

“They’re burnt.”

“They’ve got a great deal of character,” she said. Then she put the fork down on the counter, and looked at him, standing at his own stove in his T-shirt with a ruined pan in his hand and his hair on end, and said, for no reason at all, “I love you.”

He went still.

He’d heard it before. She’d said it to him in her flat in February, with her mouth still bruised from the glass room, and he’d said it back. But that had been in the middle of something, forced out by a letter and a fear and a day that had gone off like a bomb. This had nothing in it. No crisis, no question. Just burnt eggs and a Tuesday’s worth of rain on the window. She’d simply wanted him to know.

“I love you too,” he said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes. I’m learning from you.”

He reached across the counter and took her hand and kissed her fingertips, and then he said it, the thing from the board, very quietly.

“For all n.”

She laughed, and her eyes filled, both at once.

“For all n,” she said.

He made toast.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first of September was bright and clear. He carried her bag to the station. They were early, and she bought a coffee and didn’t drink it, and he stood beside her watching the departures board turn over.

At eight minutes past nine they called her train.

“I don’t want to go,” she said.

“I know.”

“I want the job.”

“I know.”

“I don’t want to leave you.”

“You’re not leaving me. You’re going to work.” He kissed her forehead. “Go and do the work you want. I’ll come up on Friday. You’ll come home the week after. We’ll have dinner and I’ll complain about the timetable and you’ll tell me I’m being dramatic.”

“You are dramatic.”

“Occasionally.”

She got on. He stood on the platform. She found him through the window straight away, and he lifted his hand, and the doors began to close.

Then, with the doors halfway shut, she stepped back out.

“Yu Jie—“

She caught his face and kissed him. Somebody on the train laughed.

“That’s two,” she said, breathless.

“I counted.”

She kissed him once more, quickly. “That one’s for the week.”

“Understood.”

She got back on. This time the doors shut and she stayed behind them, and he stood on the platform till the train had gone round the bend and there was nothing left to look at.

Twenty minutes north of the city she opened her book on the tray table, and a small yellow square fell out of it into her lap. It was folded once. Inside, in his handwriting, in brackets, as if it were a footnote to something he’d already proved:

(I love you.)

She turned it over. There was nothing on the back.

Yu Jie: I found your note.

White Rabbit: Good.

Yu Jie: You could have just said it.

White Rabbit: I did. I wanted you to have it in writing.

She took a photograph of it on her open palm and sent it to him.

Yu Jie: I’m keeping this.

White Rabbit: I hoped you would.

Outside, the city was thinning into fields and low hills. She looked at the yellow square a little longer, and then she put it in her purse, in the little pocket behind her card, where he kept a sweet wrapper in his.

chapters.title: Long Distance Is Just a Variable
chapters.desc: The 18:20 and the 21:10. Calls at midnight. A whiteboard screwed to his kitchen wall. A storm, a cancelled train, a handsome postdoc, and a black hole made of water that finally holds.
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to be the first thing you saw.”
chapters.content:
By October, Miles had a relationship with the railway timetable.

He knew the 18:20 north on a Friday was usually on time and the 21:10 south on a Sunday was usually full. He knew the coffee at the station café got worse after eight, and which carriage stopped nearest the barrier at the other end. He knew she liked the window seat, and bought a carton of milk tea before every journey, and would forget to eat anything proper if her Friday ran late. Every other Friday he took the 18:20 up to her. Every other Friday she took it down to him. He kept a record of it in a small black notebook.

2 October. 18:20, twenty-three minutes late. She was waiting at the south exit in the blue scarf.

16 October. On time. Noodles by her residence. She said the new group is better than she feared.

30 October. Signal failure. She’d bought two coffees and drunk both by the time I got there.

He didn’t need to keep it. He had the tickets and the calendar. But on the inside cover he’d written Distance: about 480 km, and underneath, smaller, not a useful measure, and once he’d started he found he didn’t want to stop.

Ling Hao found it one Wednesday in the basement, picking up the wrong notebook off the bench while he was looking for calibration records.

“Wei. Are you keeping a railway diary?”

“It’s a travel record.”

“Of your romantic suffering?” Ling Hao turned a page and read aloud. “She laughed when the coffee machine made a noise like a goose.”

“Give that back.”

“She fell asleep on my shoulder before the taxi came. I didn’t wake her.” Ling Hao held it out of reach. “Most people just take photographs.”

Miles took it back. He thought about the question, because it was a real one under the teasing.

“I don’t want to forget the ordinary parts,” he said.

Ling Hao’s face softened. Then, because he was Ling Hao, he said, “That’s disgusting,” and went back upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it herself in a restaurant by the station in the capital, going through his coat pocket for his mints, and read three pages before he could stop her. Then she gave it back and leaned across the table and kissed him, in the middle of the restaurant, with the waiter standing there holding their bill.

“What was that for?”

“For the ordinary parts,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By November the capital had turned cold, and she was still in the light coat she’d brought up in September, which she insisted was perfectly adequate. He disagreed. He disagreed a great deal more when he came out of the barrier on the second Friday of the month and found her waiting under the canopy hunched over a paper cup of tea, with her shoulders up round her ears.

“That isn’t warm enough.”

“Hello to you too.”

“Hello.” He kissed her. Then he took a big paper bag out of his holdall.

“What have you bought?”

“A coat.”

“For who?”

“For you. It’s cold.”

“I’ve got a coat.”

“You’ve got something shaped like a coat.”

It was long and soft and charcoal, with a deep warm lining and a wide collar, plain and beautifully made, exactly what she’d have chosen herself if she’d still been willing to spend money on herself. She took off the old one and put it on, there on the concourse, and before she could reach for the buttons he’d reached for them.

He did them up one at a time, from the collar down, the way he’d once done up her cardigan in November in office 412 with his face perfectly serious and his ears scarlet. His knuckles brushed her collarbone. He turned the collar up round her neck and settled it.

“Too tight?”

“No.”

“Can you move?”

She lifted both arms. People were walking round them. She didn’t care.

“You’ve bought me something expensive.”

“It’s warm.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the relevant property.”

She laughed, and took his hand inside her new sleeve. “Now I have to buy you something you don’t need.”

“That’s not a sensible use of money.”

“It’s a romantic use of money.”

He considered that.

“Then I accept,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Friday it was her turn to come south, and her train was late. Then later. A run at the institute had gone unstable near a boundary at four o’clock and she’d stayed to chase it, and missed the 18:20, and caught the 19:40, and the 19:40 sat outside a junction for an hour for reasons nobody explained.

It was after midnight when she came through the barrier. The concourse was nearly empty. A cleaner was going round with a trolley. And on a bench by the departures board, in his coat, with two paper cups of tea gone cold beside him and a printed paper on analogue gravity sliding off his knee, Miles was asleep.

She stood in front of him.

His glasses had slipped down his nose. His head had tipped back against the wall. He looked younger than she’d ever seen him, and very tired, and he’d waited three hours and forty minutes on a station bench for a train that kept being late, and he hadn’t sent her one single message to say so, because she’d have felt she had to answer.

She took the paper off his knee before it fell. She took his glasses off and folded them. Then she bent down and kissed him.

He didn’t wake. She kissed him again, and felt him come up out of sleep under her mouth, and his hand found the back of her neck before his eyes had even opened. She was laughing when she drew back. He blinked at her without his glasses.

“You’re here.”

“I’m here. You fell asleep.”

“I was resting my eyes.”

“For how long?”

“What time is it?”

“Twenty to one.”

He looked at the departures board with naked, short-sighted eyes. “About an hour.”

She sat down beside him on the bench, in her new coat, and kissed him a third time, slowly, while the cleaner went past them without looking.

“You should have gone home.”

“I wanted to be the first thing you saw.”

“You were,” she said, and gave him back his glasses.

In the notebook, the next morning, at his kitchen table, he wrote: 20 November. Her 19:40 two hours late. I slept. She woke me, three times. He looked at it. Then he added, underneath: Worth it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday nights became physics.

It began by accident. She rang one evening at nine and he answered standing in front of the whiteboard he’d screwed to his kitchen wall in October, because he kept running out of paper. She saw it over his shoulder.

“Are you working? Show me.”

He propped the phone against the kettle. The board was full of the tank: the water drawn in towards the drain, faster and faster, and the circle where its inward speed matched the speed of a ripple on its surface. He’d written the condition up in the middle of it and drawn a box round it.

|v(r)| = √(g h)

“Inward speed equals wave speed,” she said. “That’s your horizon.”

“That’s where it ought to be. It won’t stay there. Every time I change the flow, it drifts.”

“Write your boundary condition again. No, not that one. The one from before you approximated it.”

He rubbed out a corner of the board and wrote it again. She leaned closer to her screen, five hours away, with a blanket round her shoulders and her hair up round the purple cat, and frowned.

“You’re assuming the flow’s steady everywhere.”

“Locally.”

“Your boundary doesn’t keep it steady. Look at your join. You’re treating it as smooth, and it’s not.”

He looked at the board for a long time. Then at the phone.

“Show me.”

They worked for forty minutes. He stood barefoot on his kitchen tiles with marker on his fingers. She sat at her desk in the capital with a pencil in her teeth. At a quarter past ten she sat back.

“It’s the matching condition.”

“Yes.”

“You were wrong.”

“I was.”

“And I found it.”

“You did.” He reached for the marker. “Now if we change this term—“

“It’s a quarter past ten, Miles. I said I’d help. I didn’t say I’d work till midnight.” She waited till he’d put the marker down and come back to the camera. “Hello.”

“Hello.”

“Now tell me something that isn’t physics.”

He told her Shu Mei’s new oven had come and was too big, and made the bakery look like a factory. She said that was because it was a factory. They talked until nearly one.

After that, every Wednesday. The phone against the kettle. Sometimes she caught him and sometimes he caught her, and sometimes they spent twenty minutes on one small assumption before remembering neither had asked how the other’s day had been. It grew into a shared file, and then a draft, about corners and boundaries and the edges of things, with Dr. Mao on it and his group’s name, and every contribution written down at the top so that nobody could ever ask whose was whose. They submitted it on a Wednesday in December at eleven at night and raised two cups of tea at each other through two screens.

“I think we should write another one,” she said.

“Let’s wait for the referees first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time he told her he was jealous, it was of Dr. Lam.

“He’s so good,” she said on a Thursday, telling him about the cluster. “He saw the problem with the mesh before I did. He spent two hours showing me how to set up the new boundary test. He’s got a terrible sense of humour. And he’s quite handsome.”

Miles went quiet.

“What?” she said.

“Is Dr. Lam married?”

There was a pause. Then, slowly, all over her face, a smile.

“Oh.”

“What?”

“Dr. Wei. Are you jealous?”

“No.”

She waited.

“Possibly,” he said.

“Of my postdoc?”

“I’m not proud of it.” He shut the book he’d been pretending to hold. “He sees you every day. He can walk down the corridor and find you when something breaks. He can have lunch with you without a timetable.” He looked at her through the screen. “I know it isn’t reasonable.”

“It’s reasonable to miss me,” she said gently. “Dr. Lam has a wife. And a daughter of four who comes in on Saturdays and steals his pens.”

He took that in. She watched the relief go across his face before he could hide it, and laughed till she cried.

“You’re the one I want to come home to,” she said, when she could talk again. “Every other Friday. On the 18:20.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The storm came in on the second Friday of December.

He was on the platform at six with his holdall and a bag of oranges when the board changed. 18:20 DELAYED. He rang her.

“I’ve seen,” she said. “There’ll be another.”

18:20 CANCELLED. Then the one after it. By half past six every train on the northern line had been suspended until further notice, and the wind was coming down the platform hard enough to rock the departure boards on their chains.

He stood in the middle of the concourse with his bag. It was the first one they’d lost. Not shortened. Not delayed. Gone. He had the tickets and the oranges and the notebook, and no train.

“Come home,” she said, in his ear.

He went home.

That night she lay in bed in the capital with the phone on the pillow, and he lay in his, with the call open between them. The storm was on both their windows at once, five hours apart. They talked about the trains and then about dinner and the paper and Shu Mei’s oven, and then about nothing at all.

“I hate this,” she said at half past eleven.

“So do I.”

“I bought the good tea.”

“I bought oranges.”

She laughed. “Of course you did.”

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“What for? You didn’t make the storm.”

“For not being there.”

“I’m disappointed,” she said. “I’m not disappointed in you. That’s different, and you know it is.”

At some point she fell asleep. He stayed awake a while longer, watching her face on the little screen, half of it in shadow on the pillow.

At fourteen minutes past two her phone buzzed against her cheek and woke her. The screen said the call had ended at four minutes to two. Somewhere between them, the storm had taken down a line. Under it, a message had come in.

White Rabbit: I love you, Yu Jie. I wish you were here.

No joke in it. No atom. Nothing clever. She rang him back before she was properly awake. He answered on the first ring, his voice low and rough out of the dark.

“Sorry. You were asleep.”

“I love you too,” she said. “I’m here. Five hours away, but I’m here.”

He didn’t say anything for a moment. She heard him breathe.

“For all n,” he said.

“For all n.”

They slept with the call still connected. In the notebook, on the Monday, he wrote: 11 December. Storm. No trains. First missed weekend. He looked at that for a while. Underneath it he wrote: We stayed together anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

The horizon held on the nineteenth of January, a Tuesday, at twenty-two minutes past nine at night.

He’d been chasing it since October. Under the right flow the tank was supposed to make a circle that ripples couldn’t climb back out of, and for three months the circle had refused to stay where the mathematics said it would. It moved when the pumps warmed up. It smeared when the flow rate changed. It vanished altogether when the boundary drifted. He’d rebuilt the inlet twice. He’d re-matched the join she’d found on a Wednesday night in November. The technicians had learned to tell his footsteps on the basement stairs.

On Tuesday night the flow went steady and stayed steady. He sent a wave train in from the rim. The cameras watched it run inwards, and slow, and pile up, and stop where the water was running in exactly as fast as it could run out. The data came through clean. The circle held.

He looked at it. He checked it. He ran it again. He rang Ling Hao, who came down the stairs in his coat over his pyjamas with a coffee, looked at the screen, put the coffee down very carefully on the bench, and said, “Is that it?”

“It’s holding.”

“Wei. It’s actually holding.”

Miles smiled. Not the small one. The whole of his face, open and astonished, like a boy.

“Ring her,” said Ling Hao. “Go on. I’ll pretend I’m not here.”

She answered at nine thirty-seven, at her desk, in a jumper, with a notebook open. She saw his face and stopped.

“What’s happened?”

He turned the phone round. The dark basement. The tank. The screen. He brought it close.

“Look.”

She leaned in. He watched her face in the corner of his screen as she read the data, and saw the exact second she understood it.

“Miles,” she said.

“It holds.”

“You did it.”

“We did. You found the join.”

“That’s not the same. This is yours.”

“It mattered,” he said.

She laughed, and her eyes went bright, and she put both hands over her mouth.

“I wanted you to see it first,” he said. “Well. After Ling Hao. He was already here.”

“He’s in his pyjamas, isn’t he.”

“Yes.”

“That’s acceptable,” she said.

He talked her through it again, all of it, the flow and the waves and the clean signal, and she asked questions, some of them sharp and some only so she could listen to him answer. At the end she lifted her hand flat to the screen, palm out, the way she’d done once across a corridor outside room 301. He lifted his. Their two hands met through glass and light, four hundred and eighty kilometres apart, which was not a useful measure.

“Friday,” she said.

“I’m coming north.”

“Tell me all of it again when you get here. Even the bits I already understand.”

“Especially those,” he said.

chapters.title: Her Mother Comes to Tea
chapters.desc: No warning, no appointment, pale grey silk on a basement ramp. Mrs. Shen inspects the physics lecturer, his tank, and his only clean mug. He explains entropy. She brings something she was supposed to have thrown away.
chapters.epigraph: “She talks as if the question were the point, not the answer.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that Shen Ruolan had come was the sound of her heels on the basement ramp.

Miles looked up from the control desk. It was a particular sound, measured and unhurried and entirely wrong for a concrete ramp built for forklifts. It was a Tuesday in March, a little after three, and the basement was empty except for him and the tank and the low hum of the pumps.

A woman stood at the top of the ramp in pale grey silk, with a small handbag held in front of her in both gloved hands. Her coat was buttoned to the throat. Her face said she’d already formed an opinion of the building and was waiting to see whether the man inside it would improve it.

He put his pen down.

“Mrs. Shen.”

“Dr. Wei.” She came down the ramp as if it were a staircase in her own house. “I hope I’m not interrupting.”

“You are,” he said. “But you’re welcome to come in.”

She stopped at the bottom and looked at him. He had the impression that nobody had told her she was interrupting anything in a great many years.

Then she walked into the laboratory.

She looked at everything. The drum of clear water four metres across, turning slowly, with its dark eye at the centre. The cameras on their gantry. The cables taped along the floor. The screens. She didn’t touch anything.

“This is the laboratory my mother-in-law’s trust pays for.”

“Yes. The trustees looked at it again in May, after the council, without your daughter in the room. They voted for it a second time.”

“And this time you accepted.”

“Yes.”

“I’m told you refused it at first.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

He thought about it, because she’d asked it as a real question.

“Because I was wrong about what taking it meant.”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she turned back to the tank.

“What does it do?”

“It makes a horizon. A circle on the water that ripples can’t get back out of.” He went and stood beside her. “The water runs in towards the drain faster and faster. At one radius it’s running in as fast as a ripple can run out. Inside that line, nothing on the surface escapes.”

“A black hole.”

“No. The same mathematics as one, for the waves. Nothing’s being crushed.”

“So it’s an imitation.”

“A model.”

“An imitation with a more respectable name.”

He smiled slightly. “That’s one way to put it.”

She was deciding, he could see, whether she disliked his sense of humour. She hadn’t decided.

“Show me,” she said.

He brought up the morning’s run on the screen and took her through it. The flow. The wave train coming in from the rim. The place where it slowed and bunched and stopped. He kept it plain without making it stupid. She asked two questions. Both were good ones.

“You seem very pleased with it.”

“It took a long time to make it work.”

“And now it works.”

“Now it works well enough that we can start asking more interesting questions.”

“You sound like my daughter,” said Shen Ruolan. “She talks as if the question were the point, not the answer.”

“She’s right.”

Something in her face moved, very slightly, and went still again.

“Would you like some tea?”

✦ ✦ ✦

There were two mugs on the shelf by the kettle. One had a cartoon cat on it and a crack down to the base. The other was white, chipped by the handle, with WORLD’S OKAYEST SON across the front in large blue capitals.

She looked at it for some time.

“It’s clean,” said Miles.

“Have you another?”

“Only the cat, and it leaks.”

“Then this will do.”

He made jasmine tea in it and gave it to her. She held it in her gloved hands and took a careful sip.

“Your equipment is very expensive,” she said. “Your mug is not.”

“No.”

“Does your mother know you use this?”

“She gave it to me. When I was made permanent.”

That surprised her. “Your mother gave you a mug that says you’re adequate.”

“She thought it was funny.”

“And you?”

“I agreed with her.”

She looked at him over the rim. Then, unexpectedly, she drank some more.

They stood side by side looking at the water. It was not quite a comfortable silence. It was no longer quite a hostile one.

“My husband told me something,” she said. “In November. He went to her graduation.”

“I know.”

“He didn’t tell me at the time. He sat at the back. He watched her take the medal.” She turned the mug a quarter turn in her hands. “He said he stood up and clapped until his hands hurt. He said she saw him.”

Miles didn’t say anything.

“I was very angry when he told me. That he’d gone without me.” She looked at the tea. “And that he’d been proud of her, and I’d made it so difficult for him to show it that he went in secret, like a thief.”

“She looked for you,” said Miles. “When she came off the stage. I wasn’t there, but I know she did. She wanted you there.”

“And she didn’t have me.”

“No.”

“Do you think she still wanted me?”

He was careful with it.

“Yes. And I think wanting you there doesn’t mean she was wrong to graduate without you.”

Her eyes sharpened. “You’re very direct.”

“I try to be.”

“Does she like it?”

“Sometimes. The rest of the time she tells me I’m being difficult.”

The corner of Shen Ruolan’s mouth moved, reluctantly. “That sounds like my daughter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him about entropy.

“She told me at dinner once that her bedroom wasn’t untidy,” said Shen Ruolan. “She said it had high entropy. She was fourteen. I’ve wondered for eight years whether she was insulting me.”

He took a paper towel off the roll by the sink and spread it flat on the desk and drew four small boxes.

“Imagine four socks and two drawers. If you only care how many socks are in each drawer, not which ones, then all four in the left can only happen one way. But two and two can happen six different ways.” He drew them, quickly, the six. “Entropy is a count of the ways. The state that can happen in the most ways is the one you’ll nearly always find. That’s why rooms go untidy and never tidy themselves. There are far more ways to be untidy.”

He wrote it under the boxes, because it belonged there.

S = k log W

“W is the number of ways,” he said.

She looked at the paper towel for a long time.

“So she was insulting me.”

“She was telling you the truth in a way you couldn’t argue with,” said Miles. “Which is a kind of insult, I suppose.”

Shen Ruolan laughed. It was very short and it seemed to startle her as much as him. She put the mug down on the desk.

“She used to draw everything,” she said. “When she was small. Stars, plants, the inside of clocks. She’d draw what she didn’t understand and bring it to me and ask me what it was. I never knew.” She looked at the paper towel. “She took a kitchen timer to pieces when she was four. She wanted to know why the numbers moved when the spring turned.”

“That’s a reasonable question.”

“She was four.”

“Still reasonable.”

“You have a great deal of patience, Dr. Wei.”

“I’ve had a lot of practice. With difficult questions.”

“Is that what you think she is?”

“No,” he said. “I think she’s someone who keeps asking until she understands. It’s not the same thing.”

Shen Ruolan opened her handbag.

She took out a flat oblong parcel in old brown paper, soft at the corners, one side held together with tape that had gone yellow. She put it on the desk beside the paper towel.

“I kept something,” she said. “I was supposed to throw it away.”

She unfolded the paper. Inside was a child’s chemistry set in a faded cardboard box, with a picture on the lid of test tubes full of jolly colours and a cartoon girl in goggles. A corner was crushed. One of the little plastic bottles had lost its label. The rack inside had cracked across.

“My mother-in-law bought it for her fourth birthday,” said Shen Ruolan. “Before the glasshouse, before the proper set. It lived in her bedroom. When she was seven she knocked the spirit lamp over and set fire to her curtain, and I took the box away and told the whole house I’d put it out with the rubbish. Lihua was furious with me. She gave her the good set the next week, the one with six bottles, and kept it at her own house where I couldn’t touch it.” She smoothed the paper. “I didn’t throw it away. I put it on the top shelf of my wardrobe behind my winter hats. It’s been there fifteen years.”

Miles looked at the little box and didn’t touch it.

“Why did you keep it?”

She was quiet for a long time.

“I don’t know,” she said at last. “I’ve asked myself every winter when I take the hats down.”

She pushed it an inch towards him across the desk.

“Will you give it to her? I don’t think she’d take it from me.”

“I think she might,” said Miles. “But I’ll give it to her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the foot of the ramp she stopped and turned round.

“Do you mean to stay here, Dr. Wei? In this university?”

“Yes.”

“Even if she stays in the capital?”

“Yes. I’d like her to come home. I won’t ask her to give up work she wants.”

“And if she doesn’t come home?”

“Then I’ll go on finding ways to see her.”

“You make it sound very simple.”

“It isn’t. It doesn’t change what I mean to do.” He held her eyes. “I love your daughter, Mrs. Shen. I’m not going anywhere because she has a job five hours away, or because things are inconvenient, or because you don’t approve of me.”

Her face didn’t soften. Something behind it did.

“You don’t seem afraid of losing her.”

“I am. Very.” He didn’t look away. “But loving her isn’t the same as keeping her. I learned that from her.”

Shen Ruolan looked at him for a moment more. Then she adjusted the strap of her handbag on her wrist.

“She likes her eggs soft,” she said. “Scrambled. A little milk. Low heat. Salt at the end, never before, or they go watery. She won’t eat them if they’re dry. She’ll pretend she isn’t hungry.” She turned to go up the ramp. “Good afternoon, Dr. Wei.”

He stood at the bottom of the ramp until the sound of her heels had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell her on the phone. He wanted her to have it in her hands.

On Friday her train came in at eighteen minutes to ten. He was at the barrier with the brown-paper parcel under his arm. She came through in the charcoal coat and saw him and walked faster, and then saw his face and slowed.

“What’s happened?”

“Nothing bad. Come and sit down.”

They sat on the bench by the departures board, the same one, where he’d once fallen asleep. He put the parcel in her lap.

“Your mother came to the laboratory on Tuesday,” he said. “She brought you this.”

She looked at the brown paper for a long time. Then she unfolded it, and saw the faded lid, the girl in goggles, the crushed corner. She made a sound he’d never heard from her.

“She said she threw it away.”

“She didn’t. It’s been on the top shelf of her wardrobe for fifteen years. Behind her winter hats.”

Yu Jie opened the lid. She touched the cracked rack, and the bottle with no label, and inside the lid, in a child’s enormous capitals, in felt-tip, SHEN YU JIE SCIENTIST AGE 6.

Then she put both hands over her face and sobbed.

He gathered her in, parcel and all, and held her on the bench by the departures board while the last trains of the evening were called over their heads. She cried for the girl with the felt-tip pen, and the curtain, and for her grandmother, and for fifteen years of thinking her mother had thrown that girl out with the rubbish. She cried because her mother hadn’t. He didn’t tell her it was all right. He put his cheek against her hair and kept his arms round her and let her hold the front of his coat in both fists.

“I thought she didn’t care,” she said into his shoulder, when she could.

“I know.”

“She kept it.”

“Yes.”

“For fifteen years.”

When at last she lifted her head, her eyes were swollen and the front of his coat was dark. He gave her his handkerchief.

“I’ve cried all over you.”

“It’s washable.”

She laughed, weakly, and leaned back against him, holding the box on her knees. After a minute she took out her phone. He watched her type and delete and type again, and then send it.

Yu Jie: Ma. Dr. Wei gave me the chemistry set. Thank you for keeping it.

They sat there. The board turned over. Her phone lay face up on top of the box, and nothing came, and nothing came, and she put her head on his shoulder.

At eight minutes past ten it lit up.

Ma: You’re welcome.

And then, a minute later, by itself:

Ma: Darling.

Yu Jie looked at that one word for a long time. Then she turned the phone face down on the lid of the box, very gently, as if it might bruise.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning she woke in his bed to the smell of butter.

She found him at the stove in a T-shirt with a wooden spoon, standing over a pan on the lowest flame with the deep concentration of a man defusing something.

“What are you doing?”

“Eggs.”

She came and looked into the pan. They were soft, still glossy, nowhere near brown. There was a little jug of milk by the stove. There was the salt, unopened, waiting.

“Who told you?”
