“Your mother. Low heat. A little milk. Salt at the end, or they go watery.”

She stared at him. Then she took the spoon out of his hand, and stirred them once, gently, and turned off the flame, and put the salt on herself.

“Salt at the end,” she said.

“I remember.”

She put them on two plates. Then she stood with her back to the counter looking at the plates, and not at him.

“Thank you for not making me forgive her straight away.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I can be glad she kept it and still be angry about everything else.”

“Yes.”

“I can want her to be my mother and not pretend she hasn’t hurt me.”

“Yes.”

“You’re being very agreeable this morning.”

“I’m trying not to ruin breakfast.”

She laughed. Then she put both hands flat on the counter behind her and hopped up onto it, beside the plates.

“Careful,” he said.

“I am.”

“You’re sitting next to the eggs.”

“I know.”

She hooked a finger into the neck of his T-shirt and pulled him in, between her knees. “Come here.”

“Yu Jie. The eggs.”

“They’ll survive.”

She kissed him. It started soft and didn’t stay that way, because she wouldn’t let go of his shirt and he didn’t try to make her. His hands came to her waist on the cold edge of the counter. She kissed him again before he could say anything, and again, and somewhere behind her elbow a plate slid an inch and neither of them did anything about it.

“Breakfast’s getting cold,” he said against her mouth, eventually.

“Then you should have kissed me faster.”

“I’ll remember.” He leaned his forehead on hers. “Do you think your mother likes me?”

She considered it seriously.

“She drank tea out of your mug.”

“She did.”

“Out of that mug.”

“All of it.”

“Then it’s practically an engagement,” said Yu Jie, and slid down off the counter into his arms, and they ate the eggs, which were exactly right.

chapters.title: Miles Meets His Own Past
chapters.desc: A flower shop in the Walled City on a Saturday in May. Elowen and Aurelia, together, at last on the same side, telling him he finally chose correctly. And a glass globe that has been quietly setting the roses on fire.
chapters.epigraph: “You give them to somebody. It isn’t physics.”
chapters.content:
The invitation had come on Tuesday, as a photograph: a small bunch of forget-me-nots in cream paper on a scarred wooden counter, and under it one line.

Saturday afternoon. Bring her. Don’t pretend the tank needs you. — E.

Yu Jie had said yes before Miles had finished reading it over her shoulder. He’d asked whether Elowen meant a particular time. Yu Jie had told him he was impossible.

So on Saturday the eighth of May, with Yu Jie home for the weekend, they walked through the Walled City in the afternoon sun, up and down the stepped lanes between old brick walls, past a man selling caged songbirds and a stall of paper umbrellas and a temple door so old the paint had gone soft as felt. The shop was halfway down a narrow street between a tailor and a noodle shop. Its window was a wall of colour. Over the door, on a board gone silvery with weather, someone had painted Elowen’s in looping green letters, and painted it well, and a long time ago.

“She did the sign herself,” said Miles. “At nineteen.”

Yu Jie looked at him.

“How do you know that?”

“She told me at the reunion. In 2020. She’d just married a man everyone was frightened of and she wanted to talk about paint.”

Yu Jie looked at the sign again, and then at him, and something passed over her face that she put away quickly.

“She’s very beautiful,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And she knew you when you were funny.”

He stopped on the step. He looked at her properly. Then a slow, enormous, wholly undignified smile came over his face.

“You’re jealous.”

“I’m a little jealous.”

“Of Elowen.”

“Don’t look so pleased.”

“I can’t help it,” he said. “Nobody’s ever been jealous over me in my life. I’d like a minute.”

“You’re not getting a minute,” said Yu Jie, scarlet, and pushed the door open, and a bell rang over their heads.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was cool and dim and smelt of wet stems and earth. Buckets of roses stood along the floor. Lilies leaned out of tall jars at the back. On the counter, in a row of small glass pots, were forget-me-nots.

Elowen came out from behind a screen of white tulips in a dark green apron over a red silk blouse, with her long black hair coming loose round a gold clip above one ear. She looked less like the woman in velvet at the gala and more like herself, which was more beautiful, not less.

“You came.” She hugged Yu Jie, and held her at arm’s length and looked at her. “I wasn’t sure he’d let you.”

“I’m standing right here,” said Miles.

“I know. That’s why I said it.” Elowen kissed his cheek. “Still serious, Miles?”

“Usually.”

“Shame.” She put a little bunch of forget-me-nots in pale blue paper into Yu Jie’s hands, and another into his. “One each.”

“I don’t know what to do with flowers.”

“You give them to somebody. It isn’t physics.”

He gave his to Yu Jie. She stood with a bunch in each hand and laughed, and Elowen looked between the two of them with her head on one side, as if she’d been asked to check a sum and found it came out.

From the back of the shop came a crash, and a man’s voice saying something low and vicious to an inanimate object.

Elowen shut her eyes. “Again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong was standing in the back room in front of a great urn of crimson roses, in a beige suit with his collar open and his rings on, holding a plant mister like a weapon. A thin curl of smoke was going up from the middle of the roses.

He saw Miles.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re about to.”

“I am,” Miles agreed.

Yu Jie leaned towards the urn. “Are they on fire?”

“Not exactly.” Zhao jerked his chin at the windowsill behind the urn. On it, on a little brass stand, sat a glass sphere the size of a large orange, filled to the brim with clear water, catching the afternoon sun from the high window. “It’s that.”

“Has anybody moved it?” said Miles.

“Three times. They still smoke.”

“Only in the afternoon?”

Zhao hesitated. “Yes.”

“And only since about a week ago? Not when you first put it there?”

A longer hesitation. “Yes.”

Miles looked at the sphere, and at the window, and at the roses, and then at a small, bright, fierce white point of light resting on one red petal, which was beginning, very gently, to brown.

“When did you give it to her?”

“March. The seventeenth.” Zhao’s face did something guarded. “It’s our anniversary.”

“In March the sun was lower,” said Miles. “It came in through that window at a flatter angle and the sphere put its focus somewhere on the wall. In May the sun’s higher. The focus has come down.” He pointed, without touching anything. “A sphere of water is a lens. It’s collecting all the light that falls on it and putting it on one petal. That’s the smoke. Move the roses out of that line, or move the globe out of the sun. Either.”

Zhao looked at the white point on the petal. Then at Miles.

“You’re telling me my anniversary present is trying to burn down my wife’s shop.”

“I’m telling you it’s focusing sunlight.”

“That’s worse.”

Yu Jie had her hand over her mouth.

“Don’t laugh,” Zhao told her. “Those were expensive.”

“They were my anniversary roses,” said Elowen, from the doorway, with her arms folded.

“You told me the globe was a symbol of the world,” Miles said.

“It is.”

“It’s also a lens.”

Zhao looked at him for a long, heavy-lidded moment. “Do you always have to be right?”

“No.”

“Then try being wrong for once.”

Miles considered it. “I could say the roses are fine.”

Another curl of smoke went up between them.

“Don’t be clever with me,” said Zhao.

Elowen lifted the sphere off the sill and set it on a low shelf in the shade, and Zhao carried the urn across to the other side of the room in both arms, and the smoke stopped. He looked at the browned petal and pinched it off.

“I preferred them when they were just flowers,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bell over the door rang again.

Aurelia came in first, in pink cashmere with a soft headband and pearls, holding a paper bag from the bakery up the street, and behind her, as he always was, came Chen Si in a white shirt, with two coffees and his very still hands.

Aurelia stopped when she saw Miles. Then she smiled.

“Well.”

“Aurelia.”

She turned to Yu Jie and kissed her on both cheeks. “Somewhere without a ballroom or a committee or a man trying to arrange your future. At last.”

“It’s much quieter,” said Yu Jie.

Aurelia looked past her at the smoking urn and the plant mister. “Is it?”

“Don’t start,” said Zhao, from the back.

“Physics?” Aurelia asked Miles.

“Optics.”

Chen Si handed her a coffee. “You’ve been here thirty seconds.”

“And I’ve learned something already.” She put the bakery bag on the counter. “Pastries. Elowen, sit down before Zhendong starts arguing with the furniture.”

“I don’t argue with furniture.”

“You argued with the display cabinet on Thursday,” said Elowen.

“It was in the way.”

They sat round the little table at the back between the lilies, the six of them, with jasmine tea in Elowen’s mismatched cups and Aurelia’s pastries on their paper. Zhao sat with his arms folded and the expression of a man forced to admit that his anniversary present was a danger to the local flower population. Chen Si sat beside Aurelia and said almost nothing and watched everything, the way he always did.

“Your mother sat beside me at the hospital lunch on Thursday,” Aurelia said to Yu Jie, over her cup.

Yu Jie’s hand went still on the forget-me-nots.

“She asked whether you were eating,” said Aurelia. “Whether you looked tired. Whether you’d seen your father. She didn’t once ask what you were doing for the family.” She stirred her tea. “She’s stopped telling people at lunches about the Yans, too. Somebody brought it up and she changed the subject to orchids.”

“That’s different,” said Yu Jie, very low.

“Yes. And she asked whether Dr. Wei was still employed.”

Miles raised his eyebrows. Yu Jie laughed in spite of herself.

“I told her he was permanent,” said Aurelia, “and that he’d made it perfectly clear to me at a gala that he wasn’t going anywhere, and she said, Yes, he said that to me too, in the voice she uses when she’s lost an argument and is deciding whether she minds.”

Under the table Miles found Yu Jie’s hand. He didn’t ask. She held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re different,” Aurelia said to him, later, when the pastries were gone. “From the boy I remember.”

“Not completely,” said Elowen.

“No. Not completely.” Aurelia put her cup down. “Do you remember the library?”

The back room went quiet. A tap was dripping somewhere among the buckets.

“Yes,” said Miles.

“Have you told her?”

“Some of it. You told her most of it. In a powder room.”

Aurelia had the grace to colour.

Miles looked at his tea for a while.

“There’s a part I’ve never told anyone,” he said. “After the fire drill. After I stood between you on the field and couldn’t even look at Elowen’s face.” He turned his cup round once on its saucer. “The next week, she came and sat at our table in the library, the way she always had. And I picked up my books and walked out. I did it every day for a month. I told myself I was angry. With Aurelia, with the school, with the whole business. That I was finished with the place.” He looked up. “I wasn’t angry. I was frightened. I thought if I sat down at that table, everyone would see how much it had mattered. That they’d know they’d made me ashamed of something I’d written. So I left the room. I was seventeen, and I thought leaving meant I’d won.”

Yu Jie had moved her chair closer without noticing.

“Did it?” said Elowen.

“No. I stopped writing anything down. I stopped laughing. I didn’t sit at a table with anyone for about fourteen years.” He looked across at her. “I’m sorry. It was your table first.”

Elowen’s red mouth went soft.

“We fought each other, you know,” said Aurelia. “After.”

He blinked. “You fought?”

“Not with fists,” said Elowen.

“Speak for yourself,” said Aurelia, and Elowen laughed out loud, a real laugh, and Zhao looked at his wife with something unguarded in his face that he put away before anyone but Miles could see.

“For years,” said Aurelia. “Two silly girls. We were both completely certain we understood you. She thought you were too proud to let anyone help you. I thought you were too frightened to let anyone see you needed it. We argued about it all through school and half of our twenties, and neither of us ever once asked you.” She looked at Elowen across the table, and something old and finished passed between them. “We were both wrong. You didn’t need either of us to tell you what you needed. You needed to choose.”

“And you finally chose correctly,” said Elowen.

He looked from one to the other. “Chose what?”

“Somebody who doesn’t ask you to be less careful with your heart,” said Elowen.

“And who doesn’t mistake you being quiet for you not caring,” said Aurelia. “Somebody who knows you’re frightened sometimes and loves you anyway.”

“And who’ll argue with you about how much milk goes in tea,” said Elowen.

“That’s important,” said Yu Jie.

“It’s essential,” said Miles.

He looked down at their joined hands under the table, hers and his, on her knee, among the forget-me-nots.

“I did choose,” he said. “I go on choosing. Every day.”

Aurelia made a small sound.

“You’re crying,” said Chen Si.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“It’s the lilies.”

“There aren’t any lilies near you.”

“Drink your coffee,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before they went, Elowen took Yu Jie through to the front of the shop and came back from the cold room with a small sheaf of lily of the valley, the little white bells hanging along their stems.

“For you,” she said, wrapping it. “They look very delicate. They come up through frost.”

“That’s a very specific compliment.”

“I’ve a very specific opinion of you.” Elowen tied the ribbon. Then, lower, so it wouldn’t carry to the back room: “Your mother’s learning she can’t keep you by holding tighter. Let her take as long as she needs. And don’t hurry yourself, either.”

In the back room Zhao had the glass sphere in both hands and was holding it out at Miles like a hostage.

“Again.”

“It’s curved. It bends light inwards and brings it to a point.”

“And if I put it here?”

“Then the point lands on the table.”

“And if I turn it?”

“The point moves.”

Zhao looked at the sphere, and then at Miles, with narrow, considering eyes.

“Teach me.”

“Teach you what?”

“Lenses. Prisms. Whatever it is you do.” He set the sphere down on the shaded shelf with great care. “I’m not buying her another present that tries to kill the roses.”

“That’s a reasonable motive,” said Miles. “We could start with a prism.”

“Saturday.”

“I’ll have to check my schedule.”

“You need a schedule to tell me how light works?”

“Light doesn’t wait for either of us.”

Zhao stared at him. Then he laughed, a short, low, startled sound, as if it had got out without his permission.

“Fine,” he said. “Check your schedule.” And then, as Miles turned to go: “Wei. At the gala. You weren’t stupid about it.”

Miles stopped.

“No,” he said. “I tried very hard not to be.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The street outside was gold with late sun. Across the lane, by a dark car at the corner, stood three of Zhao’s men, the biggest of them broad as a door with a shaved head and a scar through one eyebrow. They’d been there when Miles and Yu Jie arrived. They hadn’t moved.

“Do they always watch the door?” said Yu Jie.

“Apparently.”

“Does it bother you?”

“No.”

“Not even a bit?”

He thought about it honestly. “No. I’m leaving with you.”

She laughed, and stood on the step below him with lily of the valley in one hand and forget-me-nots in the other, and looked up at him, and said, “I like you.”

“I know.”

“I like you very much.”

“I know that too.”

“Do you?”

He took the flowers out of her hands and laid them on the windowsill of the shop, among Elowen’s colours. Then he took her face in both hands and kissed her, on the step, under the green sign, in the middle of the afternoon, with three of Zhao Zhendong’s men across the road and the tailor watching from his doorway. He didn’t look round first. He didn’t look round after. He kissed her as if there were nobody else in the Walled City at all.

When he let her go, the man with the scar was examining the sky with tremendous interest.

“They saw,” said Yu Jie, pink.

“Good,” said Miles, and picked up her flowers.

Behind them the shop door opened, and Zhao stood in it with the sphere.

“Wei! Does it work with moonlight?”

Yu Jie started laughing before Miles could answer.

“Not the same way,” Miles called back.

“Why not?”

“That’s next Saturday’s lesson,” said Miles, and let Yu Jie pull him away down the steps by the hand.

At the bottom of the lane, she looked up at him.

“You told them the truth,” she said. “About being frightened.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t have to be seventeen any more. You don’t have to leave the room.”

He looked at her for a long moment, in the gold light, with her flowers in his hand.

“I know,” he said. “I’m staying in it.”

Up in the doorway of the shop, two women stood side by side, the one in pink and the one in red, watching them go.

“Well?” said Aurelia.

“He chose correctly,” said Elowen.

“Finally,” said Aurelia, and they both laughed, and went back inside together.

chapters.title: The Apartment With Two Desks
chapters.desc: A one-line letter to the Head of Department. Two flights up on Bell Street. Two second-hand desks that face each other, and a cactus that moves house in a bicycle basket.
chapters.epigraph: “Of course I counted. I’m a physicist.”
chapters.content:
On the first Monday of August, Shen Yu Jie came back to the university with a doctoral offer in a folder, two suitcases, and a cactus in a bicycle basket.

The suitcases had come down from the capital on the train the night before. The cactus had refused to. It rode now in a plastic pot wedged into the front basket of Tao Tao’s old bicycle with a scarf tied round it like a seatbelt, and it looked a great deal more confident about the journey than the woman steering.

Miles was waiting outside the physics building. He saw the bicycle first, then the cactus, and then Yu Jie, steering with one hand and holding the pot upright with the other, wobbling across the square.

“That isn’t safe.”

“Good morning to you too.”

“You’re carrying a cactus on a bicycle.”

“It’s a passenger.”

“It’s a plant.”

“It’s a passenger with limited mobility.” She put a foot down. “Careful. He’s got feelings.”

He steadied the handlebars while she climbed off, and then lifted the cactus out of the basket and held it at arm’s length. “Does it have a name?”

“Of course it has a name. Professor Thorn.”

He looked at the cactus. The cactus looked back.

“He’s very clever,” said Yu Jie, “and he doesn’t like being questioned.”

“Then he’ll fit in on the fourth floor.”

She laughed and took the pot back and kissed his cheek.

“I’m not visiting, you know,” she said. “This time.”

“I know.”

“I’m staying.”

“I know that too.”

He smiled, and she saw at once that it was a different smile from any of the ones she’d collected on platforms over the past year. Not the Friday one. Not the Sunday one. It was the smile of a man who’d been told something he’d wanted very badly to hear and was trying, without much success, not to look too pleased.

“Hello, Miles.”

“Hello, Yu Jie.”

He kissed her properly, there outside the door of the physics building, with a cactus held carefully between them so that neither of them got spiked.

✦ ✦ ✦

The offer had come in July.

Dr. Mao had been pleased with her year. The paper with her name and Miles’s and his had come back from its referees with one round of corrections and three paragraphs of compliments, which Ling Hao had printed and stuck to the door of 412 until Miles took it down. There was a great deal more to do with the corners. Mao had offered her a doctoral place in the capital.

She’d thought about it for a week. Then she’d asked him whether the work could be done from home.

It took some arranging. Ruan would supervise her in the department, and Mao from the capital, with a week up there every term. Every piece of it was written down, and Miles was written out of all of it: no supervising, no examining, no committee, no say. She’d told him over dinner. He’d asked about the project, and the funding, and whether she’d talked to Ruan. Then he’d asked what she wanted.

“I want to come home,” she’d said.

He’d looked down at his tea.

“I think that’s a very good decision.”

“You’re not even going to pretend to be neutral?”

“No,” he’d said. “I’m extremely pleased.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His letter to the head of department was three lines long. He wrote it at eighteen minutes to twelve on Monday morning and spent longer choosing the paper than writing it.

Cen read it once. Then again. He looked at Miles over the top of his reading glasses.

“Three lines.”

“It’s a simple disclosure.”

“It’s certainly brief.” Cen read it out. “Shen Yu Jie and I will be living together from the end of August. Her supervision and assessment are as set out in the attached; I have no part in either. We are both very happy.” He lowered the sheet. “Is the last sentence necessary?”

“No.”

“Then why is it there?”

Miles thought about it, honestly.

“Because it’s true.”

Cen looked at the letter for a while, rather than at him. Then he smiled, slowly, his long face creasing all the way up.

“I’ll put it on file.”

“Thank you.”

“Very happy,” said Cen, to the folder.

When Miles got back to 412 there was a yellow square on his desk in her slanting hand. I hear you told Cen we’re VERY happy. Underneath it was a small drawing of a cactus in round glasses.

He wrote underneath: It didn’t seem to need a diagram. Then he put it in his drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat was on Bell Street, on the other side of the road from Ling’s, two floors up above a man who mended watches. It wasn’t big. Two bedrooms, one of them small. A sitting room with two tall windows. A kitchen you could touch both walls of. A narrow balcony looking across at the bakery’s sign and the old brick fronts beyond. The floors were wooden and the walls were pale and a radiator in the corner clicked every few minutes like someone thinking. In the mornings, with the windows open, the whole place smelt of bread.

Yu Jie loved it the moment she was through the door. Miles was more cautious.

“The kitchen’s very narrow.”

“It’s a kitchen.”

“There isn’t much storage.”

“We don’t own much.”

“The second bedroom’s smaller than the photographs.”

“It only has to take desks.”

He looked round again. The sun on the boards. The windows that actually opened. Somebody laughing in the street below, and Shu Mei’s voice across the road shouting about a delivery.

“Yes,” he said. “I like it.”

They signed on Thursday. On Friday they had their first argument about furniture.

It was about the desk. They’d found two second-hand online, both old wooden teachers’ desks from the sixties with deep drawers and brass handles. She wanted the bigger one by the window for the light. He wanted it against the wall for the space. She said his notebooks were not entitled to a better view than she was. He said her papers would fade in direct sun. She said she was a physicist, not a houseplant. He said he was aware of that.

“You’re on Professor Thorn’s side,” she said, pointing at him.

“Professor Thorn hasn’t expressed a view.”

“He doesn’t have to. I understand him.”

They stood in the empty little room arguing for twenty minutes. Then the man selling the desks rang back to say he’d found the rest of the set, the school was closing, there were six of them in a gymnasium, did they want another.

They bought two that matched.

The desks came the following Tuesday, enormously heavy, scratched, with decades of other people’s initials in them. One drawer stuck. Under the lid of one, in faded stencil, it said PROPERTY OF EAST STREET SECONDARY SCHOOL.

“Should we sand that off?”

“No,” said Miles. “It’s part of the desk.”

“Sentimental.”

“Historical.”

“Sentimental.”

“Would you like me to agree?”

“Yes.”

“Then yes.”

They put them in the little room facing each other with the window between, so that the light came in from the side across both. He put his monitor on one and she put her laptop and her nine thesis notebooks on the other, and then they stood in the doorway and looked at it: two desks, two chairs, two lamps, a lot of books, a room so absurdly serious it looked like an exam hall.

She went and sat down at hers. He sat at his.

“Hello,” she said, across the space between them.

“Hello.”

“Do you need an appointment?”

“Possibly.”

“Office hours?”

“By arrangement.”

“I’m not your student.”

“I know.”

She looked at him across eighty centimetres of old wood. Then she got up and came round the end of the desks and kissed him, and went back and sat down again, and he sat with his hands on his keyboard and a look on his face he couldn’t do anything about.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“Your face is doing something.”

“I’ll try to control it,” he said, and didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The move took the rest of August. Shu Mei gave them three bread crates and forbade them to put anything breakable in them. Ling Hao lent them a trolley, then complained about the trolley, then about how Miles had loaded it, then about Yu Jie supervising instead of carrying. She told him supervising was an essential contribution to science. Tao Tao came on two Saturdays and put up curtains crookedly and cried once in the kitchen for no reason and said it was the onions, though there weren’t any.

Books first. Then clothes. Then the kitchen. Miles carried the heavy boxes up from the attic across the road and the street and up two more flights. Shu Mei sent over bread and a bag of oranges and a jar of plum jam with a label that said DON’T, which nobody could explain.

Late one afternoon Yu Jie came down out of the attic for the last time with a shoebox in both arms.

“Your treasures,” said Miles.

She sat down on the floor of the new sitting room among the boxes and took them out one by one. The chemistry set with the girl in goggles, which went on the shelf by her desk. Her grandmother’s photograph, in its new frame. The little yellow-handled screwdriver. The box of chalk from the glass room, which went into the drawer of her desk and not on the shelf, because it was hers and not for show.

At the bottom was a biscuit tin.

She opened it. Inside were sticky notes. Hundreds of little squares, yellow and pink, some curled, some faded, some with tea rings on them. Every note he’d stuck to the side of her mug since the October before last, and every one she’d stuck to his door in answer, which she’d taken back off the door herself, one at a time, when Ling Hao’s score had got too embarrassing. I heard you. Still angry. Still peeling oranges. (I love you.) A cat in glasses. A bad joke about fermions that she’d never forgiven him for.

“How many?” he said.

“A hundred and twelve.”

“You counted.”

“Of course I counted. I’m a physicist.” She got up with the tin and went into the little room, and opened the top drawer of his desk, his new old desk, and put them all inside, every one, in two neat stacks, yellow and pink, side by side.

“You could keep them in your own drawer,” he said from the doorway.

“I know.”

“Why mine?”

“Because you kept them first,” she said, and shut the drawer. “Now they’re home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday of August they went out at dusk for groceries and came back up Bell Street with rice and eggs and milk and greens and a packet of biscuits she said were medically necessary. There were three iron lamps on that stretch of pavement, older than the street lights, and the third stood outside their own front door, throwing a round yellow pool across the brick.

He reached for the shopping bag.

“I can carry it.”

“I know you can.”

“Then why?”

“Because I’d like to.”

She gave it to him. They passed the first lamp, and the second. Under the third she stopped and looked up at their windows. The crooked curtains. A light left on in the kitchen.

“We live here,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I used to count weekends. I used to count stations. Now I can just go upstairs.” She looked at him. “Are you happy?”

He put the shopping down by his feet.

“Very,” he said, and kissed her.

He didn’t look round first. He didn’t check the bakery windows, or the watchmender’s door, or the man going past on a bicycle with a crate of cabbages, or Shu Mei, who had come out onto her step with a broom and was watching them openly with deep satisfaction. He put his hand along her jaw under the third lamp and kissed her with the eggs at his feet as if the street had been built for nothing else. A bicycle bell went somewhere. Someone whistled. Neither of them moved.

“You didn’t look round,” she said, when he let her go.

“There’s nothing to look round for,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last night of August the bed still hadn’t come, so they put the mattress down on the sitting-room floor.

There were boxes along the walls. The curtains in the little room needed taking up. A kitchen cupboard had a loose hinge and the radiator clicked. Professor Thorn had the balcony. Two mugs stood on the counter, side by side, and a pair of her shoes lay where she’d kicked them off by the door.

It wasn’t finished. It was theirs.

She sat on the mattress in his shirt with her knees up and looked round at all of it in the light of the one lamp on the floor.

“Are you nervous?” she said.

“A little.”

“Why?”

He sat down beside her. “Because this matters.”

She leaned against him. It wasn’t their first night. There’d been his staff flat in January and her attic in April and the long string of borrowed weekends since, hotel rooms and her narrow residence bed and his sofa at one in the morning after the 19:40. But there’d always been a train in it somewhere. A suitcase by the door. A question about whether she’d stay.

There wasn’t one tonight. She was already home.

He kissed her very slowly, as if they had all the time there was, and for the first time they did. No last train. She pulled the shirt off over her head herself and laughed at his face. He laid her back on the bare mattress in the lamplight and kissed his way down from the place under her ear to the line of her collarbone and further, unhurried, attentive, as if he were learning a room he was going to live in. Every time he asked, she answered him with her hands, and then she pulled him up and guided him into her, and he moved slowly, deep, his forehead on hers. The mattress creaked on the floorboards. Somewhere below a watch began, faintly, to chime the hour, and then another, and she didn’t hear the rest because she’d stopped hearing anything but him. Afterwards they lay tangled in a single sheet on the floor of their own sitting room with the window open to the street and the smell of tomorrow’s bread just beginning to come up from across the road.

“Do you think we’ll argue?” she said into his chest.

“Yes.”

“That’s not very romantic.”

“We’ve argued about the desks already.”

“And solved it.”

“We bought two.”

“Exactly.” She traced a line down his arm. “We’ll argue about the kitchen.”

“Certainly.”

“And your books. They take up too much room.”

“Your notebooks take up more.”

She lifted her head. “Are you starting our first domestic argument?”

“I’m observing a fact.”

She laughed and kissed him and put her head back down.

“Goodnight, Dr. Wei.”

“Goodnight, Shen Yu Jie.”

“Just Yu Jie. Here.”

“Goodnight, Yu Jie,” he said, and kissed her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke first.

He lay still and listened. The bakery across the road beginning its day. A van. A shutter going up. Yu Jie asleep beside him with one hand near his shoulder and her face turned towards the window.

He’d spent his whole adult life arranging things he could control. Work. Data. Timetables. The distance between a question and its answer. Now there was another toothbrush beside his in the bathroom. A second mug. A pair of shoes by the door that weren’t his and a cactus on the balcony with a name. He found he liked every single bit of it.

His coat was hanging over the back of a kitchen chair, where it had hung all month, though it was August and thirty degrees.

In its inside pocket, for three weeks, there had been a small square box.

He’d carried it everywhere since the first Saturday in August. Down to the basement. Across the road to the bakery. Up and down the stairs with every box. He hadn’t asked her. Not because he didn’t know. Because he wanted to ask her properly, when she wasn’t tired or rushing for anything, when nothing about the question could look like a reward for coming home or a price for living with him. He wanted her to have all the room in the world to say yes, or not yet, or no.

She stirred, and opened one eye.

“Are you awake?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I’m looking at you.”

“That’s not a reason to wake up.”

“It’s a reason to stay awake,” he said, and she smiled and pulled him back down.

Later, she came into the narrow kitchen in his shirt while he was making eggs, soft, on the lowest flame. She leaned in the doorway and looked at the coat on the chair.

“Dr. Wei.”

“Yes?”

“It’s August.”

“Yes.”

“Why are you still carrying that coat everywhere?”

He turned the flame off.

“It’s useful.”

“It’s thirty degrees.”

“I don’t wear it outside.”

“You took it across the road to the bakery yesterday.”

“My keys were in it.”

“And the day before?”

He put the eggs on a plate and salted them, at the end, never before.

“Yu Jie,” he said.

She looked at him, and then at the coat, and then back at him. And then she smiled to herself, as if she’d seen the answer at the back of the book and had decided, very deliberately, not to turn to it yet.

“All right,” she said, and sat down at the counter, and ate her eggs.

chapters.title: A Ring Hidden in a Problem Set
chapters.desc: The second Wednesday of September, two years on, 3:47 p.m. Three problems on graph paper, a man who is a very bad liar, and a 113th sticky note.
chapters.epigraph: “You know the distance. You measured it three times.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to four on the second Wednesday of September, Shen Yu Jie knocked on the open door of office 412.

She’d been doing it, give or take a glass room and a year of trains, for two years.

Miles was at his desk with a paper and a red pen, his glasses low on his nose. There was a cup of jasmine tea by his right hand and a second already poured in the blue mug on the far side of the desk, steaming gently, waiting.

“You’re late,” he said, without looking up.

“It’s a quarter to four.”

“Precisely.”

“Then I’m on time.”

“That’s one interpretation.”

She came in and pushed the door half shut behind her with her heel and put her bag on the chair. She was in the second week of a doctorate. She had a desk of her own now in Ruan’s group on the third floor, a key to the building, a stipend, and a cactus. She still came up at a quarter to four on Wednesdays, because she wanted to, and because he still poured the tea.

Then he looked up, and she stopped.

His ears were red. Not pink, the way they went when she said something outrageous in a corridor. Scarlet, right to the tips, the way they’d gone in the seminar in December when he’d laughed out loud in the front row. There was a mark on the bridge of his nose where he’d been pushing his glasses up and up.

“Your ears are red,” she said.

“It’s warm.”

“It’s September.”

“September can be warm.”

“Of course it can,” she said, and sat down, and then saw the graph paper.

Three sheets, squared exactly, lay on top of his usual heap of papers on her side of the desk. Each had a handwritten problem at the top in his small straight capitals.

“What’s this?”

“A problem set.”

“For who?”

“You.”

“Am I being assessed?”

“No.”

“Then what is it?”

He took his glasses off, and cleaned them on his shirt, and put them back on.

“Something I’d like you to solve,” he said. “In order, please.”

She looked at him. He looked at his tea.

“Are you nervous?”

“No.”

“Your ears are getting worse.”

“Problem one,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

PROBLEM 1. Let W be the set of Wednesdays from the second Wednesday of September two years ago to today, inclusive. For each, record whether S.Y.J. came at 15:45. Find the number of Wednesdays and classify them. (Data: see Appendix A.)

Appendix A was four pages long.

It was a table. The first column was a date. The second was a place. The third was a remark, in his hand, and some of the remarks were one word long and some ran into the margin.

10 Sept. 412. Harmonic oscillator. Already solved. Pen under my chair.

17 Sept. 412. Two inks. Said I hadn’t seen the pen.

24 Sept. 412. Bent oscillator. She was right. Stayed till 18:02. Chalk handprint on the board, left side.

1 Oct. 412. Door wedged open.

15 Oct. Back stairs.

She stopped there for a moment with her finger on the line. Two words. He hadn’t needed to write anything else.

She went on. The flu: 26 Nov. My flat. 39.1. She peeled five oranges. The ginger tea. The gala Wednesday, 17 Dec. “Up here I’m just loud.” Two in January with nothing in the remarks column but the page numbers of her draft. Then February, and the place changed. Glass room. Glass room. Glass room.

4 March. Glass room. I said a cruel thing.

11 March. Glass room. Absent. 18 March. Glass room. Absent. STILL HERE. 25 March. Glass room. Absent. Her cup was cold by eleven.

She had to put the page down for a second. Then she picked it up again.

April, May, June. 20 May. Glass room. She brought me the corrections to read and I didn’t. Then July, after graduation, when there’d been no reason to come at all, and she’d come anyway, every single week. And then September, the trains, and the place column changed again.

Screen. Screen. Screen. Her desk, my kitchen. Screen. Matching condition. She found it. Screen. 47 minutes. Snow on her windowsill. Absent. Flu. She texted at 21:14 to say don’t worry, which I did. Screen. Paper submitted. Screen. “I wish you were here.”

The whole year was there. Forty-eight Wednesdays, five hours apart, and he’d written down every one.

At the bottom of the last page he’d added it up.

Wednesdays: 105.

In 412 or the glass room: 52.

On a screen: 46.

Neither: 7.

And underneath, smaller:

An absence isn’t the same as a choice not to come.

The room was very quiet. A door went somewhere down the corridor.

“You recorded all of them,” she said. Her voice had gone odd.

“Yes.”

“Even the ones I missed.”

“Especially those.”

“Why?”

He looked at the appendix rather than at her.

“Because the important things ought to have a record,” he said.

She looked at him for a long moment across his desk. Then she leaned right over the three sheets of graph paper and the cooling tea and kissed him.

He smiled against her mouth.

“That isn’t an answer to problem one.”

“It’s an answer.”

“Mathematically?”

“Emotionally.”

“Those aren’t always equivalent.”

“They are today,” she said, and sat back down, and took his red pen out of his hand and wrote the totals under the question, and then, below them, in her slanting hand:

The set is incomplete without the person who keeps coming back to it. (Both of them.)

He read it. His ears, impossibly, went redder.

“Warm September,” she said.

“Problem two,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

PROBLEM 2. In a shared residence on Bell Street, two desks face each other. Let d be the distance between their front edges. Find d. State whether the arrangement is satisfactory.

There was a small diagram in the corner. Two rectangles, two chairs, a window between, a little arrow.

“We’ve lived there a fortnight,” she said. “You know the distance. You measured it three times.”

“I’d like your assessment.”

“Eighty centimetres.”

“Show your working.”

She wrote a line. Room to push the chairs back. Room to get past each other. Not so far that anyone has to raise their voice. Then: Arrangement: satisfactory. She looked at it. She crossed out satisfactory and wrote over it, underlined twice:

Much better.

“Much better than what?” he said, very quietly.

“Than four metres of corridor outside room 301.” She didn’t look up from the page. “Than a glass wall. Than four hundred and eighty kilometres and a screen propped against a kettle. Than not knowing if you’ll be home when I get back.” She put the pen down. “Than standing outside your door counting down to one minute past four.”

“I agree,” he said.

“You’re being very sentimental today.”

“I’ve been accused of it.”

“By whom?”

“You. Frequently.”

She looked at the third sheet. It was folded in half.

“What’s problem three?”

“It’s the last one.”

“Is it hard?”

“Not mathematically.” He took a breath. “Read it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

PROBLEM 3. The top drawer of the right-hand desk in the second bedroom on Bell Street contains N sticky notes.

N = 112. Find note N + 1.

Note N + 1 is not in office 412.

Given: one person has been carrying the necessary object for several weeks. The other has not been told. The solution must be reached without assistance.

She read it twice. She read several weeks.

Then she looked up, and he was already standing, with his coat over his arm.

“Where are you going?”

“Home,” said Miles. He looked at her for a second longer, and his whole face was naked with it, and then he said, very low, “I’ll see you there,” and went out.

She sat in office 412 and stared at the open door.

Then at the paper. Then at the door again.

Several weeks. A coat in August, at thirty degrees. A coat carried across the road to the bakery for his keys. A coat over the back of a kitchen chair while she ate her eggs and decided not to turn to the back of the book.

Her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her fingertips.

She looked at the clock. Two minutes to four. She could do it in eleven minutes if she ran.

She grabbed the three sheets and her bag, and her shoes were under his desk, because the new ones had been rubbing her heels raw all day and she’d kicked them off the moment she sat down, the way she did in every room she felt at home in. She looked at them for half a second. Then she left them where they were.

She took the back stairs, past the landing between the third and fourth floors, where she didn’t stop, though she wanted to. She came out of the side door into the warm September afternoon at a run.

Down past the canteen. Out of the east gate. Along the road, across at the lights without waiting for them, down the hill, into Bell Street. Her bare feet slapped the hot paving stones and she didn’t feel them. Shu Mei was on her step with a broom and opened her mouth and shut it again. The watchmender looked up from his loupe. She went past the first lamp and the second and the third and through their front door and up two flights, and she was crying before she got to the top, and she didn’t know when she’d started.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the little room with the two desks.

He’d hung his coat on the back of his chair. The afternoon light came in sideways through the window between the desks and lay across both of them. On his desk, by itself, in the middle of the scratched wood, sat a small square box with a yellow sticky note folded round it.

He heard the front door. Footsteps on the boards. Then nothing.

She was standing in the doorway. Barefoot. Her hair coming down out of its clip. Out of breath, with three sheets of crumpled graph paper in one hand and her face wet.

He looked at her feet.

“You’re barefoot.”

“I know.”

“Where are your shoes?”

“Under your desk. In 412.”

“You ran here without shoes?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She looked at the box on his desk. Then at him.

“Problem three,” she said.

The smallest smile. “Did you solve it?”

She nodded. She couldn’t speak.

He picked the box up off the desk and turned it over once in his hands, the way he turned a stick of chalk before he began writing.

“I should tell you one thing first,” he said. “I didn’t choose the stone. I knew I wanted something simple. Something you could wear every day, writing, and carrying trays, and pushing your hair behind your ear. I didn’t know anything about stones. So three weeks ago I went to Aurelia’s workshop and stood among the cases looking lost until she took pity on me.” He turned the box again. “She said you wouldn’t want anything grand. She said it should be set low so it wouldn’t catch on your notebooks. She chose it. She said it was the colour of the forget-me-nots.”

“Aurelia,” said Yu Jie, through her fingers.

“She made me promise not to tell you until it was on. I’m breaking the promise. I don’t want anything about this to be a secret from you.”

“Three weeks.”

“Yes.”

“In the coat.”

“Yes.”

“The coat you wore in August?”

“Yes.”

She laughed, and it came out half a sob. “I asked you about that coat every single morning.”

“I was not very convincing.”

“You were terrible.”

“I’ve been told.”

He unfolded the yellow note from round the box and held it a moment.

“Two years ago today,” he said, “you came into my office with a problem you’d already solved, and I gave you the answer the long way round because I couldn’t think of any other way to keep you in the room. I spent a year drawing lines so that nothing could go wrong. I thought if I measured every boundary carefully enough, I could keep you safe from me.” He looked at her. “You kept coming back. You kept asking me things I couldn’t answer with a graph. You still do.”

“I’m going to go on doing it.”

“I’m counting on it.” He took her hand, with the yellow note still in his. “I can’t promise you it’ll be easy. I don’t know where the work will take either of us, or how many more trains there’ll be. But I know what I want. I want to come home to you. I want to keep arguing with you about the desks and the eggs and how much room my books take. I want you to steal my tea. I want the ordinary parts, all of them, for as long as you’ll let me have them.”

He opened the box.

The ring lay in it. A narrow gold band and one small blue stone set low, the colour of the flowers on Elowen’s counter, catching the sideways light.

Miles went down on one knee on the floorboards between the two desks.

She made a small sound and put her hand over her mouth.

“Shen Yu Jie,” he said, and his voice was quite steady, and his eyes weren’t. “I loved you for a year when I wasn’t allowed to say so, and I kept a line flat on a board because I wanted every part of your life to be unquestionably yours. I’ve loved you every day since, on platforms and through screens and across eighty centimetres of somebody else’s school desks. I don’t want to have chosen you once. I want to keep choosing you. Every day. For as long as there are days.” He held up the ring. “Will you marry me?”

For a moment she couldn’t say anything at all. Then she laughed, and the tears came properly, and she took his face in both her hands.

“Yes.”

“Yes?”

“Yes, Miles. Yes. I’ll marry you.”

He let out a breath that was almost a laugh, and took her left hand, and put the ring on it. It fitted.

She turned her hand in the light. Inside the band, very small, so small she had to tilt it to see, someone had engraved two characters.

∀n

“For all n,” she whispered.

“Aurelia said nobody would understand it. I said that was the point.”

She took the yellow note from his fingers and unfolded it. On it, in his hand, it said: Note 113. That was all. She went to his desk with the note and picked up the nearest pen and wrote underneath it, pressing hard:

Yes. (For all n.)

Then she opened his top drawer, where the hundred and twelve lay in their two neat stacks, and put it on the top of the yellow pile, and shut the drawer.

He was still on one knee. She turned round, and he stood up, and he kissed her.

It wasn’t a careful kiss. It wasn’t the kind he gave her on the steps of the physics building, or on platforms with a timetable waiting. He kissed her as if an answer he’d been waiting two years to read had finally arrived, and she wound both arms round his neck and held on, and somewhere in it they ran out of standing and sank down together onto the floor between the two desks, her back against his chair and his arm round her waist and her bare feet dusty from Bell Street.

“I’m engaged,” she said against his mouth.

“Yes.”

“To you.”

“Yes.”

“Say something else.”

He thought about it.

“I’m very happy.”

“That’s already in your letter to Cen.”

“It’s still true.” He put his forehead against hers and said, so low she felt it more than heard it, “Mine.”

She touched the ring.

“Yours,” she said. And then, because she’d never once let him get away with a one-sided proof: “And you’re mine.”

He laughed, low, against her temple.

“That’s fair.”

They sat on the floor between the desks for a long time with the sun moving off the boards. After a while she held her hand up and looked at the stone again.

“Did Aurelia know you were doing it today?”

“Yes.”

“Elowen?”

“Yes.”

“Ling Hao?”

He hesitated.

“Miles.”

“He suspected. He was not informed.”

“Good,” she said. “He can find out from Shu Mei, like everyone else on this street.” She looked up at him. “She saw me run past with no shoes on. She’ll have told half of Bell Street by now.”

“Then we’d better go down and show her,” he said.

“In a minute,” said Yu Jie, and pulled him back down to her on the floor, between the two desks, in the last of the light.

chapters.title: Quod Erat Demonstrandum
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Two red booklets in the morning. A garden behind the Hall of Science at 4:01 in the afternoon. A blackboard on an easel, a cake covered in Bohr atoms, and a proof that is finally finished.
chapters.epigraph: “Hello, wife.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past eight on the morning of the twentieth of June, two years to the day after she’d knocked on his door at one minute past four, Shen Yu Jie got married in a registry office with a plastic plant in it.

She’d expected it to be more frightening. It was pale walls and a row of chairs and a counter behind glass, and a ficus in a pot that somebody had dusted that morning with real love. Miles sat beside her holding the folder. He’d checked it three times on the bus. She’d checked his face four.

“Are you nervous?” she whispered.

“No.”

She looked at his hands on the folder. His knuckles were white.

“I’m concentrating,” he said. “Identity cards. Photographs. Forms.”

“Do you want to marry me or submit a grant application?”

“Both need careful preparation.”

She laughed out loud in the quiet room, and he smiled, and his ears went red, and she slid her hand under the folder and found his, and his fingers closed round hers at once.

When their number came up they went to the counter together. The clerk looked at the photographs and the forms and asked them to confirm their names, and their dates of birth, and that nobody had made them come. Miles answered clearly. Yu Jie answered just as clearly, though she was smiling so hard the clerk began to smile too.

“You both agree to this marriage freely?”

“Yes,” said Miles.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie.

The stamp came down twice. Two small red booklets slid across the counter under the glass. He took one. She took the other. She opened hers and there they were, side by side, his face very serious and hers not serious at all.

“Hello, husband,” she said.

He looked at her. His face did something that made her chest hurt.

“Hello, wife.”

She leaned across the counter and kissed him. The clerk cleared her throat. Yu Jie said sorry. Miles said, “Don’t,” and took her hand, and they walked out into the bright morning with their red booklets, and he didn’t once look round.

✦ ✦ ✦

The garden behind the physics building had been laid out by people who knew she’d notice everything.

White flowers along the gravel path, and in among them, if you looked, forget-me-nots and lily of the valley. A plain wooden arch with green leaves woven through it. Sixty chairs in a curve on the grass. Not two hundred. No ballroom, no committee table, no seating plan drawn up to show the family’s reach. Just the people who’d watched the two of them become who they were. Behind it all the old building stood with its windows full of afternoon sun, and on the fourth floor, if you knew where to look, the window of 412.

Beside the arch, on an easel, with white roses wired round its frame, stood a blackboard.

Miles had insisted on it. Yu Jie had insisted it mustn’t be the only decoration. The roses were the compromise.

Ling Hao came across the grass at half past two carrying an enormous cake box in both arms and stopped dead in front of the easel.

“Of course.”

“It’s a useful surface,” said Miles.

“It’s a wedding, Wei, not a seminar.”

“It’s a very beautiful blackboard,” said Yu Jie, coming up with her flowers.

“You’re encouraging him.”

“I’m his wife,” she said.

Ling Hao looked at her. Then at Miles. Then he put the cake down very carefully on the table and took off his glasses and wiped them, which he didn’t need to do.

“I’m going to need some time with that,” he said.

It was Shu Mei’s cake, three tiers, the sides covered in tiny piped atoms in blue and gold, a nucleus and three circles each, all of them physically inaccurate. On the top, in white, it said Q.E.D.

“I supervised the design,” said Ling Hao.

“Some of the orbits are wrong,” said Miles.

“It’s a cake.”

“Still.”

Yu Jie took his hand and squeezed it, and he closed his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came in ones and twos all afternoon. Ruan, in a dress she’d clearly been made to buy and a hat she’d clearly refused, who held Yu Jie for a long time and gave her a fountain pen in a box. “For the next chapter,” she said. “And the one after. You’ve earned every page.” Cen, in his camel coat although it was June, who looked at the blackboard and sighed and asked whether there’d be a proof, and was told there would.

Tao Tao, who seized Yu Jie’s left hand the second she arrived and held it up to the light and said Aurelia had done very well and cried for the first of what turned out to be eleven times. Yan Zhiyuan, relaxed in a pale suit, with Remy beside him carrying a camera and a parcel that he said wasn’t a cake, it was a book of photographs from mountain observatories, and Miles turned the pages and said it was a very good choice, and Zhiyuan said, “Don’t sound so surprised,” and Remy laughed.

Miles’s father and mother came up the path together, small and grey-haired and neat in their good clothes, the maths teacher and the literature teacher from the secondary school in the suburbs. His mother cried before she’d even reached the arch. His father shook his son’s hand and then, without warning, pulled him into a hug and held on, and said something in his ear that nobody else heard, and Miles stood very still in his arms with his eyes shut. Behind them came Wei Lan with her husband and both her children, already telling everyone that she’d known since a flu in November.

Then Elowen, in deep red with a gold clip in her hair and white peonies in her arms. Aurelia and Chen Si, in pink and in black. And Zhao Zhendong behind them with a long wooden case under his arm, which he opened on the gift table without a word. Inside, on a dark wooden base, sat a prism, beautifully cut, throwing a small sharp rainbow onto the tablecloth.

“That’s a very good prism,” said Miles.

“I know,” said Zhao.

“He’s been practising,” said Elowen.

“I can explain refraction now.”

“Can you?”

“Yes.”

“Go on, then.”

Zhao looked at him for a long moment. “Not now.”

Yu Jie laughed so much she had to hold onto Aurelia.

At twenty to four her father came across the grass in a dark suit with a white flower in his lapel, and stopped in front of her, and looked at her for a long time.

“You look beautiful,” he said. He looked at the ring. “Your grandmother would have liked this very much.”

“Ba. You asked me in February.”

“I did. Whether I might walk you to him.” He held out his arm. “I’m asking again.”

She put her hand through it.

And then, at the very back of the garden, by the last row of chairs, there was her mother.

She’d come in last, when everyone else was sitting down. She was in yellow. Not the pale gold she wore to foundation dinners, not the cold ivory of formal things. A warm, soft yellow, like the inside of a lemon, and at her throat a single strand of old pearls that Yu Jie had last seen in a photograph in the east gallery of the museum, round the neck of a young chemist looking straight into the camera.

Her mother didn’t come forward. She didn’t beckon. She stood by the last row of chairs with her handbag held in both hands and waited.

Yu Jie looked at her father. He let go of her arm.

She walked to the back of the garden on her own.

“Ma.”

Shen Ruolan looked at her. Then she reached up and straightened the little spray of lily of the valley at Yu Jie’s shoulder, which didn’t need straightening.

“You look lovely, darling.”

Then her eyes went past Yu Jie, all the way down the aisle, to the man under the arch, who hadn’t moved, who was simply standing there waiting with his hands at his sides.

She looked back at her daughter. And she nodded. Once.

There was no speech in it. No apology. Nothing undone. But Yu Jie understood every word that wasn’t in it. She took her mother’s hand, and her mother held hers back.

“Go on,” said Shen Ruolan.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles stood under the arch in a dark suit and a white shirt open at the throat. He’d meant to wear a tie. She’d told him she wanted to see his face, not his collar.

He watched her come down the grass on her father’s arm in ivory, with forty-one tiny buttons down her back and her hair half up and her grandmother’s earrings, carrying white flowers and forget-me-nots. He’d seen her in a great many beautiful things. Silver sandals in a back street at one in the morning. A charcoal suit outside room 301. His own shirt, in a kitchen, laughing at burnt eggs. None of them had been this. She was smiling, and it wasn’t the jewel’s smile. It was hers.

Her father put her hand into his.

“Look after each other,” said Shen Guoqiang, and stepped back.

“You look very handsome,” said Yu Jie, very low.

“Thank you.”

“Your ears are red.”

“It’s warm.”

There was no celebrant. There was Ruan, in front of them both, with a sheet of paper in her hand.

“I was asked to say something,” she said to the sixty chairs. She looked at the paper. “I wrote a speech.” She folded it in half and put it in her pocket. “I’m not going to use it.”

People laughed.

“I taught this man mechanics when he was eighteen,” said Ruan. “He was careful then. He thinks before he speaks and measures before he moves and he can make a simple decision so complicated you’d need a supercomputer to finish it. And I’ve supervised this young woman for three years, and she has never once been impressed by any of that.” She waited for the laugh to finish. “They met in an office. She was a student who asked questions, and some of them weren’t about physics. They were careful. They respected the work and they kept to the lines they’d drawn, and when they made mistakes, and they made one or two, they learned to listen. I’ve watched them choose each other through a great deal. Distance. Families. Bad trains. Worse coffee.” She looked at them both over her half-moon glasses. “They’re not promising each other it’ll be easy. They’re promising to keep choosing. Do you?”

“Yes,” said Miles.

“Yes,” said Yu Jie.

“Good,” said Ruan. “Then get on with it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d written his vows on a sheet of paper and put them in his inside pocket. Looking at her, he forgot they were there.

“I used to think that if I understood something completely, I could stop it going wrong,” he said. “I thought if I kept enough distance I’d never hurt anyone by wanting too much. I was wrong. You taught me that love isn’t a problem you can solve in advance. It’s a choice you make again, on ordinary days, when nobody’s watching. I want to make it with you. When the trains are late. When the work won’t come. When you steal my tea.” His voice didn’t shake. His hands did. “I choose you, Yu Jie. Today, and every day after it.”

She was crying. She didn’t wipe it away.

“When I met you,” she said, “I thought you were impossible. You had a rule and a graph and a metre rule, and you looked at an equation as if it had personally let you down.” The guests laughed. Ling Hao laughed loudest. “I didn’t know I’d end up being the one who knows when you’re frightened, and when you’re tired, and when you just need somebody to sit beside you and not ask you to explain. You have never once asked me to be smaller so that you could be bigger. I promise to keep asking you questions. I promise to tell you when I’m angry, and when I’m happy. I promise to keep coming home.” She held his hands. “I love you. For all n.”

“For all n,” said Miles.

Ruan stepped aside. Miles picked up a stick of chalk from the ledge of the easel.

He wrote at the top of the board, in his small straight capitals: PROPOSITION. For every n ≥ 0, M and Y choose each other on day n.

She took the chalk from him. BASE CASE. n = 0. Today. True.

He took it back. HYPOTHESIS. On day k, both choose freely.

She took it. STEP. On day k + 1, each is free to choose again, knowing the other, owing nothing.

He wrote the last line, and stood back.

Therefore, for every n ≥ 0: they choose each other.

Yu Jie took the chalk out of his fingers one last time and drew a small square box at the end of it, the way every proof is closed, and inside the box she wrote three letters.

Q.E.D.

“I believe that’s the conclusion,” said Ruan.

“FINALLY,” shouted Ling Hao, from the third row.

Miles put the chalk down. He turned to her.

“My wife.”

“My husband.”

He kissed her. In front of sixty people. In front of her father, and her mother in yellow, and his own parents, and Ruan, and Cen, and two women he’d known when he was sixteen and their two dangerous husbands, and Tao Tao crying for the sixth time. He didn’t look round first. He held her face in both hands and kissed her under the green arch as if there were nobody in the garden at all, and she held his wrists and kissed him back, and the whole garden stood up and clapped.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came home at ten to the flat on Bell Street. Flowers on every surface. Presents along the wall. Two red booklets on the shelf by the cactus.

She kicked off her shoes by the door. Then she turned round and gathered her hair over one shoulder.

“There are forty-one,” she said.

“I know. I counted at the arch.”

He undid the first one. Then he bent and kissed the skin it had covered, at the top of her spine. Then the second, and a kiss. Then the third. He went slowly. She started laughing at the fifth and stopped at the twelfth. At the twentieth she leaned back against him with her eyes shut. At the thirty-second she reached back and found his wrist and held it. At the forty-first the ivory slipped and he let his hands rest at her waist and didn’t move them until she turned round in his arms.

“Did you really count every one?”

“All forty-one.”

“You’re impossible.”

“I’m your husband,” he said, and she pulled him down by the open collar of his shirt.

There was no hurry in any of it, and no audience, and nothing to prove. The dress went over the chair with its forty-one open buttons, and he laid her back on the bed in nothing but her ring and kissed every inch he’d unbuttoned, down her spine and back up, before he turned her over and came into her, slowly, watching her face. He said her name against her throat as if he’d been saving it all day. She held his face and looked at him in the lamplight and told him she loved him, three times, and he answered every time, and the third time neither of them could finish the sentence.

Much later, when she was half asleep against his chest with the ring catching the lamp, he reached over to the bedside table and put an envelope on the sheet in front of her.

Inside were two tickets. A train, and then a bus, and then a road that went up and up into mountains to an observatory above the clouds, with a guesthouse beside it and a programme for visitors.

“Miles.”

“Five nights. Telescopes.” He hesitated. “And one day with nothing planned in it at all.”

She looked up at him.

“That’s the most romantic thing you’ve ever said.”

“The telescopes?”

“The nothing,” she said, and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes to midnight she got out of bed.

“Where are you going?”

“The calendar.”

It was on the wall above her desk in the little room, between the two desks, where it had lived since the end of August. Two hundred and fifty-five atoms, every one of them coloured, and the star on the twentieth of June two years ago, with a small door drawn under it. And after the star, the squares she’d added the morning after the museum stairs, and all the ones she’d added since, in rows down the wall: trains, and a loaf of bread, and a tank, and a yellow note, and a ring.

She found the square she wanted. Beside the old star, inside the little door, she drew a small box. In it she wrote:

Q.E.D.

He’d come up behind her in the doorway. He looked at the box. Then at the empty squares running on beyond it, off the edge of the paper.

She picked up her purple pen and drew another square. And another. And another.

“What are you doing?”

“Making room,” said Yu Jie.

“For what?”

She turned round and held out her hand to him.

“For every day after today,” she said, and he took it, and they stood together in front of the wall in the dark, with the bakery quiet across the road, and a great many Wednesdays still to come.

chapters.title: Who Hid Miles Wei’s Glasses (Again)
chapters.desc: A short investigation, conducted by Dr. Ling Hao, into the fourteenth disappearance of a pair of glasses on Bell Street. There is one obvious suspect. There is also a motive nobody expected.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the reason I come home.”
chapters.content:
At sixteen minutes past seven on the second Wednesday of November, in their second autumn on Bell Street, Miles discovered that his glasses had gone.

He checked the bedside table. The bathroom shelf. The kitchen counter. The pocket of yesterday’s trousers. Then he checked the bedside table again, in case the glasses had thought better of it.

“Have you seen my hair clip?” called Yu Jie from the kitchen.

He stood in the bedroom doorway, a blur in a shirt. “No.”

“It’s on your desk.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I put it there.”

“Then why did you ask?”

“To check you were awake,” said his wife, and laughed.

He narrowed his eyes at the shape of her by the kettle. It was the fourteenth time.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes to eight Ling Hao’s phone buzzed.

Miles: Have you seen my glasses?

Ling Hao: again??

Miles: Yes.

Ling Hao: have you checked your face

Miles: Very funny.

Ling Hao: have you checked your wife

Miles looked up from the phone. Yu Jie was at the counter in his old grey jumper, eating toast and reading something on her tablet. She looked entirely innocent. He knew that expression. He had married it.

“I’ll be late,” he said.

“Oh no. Why?”

“My glasses are missing.”

“That’s very unfortunate,” said Yu Jie, after the smallest pause, and took another bite of toast. “Very.”

He bent and kissed the top of her head, which he could find without them.

“Good luck finding your eyes,” she said.

He went. She waited till she heard the street door. Then she put down her toast.

✦ ✦ ✦

By three minutes past eight, Ling Hao had opened an investigation.

He had a notebook. He had a pen. He had, in the opinion of Mr. Pei from the department office, a great deal too much time on his hands for a man with three doctoral students.

“The first was in March,” he told Mr. Pei, who’d come into 413 with the post and couldn’t now get out again. “Then April. May. Two in June, before the wedding. One in July. Three in August. Several since. Fourteen.”

“Perhaps he’s careless.”

“With his glasses? He can’t read a menu without them. He can’t find the door.” Ling Hao underlined something. “And eleven of the fourteen were on Wednesdays.”

Mr. Pei thought about it, holding the post.

“Perhaps she likes him better without them.”

Ling Hao stopped writing. He turned round slowly in his chair.

“Pei,” he said. “That is a very interesting hypothesis.”

At nineteen minutes past eight, on his way past the doctoral room on the third floor to borrow a stapler he didn’t need, he found the evidence.

It was under a pile of printouts on Yu Jie’s desk: a small notebook with a pale yellow cover. He knew he shouldn’t. He really did. Then he saw the tiny drawing of a pair of round glasses beside the first line, and his conscience lost.

Things I have found out about my husband, it said inside the cover. It went on in her slanting hand.

12 March. He left them by the kettle and came all the way back up for them. I kissed him before I gave them back. He looked very pleased.

2 April. I put them in the cutlery drawer because he was leaving too early. Six minutes looking. I gave them back with coffee. He suspected nothing.

7 May. He was going to leave without saying goodbye properly. I hid them. He came back. He said goodbye properly. This is a very effective method.

18 June. Working too late, two days before the wedding. Glasses in my desk drawer. He came looking for them and found me instead. He said I was impossible and then he didn’t say anything for some time.

Ling Hao turned the page with one finger, like a man defusing something.

The last entry was dated last Wednesday.

I think he knows. I think he lets me.

He shut the notebook very carefully and put it back under the printouts exactly as it had been. Then he went back to 413 and wrote one line at the bottom of his investigation and underlined it twice.

Case closed. Motive: affection, apparently.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight Miles was in Lecture Theatre C in front of a hundred and sixty second-years, in his spare glasses.

They lived in his desk drawer in 412. They were five years old, too narrow, and an old prescription, and after twenty minutes they gave him a headache behind the left eye. He’d put them on anyway. The lecture was on the hydrogen atom, and he’d got as far as the energy levels, and written them up in the middle of the board, large, the way you write the first thing a student ought to remember about the universe.

Eₙ = −13.6 eV / n²

“One electron,” he said. “One proton. And only these energies allowed, and nothing in between. The minus sign means it’s bound. It would cost you thirteen point six electronvolts to pull it free from the lowest state. The higher you go, the less it costs, until at the top the electron’s hardly held at all.”

He was halfway through the radial equation when Mr. Pei appeared in the doorway at the back of the theatre and came down the steps holding a black glasses case aloft like a relic.

A hundred and sixty heads turned.

“Dr. Wei. Department kitchen. Behind the tea tins.”

“Thank you, Mr. Pei.”

It was eight forty-four. Miles opened the case. There they were. He took the narrow pair off and put his own on and the theatre came back into focus, every face in it, grinning.

“Are those the ones that went missing?” said somebody in the third row.

“Yes.”

“Again?”

The theatre laughed. Miles looked at the board.

“Apparently,” he said. “Now. The radial part.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles: Found them. Kitchen. Behind the tea tins.

Ling Hao: fascinating

Miles: Very.

Ling Hao looked at the message for a long time. Then he looked at the ceiling, towards the third floor, and smiled, and didn’t reply.

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past twelve Miles came home for lunch.

Yu Jie was at her desk in the little room, typing, with her feet tucked up on the chair. She looked up.

“Did you find them?”

“Behind the tea tins.”

“How strange.”

“Very.”

He put the case down on the corner of her desk, eighty centimetres from his, and kissed her. She put her hand flat on his chest.

“Good lecture?”

“Very good. I told them about the hydrogen atom.”

“Did they understand?”

“Some of them.” He looked at the yellow-covered notebook, which was now, curiously, on her desk at home, peeping out from under a journal. “Working?”

“Research.”

“Of course,” said Miles, and went to put the kettle on.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening they made dumplings at the kitchen counter, the way the old woman at the night market had taught them, prawn and chive. He did the filling and she did the folding, because after two years his pleats still ran off in different directions. His glasses were on. She kept looking at them.

“Something the matter?”

“No.”

“You keep looking at me.”

“I’m allowed.”

He put a spoonful of filling on a wrapper.

“Ling Hao was asking about my glasses today,” he said.

Her fingers stopped. Then started again.

“Why?”

“He seems to have opened an investigation. He’s noticed most of the disappearances are on Wednesdays.”

“That’s a strange thing to notice.”

“Very strange.”

“He needs a hobby.”

“He has one. Investigating his colleagues.” He watched her press a pleat shut with great concentration. “I wonder what he’d find, if he did it properly.”

“Probably nothing.”

“Probably.”

She put a dumpling on the tray. Then another. She looked up at him and narrowed her eyes, because he was smiling at the filling.

“What?”

“Nothing, wife.”

“Miles.”

He bent and kissed her cheek, which had gone pink. “Nothing at all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, while she was in the bath, he found a yellow note under his glasses case on the kitchen table, folded in half.

I know you can find your glasses without me. I know you’d come back upstairs anyway. I just like being the reason you turn round. I like seeing your face when you look for me. I like having you inside my focal range.

He read it twice. He folded it again and put it into his wallet, behind his staff card, with a sweet wrapper that said never zero.

She came out in his dressing gown with her hair wet and saw his face and went very still.

“You found that.”

“I found it.”

“It’s silly.”

“It isn’t.” He held out his hand and she came and took it. “You don’t have to hide them, you know. I’d come back anyway. I’ll always come back.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

She thought about it honestly, the way she thought about everything.

“Because sometimes I like being the reason you turn round,” she said. “Not the trains. Not the work. Me.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“You’re the reason I come home.”

She leaned into him. He put his chin on her wet hair.

“I would prefer to keep my glasses,” he said.

“Fine.”

“Thank you.”

“I make no promises about Wednesdays,” said Yu Jie into his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seventeen minutes past nine, with his wife asleep on the sofa under the grey blanket and her feet in his lap, Miles sent one more message.

Miles: Please don’t ever tell Yu Jie you read her notebook.

Ling Hao: I wasn’t going to

Ling Hao: does she know you know

Miles: No.

Ling Hao: are you going to tell her

He looked down the sofa at her. She had a pencil still in her hand. She’d fallen asleep in the middle of a sentence.

He had known since the fourth time. He had, more than once since, left his glasses somewhere slightly wrong on a Wednesday morning, on purpose, so that she’d have something to hide.

Miles: No.

Ling Hao: why

Miles: I like being inside her focal range.

Across the road, in the flat over the bakery, Ling Hao put his phone face down on the table and told Shu Mei that the two of them were exactly as ridiculous as each other, and always had been, and he’d known it before anyone.

chapters.title: The Night She Made Him Dance in the Empty Lab
chapters.desc: Midnight in the basement of the east wing. One pair of headphones, two people, a horizon holding in a tank of water, and a man who has never danced in his life.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve stopped a black hole for a cork.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes to midnight on a Thursday in October, four months after his wedding, Miles got an email that made him forget how to breathe.

He was still in the basement, because he was always still in the basement. He read it once. Then again. Then a third time, slowly, as if the words might rearrange themselves if he took his eyes off them.

We are pleased to tell you that your manuscript has been accepted for publication.

The horizon paper. Three years and eight months of it. The inlet rebuilt twice. The join she’d found on a Wednesday night by video in her blanket. A hundred and forty nights of watching ripples run in towards a drain and refuse, for months, to stop where they were told. The best journal in the field, the one with the cover he’d pinned above his desk at twenty-six and never told anybody about.

He sat back in his chair. For several seconds he did nothing at all.

Miles: Are you awake?

Not Stuck: I’m married to a physicist. Of course I’m awake.

Miles: It’s accepted.

The phone rang before he’d put it down.

“Tell me you’re serious.”

“I’m serious.”

“The journal?”

“Yes.”

She made a sound down the line that he had only heard from her once before, on a station bench, over a chemistry set. Then she said, “I’m coming down,” and he said, “It’s nearly midnight,” and she’d already hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past twelve she came down the basement ramp in his old grey jumper and pyjama trousers and her slippers, with her hair falling down and a bottle of champagne under one arm and two glasses held by their stems in the other hand.

“You brought champagne.”

“Obviously.”

“You could have waited till tomorrow.”

“Absolutely not.” She put it all down on the bench and came straight to him and put her arms round his neck. “Congratulations, Dr. Wei.”

“Thank you.”

“You did it.”

“We did the work.”

“You did the work.” She kissed him. “And I’m going to be completely unbearable about it. I’m going to tell everyone.”

“Please don’t tell the entire department at midnight.”

“I’ll tell them at eight,” she said, and went for the bottle.

The cork had ideas of its own. She twisted. Nothing. She braced the bottle against the edge of the bench, frowning, and twisted again, and he asked whether she’d like help, and she said no in the voice she’d used on Dr. Mao, and the third time the cork went off like a shot. It hit the underside of a shelf, ricocheted off a box of cable ties, and dropped with a small neat plop into the tank.

They both looked at it.

The pumps were running. The water was drawing in towards the drain at the centre in its slow, tightening spiral, the way it had been all week, and the cork rode the surface round. Once. Twice. Faster each time, a little nearer the middle with every lap. It wasn’t going anywhere. It wasn’t getting out.

“Your horizon’s got our cork,” said Yu Jie.

“The horizon’s for waves, not corks. The cork’s just following the water.”

“It’s going round and round.”

“It’ll go down the drain in about ninety seconds, and get stuck on the grille.”

“Can you save it?”

He leaned over and turned the flow down two notches at the desk. The spiral slackened. The cork slowed, and bobbed, and came to rest circling lazily a hand’s breadth outside the line on the water that he’d spent nearly four years trying to hold.

“There,” he said.

“You’ve stopped a black hole for a cork.”

“An analogue one.”

“For a cork,” she said, and laughed until she had to sit down on the crate, and he tried very hard not to, and failed.

She poured. They clinked glasses beside the tank.

“To the paper,” she said.

“To everyone who made it possible.”

“And to the man who spent four years arguing with a bathtub.”

“Three years and eight months.”

“Don’t correct me at your own celebration.”

They drank. Then they stood together by the clear wall of the tank, watching the water turn under the work lights.
