A wave train went in from the rim, the way he’d set it to every five minutes all week, and ran inwards, and slowed, and stopped dead at the line, and stayed there. It looked like nothing. A ripple that wouldn’t move. He watched it with the face she knew from the January call: a man looking at something he’d once believed would never work.

“What are you thinking?” she said.

“That it holds.”

“You sound surprised.”

“I’m not.”

“You are, a little.”

“Perhaps,” he admitted.

She took her phone out of the jumper’s pocket and put one earbud in her own ear. She held out the other.

“What are you doing?”

“Music.”

“Now?”

“Now.”

He took it. Something slow and old came into his ear, a woman singing over a piano, a song older than either of them. She took his hand.

“Yu Jie.”

“We’re dancing.”

“Here?”

“Unless you’d prefer the corridor.”

“I’ve never danced in a laboratory.”

“There’s a first time for everything.”

“I’ve never danced anywhere.”

She stopped and looked at him. “You’re serious.”

“Yes.”

“Not at the wedding?”

“We walked round in a circle and you led. I counted. That isn’t dancing, that’s orbit.”

Her whole face lit up. “Then this is a historic scientific milestone.” She put his hand at her waist and took the other in hers and set her own on his shoulder. “Just follow me.”

“I don’t know how.”

“You know how to walk.”

“That’s not the same.”

“It’s a very similar principle,” she said. “Trust me.”

He did. He was dreadful at first. He watched her feet and his own and the floor and the cables taped to it, and held himself as if he were about to give evidence. She laughed, and moved in closer, and steered him with small shifts of her weight.

“Relax.”

“I am relaxed.”

“Your shoulders don’t agree.”

He let them down. She put her cheek against his chest.

“Don’t think so much.”

“That’s difficult.”

“I know,” she said. “I married it.”

The basement was dark except for the work lights and the faint blue glow coming up through the tank. Their two shadows went round together across the concrete floor. Somewhere in the second verse he stopped looking at his feet. He looked at her instead. The loose hair by her cheek. The corner of her mouth. The way she looked up every time she felt him catch the beat, as if she’d just watched an experiment come out.

“You’re learning,” she whispered.

“The instruction is adequate.”

“Only adequate?”

“Very good.”

“Better.”

Halfway through the song he bent his head and kissed her, still moving, and she smiled into it, and the wave train went in again from the rim behind them and stopped at the line and held.

When the song finished she took her earbud out. He was still holding her hand.

“Again?” she said.

“Perhaps.”

She reached up and undid the top button of his shirt.

“Or,” she said, “we could celebrate another way.”

He went still. “Here?”

“Is there a problem?”

“It’s a laboratory.”

“An empty one. Your empty one. With a lock on the door, which I turned on the way in.” She took his coat off the back of the chair at the control desk and shook it out and spread it over the clean bit of floor beyond the cable runs, between the bench and the tank, in the blue light. Then she held out her hand. “Come here, Dr. Wei.”

He came.

She didn’t let him be careful. She pushed him down onto his coat by both shoulders and knelt astride him and kissed him until he forgot where they were, and when he tried to sit up and take charge, the way he took charge of everything, she put one hand flat on his chest and held him there, and laughed when he let her. She took her time with his buttons, one by one, as he once had with hers. She took his glasses off and put them on the bench and kissed his closed eyes. She pushed her pyjama trousers off and undid his belt and sank down onto him there on the coat, slowly, and he said her name in a voice she’d never heard him use in that building, and she said his back, low, against his throat, and rode him until neither of them said anything that made sense for a long while. The pumps hummed. The light came up blue through the clear walls and moved on the ceiling as the water turned. Every five minutes a ripple ran in from the rim and stopped at the horizon and held, and neither of them saw a single one.

Afterwards she lay on his chest on his coat with her hair all over him, listening to his heart come down.

“Are you happy?” he said.

She lifted her head. “Your paper’s accepted. We drank champagne in a basement. I danced with a man who has never danced in his life.” She kissed him. “And I’m married to him.”

“Is that yes?”

“That’s a great deal more than yes,” said Yu Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-four minutes to eight the next morning, Ouyang came down the ramp to check the overnight run.

He was Miles’s first doctoral student: tall, careful, unfailingly polite, the sort of young man who labelled the labels. He stopped at the bottom of the ramp.

There were two champagne glasses on the bench. A bottle beside them. A pair of earbuds still plugged into nothing. And in the tank, circling slowly a hand’s breadth outside the horizon line, as the flow had been left turned down two notches all night, a champagne cork.

Ouyang looked at it for a long time. He looked at the flow rate on the desk. He looked at the bench, and at a long dusty patch on the clean bit of floor where somebody’s coat had evidently been, and was not any more.

He took out the lab book, and under the night’s observations, in his tidy hand, wrote:

07:42. Flow found at −2 on dial. One champagne cork recovered, outer region. Not part of the protocol.

He considered this. Then he added:

Classification: celebratory.

At eleven minutes past eight, Miles came down the ramp with his hair on end and his shirt buttoned one hole out of true all the way down, and stopped at the sight of Ouyang standing by the tank holding a wet cork between finger and thumb.

“Good morning, Dr. Wei,” said Ouyang. “Congratulations on the paper.”

“Thank you.”

“I’ve logged the cork.”

“I see.”

“As celebratory.”

Miles pushed his glasses up his nose. “That seems reasonable.”

He went to the desk to look at the night’s data. His phone buzzed on the bench where he’d left it.

Not Stuck: You danced.

Miles: I did.

Not Stuck: You were very good.

Miles: You were very kind.

Not Stuck: I have video. I’m keeping it forever.

He stood still in the middle of his laboratory, with Ouyang three metres away pretending with great tact to be fascinated by a pump, and smiled at his phone like a fool.

Miles: I love you.

Not Stuck: I love you too. Do your buttons up properly.

He looked down at his shirt. Ouyang, very carefully, did not.

On the bench beside the printout of the paper’s first page, the cork sat drying, where it would stay for years. For once, Miles decided, not everything needed explaining.

chapters.title: Miles Calculates Before Holding Hands
chapters.desc: The second date. A cinema, a shared armrest, and a man with a napkin and a pencil in the dark, working out the optimal moment. She has already done the calculation. Hers is shorter.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to ask the universe for permission.”
chapters.content:
Miles planned his second date in three lines, on a yellow sticky note, at twelve minutes past eight on the Tuesday after graduation.

1. Dinner.

2. Cinema.

3. Hold her hand.

He looked at the third line for some time. Then he drew a small box round it.

At nineteen minutes past eight Ling Hao came into 412 with two croissants and read it upside down.

“You’re planning to hold her hand.”

“Yes.”

“On your second date.”

“Yes.”

Ling Hao waited. Miles put his pen down.

“What?”

“Nothing. I’m only trying to understand why you look as though you’re about to defend a thesis.” Ling Hao put a croissant on the desk. “Wei. You’ve been with that girl since October. You’ve been to her attic. Zeng Bo has told the entire fourth floor about your proof.”

“That’s not the same.”

“How is it not the same?”

Miles looked at the note.

“Because I’ve never once done it first,” he said. “In public. Not once. Every time we’ve held hands where anyone could see, she’s the one who took mine.”

Ling Hao opened his mouth. Then he shut it again, and looked at his friend with a sudden, unwelcome tenderness, and took his croissant back, because he needed something to do with his hands.

“Then do it first,” he said, from the door. “And for God’s sake don’t draw a graph.”

When he’d gone, Miles turned the yellow square over and, because he couldn’t help it, made a list on the back.

Hill road, December, one in the morning. He’d held his hand out and waited, and she’d been the one to take it. Museum stairs, February. She’d taken two fistfuls of his coat. The corner by the drain, March. She’d held out her hand to be pulled up off the pavement, and kept it. The glass room. Hers. The second lamp. Hers. The corridor outside 301. Not even a hand. A palm, held up in the air across four metres of carpet, because he hadn’t dared cross it.

He looked at the list for a long time. Every time, she’d been the one to close the gap. He had kissed her against blackboards and carried her through doorways and spun her round his office until the scripts flew. But in eight months he had never once, where another living person could see it, reached out first and simply taken her hand.

He’d spent so long making sure he never took anything from her that she hadn’t offered. He had got very good at it. He’d forgotten there was any other way to be.

He turned the note back over, and looked at line three, and the box round it, and put the note in his breast pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was outside the cinema at half past six in a cream cardigan and a dark skirt, with her hair loose, and when she saw him coming down the street she smiled and came to meet him.

“You look beautiful,” he said.

“You look very handsome. You look very nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“Your ears are pink.”

“It’s June.”

They had an hour before the film, and they walked it, down to the harbour and back along the front with the evening coming on. Three times he nearly did it. At the crossing by the ferry pier, when the lights changed and she stepped off the kerb and her hand swung back towards him. Outside a bookshop, when she stopped to look in the window and he stood beside her with his hands at his sides like a man at a funeral. At the bus stop, where a family went past all holding hands in a chain, the smallest one at the end swinging off it. Three times his fingers moved, and three times he thought not yet, not while she’s looking at something else, not if she’d rather not, and the moment went by.

She noticed all three. She didn’t say anything. She’d waited two hundred and fifty-five days once. She could wait a walk.

At the cinema he gave her the ticket. She took it, and then looked down at his other hand, which was hanging at his side, not holding hers. Then back up at his face. Then she went in through the doors he was holding, smiling to herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The film started at five past seven. She’d chosen it, because he’d said he’d watch anything, and he hadn’t realised that anything could include two hours of two attractive people misunderstanding each other because neither of them would simply ask a single direct question. He watched it with close attention and growing indignation.

She watched him.

Their arms lay side by side on the armrest between their seats. His hand was very near hers. A centimetre, perhaps less. Not touching.

At first she thought he was being polite. Then she saw his fingers move. Not towards her. On his knee.

She looked down. There was a paper napkin from the kiosk spread flat on his thigh, and a pencil in his hand, and in the flickering light off the screen he was writing on it.

She leaned over, very slowly, as if reaching for her drink.

Let t be the optimal moment.

Factors: (a) her attention to the film. (b) distance between hands, about 1 cm. (c) probability of interrupting a scene she likes. (d) whether the armrest is mine or hers. (Unclear. Check convention.)

Under it, he’d drawn a small graph. Time along the bottom. Something up the side she couldn’t read. A curve with a peak in it, and an arrow pointing at the peak, and a question mark.

She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt. She looked at him. He was frowning at the napkin with exactly the face he wore in front of a bad derivation.

She took the pencil out of his fingers.

He turned. She bent over the napkin on his knee and, under his graph, in her slanting hand, wrote one line.

t∗ = now

Then she put the pencil back in his hand and sat back in her seat and looked at the screen.

He read it. In the light from the film she saw him read it twice. She felt him look at her. She didn’t look back. She was smiling so hard at the film that a man two seats along glanced over to see what was funny.

“Your model’s taking too long,” she whispered, to the screen.

And then he moved.

His fingers slid between hers on the armrest, all at once, not testing, not asking, as if they’d always meant to be there and had only been waiting for him to stop thinking. His thumb settled over her knuckles. He held on.

She looked down at their two hands. He had taken hers. First. In the dark, in a cinema, in front of two hundred strangers who weren’t watching, but still.

Then he lifted her hand off the armrest and kissed her knuckles, one after another, and put it back down, and kept it.

“Dr. Wei,” she whispered. “You’re missing the film.”

“I’ve seen enough of it,” he said. “They should ask each other.”

She laughed out loud, and somebody behind them hissed, and she put her head on his shoulder and stayed there till the credits. He didn’t let go once. The napkin slid off his knee onto the floor in the second hour, and neither of them picked it up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they went to a noodle shop round the corner with steamed-up windows and six tables. She had beef noodles. He had dumplings and tea. They shared a bottle of chilli oil, unequally.

“Did you enjoy the film?”

“It was entertaining.”

“You mean you spent half of it working out when to hold my hand.”

“Not half.”

“How much?”

“About seventeen minutes.”

“Miles.”

“I was considering the conditions.”

“What conditions?”

He thought about it, seriously, with a dumpling halfway to his mouth.

“I didn’t want to interrupt you,” he said. “You were enjoying it. I’ve spent a year making sure that nothing I did ever got in the way of anything you wanted. I suppose I’ve got into the habit.”

She looked at him across the table, and everything in her face went soft.

“You can just take my hand,” she said. “You don’t have to ask the universe for permission.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I’m learning.”

They talked about the ending, which was terrible. He said the hero’s development hadn’t been adequately demonstrated. She said he was banned for life from reviewing romantic films. He accepted the ban.

The waiter came to fill their teapot. And while the man was still standing there with the kettle, in the middle of Miles explaining why the final reconciliation lacked sufficient emotional preparation, he reached across the table and took her hand.

Just like that. No napkin. No pencil. No peak on a curve. He went on talking about the film as if nothing had happened, and his fingers closed round hers on the formica beside the chilli oil, warm and certain, while the waiter filled the pot and went away.

She looked at their hands. Then at him. He was entirely calm.

“Much better,” she said.

He glanced down, as if he’d only just noticed what his hand had done without him.

“I didn’t calculate that one,” he said.

“I know.”

He lifted her fingers and kissed them, there in the noodle shop with its six tables and its steamed-up window, where anyone on the street could have looked in.

He hadn’t worked out the moment. He’d simply wanted to. And that, she thought, sitting back with her hand in his and the chilli oil burning her mouth, was the best correction anyone had ever made to a model.

chapters.title: The Sticky Note Archive
chapters.desc: For his thirty-fourth birthday, she gives him a binder. A hundred and twelve sticky notes, catalogued, dated, cross-referenced, and annotated. Some of them he doesn’t remember writing. One of them she never showed him.
chapters.epigraph: “Some things take longer to say.”
chapters.content:
Miles had been given a great many presents in his life. Books. Pens. A mug from his mother that said WORLD’S OKAYEST SON. A bottle of whisky from Professor Cen when he was made permanent, which he had never opened and never would, because it was the only thing Cen had ever given anyone.

At twelve minutes past nine on the morning of his thirty-fourth birthday, a Saturday in February, at the kitchen table on Bell Street, his fiancée gave him a binder.

It was dark blue cloth and much heavier than it looked. On the spine, in her slanting capitals on a white label, it said THE STICKY NOTE ARCHIVE.

He went very still.

She sat down across the table from him with her chin on her hand, looking enormously pleased with herself.

“Open it.”

He opened it.

A Complete and Annotated Catalogue of the Bell Street Sticky Notes. 112 items, plus one. Arranged by date. Cross-referenced. With commentary.

He turned the page.

Every note was there. Each original had been slid into a clear sleeve, his yellow and her pink, curled and faded and some with tea rings, and beside each one, in her hand, a number, a date, a place, a transcription, and a line or two of notes. She’d done it in the week in January when he’d been away at a meeting in the north, he realised. She’d taken every one of them out of his drawer, and put every one back into this.

No. 1. Wed 22 Oct. On her tea, 412. “Why can’t you trust atoms? They make up everything.” Annotation: The worst joke in the archive. It was also the first. I laughed for ten minutes in the toilets so he wouldn’t see.

No. 4. Wed 5 Nov. On his door, 412. (Mine, the first pink one.) “Because you’re cute.” Annotation: Reply to No. 3. I was very brave. Ling Hao saw it before he did and put a mark on the inside of his door.

He laughed, and turned the pages slowly, and she watched him.

No. 17. “You’re my favourite boundary condition.” Annotation: Mine. On the edge of his keyboard, the day of the four papers. He read it twice. I know, because I watched him through the glass of the door.

No. 19. “Tea’s on the left. You’ve got three minutes before the seminar.” Annotation: He was pretending he didn’t care whether I was late. He was very bad at it.

No. 21. Wed 26 Nov. On the lid of a box of oranges in his fridge. “Eat these. All of them. That’s not a request.” Annotation: Mine. He had 39.1. He ate all of them, and kept the lid.

Then he reached number twenty-two, and stopped.

It was one of his. A yellow square, small, written in pencil, not pen.

Today’s best question:

That was all it said, on the face of it, and the date beside it in her hand was a Wednesday in December of the first year. He remembered it. He used to write that on a yellow square at the end of each Wednesday’s office hour and stick it on the side of her mug, with the question written after the colon, and he’d done it for a month, and then stopped. This one had nothing after the colon at all.

He took the sleeve out of the rings and held it up to the window.

The light came through the paper. And underneath the line, so faint it was hardly there, pressed into the fibres and then rubbed out with the end of the pencil, were two more words in his own hand.

(from you)

He remembered now. He’d sat in 412 at six o’clock with the square in front of him and written the line, and then the two words, and then looked at them for a long time and rubbed them out, because they said far too much for a man with a rule on his board. He’d stuck it on her mug blank. He’d thought it was a joke she wouldn’t get.

“You found this,” he said.

“I hold all of them up to the light,” said Yu Jie. “I’m a physicist.”

“When?”

“The night before I left your oranges with Shu Mei.” She looked at the sleeve in his hand. “I was so angry with you, that fortnight. I went through the whole tin trying to stay angry, and then I held that one up to the lamp, and I couldn’t.”

He put it back into the rings very carefully.

At the back of the binder was a section with its own divider. Appendix A. The Wednesdays apart.

The pages behind it were nearly empty. Each had a date at the top in her hand, and a short line under it. Capital. Capital. Conference. Her flu. Storm, no trains. Capital. Some had nothing but the date. There were forty-eight of them, and nothing stuck to any.

“Why are these blank?” he said.

“Because there weren’t any notes.”

“You could have put something.”

“I could.” She turned her teacup round on its saucer. “I didn’t want to pretend we’d been together on those Wednesdays when we weren’t. But I wanted to keep the room for them. They were still ours. We just spent them on a screen.”

He looked at the forty-eight blank pages for a long time. They weren’t gaps. They were the record of every Wednesday they’d been five hours apart and had chosen each other anyway.

Then he frowned, and went back to the front, and ran his thumb down the contents page.

“The count’s wrong.”

She went pink. “No, it isn’t.”

“There were more than a hundred and twelve. I remember the drawer. There were more.”

“There were a hundred and twenty-seven,” said Yu Jie, to her tea. “I bent the count.”

“How?”

“I put two on one page if they were the same day. I left out three that were only times. Four-fifteen? Five? You know. And some of Ling Hao’s, from your door, which were insults.”

“Why?”

She put her cup down.

“Because it’s a hundred and twelve days,” she said, “from the back stairs to my flat. From the fifteenth of October to the fourth of February. From the first time you kissed me to the first time either of us said it.” She looked up. “I counted it the night of the intercom, after you asked me what I needed. I wanted the archive to come out at a hundred and twelve. So I made it.”

He stared at her.

“You falsified a catalogue.”

“It’s not a paper, Miles.”

“It’s still a record.”

“It’s a romantic record.”

“Those ought to be accurate.”

“Do you want your birthday present or not?”

He looked at her across the kitchen table. Then he laughed, helplessly, with his head down over the binder, and she watched him do it with her chin on her hand.

“Plus one,” he said, when he could. “On the front.”

“That’s the hundred and thirteenth. You know that one.”

He did. It was in the last sleeve, after the appendix, yellow, with his two words on the front, Note 113, and hers underneath, pressed so hard into the paper that the pen had nearly gone through: Yes. (For all n.)

“There’s something in the back cover,” she said, quite differently.

There was a pocket inside the back board. In it was a single pink square, alone. It had no number. No sleeve. No annotation. Only a title at the top in her hand, and some lines under it that had been written very small, as if by somebody who was afraid of being overheard.

No. 0. Wednesday 10 September.

I came to 412 because I wanted to see you. I wasn’t stuck. I’d done the oscillator twice on the bus. I thought you were the most beautiful man I’d ever seen and I liked the way you explained things, as if they mattered, and I wanted you to look at me for one minute longer than you looked at anyone else.

I don’t know what will happen. I don’t know if you’ll ever look at me like that.

I’m not going to give you this. I’m too frightened.

But I think I’m already hoping.

He read it. Then he read it again.

The kitchen was very quiet. The bakery across the road was loud with its Saturday queue, and none of it came in.

“You wrote this on the first day,” he said. “Before anything.”

“On the bus home. After the pen went under your chair.”

“Why didn’t you give it to me?”

She shrugged, but her smile had gone small.

“I was your student. You were going to have rules. I could see them on you, the minute I walked in, like a coat. I didn’t know if you’d ever want me to be anything else.” She looked at the pink square in his hand. “So I kept it. I’ve had it in every bag I’ve owned. It was in the canvas bag on the pavement by the drain.”

He closed the binder.

He sat for a moment with his hand flat on the cover. Then he stood up, and came round the table, and she looked up at him and said, “Miles?” and he went down on his knees on the kitchen floor beside her chair and put his face in her lap.

His arms went round her waist. She went perfectly still. Then she put her hand on the back of his head, and smoothed his hair, very slowly, the way you would for a child, or for someone you’d been waiting for.

“You kept all of it,” he said, into her skirt.

“Yes.”

“Even the ones I’d forgotten.”

“Yes.”

“And the one you never told me.”

“Some things take longer to say.”

He was quiet for a long time, with his face in her lap and her hand in his hair. When he lifted his head his eyes were wet and his face was softer than she’d ever seen it.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Happy birthday.”

He kissed her palm, and then the inside of her wrist where her pulse was going, and then he came up off his knees and took her face in both hands and kissed her properly, slowly, at the kitchen table on Bell Street, with the binder between his elbow and her teacup, until the tea was cold.

“Do you like it?” she said, against his mouth.

“I love it.”

“Even the falsified count?”

“Especially the falsified count.”

He took the pink square, note zero, and folded it once, and put it in the inside pocket of the coat hanging on the back of his chair, the coat he’d carried a ring in all August, over his heart. Then he took a yellow pad and a pen out of the kitchen drawer.

“The archive’s missing an entry.”

“Which one?”

He wrote, and stuck it on the inside of the binder’s front cover, where it would be the first thing anybody saw.

No. 114. My thirty-fourth birthday. I found out she loved me before I knew how to ask her to stay. I’d like to spend the rest of my life finding out everything else she hasn’t told me yet.

She read it. Then she took him by the collar and pulled him down and kissed him again, and outside, Bell Street went on buying its bread, and for once Miles Wei didn’t feel the slightest need to correct anybody’s count.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Glaring at Me From Across the Room
chapters.desc: The Shen Foundation gala, from inside Miles’s head. A running log of one arms dealer’s stare, the reunion he has spent five years being embarrassed about, and the moment the glaring changed direction.
chapters.epigraph: “Then she really doesn’t look like she wants to run.”
chapters.content:
Written at the kitchen table, staff flats, 3:12 a.m., Sunday 21 December. Times from my phone where I have them, and from memory where I don’t. I can’t sleep. This seems the next best thing.

19:52. Arrived. Ballroom of the Harbour Hotel, same room as the reunion five years ago, same stage at the far end where I dropped the clicker. Ruan took me by the elbow within thirty seconds and steered me to the dean. Ling Hao’s first rule (don’t stand on your own by the desserts) is annoyingly good.

19:58. Zhao Zhendong is by the second marble pillar on the east side.

He is in navy, with his collar open and his arms folded and his rings on, and he is holding up the pillar with one shoulder as if it would fall without him. I knew him at once. In 2020 I walked straight up to him at the reunion and asked whether he was with the hotel.

He is looking at me.

20:04. Still looking at me.

20:09. Aurelia has retied my bow tie, in the middle of the ballroom, with her own hands, telling me the hire shop had done it like a parcel. Chen Si watched her do it. Chen Si’s look was the look of a man filing something for later. Zhao, by his pillar, watched Chen Si watch, and I would swear in a court of law that this improved his evening.

Then Zhao looked back at me.

20:16. Elowen. In deep red velvet, with a gold clip above one ear, and people moving out of her way without seeming to know they were doing it. She came straight over and stood rather close and asked whether I’d been dragged here, and laughed at something I said, properly, with her head back. I think I made a joke. I have no idea what it was.

She told me Zhendong had been holding up that pillar for a quarter of an hour. I said I’d noticed. She said that was either her or he’d decided the pillar was the most interesting person in the room, and she’d better go and rescue it.

She went. He unfolded one arm and put it round her without looking down, and went on looking at me over the top of her head.

20:17. I am beginning to think the pillar isn’t the problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

Concerning the reunion, 14 December 2020, since I have been thinking about nothing else for an hour.

I gave the speech. I dropped the clicker in front of three hundred people and laughed, at myself, for the first time in nine years, which nobody but Aurelia noticed. Afterwards I went out onto the balcony, because Elowen Lin was out there on her own with her face to the water, and I’d seen her across the room with a man by a pillar and the way she looked at him, and I went out after her for no reason I could have given you. I asked her whether she was happy. She took a long time to answer and then she said yes.

Then I went back inside and saw the man by the pillar watching the balcony door as if it might be stolen. I took him for hotel security. Or somebody’s security. It was that sort of event.

I went over.

“Excuse me. Are you with the hotel?”

“No.”

“Oh. It’s just you’ve been watching that door for some time. If you’re worried about the woman on the balcony, she’s fine. I was just talking to her. She doesn’t look like she wants to run.”

He said nothing for a moment. Then, “Good.”

I told him she was an old friend from school, married now, apparently, I hadn’t caught to whom. I held out my hand and said I’d given the speech. He said he knew. He shook it. His hand was very dry and very strong and there was a heavy ring on it. “Zhao Zhendong,” he said. “I’m her husband.”

“Oh,” I said.

I did what I’m good at, which is working out what a thing is from what’s around it. And I said, “Then she really doesn’t look like she wants to run. Congratulations.” And I went to find the committee, and I have been embarrassed about it, on and off, for five years.

I think now that it may have been the most useful thing I ever said to anyone. I think he’d been waiting quite a long time for somebody to tell him.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:41. She’s here.

She has been here since eight, on the great staircase beside her mother and her father and her brother, being looked at. Ivory silk, straight from the shoulder to the floor. Her hair up, high, with something holding it that catches the light. She looks like a girl in a painting of a girl who is being given away.

She is at a table of trustees now, listening to a conversation about bursaries, and smiling the smile she uses on people who think a scholarship is a kind of gift.

I sent her a message. I’m not proud of the message. It’s the first one I’ve ever sent her that wasn’t about time or tea.

Miles: You look beautiful.

20:43.

Not Stuck: You look

That was all. Two words, unfinished. So I looked.

She was already looking at me.

The quartet went on playing. A waiter walked between us with a tray of glasses and out the other side and she was still looking. Then she smiled. Not the one for the trustees. The other one, the small crooked wicked one she gives me across my desk when she’s caught me out. It lasted perhaps a second and a half, and it was entirely mine.

I’m writing the time down because I want to keep it. I have apparently become a man who writes down the minute a woman smiles at him across a room. I don’t think I’ll stop.

Miles: I am.

Not Stuck: That wasn’t finished. My mother touched my arm. I was going to say you look very handsome.

Miles: Your mother’s looking at you now.

Not Stuck: I know.

Miles: Be careful.

Not Stuck: Look at me again when you can.

20:47. I looked down at my phone. Across the room, a second later, so did she.

20:48. Zhao has stopped glaring at me.

I didn’t see it happen. I looked up from the phone and he was still by the pillar, with Elowen beside him with a glass of water and her shoulder against his arm, laughing into it. And he was looking at me. Only it wasn’t the same look. It was the way you look at a man who’s just walked out onto a frozen lake. Not hostile. Rather sorry for me.

Elowen told me much later what he said. “Poor bastard.” I’ve decided to take it as a compliment.

I understand now what I was wrong about all evening. He was never glaring at me. He was glaring at the whole room, at every man in it who might stand too close to his wife and laugh at her jokes. I happened to be the one she’d come over to. And then he’d watched me fail to look at her even once after she walked away, and look instead at a girl in ivory on the other side of the ballroom, and he’d worked out from what was around a thing what the thing was. He’s good at it. Better than me, I suspect.

21:10. Terrace. Elowen asked me, five years after I asked her, whether I was happy. I didn’t answer at first. I looked through the glass at Yu Jie bending to hear an old woman in a wheelchair.

“I’m happy on Wednesdays,” I said.

Elowen looked at me the way she used to look at Mr. Hui when she already knew the answer and was waiting to see if he did. Through the glass, at the edge of the dance floor, Zhao had been watching us both. When I looked at him, he nodded. I nodded back.

22:03. A diplomat in a very good suit arrived and waltzed with her. I didn’t watch. I watched.

✦ ✦ ✦

01:04. The lobby.

I’d been told by Aurelia to make sure she got home. I’d said that was what I was waiting for. The lifts opened and Elowen came out in a long black coat over the red, and Zhao behind her with his hand flat at the small of her back, steering her through the crowd as if nobody else were in it. When they got to me he stopped.

We looked at each other.

“Don’t be stupid about it,” he said.

It was low, and Elowen had turned to say goodnight to Aurelia, so I was the only one who heard.

“About what?”

He looked at me as if I’d asked what water was.

“Her.” An inch of his head, towards the girl in ivory across the lobby with her silver shoes in her hand. “Whatever you’re doing with her, don’t let being frightened make you careless. And don’t make her be the one who pays for it.”

From Zhao Zhendong, I suspect, that was an enormous speech.

“I’ll remember,” I said.

They went out into the cold to a dark car. I still don’t know whether I was threatened or blessed. I’ve been sitting here two hours and I think, on balance, both.

03:40. I gave her my jacket on the old wall. She’s still got it. I don’t want it back.

Going to bed. Will not sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

Postscript. Same notebook. June, a year and a half later.

Zhao Zhendong now comes to the basement on Saturday mornings for lessons in optics. He says it’s so that he’ll stop buying his wife presents that set fire to her roses. I suspect it’s mostly so that he can ask me questions that sound exactly like interrogations. What’s a focal length. Why. How do you know. Prove it.

He pays me in tangerines. Three a lesson, in a paper bag, put down on the bench without comment. I told him the first week that it wasn’t necessary. He said, “Take them.” I took them.

Last Saturday he held a prism up to the window and watched the colours come out on the wall, and asked me whether a prism could make a person look more beautiful. I said it changes where a thing appears to be, not what it is.

He thought about that for a while. “Shame,” he said.

I’ve decided not to ask what he meant.

Yu Jie says I’m making a friend. I’m not convinced. But the tangerines are excellent. I ate one on the train north that evening, and gave her the other two on the platform, and she peeled them for both of us on the bench by the barrier, every scrap of pith off, while I told her about focal lengths.

I’m writing the time down. 21:14.

chapters.title: Miles Tries to Text With Emojis
chapters.desc: The long-distance year, as told through a phone. The atom is not romantic. The cactus is a cry for help. And one message, at 2:14 in the morning, that needed no emoji at all.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time just tell me you’re lonely.”
chapters.content:
On the first night she was five hours away, Miles found the button on his phone with the small pictures on it.

He was sitting at his kitchen table in the staff flat at a quarter past ten with a cup of tea going cold and nobody across the table, and he pressed it by accident, and a great grid of tiny faces and animals and objects came up, and he scrolled through it for some time with the expression of a man reading an unfamiliar journal.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday 1 September, 22:17

Miles: I’ve discovered that this phone can insert small illustrations into messages.

Not Stuck: You mean emojis?

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: Congratulations, Dr. Wei. Welcome to the twenty-first century.

Miles: ⚛️

Not Stuck: ...

Not Stuck: Is that an atom

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: That isn’t what an atom looks like

Miles: I know. The electrons are in orbits. They aren’t in orbits. It’s a hundred years out of date.

Not Stuck: You sent me a physically inaccurate atom to say goodnight

Miles: It seemed appropriate.

Not Stuck: It’s the most romantic thing anyone’s ever sent me

Miles: I thought it might be.

Not Stuck: ❤️

Miles: Is that a red heart?

Not Stuck: Yes. Don’t analyse it

Miles: I wasn’t.

Not Stuck: You’re typing

Miles: I was considering whether it has a physical interpretation.

Not Stuck: Goodnight, Miles

Seven minutes later, when he’d put the phone down and picked up his tea and put the tea down again, one more came.

Not Stuck: ⚛️

Not Stuck: Now we’re two atoms in the same universe

He looked at that for a long time. He didn’t know what to say to it. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t delete it, either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday 13 September, 21:40

She’d been home for the weekend, her first. He’d walked her to the 21:10 and stood on the platform till it went round the bend. Then he’d gone back to the flat, and it had been very quiet.

Miles: 🌵

Not Stuck: ...

Not Stuck: Why have you sent me a cactus

Miles: It seemed appropriate.

Not Stuck: Are you calling me prickly

Miles: No.

Not Stuck: Are you saying we’re going through a dry spell. I left forty minutes ago

Miles: No.

Not Stuck: Miles. Did something happen

Miles: Nothing happened.

Miles: The flat’s quiet.

Miles: I made two cups of tea.

Not Stuck: Have you eaten

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: Properly

Miles: Define properly.

Not Stuck: I’m ringing you. Pick up

He picked up. The call lasted three hours and seventeen minutes. They talked about her new desk and the cluster and the woman next door with the running club, and the tank, and whether a cactus could survive the department kitchen. At some point after midnight he stopped talking, and she listened to him breathe down the line from five hours south.

“Miles?”

“I’m here.”

“Next time just tell me you’re lonely.”

“I know.”

She was quite sure the cactus would come back. She was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday 2 October, 18:31

Miles: The 18:20 is delayed.

Not Stuck: How long

Miles: Twenty-three minutes, they say.

Not Stuck: That’s horrible. Are you on the platform

Miles: Yes. I’ve been thinking about Sundays.

Not Stuck: What about them

Miles: When you leave, the platform stays exactly the same. The train goes, and gets smaller, and at a certain point it goes round the bend and you can’t see it any more, as if it had crossed a horizon.

Not Stuck: That’s a very dramatic way to say you miss me

Miles: I was describing a physical phenomenon.

Not Stuck: Of course you were

Miles: In the tank, a wave that reaches the horizon doesn’t come back.

Not Stuck: But I always come back

Not Stuck: The train doesn’t stop existing round the bend, Miles. It’s just too far for you to see

Not Stuck: That’s all a horizon is

There was a long pause on the platform. The board turned over.

Miles: I miss you.

Not Stuck: I miss you too

Not Stuck: Much better description

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday 21 October, 16:33

Miles: 💛

Not Stuck: !!!!!

Not Stuck: MILES WEI

Miles: Yes?

Not Stuck: A YELLOW HEART

Miles: I’ve been told that the colours carry different meanings.

Not Stuck: By who

Miles: Ling Hao.

Not Stuck: oh no

Miles: He provided a table.

Not Stuck: Please tell me you didn’t keep the table

Miles: I’ve pinned it above my desk.

Not Stuck: What does yellow mean

Miles: According to the table: warmth, happiness, friendship, affection without excessive romantic intensity.

Not Stuck: And why did you choose it

Miles: Because it’s Wednesday and you’re working and I wanted to send you something warm. And because it’s the colour of the notes.

Not Stuck: oh

Not Stuck: That’s so sweet I have to go and stand in the corridor

Miles: I also considered orange.

Not Stuck: Don’t overthink it

Miles: Understood.

Miles: 💛

Not Stuck: I love you

Miles: I love you too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday 12 November, 23:51

Miles: 💚

Not Stuck: A green heart?

Not Stuck: What’s green on the table

Miles: Jealousy.

Not Stuck: ...

Not Stuck: Miles

Miles: You stayed until ten with Dr. Lam to fix the mesh.

Not Stuck: Dr. Lam has a four-year-old who thinks my laptop is a colouring book

Miles: I know. You told me on Saturday.

Not Stuck: Are you jealous of my postdoc

Miles: A little. I’m not proud of it.

Not Stuck: Ring me

He rang her. She told him about Dr. Lam’s wife and daughter, and laughed at him until she cried, and then stopped laughing and told him he was the one she wanted to come home to, every other Friday, on the 18:20. In the morning she sent him a photograph of her simulation results, on which somebody small had drawn a large purple dinosaur in felt-tip.

Not Stuck: Scientifically significant

Miles: 💚

Not Stuck: Come up and be jealous in person

Miles: A fortnight on Friday.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday 11 December, 18:31

Miles: Every train on the line is cancelled. The storm.

Not Stuck: oh Miles

Not Stuck: All of them?

Miles: Until further notice. I’m still on the platform. I’d bought the good pastries.

Not Stuck: Save them for me

Miles: They’ll be stale.

Not Stuck: I’ll eat them stale

A few minutes went by. The wind was rocking the departures board on its chains.

Miles: 💛💛💛❤️

Her phone rang in his hand before he’d put it in his pocket.

“Three yellow and a red?” she said. He could hear her radiator ticking five hours north, and his own storm on the station roof. “What does that one mean on the table?”

“It isn’t on the table,” he said.

She was quiet.

“I’d planned the whole weekend,” he said. “I’d booked the restaurant. I was going to take you up to the old observatory on the hill in the morning if it was clear.”

“I know.”

“I miss you.”

“I miss you too,” she said. “Go home. Ring me from bed.”

He went home. He rang her from bed. They stayed on the line until they both fell asleep, five hours apart, with the storm on both their windows.

At four minutes to two the line dropped.

He woke with the phone on the pillow and the screen dark and call ended on it, and lay in the black with the rain on the glass. He opened the button with the little pictures. He looked at the hearts, all the colours, and the atom, and the cactus, and the whole long grid of them. He closed it again.

02:14

Miles: I love you, Yu Jie. I wish you were here.

She rang back before it had finished sending.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday 25 December, 00:14

Not Stuck: Happy Christmas, Dr. Wei

Miles: Happy Christmas.

Not Stuck: Did you open it

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: And

Miles: I like it.

Not Stuck: You like the scarf

Miles: I like the scarf.

Not Stuck: That’s a very restrained review

Miles: It’s warm.

Not Stuck: MILES

Miles: And it smells of you.

Not Stuck: Better

Not Stuck: It’s something you don’t need. I told you I’d get you something you didn’t need

Miles: I need it.

Miles: I have something for you as well.

A photograph arrived. It was a screenshot of a message thread, months old, scrolled all the way back to the first of September. His atom. And seven minutes under it, hers.

Not Stuck: ⚛️

Not Stuck: Now we’re two atoms in the same universe

Not Stuck: You saved that

Miles: Of course I saved it.

Not Stuck: You never answered it

Miles: I didn’t know what to say. I’ve been trying to work it out since September.

The dots came, and went, and came.

Miles: Two atoms on their own just go past each other. Two that are close enough make a bond. They share. They have less energy together than apart, which is the most stable thing in the universe, and the only reason anything at all holds together.

Miles: That’s what I should have said.

Miles: I didn’t have an emoji for it.

Her phone went quiet for a long time. Then it rang.

“I’m on the 10:05,” she said, before he could say hello. “Tomorrow. I’ll be home by three.”

“I know. I’ll be at the barrier.”

“And Miles. If you send me one more cactus this year, I’m hiding your phone.”

He laughed, low, into the dark of the staff flat.

“Understood,” he said.

“Happy Christmas, my love.”

“Happy Christmas.”

And for once he didn’t send anything after it. He didn’t need to.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Teaches First Years
chapters.desc: Doctoral student, first-year problem class, Thursday mornings, room 104. She is terrifying. They are terrified. By November, there is a queue outside the door on the wrong day.
chapters.epigraph: “Because you’re good at explaining hard things.”
chapters.content:
Professor Ruan gave her the class on a Monday in September, the week after the ring, by dropping a folder on her desk in the doctoral room and lighting a cigarette she wasn’t allowed to light.

“First-year mechanics. Problem class. Thursdays at nine, room 104. Twenty-six of them.”

“Why me?”

“Because you’re good at explaining hard things.”

“I’m also good at complaining about hard things.”

“I’d noticed.” Ruan blew smoke at the window. “Try not to frighten them.”

“I’ll be very nice,” said Yu Jie.

Ruan looked at her over her half-moon glasses for some time, and then went out without saying anything, which was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Thursday, twenty-six first-years had found out that their new tutor was young and pretty and smiled a great deal. By a quarter past nine they had also found out that this meant nothing whatsoever.

She wrote her name on the board. She turned round.

“Good morning. I’m Shen Yu Jie. You can call me Miss Shen, or Yu Jie. Three rules.”

She wrote them up.

1. Ask.

2. Show your working.

3. Never trust an equation just because it looks confident.

A boy in the second row put his hand up. “What’s the third one for?”

“You’ll find out,” said Yu Jie, and smiled at him, and he sat back as if he’d been shoved.

She began with Newton’s second law. Free-body diagrams. Forces as arrows. Choosing your axes before you put a single number anywhere. For twenty minutes it was all perfectly reasonable, and they wrote it all down, and relaxed. Then she drew a block on a slope and worked it through on the board, step by careful step, starting from rest, out to the distance it would cover in a given time.

s = a t²

“There,” she said, and put the chalk down. “Any questions?”

Silence.

“Are you sure?”

Somebody looked at somebody else. She waited. She could wait a very long time. She’d learned it from an expert.

Then, very slowly, a girl by the window put up her hand. She was small, with a fringe and enormous glasses, and she was pink to the ears with the effort of it.

“Miss Shen? Isn’t there a half missing?”

“Is there? Why?”

The girl swallowed. “Because if it starts from rest and the acceleration’s constant, the speed goes up in a straight line, so the distance is the area under it, and that’s a triangle, and a triangle’s half.”

Yu Jie looked at the board. Then at the girl. Then she smiled, a real one, and took a stick of chalk and wrote the half in, large, where it belonged.

s = ½ a t²

“What’s your name?”

“Li Xiaoqing.”

“Li Xiaoqing, you’ve just won a bag of White Rabbits.” She took one out of her desk drawer and walked down the room and put it on the girl’s desk, and twenty-five heads turned to look at it. “Rule three, everyone. That equation looked very confident. It was wrong.”

She circled the mistake on the board. She left it up for the rest of the hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fourth Thursday they had learned that Miss Shen’s problem class was not easy.

She asked questions and then she waited for the answers, in a silence that went on until somebody broke. She could see an unexplained minus sign from the back of the room. If somebody said I just remembered the formula she would smile and say, “Lovely. Derive it,” and hand them the chalk. A boy called Chen wrote obviously in the middle of a working, once, and was made to explain to the whole class what, exactly, had been obvious, and after a quarter of an hour of it everyone agreed that nothing had.

They were terrified. They were also, without quite noticing, starting to enjoy it.

Li Xiaoqing won three bags of sweets in October. By the end of the month she had stopped going pink when she put her hand up.

By November, there was a queue outside room 104 at ten to nine on Thursdays. Yu Jie pretended not to be pleased. She was enormously pleased.

Then the queue started turning up on Wednesdays.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to four on the third Wednesday of November, Yu Jie was gathering up her things in the doctoral room to go up to the fourth floor, the way she had at a quarter to four on a Wednesday for more than two years, when somebody knocked on the open door.

Li Xiaoqing, with a notebook clutched to her chest.

“Miss Shen? I know it’s Wednesday.”

“Your class is tomorrow.”

“I know. I did the extension problem and I think I’ve got the boundary condition wrong, and I couldn’t sleep.”

Yu Jie looked at the clock. Then at the girl. Then she put her bag down and pulled out a chair.

“Show me.”

It was a perfectly reasonable mistake about which way a force pointed. It took ten minutes. At two minutes past four a second first-year appeared in the doorway with the same problem. At eleven minutes past, a third. By twenty past, there were four of them round her desk, and two were arguing furiously about whether an approximation was allowed, and she was explaining the difference between an assumption and a conclusion, when a voice from the doorway said, “Busy?”

Miles was standing there with two cups of jasmine tea.

He looked at her. At the four first-years. At the fifth, hovering in the corridor with a ring binder.

“Quite busy,” he said. “Apparently.”

Four first-years sat bolt upright.

“Good afternoon, Dr. Wei.”

“Good afternoon.” He came in and put her blue mug down by her elbow. He was perfectly polite. He was so polite it was suspicious.

“You brought it down,” said Yu Jie.

“It’s a quarter past four on a Wednesday. The tea was getting cold. I thought I’d better bring it to where you are.” He looked at the boy nearest her chair. “Are you getting enough help?”

The boy nodded very fast.

“Good,” said Miles, and looked at Yu Jie. “I’ll wait.”

“Are you jealous of my office hours?”

“I’m monitoring the situation.”

“What situation?”

“The situation in which four first-years have taken over my fiancée’s Wednesday afternoon.” He sat down at the empty desk across the aisle, took a paper out of his jacket, and opened it. “Carry on, Miss Shen.”

Five first-years had heard the word fiancée. Yu Jie watched it go round them like a current. She bit the inside of her cheek, very hard, and carried on.

At six minutes past five the last of them went, clutching the notebook, saying thank you three times. The room was quiet. Miles was still at the desk across the aisle, reading.

“You waited.”

“I said I would.”

“Were you really monitoring the situation?”

He looked up. “I was monitoring whether you remembered to drink your tea.”

She looked at the mug. It was empty. She had no memory of drinking it.

“Good,” said Miles.

She came and leaned on the edge of his borrowed desk. “They’re sweet, really. Li Xiaoqing’s the cleverest. She’s going to be better than me.”

“I heard you take her through it. The door was open.” He put the paper down. “You’re good at this. You don’t give them the answer. You make them find out they already had it. It’s the hardest thing there is to teach.”

“That’s what you taught me.”

“I think you’ve improved on it,” he said.

She looked down at him for a moment, at the paper on the desk and the empty mug and his face, which had become, over two years, so easy to read. Then she leaned across the eighty centimetres of aisle between the doctoral desks and kissed him.

He caught her by the waist, smiling against her mouth.

“Your students might come back.”

“Then they’ll learn something about momentum,” said Yu Jie, and kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The feedback forms came back in December. Ruan dropped the envelope on her desk on the way past without stopping. “Read them,” she said over her shoulder, “and don’t let them go to your head.”

Yu Jie read them that evening on the sofa on Bell Street, with Miles at one end and Ling Hao, who had come over for dinner and stayed, in the armchair.

Miss Shen is strict, but she never makes you feel stupid for being wrong.

She keeps asking until you understand WHY your answer’s wrong. This is terrifying. It also works.

I hated mechanics. I don’t any more.

She went quiet. She came to the last one, in small careful writing, and read it twice.

She remembers what each of us finds hard. She once stayed twenty minutes after class to go through something I was too embarrassed to ask about in front of everyone. I think she actually wants us to understand it. She is the first person who ever made me feel that physics is something you can learn and not something you have to be born with.

She passed it to Miles without a word. He read it. His face changed. He passed it to Ling Hao, who read it, and made a small noise, and then another, and took his glasses off.

“I’m not crying,” said Ling Hao.

“Of course not,” said Miles, who was.

“You’re both ridiculous,” said Yu Jie, wiping her own eyes with the cuff of her jumper.

“I’m going home,” said Ling Hao, with great dignity, and went across the road to Shu Mei.

Miles put the forms back in the envelope very carefully, the way he put things into his top drawer. Then he went into the kitchen and came back with her blue mug, full, and a yellow square stuck to the side of it.

To the best teacher in room 104. They’re lucky. So am I.

She smiled at it. Then she turned the mug round in her hands, because she’d learned by now that he never wrote on just one side.

P.S. I’m still monitoring the Wednesday situation.

She laughed so hard she nearly spilt the tea. He watched her do it, from the other end of the sofa, with an expression she was going to keep for the rest of her life. Then he held out his hand.

“Come here, Miss Shen.”

“Coming, Dr. Wei,” she said, and did.

chapters.title: The Department Christmas Party
chapters.desc: The first department party Miles Wei has attended in seven years. There is a quiz. He wins it. There is also karaoke, a secret gift exchange and a dance-off with the Head of Department. She wins everything else.
chapters.epigraph: “I enjoyed watching you.”
chapters.content:
Miles had been to exactly one department Christmas party in seven years. He had left after twenty-three minutes. Ling Hao still talked about it as a personal best.

“You’re coming this year,” Yu Jie told him, standing in front of his desk in 412 on the Monday of the last week of term.

“Am I?”

“You are.”

“Is it compulsory?”

“I’m your fiancée. I have authority.”

He took his glasses off. “That isn’t how authority works.”

“Then it’s a research requirement. Whether Dr. Wei can survive a room full of physicists enjoying themselves.” She was already at the door. “Six o’clock on Friday. I’ll collect you.”

When she’d gone he opened his calendar and typed Friday, 18:00. Party. He looked at it. Then he added, underneath, Yu Jie, as if that settled the matter, which it did.

✦ ✦ ✦

By twenty to seven on Friday he had discovered that a department Christmas party involved a great deal more than dinner.

There were paper snowflakes on threads from the ceiling of the seminar room, each with a different equation on it, which somebody had evidently spent a week cutting out. There was a bowl of punch the colour of a warning light. There was a table of prizes, and at the front of the room, with a microphone and a paper crown, stood Professor Cen.

“Welcome,” said Cen, “to a quiz, a secret gift exchange, karaoke, and several other activities.”

Miles leaned down to Yu Jie’s ear. “What other activities?”

“You’ll find out.”

He didn’t care for the way she said it.

The quiz came first, in teams of four, drawn out of a hat. Yu Jie drew Miles, which several people said was rigged, and Ling Hao, and Zeng Bo, who looked round the table and announced that they had a lecturer, a doctoral student, a postdoc, and a man who’d been avoiding social contact since before he could vote.

“I’m sitting beside you,” said Miles.

“Exactly my point.”

Question one: the energies of a particle in a box, the ratio of the third level to the first. Miles had written 9 on the answer sheet before Cen had finished reading it. Question two: which conservation law follows from the laws of physics not changing over time. “Energy,” said Yu Jie, a beat ahead of him, and he looked at her with naked pride. Question three: the speed of sound in air at room temperature. Zeng Bo, who did lasers, got that one, and was insufferable for a quarter of an hour.

Question four: “In what year was the sundial in the department courtyard put up?”

“Nineteen fifty-eight,” said Miles.

“Correct,” said Cen, consulting his card. “Bonus point. Is it accurate?”

Miles looked out of the window at the dark courtyard. “No.”

The room laughed. Cen did not.

“Why not?”

“It’s about three degrees out of true. The gnomon isn’t aligned to the pole. It varies through the year, of course, but the error’s there in every season.” He paused. “I checked it. In 2019.”

“Why?”

“It was bothering me.”

Ling Hao put his face in both hands. “Wei. It’s a Christmas quiz.”

“That sundial,” said Cen, with great dignity, “was put up by the founding head of this department, with his own hands.”

“I know. He put it up three degrees out.”

Yu Jie laughed so hard she had to lean on him. Their team won by eleven points, and the prize was a small silver trophy shaped like an atom, nucleus and three bent orbits, every bit as inaccurate as the one on his phone. Miles held it with the expression of a man who has been handed an administrative duty.

Yu Jie took it off him. “I’m keeping this.”

“It’s a team prize.”

“I’m the team. I contributed emotional support.”

“She did,” said Ling Hao. “I felt very supported.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The gift exchange came next. Yu Jie had drawn Miles’s name, which she said was destiny and Ling Hao said was fraud. Miles had drawn Ruan’s.

He gave Ruan a small, old book on the history of scientific instruments, with a brass armillary sphere on the cover, found in a shop by the harbour that had been selling the same three hundred books for forty years. Ruan turned it over in her hands, and looked at him over her half-moon glasses, and said, “You actually thought about this.”

“I was told it was a gift exchange. Not an experiment in random allocation.”

“Hm,” said Ruan, which from her was a medal.

Yu Jie unwrapped hers and found a tiny knitted moon wearing a knitted scarf.

“He’s adorable,” she said.

“He’s slightly asymmetrical,” said Miles.

“Don’t you dare insult my moon.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Karaoke began at a quarter past eight. She had mentioned it three times at dinner, which was how he knew.

“I’m not singing,” he said.

“You don’t have to.”

“Good.”

“I am, though,” said Yu Jie, and walked up to the front of the room.

The first notes came out of the speaker and he knew them at once. It was the old song about the moon that her grandmother used to sing in the kitchen of the house on the hill, in the dialect of the old woman’s own village, not the language of the city. Yu Jie had played it for him one Sunday in the attic and gone through it line by line, what each word meant, and why the moon in it was always on the water and never in the sky. He’d asked her to say some of the lines again. He’d practised them since, under his breath, on the 18:20, on the basement stairs, when she wasn’t there to hear him get them wrong.

She didn’t sing it perfectly. She sang it low, and the room went quiet and leaned in.

At the chorus she looked straight at him across the seminar room.

He said the line back to her. The first half of it, in her grandmother’s words, not loudly, just clearly enough to carry.

She nearly lost the next note. Her eyes went wide. He said the second half, a little more surely.

She sang the rest of it to him, and only to him, and her voice shook on the last line, and sixty people pretended hard to be looking at the snowflakes.

“That’s disgusting,” Ling Hao said, beside him, with deep feeling.

“What is?”

“You. Being romantic in front of colleagues.”

The song finished. The room clapped. She came back to him with her cheeks scarlet.

“You learned it.”

“Some of it.”

“When?”

“On trains. I wanted it to be a surprise.”

She stared at him. Then she went up on her toes and kissed him, there, in the middle of the seminar room, in front of Cen and Ruan and Mr. Pei and the entire condensed matter group, with the snowflakes turning on their threads overhead. Somebody cheered. Somebody else whistled. Zeng Bo said, finally, a measurable result. Miles kissed her back without once looking round, and when she let him go he was smiling.

“Worth learning,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dance-off was Cen’s idea, and in Yu Jie’s opinion the best chance she’d ever be given to humiliate a head of department.

“Surely,” said Cen into his microphone, still in his paper crown, “somebody here can dance better than me.”

Yu Jie’s hand went up.

“No,” said Miles.

“Yes.”

“Yu Jie.”

“Trust me.”

“I do. That’s what worries me.”

Cen, it turned out, could dance. He had rhythm, and three rehearsed steps from somebody’s wedding, and the confidence of a man who’d chaired four international conferences. Yu Jie had none of those things. She simply danced, laughing, spinning, dragging Tao Tao into the circle from the doorway where she’d turned up uninvited, and then Ling Hao, who protested and then didn’t, and then half the second-year doctoral students. By the end the whole room was clapping in time. Cen tried a final flourish. Yu Jie answered it with a turn and a deep bow, and the room came apart.

The judges, who were Mr. Pei and two first-years, gave her the prize: a gold trophy in the shape of an electron, a little blob on a stick.

“I’m taking this home,” she shouted, holding it up.

“I have been betrayed by my own department,” said Cen, and took off his crown and put it on her head.

She came running back to Miles with the trophy and the crown, and he caught her round the waist.

“You were excellent.”

“I won.”

“You did.”

“Are you proud?”

“Very,” he said, and she kissed his cheek and put the crown on him instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home at half past ten down Bell Street, past the old wall, in the cold. She had the electron in one arm and the knitted moon in the other. He had the atom, and the paper crown still on, because she wouldn’t let him take it off.

“Your first department party in seven years,” she said, “and you stayed till the end.”

“Yes.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

He thought about it honestly.

“I enjoyed watching you.”

“That isn’t the same as enjoying the party.”

“It was the best part of it.”

She stopped under the third lamp, the one outside their door, where it threw its yellow circle on the old stones of the wall, and put the trophies and the moon down on the low ledge.

“You came because I asked.”

“I did.”

“You sang to me.”

“Two lines.”

“You kissed me in front of everyone.”

“I believe you started that one.”

“And you didn’t run away,” said Yu Jie.

“I didn’t want to,” he said.

She took hold of his coat in both hands and backed him up against the cold stones of the old wall, under the lamp, and kissed him, much longer than in the seminar room, much less politely, with the paper crown sliding sideways off his head. His hands came to her waist. Somebody came out of the bakery opposite with the last of the day’s bread and went straight back in again.

“Next year as well?” she said against his mouth.

“If you take me.”

“Every year.”

“Then I’ll come,” said Miles, and picked up the atom, and the moon, and the electron, and her hand, and took the lot of them upstairs.

chapters.title: Physics Puns, Ranked
chapters.desc: A speech given at the first wedding anniversary dinner, in the back room of a dumpling stall at a night market, by the woman who has heard them all. Fifteen jokes. Ranked. With notes.
chapters.epigraph: “I keep all your notes. It isn’t an endorsement.”
chapters.content:
The back room of the dumpling stall behind the station was barely big enough for six people and two folding tables, and Yu Jie had filled what was left of it with decorations. Red paper lanterns. A small cake by the teapot, with one Bohr atom piped on it, inaccurately. And a sign, hand-lettered, taped to the wall above the window onto the lane.

ONE YEAR MARRIED. FIFTEEN YEARS OF BAD PHYSICS JOKES.

Miles looked at it for some time.

“Fifteen years?”

“Emotionally,” said Yu Jie.

“I’ve known you for less than four.”

“Your jokes have aged me.”

It was the twentieth of June, their first anniversary. They had kept it small on purpose: the old woman’s stall, where he’d once made twelve dumplings, eleven and a half of them structurally sound; the old woman herself in the doorway with her sleeves rolled, pretending not to listen; Ruan; Ling Hao and Shu Mei; and Yu Jie’s father, in his dark suit, with his phone face down beside his bowl, as it always was now when he sat at a table with her.

When the first trays were empty Yu Jie stood up with her teacup and unfolded a sheet of graph paper.

“I’ve prepared a speech.”

“Should I be worried?” said Miles.

“Very. Tonight I’ll be ranking the fifteen worst physics jokes my husband has ever made. With notes.”

“Worst?”

“Don’t interrupt the speaker.” She cleared her throat. “Number fifteen. Why can’t you trust atoms? They make up everything.” She looked at him. “October the twenty-second, two thousand and twenty-five. Written on the side of my tea. The first note. I laughed for ten minutes in the toilets so you wouldn’t see. Two out of ten, for longevity alone.”

“Technically sound,” said Miles.

“Number fourteen. I’m attracted to you. It’s not personal. It’s gravitational.”

“You laughed.”

“I was being polite.”

“You kissed me afterwards.”

“To stop you talking.” She turned the page. “Number thirteen. The sodium joke.”

Across the table, her father put down his chopsticks and began, without a sound, to laugh.

“For those of you who weren’t there,” said Yu Jie, “Dr. Wei came to tea at my parents’ house for the first time last October. The first time ever. My mother had made the soup herself, which she hasn’t done since I was nine. She passed him the salt, and said, Do you take salt, Dr. Wei? And he said—“

“Na,” said her father, and laughed out loud, so loudly that the old woman in the doorway turned round.

“My father,” said Yu Jie, “is the reason he keeps doing it.”

“It was very funny,” said Shen Guoqiang, wiping his eyes. “Your mother didn’t understand it for a full minute. Then she did. She’s still angry.”

“Three out of ten,” said Yu Jie. “Plus two for making Ba laugh. Five.” She went on. “Number twelve. Schrödinger’s cat, as explained to Zhao Zhendong. At the Zhaos’ anniversary dinner, in March, in a flower shop, in front of eleven people.”

Miles looked at his tea.

“Zhao asked what happens to the cat,” said Yu Jie. “Miles said that until you open the box, it’s in two states at once, and both are true. And Zhao thought about it with that face he has, and asked whether that meant his wife was simultaneously furious and delighted with him until she opened her present.”

“That wasn’t part of the original question,” said Miles.

“And Zhao went straight out, in the middle of dinner, and came back with a different present, because he decided he wasn’t going to risk the superposition.” She marked something. “Four out of ten. Five for the outcome. Elowen sends her regards.”

“Number eleven. You’re the only constant in my universe.” She sighed. “Too sentimental. Minus points.”

“You kept the note.”

“I keep all your notes. It isn’t an endorsement.” She looked down at the next line, and stopped.

The back room went quiet.

“Number ten,” she said, more slowly, “is from our first winter on Bell Street.”

Miles’s face changed.

She didn’t tell them all of it. She didn’t have to. It had been January, the first winter in the flat with the two desks, and she’d been in the laboratory till two every night for a week chasing a result that wouldn’t come, and he’d decided, without asking her, that she needed rescuing from it. He’d turned up at midnight to take her home. She’d told him to go. He’d said a thing about her not looking after herself in the voice her mother used, and she’d said a thing back about men who decided what was good for her. And then, in the kitchen at half past two, trying to mend it, he’d made a joke. I’m sorry. I was being acidic. Can we neutralise it? And she’d said, I don’t want chemistry, Miles, I want you to listen, and gone to bed, and shut the door.

In the morning she’d found him asleep on the sofa under the grey blanket, with his glasses still on and one arm over his eyes. There’d been salt on his cheek. He’d cried himself to sleep, at thirty-three, on a sofa, without making a sound, because he’d heard her mother’s voice come out of his own mouth and couldn’t bear it. She’d sat on the floor beside him until the light came round the blind before she woke him.

He hadn’t made a joke when he apologised. He’d asked her what she needed. And that week, and every week since, he’d brought dinner to the laboratory at eight, in a tin, and left it on the bench with a yellow note, and gone home without being asked twice, and never once told her to stop.

“The acid joke,” said Yu Jie, to the room. “Zero out of ten.”

“I deserved that,” said Miles.

“You did.”

“I’ve improved.”

“You have.” She looked at him across the folding table. “You still bring dinner.”

“Every night.”

“Not every night.”

“Almost every night,” he said, and reached across the cake and took her hand, and Ruan looked at the lanterns and Shu Mei blew her nose.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Number nine,” said Yu Jie, recovering. “I’d tell you a joke about photons, but you’d find it too light.”

“Photons are massless,” said Miles. “It’s a good joke.”

“Your joke is massless. It has no substance.” Ling Hao choked on a dumpling. “Number eight. Our love has no uncertainty. Heisenberg would like a word. One out of ten. Number seven. You make my heart oscillate.”

“That’s a good one.”

“It’s a cardiac event. Number six. We have such good chemistry.”

“That’s not even a physics joke,” said Ruan.

“Interdisciplinary,” said Miles.

“Don’t defend yourself,” said his wife. She looked down at the paper. “Number five.”

Her voice changed.

“Still here.”

Nobody laughed. He’d written those two words on a whiteboard in a glass room, in the March when she’d asked him for room and he’d given it to her, every day, without once making her pay for it.

“Ten out of ten,” said Yu Jie.

“That isn’t a joke,” said Miles, very low.

“I know.”

She sat down for a moment. He leaned across and kissed her forehead, and she let him, and then she stood up again.

“Number four. For all n.”

“That’s a mathematical statement.”

“It’s an annoying one. You say it every time you lose an argument.”

“I never lose arguments.”

“Exactly. Number three. You’re my favourite solution. Too easy. Number two. I would choose you in every possible state.” She lowered the paper. “That one’s actually quite good.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t get excited. And number one.”

She looked at the last line. She’d written it in herself, at the bottom of the page. It was the text that had come at fourteen minutes past two in the morning, on the night the storm cancelled every train, after the line had dropped.

I love you, Yu Jie. I wish you were here.

No atom. No cactus. Nothing clever.

“Number one is the worst one,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because it made me cry, and I was alone, in a residence three hours up the line, and you weren’t there to see.”

He didn’t answer at once.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“No, you’re not.”

“No,” he admitted. “I’m not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dumplings went round again. Ruan told the story of a conference dinner in the north at which a Nobel laureate had set fire to his own tie. Ling Hao proposed that all of Miles’s future jokes should be sent out to referees before being inflicted on the department. Shen Guoqiang ordered another plate, and then another, and asked the old woman how she pleated them, and was made to try, and was hopeless at it.

And Miles, who had spent the evening listening to his wife take his sense of humour apart in public, said at last, “May I give a ranking of my own?”

Yu Jie narrowed her eyes. “Of what?”

“Your jokes.”

“I don’t make physics jokes.”

“You do. Every time you hide my glasses.”

Yu Jie froze.

Ling Hao very slowly put down his chopsticks.

“In the cutlery drawer,” said Miles, perfectly calmly. “Behind the tea tins in the department kitchen. Once behind the books in 412. Once in your own desk drawer two days before our wedding.”

“How long,” said Yu Jie, “have you known?”

“Since the fourth time.”

“That was a year and a half ago!”

“Yes.”

“You let me go on doing it?”

“You seemed to like being the reason I turned round,” said Miles. “So did I.”

She turned on Ling Hao. “Did you know?”

Ling Hao held up both hands. “I know nothing. I’m an innocent bystander. I’ve never read a notebook in my life.”

“Then what’s your number one?” said Yu Jie to her husband, scarlet.

He took his wallet out of his jacket. From behind his staff card, next to a sweet wrapper that said never zero, he took a small yellow square, folded in half, soft at the edges, and unfolded it on the table among the dumpling baskets.

I like having you inside my focal range.

“Ten out of ten,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the others had gone and the market was packing up round them, they walked back through the lane under the strings of lanterns, her with the leftover cake and him with the sign, which she’d insisted on keeping.

At the corner where the dark street ran down past the tailor’s green shutter, she stopped.

“Miles?”

“Yes?”

“Are you happy?”

She still asked him sometimes. She knew the answer. She liked to hear him give it.

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“For all n,” he said.

“That’s not a proper answer.”

“It’s the most accurate one I have.”

She stepped in close. He kissed her, there, under a red lantern, against the tailor’s green shutter, slowly, with the cake squashed between them and neither of them caring.

“One year,” she said.

“One year.”

“Fifteen terrible jokes.”

“Sixteen. There’s one I haven’t told you yet.”

“Miles Wei.”

He was smiling. In his inside pocket, folded once, beside his wedding vows, was the sheet of graph paper with her rankings on it. He was going to keep it for the rest of his life. Even the zero.

chapters.title: Miles at Sixteen
chapters.desc: A boy at the back of Mr. Hui’s advanced class who does impressions of the teacher, a tired girl at the end of his table, a girl who reads his notebook out loud, and eight days that taught him to stop wanting things. And the man who, fourteen years later, unlearned it.
chapters.epigraph: “That isn’t a choice, son. That’s a hiding place.”
chapters.content:
At sixteen, Miles Wei was funny. Most of the people who knew him later found this hard to believe, and he’d stopped trying to convince them.

Mr. Hui’s advanced class took the best of three year groups and put them round two long tables in the room at the end of the maths corridor, and Miles sat at the back, where he had perfected Mr. Hui. The voice was easy. The trick was the pause before the last word, and the way he pushed his spectacles up with one knuckle.

“Class,” said Miles, in the voice, pushing up spectacles he didn’t have, “the universe is expanding. Unfortunately, so is your homework.”

The boy beside him nearly choked.

“And if you cannot solve question seven,” said Miles, “I suggest you look for a different universe.”

The whole back table went. Somebody put his head down on his exercise book and shook.

“Mr. Wei.”

Mr. Hui was standing at the end of the table.

“Yes, sir?”

“Since you know my teaching so well, perhaps you’d like to do the next derivation.”

Miles went up to the board, still smiling, and did it. All of it, without stopping, in the neat small hand he’d later be known for. Mr. Hui looked at the board for a while, and then at him, and said, “Sit down,” and Miles went back to his seat looking unbearably pleased with himself.

At the front, a girl turned round in her chair and laughed. Her name was Aurelia Song. She’d come from Milan that year, at fifteen, with an accent she was already losing on purpose and a way of sitting as if every chair she chose was the best one in the room. She was pretty, and confident, and used to being looked at. She’d noticed Miles before. That afternoon, watching him walk back down the room with chalk on his sleeve, she decided she wanted him.

At the far end of the table, another girl wasn’t laughing.

Elowen Lin was fourteen, the youngest in the room, there by special permission because her own year’s class had nothing left to teach her. She had shadows under her eyes and a stack of library books at her elbow, and she looked too tired to be pleased about any of it.

Miles noticed her on the way back to his chair.

“Are you all right?”

She blinked at him. “Yes.”

“You look like you’ve been awake since the invention of calculus.”

She looked at him. Then, without meaning to, she smiled.

“I’m just tired.”

He pushed his packet of biscuits across the table to her, unopened.

“Emergency supplies.”

“Do you always carry biscuits?”

“For emergencies.”

“What counts as an emergency?”

“Someone about to fall asleep on a differential equation.”

She laughed under her breath, and kept the biscuits.

After that it became a habit. They shared a table in the library after school, at the window end, three or four days a week. He did problems from the back of university books. She read chemistry. Sometimes they didn’t speak for an hour. Miles liked that more than he could have explained. Elowen never expected him to be funny. With her he could stop performing and just think, and she’d look up when he swore at a sign error and go back to her book without a word.

He didn’t notice Aurelia watching him from across the library. Or he noticed, and liked it, and thought nothing of it, which at sixteen came to the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was a notebook.

He kept it at the bottom of his school bag under his physics. It wasn’t a diary. He wrote down problems in it, and things he wanted to remember, and now and then the things he’d never have said aloud. The winter he turned seventeen, after an argument with his father that he couldn’t win, he’d written a list.

Rules for Not Being Disappointed
