1. Never ask for something you can’t give yourself.

2. Never let anyone know how much you want them to stay.

3. If they leave, don’t follow.

4. Never let them see that it hurt.

He left the notebook on the library table one afternoon in March while he went to put a book back. When he came round the end of the shelves, Aurelia was sitting in his chair, reading it aloud.

“’Never let anyone know how much you want them to stay.’”

He stopped.

She looked up. “Is this yours?”

“Put it down.”

“It’s rather dramatic, Miles.”

“Aurelia.”

She read on, louder. “’If they leave, don’t follow.’ That’s so sad.” Three people at the next table turned round. “Who hurt you? Is it about somebody?”

He reached for it. She pulled it back out of his reach, laughing, and the laugh was the worst part.

Elowen stood up.

“Give it to him.”

Aurelia looked at her. “I’m only reading.”

“He asked you to stop.”

The library went silent. Aurelia held Elowen’s eyes for a second longer than was comfortable. Then she dropped the notebook on the table, and Elowen picked it up and held it out to him.

He took it without looking at her. He was too ashamed to thank her, and too ashamed to stay, and he walked out of the library with his face burning and didn’t go back that week.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two days later the fire bell went during afternoon break for a drill, and the whole school poured out onto the sports field. Miles was at the back of the crowd by the long-jump pit when he heard raised voices.

He only caught the end of it.

“You made me look ridiculous,” Aurelia was saying.

“I didn’t do anything,” said Elowen.

“You think he likes you?”

“I never said that.”

Aurelia stepped in close and slapped her. The sound carried across the grass like a dropped plate. Elowen staggered sideways, one hand going up to her cheek.

Miles moved before he’d decided to.

“Stop.”

Aurelia turned. Her face changed when she saw who it was. “Miles—“

“Don’t.”

He stepped between them. Elowen stood behind him with her hand still on her face, not making a sound. A teacher was already coming across the field at a run, and Aurelia had started explaining, fast, in the voice she used on teachers, and he wasn’t listening to a word of it.

He turned to Elowen. “Are you hurt?”

She shook her head. He knew she was lying. He wanted to say it wasn’t her fault. He wanted to take her inside to the nurse, and sit with her, and give her every biscuit he owned.

Two hundred people were standing on the field watching them, and he could feel every one of them.

He looked away.

He’d remember the slap, later, and the teacher, and the cold. But what he’d remember first, at three in the morning for years afterwards, was that he’d wanted to protect somebody and had still been ashamed to be seen doing it.

The next eight days were bad. The story went round the school in four versions. In one Elowen had been trying to come between him and Aurelia. In another he’d led Aurelia on. Somebody had seen the list over her shoulder and was quoting it in the corridors, with the words changed until it read like a confession. Miles stopped doing impressions. He stopped answering in class. He stopped sitting with Elowen, and when she came over to him in the library on the fifth day, holding a packet of biscuits out in front of her like a flag, he gathered up his books and left.

On the eighth day he came home at lunchtime.

His father was at the kitchen table with the newspaper and a pile of exercise books, because he taught mornings on Thursdays.

“Finished early?”

Miles didn’t answer. He put his bag down by the door and walked through the kitchen towards the hall.

“Miles?”

He stopped with his back to the room.

“I don’t want to go back.”

His father folded the newspaper. “What’s happened?”

“Nothing.”

“Miles.”

“Nothing happened,” he said, and his voice broke on it.

He put both hands over his face and cried, standing in the hall in his school blazer, with no noise at all, the way you cry when you’ve been holding something shut so long you’ve forgotten where the catch is.

His father got up and came and put a hand on his shoulder. Miles didn’t pull away.

“I don’t want people to know what I want,” he said into his hands. “Every time they know, they can use it.”

His father stood there a while before he answered.

“That isn’t a choice, son,” he said. “That’s a hiding place.”

Miles lowered his hands and stared at the floor.

“I don’t know how to do anything else.”

“Then you’ll learn.” His father pulled him in, awkwardly, the way he did everything that wasn’t arithmetic. “You don’t have to let everyone in. But you can’t spend your whole life locking every door because somebody once walked through one without asking.”

Miles didn’t answer. He didn’t believe him. It took him fourteen years to try.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night of the twentieth of June, at a few minutes past midnight, when the calendar had its new squares and Yu Jie had gone back to bed, Miles went to the chair where his wedding jacket hung and took the notebook out of the inside pocket.

His father had put it there at the garden, in front of everyone, in the middle of the hug, while he said the thing in Miles’s ear that nobody else had heard. I kept it. I think you can have it back now.

The cover had gone soft. The pages had yellowed at the edges. He hadn’t seen it in fourteen years.

“What’s that?” said Yu Jie, from the pillows.

“Something I wrote when I was seventeen.”

She sat up and held out her hand, and after a second he sat down on the edge of the bed and gave it to her.

She turned the pages carefully, past equations in a younger, rounder version of his writing, and stopped at the list. She read it twice. When she looked up, her eyes were wet.

“You believed these?”

“For a while.”

“Do you still?”

He looked at the list, and then at her, in his shirt, with her hair still crimped from the pins and her ring on.

“No.”

“What changed?”

He gave it real thought, because she’d asked properly.

“I found a counterexample.”

“Me?”

“You.”

He took the notebook back, and the purple pen off the bedside table where she’d left it, and crossed out the list one line at a time, slowly, the way he’d mark a proof that had a hole in it. At the bottom of the page he wrote:

Counterexample found.

Yu Jie leaned her head on his shoulder. “That’s a very scientific way of saying you love me.”

“I thought you’d appreciate the notation.”

“I do.” She took the pen out of his hand and put it down. Then she turned and took his face between her hands. “Tell me the rest.”

“I used to think that if I wanted someone too much, I’d be handing them a way to hurt me.” He covered her hands with his own. “Wanting you is one of the few things I’ve never regretted.”

She kissed him, and pulled him down under the sheet with her, and he went, and didn’t hold any of it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

His father rang at half past seven the next morning. Miles took the phone into the kitchen so as not to wake her.

“I wanted to say something,” said his father, “and I didn’t manage it yesterday. Your mother says I should have.”

“Go on.”

“I watched you, at the arch. You looked happy. You didn’t look like the boy who came home on the eighth day.” A pause. “I think you’ve come out of hiding, son.”

Miles looked down at the ring on his hand, and at the notebook open on the kitchen table, the old rules struck through in purple.

“Yes,” he said. “I think I have.”

When he went back to the bedroom she was awake, just. She reached for him with her eyes still shut.

“Come here.”

He got in beside her and let her pull him close. There was nothing to solve. Nothing to prepare for. He held his wife, and wanted her, and stayed.
